summary: The Food Inspector, P.W. 468 In Municipal Corporation of Delhi vs Kacheroo Mal, (I) the Public Analyst had reported that the sample was adulterated due to insect infested pieces of Kajus to the extent of 21.9% and I am of the opinion that the same is adulterated due under section 2(1)(f). The Food Inspector in his report dated 10 1 1969 stated that the samples were adulterated due on insect fect infestation, without more, but only after obtaining a certificate from the Public analyst that the article was unfit for human consumption. The Food inspector reported that "Date of Analysis: 10 1 1968 Insect infated pieces of tubes of Kajo to the tune of 21%" Sarkaria, J. speaking for himself and Gupta, JJ. has observed in that case: "In view of the construction that the expression 'insect infective ' includes infestation even by dead insects, the further point to be considered is whether mere insect insect ' without more would be sufficient to hold the article to be 'adulterated ' within the meaning of sub clause (f) of section 2 of the Act. If it is read conjunctively, that is, in association with what precedes it, sub clause(f) with slight consequent rearrangement and parenthesis would read like this: "If the article is unfit for personal consumption on account of (a) its consisting wholly or in part of any filthy, putrid, disgusting rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or because it is insect eg infested or on account Of any other cause." To fall under that sub clause an article of food must be unfit for Human consumption because it consists wholly or partly in part and partly in parts of any obscene, put uprid, Disgusted, rotten or decomeased animal. " The Food Analyst had also reported that 'Date of analysis: 10.1 1969 Insect fects infested and insect Infested ' were adulterated under section 3(2)(f) and the Public Food Inspector had reported the fact that the food was unfit to human consumption and therefore adulterated within the contemplation of section 1(1) (f). On the basis of this decision it is stated as follows in the , published by the Eastern Book Company, seventh edition, with reference to section 2 (1)(a) (i) of the . The Food Inspectors, P W. 468, in Municipal Corporation Delhi vs Tek Chand Bhatia, (supra), and the conclusion that 'it would not be necessary in such a case to prove further that the articles were unfit for ' human consumption ' is a correct statement of the law.

The appellant was convicted by the Munsif Magistrate, First Class and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for six months. The foodgrains found in his possession were also ordered to be forfeited to the State. He appealed unsuccessfully to the Sessions Judge, Santhal Parganas, Dumka and his revision in the High Court was summarily dismissed. The defence of the appellant was that he was an agriculturist and that the foodgrains were grown by him on the lands he had taken on lease from various parties. In support of his defence he produced both documentary and oral evidence. The documentary evidence consisted of certain lease deeds executed by 'him and his brother in favour of the lessors. Oral evidence showed that he and his brothers were in possession of 80 90 bighas of land on which Paddy and other foodgrains found therein were grown, 901 The case proceeded against him on that basis. He was convicted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of cl. 3 of the order. He preferred an appeal to the High court but the same was summarily rejected. The appellant appealed unsuccessfully before the Sessions judge, Santal Parganas and his Revision in the high Court was also summarily dismissed, but the defence of him was not accepted. The State appealed to the Supreme Court by special leave. HELD: (i) The presumption under section 3(2) could ,not be drawn. If that presumption is not drawn, then the case against him stands unproved because of the exemption which agriculturists enjoy. [901 B] (ii) It is obvious that sub paragraph speaks of storage for sale as a dealer although the words "as a dealer" are not there, because storage has reference to 'business as a trader and that is the essence of the Order. In the present case, the appellant produced a number of lease deeds in which leases of various parcels of land were shown to have been granted to him. He also produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed on oath that he had cultivated 80 90 bigha of land. No doubt, the lease deed is not registered but for the purpose of a criminal prosecution, it is obvious, that subparagraph speaks of store for sale As a dealer though the words 'carrying on the business" are neither there nor are they genuine or not and whether an inference of innocence can be based upon them. [1001 C D] (iii) The appellant produced receipts and proved by oral evidence that he is an agriculturist. He executed a number, of lease deed in which lease deeds were not registered. But for the purposes of a Criminal prosecution, he has successfully proved that he has been carrying on agricultural ,operations. He signed a number and of lease documents. No question was asked to put questions to the witnesses on the ground that they are interested in the appellant 's case.

The defendant was a monthly tenant in respect of the land described in schedule to the plaint. The plaintiff respondent, who was a permanent tenant under section 116 of the Transfer of Property Act, executed a Kabuliyat in 1924 for the purpose of erecting a tenancy on the expiration of the period provided for in the lease. The defendant 's father, who had been appointed as a Receiver, died on 7th December, 1926 and the suit was instituted by the plaintiff respondent for recovery of possession of the property described in Schedule to the suit. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the defendant ' s tenancy created by payment and acceptance of rent in the years 1925 and 1926, after 1926, became a tenant from month to month under him and the tenan cy was determined by a proper notice to quit. Held, that the tenancy created in 1924 was from the beginning a tenancy from monthto month under the provi sion of section 116, Transfer of property Act, terminable by fifteen days notice. The suit was one for ejectment of a lessee on the expiry of the term provided for therein and no tenancy could be created by the two payments of rent, inasmuch as the Receiver had accepted rent in 1925, it should be presumed that the parties intended to create a tenancy for one year and when he accepted rent again in 1926, such acceptance amount ed to his assenting to the defendant "s holding over. Held further, that if a tenancy created for one month only was created in the year 1925, then after the expiration Of that one year 's lease the defendant held over and the Receiver 's assent to his continuing in possession is evidenced by acceptance of rents from him in the Year 1926. The fact that two successive tenancies were created for another year each, the facts admitted and proved would go to show that the tenant held over after the second annual lease and consequently a tenancy From month to months under section 106, Transfer Of Property Act. De, appearing for the plaintiff respondents, has on the other hand, contended that even if two successive leases were created by one year each the facts proved and proved will go to showing that the tenants held over thereafter after the expiry Of that period. The High Court was right in holding that the suit filed by the defendant was one from month 'to month since its inception in 1924.

The appellant assessee, a firm of Chartered Accountants, was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1964 65 onwards. The Income Tax Officer issued notices under section 148 of the Income Tax Act, 1961 on the ground that the assessee had failed to produce the books of account and other documents in support of its claim. The assessee filed an application before the Commissioner of Income Tax seeking information under section 147(1) (b) of the Act. The Commissioner of income tax rejected the application holding that the omission of Section 137 did not make any difference and that the ban on the courts as contained in the repealed section 137 continued to remain in force by virtue of the provisions of section 138 (1)(b). The assessee appealed to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who dismissed the appeal. In the reference, the High Court held that the failure of the assessee to produce books of accounts and other relevant documents before the Income tax Officer was subject to the veto powers of the Commissioner under section 138(1)(a) of Act V of 1964 and that it could not be called in question in any court of law. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The finality attached to an order of the commissioner under Section 138(i)(b) does not affect the powers of a court to summon the production of documents from the income tax authorities after April 1, 1964 relating to assessment proceedings for 1964 65 in respect of the record filed after April1, 1964. [557G] 2. The effect of introduction of section 137 of the 1961 Act by Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act 1960 was that it entitled a person to make an application to the Commissioner to obtain information thereafter as to the amount of tax determined, as payable by an assessee in respect for any assessment made either under the 1922 Act or under the 1961 Income Tax law Act, 1922 on or after April 01, 1964 and authorised the Commissioner, to furnish or cause to be furnished the sought for information, if he was satisfied that there were no circumstances justifying its refusal. [657C] 3. The High Court fell in error in holding that section 138 did not affect powers of courts to require production of assessment records from the Incometax authorities after March 1,1964 relating to the assessment proceedings relating to 1964 65 and that section 139(1), (b). [658D] 4. Section 138 does not apply to cases where the information etc. as contemplated by the section is called for by any person other than a court of Law on summons for its production being issued by the court and that Commissioner has the authority to furnish such information, in a case pending before it. The power of the courts to summon documents from income tax Authorities after April January 1, 1965 relating to assessments proceedings for 1963 65 onwards is, thus restricted to the cases where information etc., as contemplated under the section are called for. [613D] 5. Section 139(2) does make punishable, the disclosure by a public servant of any information contained in those documents. The object of the provision is to ensure that the information sought is produced in a court on being summoned by it without the approval of the Commissioners of Income tax. [457E] 6. The provisions of Section 138 are not intended to affect the power of courts under require production or disclosure of any such information from the record even to the courts when the court, by a judicial order, requires the production or supply of the document to it, in case pending at the time of assessment proceedings before an Income tax officer, without the sanction of the Commission. [558F] 7. The words "any person" occurring in Section 138 have been used in the sense that they are not meant to be used as evidence in a civil court.

The appellant was married to Seinaba and he made a gift of his properties including immovable property to Seinsaba on April 7, 1944 by a registered deed. Mammotty died soon afterwards on February 25, 1947 without leaving any issue. The appellant 's mother accepted the gift on behalf of her minor wife to be valid must be accepted on her behalf by a legal guardian of her property under the Muhammadan Law. The gift was made by a deed which was registered and handed over by Mammottty to his mother in law and accepted by her on behalf. The respondent 's father accepted the gifts on behalf, but it was not delivered to Sewinaba but to her mother, the first appellant, and she accepted the same on behalf and took possession on behalf Of her minor daughter who had attained puberty and had lived with him for after the celebration of marriage a husband can receive a gift in respect of minor wife even though his father was living. The suit filed by the respondent was decreed by the trial court but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf the appellant that neither express acceptance nor transfer of possession is necessary for the completion of a gift when the donor is himself the guardian or the de facto guardian ' provided there is a real and bona fide intention on the donor 's part to transfer the ownership of the subject matter of the gift to the donee. HELD : (i) The gift by a father to his minor wife was completed ordinarily by the acceptance of the guardian of the property of the minor Wilayat ul Mal. [501 B] (ii) The intention to make the gift was clear and manifest because it was made in a deed registered and delivered by Mammanotty to her father in law, and accepted and acted upon by her. [558 C D] (iii) The object of making the gift is clear and apparent because it is made by an instrument which was unregistered and handed back by Mam mottty and as the gift has been made by Mammenotty, the gift would have been complete under Muhammadan law and it seems impossible to hold that by handing over the deed to his wife in law the gift can be completed by delivery of the title to the donor.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administration and governance of Hindu religious institutions in the State of Madras. Section 76(1) provides that every religious institution shall from the income derived by it, pay to the Commissioner annually such contribution not exceeding five per centum of its income as may be prescribed. The Act does not contemplate separate rules to be made in respect of each religious institution likely to obtain the benefit of services rendered by the State for which the contribution is to be levied. Under section 76(2) of the Act audit fee is not to be prescribed by rules : the Commissioner has to determine, having regard to the facts and circumstances of each case, the fee (being not more than one thousand rupees), by auditors appointed in the prescribed manner, (b) (1) 920 section 76 "(1) In respect of the services rendered for defraying the expenses incurred on account of such services every religious endowment shall from income derived By it, Pay to the commissioner annually such contributions not exceeding fifty per centum" of its annual income as the Commissioner may determine. The Commissioner has also to form an estimate of the reasonable cost which may be incurred in making an effective audit of the accounts of each temple. Section 77(1)(a) provides for the assessment and collection of contribution payable by a religious institution, the annual income of which is calculated for the fasli year immediately preceding the year immediately following the year in which it is calculated as aforesaid for the purposes of the levy of contribution under sub section (1), and the demand will not be struck down merely because it turns out that the amount demanded is not precisely equivalent to the cost actually incurred for auditing the accounts. The High Court was of the view that the Commissioner had not determined the audit fee under section 76 (2). It also held that the demand made by the petitioners ' temple for the payment of a sum of Rs. 1,000 was without jurisdiction and was "on that account without competence or authority of law". In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court had not properly determined whether the audit fees were in truth for meeting the cost of auditing the account of the petitioners temple. HELD : (i) The Commissioner had no power under section 77(2). [924 B] (ii) The High court has not committed any error in holding that the audit was without authority or jurisdiction. [925 C D] (iii) The order passed by the High court is set aside and it is directed that the case do stand remanded to the High ' Court for disposal according to law and in the light of the observations made in this judgment.

The appellant was charged with committing contempt of the High Court. The High Court dismissed his petition under section 19(1) of the Act on the ground that no appeal lies to this Court as a matter of right under section 20 of the . The High court held that an appeal does lie to this court as a question of right from any order or decision of a bench of the Court. In appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that an application under section 18 of the , is not maintainable in view of section 19 of the ; and that an appellate court has no power to entertain an appeal against an order passed by a single judge. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The preliminary objection raised on behalf of the respondents is well founded and must be accepted as correct. [501G] (2) An order merely initiating the proceeding without anything further does not decide any question. It is neither appealable under section19 nor can it be appealed against as a " matter of Right under section 21. In a given case special leave may be granted under article 136 from an order initiating the proceedings. What has been decided therein is this : that on a reference made by the Advocate General if the Court declines to take cognisance and to initiate proceeding for contempt, the order is not an order instituting contempt proceeding. [525A B] (3) An appeal would lie as a right from an Order of the Supreme Court merely initiating proceedings without anything more, does not deciding any question; it is neither possible nor advisable to make an exhaustive list of the: typo of orders which may be appealable under Section 19. In such an order, the mere order issuing the notice is not appealable. [401C] (4) An appellate court cannot be asked in such an appeal to decide whether the person proceeded against has committed contempt of its Court or not. The matter has to be decided either finally or may be. even at an earlier stage an order is made, which does decide a contention raised by the alleged contemner asking the High court to drop the proceeding on the grounds of its being barred under section20 of the the Act but the High Courts hold that the proceeding is not barred. [504D] (5) An application under Section 18 of a . is not a "appeal" within section 19.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another in the Court of the Magistrate, First Class, Delhi under section 6(1 A) of the . The trial court acquitted him. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) section 6 of the Act was repealed and, therefore, neither the conviction nor the sentence thereunder could be sustained; and (ii) if section 6 was not on the statute book there could be justification for this view as the words it wireless telegraphy apparatus " in section 4 of the 1952 Act were comprehensive enough to take in " wireless telegraphic transmitter" which had been applied, incorporated or referred to. Held, that section 6 (1 A), inserted in the Act of 1933 by the Amending Act of 1949, was repealed by the Repealing and Amending Act, 1952 (XLVIII of 1952) and that it was in force when the offence was committed by the appellant. The words " apply, incorporated and referred to" in section 6 were comprehensively enough to cover all cases where an earlier Act is amended by a later Act. Section 20 of the , repealed the amending Act by the 1952 Amendment Act of 1948 did not affect the continuance of the amendment made by the amending Acts of 1949 and 1950. The effect of the repeal was that section 4 continued to be on the Statute book even after the amending (XIII of 1885) and, consequently, it could not be said that section 5 of the Amending Acts repealed the old Act. Held further, that the words " applies, incorporated, or referred" in sections 6(i), 6(ii) and 20 of Act XIII of 1885 were comprehensive sufficient to take into account the effect of repeal of the amending statutes by the repealing Act of 1945.

The appellant, a son of Adwaita executed two decrees in favour of the respondent and one of the Shebaits. The decreeholders filed two applications under section 36(6) (a)(ii) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act praying for the reopening of the two compromise decrees mentioned above and the passing of new instalment decrees to have the properties, which were purchased in execution of the decrees. The trial court dismissed both the applications holding that the decreeholders had no bona fide acquired any right which could be protected under clause (b) of section 36 of the Act. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the judgment debtors ' claim to have been benamidars for her husband Aghore in respect of the purchase of Ga Schedule properties in court sale, and also that the Kobala executed by the Chakrabortys in favour on July 26, 1940, was a fictitious transaction. Held, that the order for restoration of possession made by both the courts below should stand. The subsequent conveyance of these properties in favour to Oramba Sundari, the appellant, has been held by both both the Courts below to be a fictitious one and as the subsequent conveyance is dealt with exhaustively in the several clauses of section36(2) (c), the court can at all enter into the question as to whether the decreeholder on record was himself a benamidar for another person in respect Of the decree. The order for restoring possession made in favour by both these courts below must stand.

The appellant company was a transferee of the decree passed by the City Civil Court, Bombay. The transfer in writing of a property which is the subject matter of a suit without in terms transferring the decree to be passed in the suit in relation to that property does not entitle the transferee to apply for execution of the said decree as a transferee or of the order itself. The appellant company filed an application under Order XXI, r. 16 of the Code of Civil Procedure for execution by transfer of the suit to the City Court, which was dismissed on the ground that it was not in existence at the date of the document it operated as an agreement to transfer the decree when it would be passed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the transfer in question was not made by a registered instrument within the meaning of Order XXI r.16, and that the transferee could apply for leave under Order 21, r., 16 of Code of C.P.C. Held: (i) The provisions of Order 21 of the Civil Procedure Code contemplate the actual transfer by an assignment in writing or by operation of law and enables such transferee to do so, while rule 16 contemplates the actual Transfer by an assignee in writing within the ambit of Order XX, r .16 of the C. P.C., and if it was found that the (1) I.L.R. , approved. (2) A.I.R., 1949 Bom. 881, approved. Per Das, J. The provisions Of Order XXI Rule 16 contemplate the delivery of possession by an assign in writing to a transferee by assignment in his own name within the time fixed for the purpose. It is not necessary that the transferor must be a party to the suit and he should be allowed to do it. In the present case there was no question of transfer of any decree by the transferors to the respondent company by assignment of the same decree. The High Court was right in holding that the appellant could claim to be a transferee only of the judgment debtor 's interest in the decree after it was passed and that while the transfer of or an agree ment to transfer a decree that may be passed, does not render the transferee a transferee a transferor of the original decree by assignment within the scope of Order XXII, r, 16. The respondent company cannot claim to have been transferees of the right of actual decree holder, which is subsequently obtained by Habib & Sons by an Assignment in writing under the provisions of Rule 16. (ii) The High Courts were wrong in holding the transfer was not transferred or agreed to be transferred to the appellant by assignment as contemplated by Order XXI rule 16.

The respondent, a contractor, was invited to supply and fixing "S.H. Windows"W ' Type ' "T.H., Window 'W ' type". The tender was accepted by the Executive Engineer on April 20, 1957. On April 20. 1957, the respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, its tender for providing and fixing the S.H.' W ' Type " '"T. H., W. C. W. W ' type "T 'H.W. Type" "T".H. C., W 'W. C.. W 'C. W "W. ' Type" 'T '.H, W 'E 'H 'W G 'W E 'H, S.S. H. W., C.W 'W F 'W H. C.' W. 'W C. 'E H. 'C 'W D 'H; S.K. Jain vs The State of Rajasthan and others, ; , followed. The contract was for work, in the execution of which some movable property passed : it was not a contract for sale of windows but a combination of two distinct and separate contracts, one for the supply or the sale of goods for consideration, was liable to tax under the Sales Tax Act. The respondent 's case that the contract with the Executive Engineers was one of sale of articles and the amount received by the respondent was not taxable, was rejected by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State of Madhya Pradesh that the contracts were for work in the executing of which certain movable property passing : it is not a "building contract" but a composite one for sale and not a composite contract for the sale or purchase of windows, and that the amount paid by the contractor was not liable to sales tax. HELD: (i) The contract of sale was a works contract and not an agreement for sale. [501 D] (ii)The contract was a composite transaction which was entered into in pursuance thereof. It was not merely to supply the windows but to "fix" the windows. If the windows were not properly "fixed" the contract would not be complete, and the respondent could not claim the amount agreed to be paid to it. [506 E F] (iii)The terms of the tender were not decisive and the Court was entitled to ascertain the true effect of the contract as disclosed by the nature of the work, and in determining whether the contract is one of service or labour or one for consideration.

The appellant State is an accused in a case under section 420 and 468 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B Indian Penal code. It was alleged that on November 8, 1967 Shanker Lal came with another man named Pandey and told him that he (Shanker Lal) could arrange for a transaction of sale of foreign goods which would result in good profit to the complainant. On November 16, 1967 Ram Avtar lodged a report with the police against Shanker Lal after his suspicion had been aroused. The appellant was charged under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal. It is contended on behalf of the State that so far as Raj Kumar Agawalla was concerned no case had been made out against him because it was the case of the prosecution itself that Raj Kumar respondent too was a party to any conspiracy to defraud or cheat Ram Avtar. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The report which was lodged by Ram Avtar in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar Agarwalla respondent because it is the case that Raj Kr. Agawalala was a Party to any agreement to defraud and cheating Ram Avtar or to cheat Ram Pal. That circumstance, as pointed out by the High Court, would hardly warrant an inference that RajKumar respondent too had been a party in any conspiracy with defraud or cheated Ram Avtar.[279A B] 2. The part which is attributed to Raj Kumar is that he was present along with Shanker Lal, when the latter brought washer plates in a taxi and demanded the price of the washer plate from Ram Avtar; that Shanker Lal and Raj Kumar Agrawalla were thereupon arrested by the police. That circumstances, as stated by the appellant, would not warrant an conclusion that Rajkumar respondent too did not commit any conspiracy or defraud Ram Avtar [279A] 3. The charge under sections420, 468, 471 Indian penal Code readwith section 120 B Indian Penal Act is framed against Raj Kumar Aggarwalla and Shanker Lal. Raj KumarAgawalla thereafter filed a revision petition in the High court for quashing the charge against him. Charges framed against him were accordingly quashed.

The petitioner, a resident of Sultanbattery area in the State of Kerala and describing himself as a commuter of the Indian Railways he has alleged that the Railways in this country are owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional, statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways, adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties is not available. The petitioner also alleged that there were as many as 27233 unmanned level crossings on the Railways and if all of them are to be manned, a capital expenditure of 330 crore rupees would be necessary and similarly an annual recurring expenditure of Rs.44 crores will have to be met. Adverting to robberies and dacoities in the running trains, it has been pointed out that they are problems of law and order, maintenance of which is an obligation of the State Governments. The commendable view to accept may be that the rates and fares should cover the total cost of service which would be equal to operational expenses, interest on investment, depreciation and payment of public obligations, if any. It was also submitted that they were problems of Law and order maintenance ofwhich is an essential part of the system. Security both to the travelling public as also to the non travelling citizens must be provided and this means that accidents have to stop. The respondents denied some of the assertions of the petitioner, yet no dispute has been generally raised to the stand taken in the writ petition. It is only in a country of that order that the common man 's mode of transport closely connected with the free play of this fundamental right should not be. least insiduous because they are novel and unprepared for. The quality of the service should improve. This means that accident have tobe avoided, attack on the persons of the passengers, prying on their property has to stop; attack on them as national works over which the Government may justly exercise and is called upon to exercise stringent and salutary control This control should not remain an arbitrary right of interference but a regulated authority defined and declared by law which is not to be needlessly or vexatiously exacted but which, in my humble judgment, is necessary at once for the interests of the state and for the protection of the public. The responsibilities cast by the Railway Act and the Rules under it must be complied with. It has been lodged in the Judges and if they have to fulfil their function as Judges, it would hardly be lodged elsewhere. The Railways Act and Rules under them must be comply with. This is worked out also in the Railways. As quickly as possible, classification conforming to this is introduced. Lord Simond in Shaw vs Director, Public Prosecution, has observed: "I entertain no doubt there remains in the Courts of Law a residual power to enforce the supreme and fundamental purpose of the law, to conserve not only the safety and order but also the moral welfare of the Government and that it is their duty to guard against attacks which may be more insidious because they were novel and Unprepened for. This control must be lodged somewhere and under our Constitution and laws, it had been lodged elsewhere." (Minutes of Lord Dalhousie, July 4, 1850). Keeping the history of the growth of the Railwaysand their functioning in view, the commendable views to accept can be that this is workedout also in this Railway track, Lord Simon, July4, 1850. Keeping the History of the spread of the railways and their functioning at the level crossing, theaikma and the then Governor General of India had said in his minutes: "Have you will ever avoid the error of viewing Railways as private undertakings and will regard them as National works, over which this public utility may justly be exercise and are called uponto exercise stringent And salutary control." The appellants were the owners of certain lands in the State of Gujarat. They claimed that they had been cultivating the said lands since 1948 and that they were entitled to be protected under section 20(1) of the Jagirs Abolition Act, 1952. The Tribunal dismissed their applications on the ground that the applications for restoration made by them were barred by limitation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, they were within 30 days of receipt of the order of dismissal and hence the applications were not within 30 day of the receipt of such order of rejection and hence they were barred under section 21(1). HELD: (i) The Tribunal committed an error of law in dismissing the applications of restoration made to them. [144 D] (ii) The orders of the Gujarat Revenue Tribunal dismissing the appellants ' applications for restoring their appeals were well within the period of limitation prescribed by Regulation 21. [145 E F] (iii) The order of the Tribunal dismissing their applications was received by the appellants on April 20 and April, 1961. It follows therefore that the Tribunal committed error of jurisdiction in dismissing them in all the four cases. [146 G H] (iv) The words "decide it on merits" but in Regulation 20 the expression used is "decided ex parte". In the context of section 20 and in view of the express language of section 17(1), the legislative authority uses the words "Decreeed ex parte" and we see no reason, either in the language or context of Regulation 20, why it should not include in its scope and ambit an application for restoration of an appeal decided on merits under Regulation 19(1); and generally for the effective exercise of its powers and discharge of its functions under this Act. [147 A B] (v) The expression used in Regulation 21 is " deciding ex parte", and we are of opinion that it is obligatory on its part to decide an appeal on merits even though there is default on the part of the appellant to appear in the appeal or application.

The appellant 's case was that Telibandha was dedicated to the temple of Shri Ramchandra Swamy as early as 1857 by Dinanath Sao himself and later in the year 1896 when a partition took place between his descendants who were up till that time living jointly, all the coshares not only re affirmed the dedication made by Dinnath Sao of this village of Teli captured but also themselves dedicated the village Teli misconstru to the deities in this temple by accepting the award made by the Panchas. The appellant ' s case was one of absolute dedication of the village for the purpose of the temple by the Panch Faisla Award of 1896 and no trust was created thereby. Held, that the document (the Panch Faishla Award) clearly and unambiguously shows an .absolute dedication of a village to Shri Ramchandra Swami temple or whether the village was given in full proprietorship to Ramsaran Lal absolutely with only a charge on it for the expenses of the Temple and did not make an absolute dedication. The fact that there is not a single word in Bagchi 's award to indicate, even remotely, that in his opinion, the award suffered from any infirmity. On the contrary, Mr. Bagchi accepted the previous award and gave his own interpretation of it, saying that by the award after "including mouzas Borsi and Teli Oriya in the partition the Panchares not merely re affirmed dedication made thereby. The document (The Panch Fairsla Award Of 1896) clearly shows an "absolute endowment of the Village Telighted" of the villages to Shri Ramachandra Swamy temple, set aside the judgment and decree of the High Court and send the case back to the High court for disposal of the appeal after deciding the other issues in the suit that require to be decided for its proper disposal.

The appeal is against the order of the High Court. Allowing:The appellants were the President of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of the Oudh Bar Association. There were three charges against the appellants. It was not necessary to refer in detail to the same. The High Court discharged the notices. The appellants filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution praying that they be punished for contempt of court. The two appellants before this Court were the president of the Lucknow Bar Association, and the chairman, Action committee of the Allahabad Bar. The question was whether contemners Nos. 1 & 2 are guilty of contumacious conduct or not. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The High Courts did not wish to proceed against the appellant. [604B] (2) The language used by them was unfortunate. Counsel for the appellants rightly said that was not proper and it should not have been passed in that manner. It is the duty of lawyers to protect the dignity and decorum of the judiciary. If lawyers fail in their duty the faith of the people in the judiciary will be undermined to a large extent. [0604C] (3) The words used by the appellants were unfortunate. They did not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion. The language employed by them is unfortunate. It cannot be said that lawyers are the custodians of civilisation. Lawyers have to discharge their duty with dignity, decorum and discipline. [2006] 3 S.C.R. 927; referred to. (4) The Judges do not want to be over sensitive in the matter keeping in view the surrounding circumstances in which the contu macious act was committed by them.

The appellants were the owners of a joint movable and immovable properties. The arbitrators made an application before the Sub Judge for registration. On 2nd September, 1978 the arbitrators made a reference to them under section 18 of the . The Sub Judge fixed the hearing of the arbitrators ' application to return the award to enable them to present the same for registration on the ground that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo the arbitrators could not take 122 back the award for presenting the same. On 3rd September, 1981 the arbitrators presented the award before the sub Registrar and made an endorsement to that effect. The Sub Registrar rejected the application holding that the limitation for registration had already expired. On appeal by the appellants the High Court ordered that the arbitrators " application dated 14th August, 1978 should be kept pending and be heard when the injunction order was vacated. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending, namely 28th January, 1978 to 24th November, 1983 should be excluded in view of the principle laid down under section 15 of the , and that the award was presented within time as the period between 28th of January,1978 to 24rd November,1983 should be included in view Of the principle enunciated under section15 of the ; and that since the award had been made on 28th November 1977, the limitation prescribed for the registration of the award has already expired; and that even if the award is in the custody of the court, he could not have taken back the awarded from the custody. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The period during Which the judicial proceeding were pending that is to say, from 28th February, 1978 till the return of the Award to the arbitrators on 24th of November, 1982 the arbitrators or the parties could not had presented the same within time. [690C] 2.1 In the instant case admittedly the award as we have noted before was presented before the Court pursuant to the order of the High court directing maintenance of status quo and 20th December, 1982 was the date of the order directing maintenance. The award as it would appear from the narration of events hereinbefore made that the arbitrator had tried to obtain the custody by the court. [613D E] 2:2 In view of this position the Sub Registrar pursuant to order of this Court on 24rd June, 1985 found that the reference was presented beyond time as it was in the court of the learned Munsif from 28st January, 1979 to 24 November, 1984. The High Court was therefore right in holding that it was the Registrar and not the Sub Court who could determine the question of limitation for the purpose of registration of a award. [686D E; 686A] 2 :3 In view thereof the period that is required to be excluded is from 28rd January 1978 to24th November 1983, but still the award being in the possession of the Court and there was ample evidence as it could appear from narration of facts hereinbefore made by the narrationof events hereinbefore referred to that the Arbitrators had triedto obtain the possession. [687F] 2(a) The period of limitation prescribed under section 12 of the Limitation Act is three years from the date when the interim order was passed directing maintenance or status quo, and 20nd December, 1983 was the day of the passing of the injunction. [688D E]. (b) In the present case admittedly, the award having been made in the Court of the Sub Munsif from 29th January 1978 till 24th October, 1983 the very next one day of getting possession of that award from the court on 24st November, 1980 to 24nd November, 1981 was the dates when the stay order was granted.

The appellant was a tenant of the respondent. The respondent gave notice to the appellant under section 13(1)(e) of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, for sub letting which it was alleged had resulted in the termination of the tenancy. The defence of the appellant was that under the terms of the lease he had the right to sub let the premises. Held, that the respondent 's suit for ejectment was not brought within the provisions of section 13 (1)(a) of that Act and section 23 of the Contract Act. The question is whether the respondent waived his right in regard to the prohibition against sub tenancy and the provision in section 13 of the Act was for the protection of his rights which he was entitled to waive. Held further, that under section 15 of the , a tenant may sublet any portion of his premises to a sub tenant provided be forthwith intimates in writing to his landlord (1) A.I.R. 1949 Bom. 881, and (2) A,I. R. 1950 Bom. 981, applied. The right of the landlord to sue for ejectment on the ground of subletting being a personal right for his benefit, the landlord must be taken to have waived it as by an express contract he had allowed the tenant to sub letting and consequently he could not evict the appellant. In the instant case the question is not merely whether waiver of statutory rights enacted for the benefit of one individual but whether the Court would aid the appellant in enforcing a term of the agreement which section 15 was declared to be illegal.

The respondent, a student of the appellant 's college, filed an application before the Divisional Board for permission to conduct examinations and also to deal with the use of unfair means at the final examination conducted by the Board. The Divisional Board rejected the application on the ground that the examinees/parents/guardians were parties to the fabrication and the fabrication was done at their behest. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of the Divisional Commissioner, which allowed the writ petition holding that the Committee had no jurisdiction to evaluate the evidence as an appellate Court and to come to its own conclusions. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the finding reached by the Standing Committee that the fabrication of moderators ' mark sheets was done in the behest of either the candidate or the parents or guardians to 790 their advantage is based on records. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The conclusion reached by a Standing Committee, as per the directions given in its order dated January 30, 1991, that the fabricated moderators 'mark sheets were done at the instance of either of the examinee or the parent or guardian is based upon the evidence on record. [798C] 2.1 In dealing with question as to whether the Committee was justified in arriving at its conclusion against the respondent it would not be reasonable to exclude from consideration the circumstances on which the whole enquiry came to be held and the general background of the atmosphere in the examination hall. The fabrication of the moderators ' Mark sheets was undertaken after the scrutiny by the concerned officials in the office of the State Board at Bombay and before the moderators' mark sheets were taken out to Pune to feed the computer. It depends on the nature and gravity of the misconduct to be dealt with by the disciplinary authority. [788E] 2:2 The conclusion arrived by the Education Standing Committee is not based on any evidence or if the order as passed in contravention of the statutory provisions of the law or in violation of the principles of natural justice, the court has no jurisdiction either to quash the order merely on the grounds that different view could possibly be taken on the evidence available on the record. The conclusion drawn by the Educational Standing Committee was based on the admission made by the respondents. It depended on the type and gravity and nature of the work done in connection with the fabrication, it is not open to the High court under article 226 or Article 136 to interfere with the finding and to quash a notification merely on that ground. [789E F] 2(a) The conclusion that the construction was done by either the examinee/guardian or their parents or guardian was based upon evidence on records, cannot be sustained. [783C D] 3:1 In the instant case, the fabrication is done at its instance and not at his behest. It is, therefore, clear that the conclusion reached in the Education Committee that fabrication ofithal ' mark sheet was done after the inspection by the officials in their office at Bombay, before theuments were taken into consideration to feed to the computer, cannot also be sustained.[789E] 3.2 The finding reached in this regard by the educational Standing Committee on the basis of admission made from the records is not supported by any evidence nor was the conclusions reached on the strength of the admissions made by them. [784F] 4:3 In dealing in question as regards the quantum of punishment, it would be open to a High Court to interfere only with the order passed in violation or violation of principles of Natural justice, if it is supported by some evidence or where the order is passed in breach of the provisions of law or is based solely on the facts available on record and is based merely on evidence on the records.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that the appellants had been charged under s.120 B of Indian Penal code for criminal misconduct and under section 409 of the IPC, to be committed by Madan Lal, one of the prosecution witnesses. The trial court acquitted the appellants but convicted them on the ground that the charge against them was not based solely on such presumption. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the intention of the Act was to create by means of clause (d) an offence different from a single act of bribery and that it could come into play only when there is no offer to give an d acceptance of a bribe by a public servant. Held, that the object of the legislation was to provide by means in cl.(d) a person who commits criminal misconduct in the discharge of his duty must be deemed to be a public servants for the purposes of Chapter IX and section 409 Of the Indian penal Code. The offence as defined in cl. (d), does not come with. in the meaning of bribery is to place too narrow a construction on the sub clause. Under the Act as it stood before it was amended by Act XVII of 1955, every railway servant was deemed to have been a public Servant for the purpose of Chapter X and section409 Of that Code. Section 5(1) of this Act provides that "every railway servant, not being a publicservant as defined under section 21 of the I.P.C., shall be deemed, to have committed the offence" of criminal conspiracy. The words "any railway servant" in cl (d)(d) are wide enough to include a person whose duty it is to perform and which act or purports to do so. The word "public servant" is not defined in section 21(1). It is only used in the sense of a person in authority who has been entrusted with the duty of performing the duties of a public office. The definition of "public servants" in section 2(2)(d), therefore, includes persons who are in charge of the affairs of a railway servant and not those who are directly or indirectly connected with the official functions of a private person.

The appellant Bank of Saurashtra (the Bank) had pledged oil tins and other personal guarantee of the surety. The surety was discharged from his liability under the guarantee. On appeal by the surety, the High Court held that the surety had agreed to become surety on the principal debtor pledging oil tin and, therefore, two securities were offered, namely, pledge of goods and the personal guarantee executed by the principal creditor in favour of the Bank Ext. 81, and the letter of guarantee Ext. 31 executed by surety in favour thereof as also the bond executed by him in favour Of the Bank was independent of the pledge of Goods given by the Principal debtor in favour o the Bank. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The surety is entitled to restitution. [83D] (2) In order to attract section 141 it must be shown that the creditor had taken more than one security from the principal borrower at the time when the contract of guarantee was entered into and irrespective of the fact whether the surety knows of such other security offered by the guarantor, if the creditor loses or without the consent of the sureties, parts with such security, the surety is discharged to the extent of the value of the security lost as provided by section 141. [84E] (3) The principal debtor had taken a more than two security from one of the principal debtors at the relevant time when he was contract of suretyship was entered and irrespective Of the fact Whether the surety knew of such security or not, and if the surety accepts the offer, partswith such security are discharged to that extent. [85F] (4) The guarantor is entitled under section 141 to restitution because it is found that a creditor has taken more or less one security on the basis of which advance was made and the surety gave personal guarantee on the good faith of other security being offered by him, which itself may be a consideration for the surety offering his personal guarantee and the creditor by its own negligence lost one of those securities. [86B] (5) The liability under section 138 is not discharged because it has taken less than one guarantee on account of the negligence of the creditor Bank. It is difficult to entertain a contention that section 141 would not be attracted and the guarantor would not have been discharged even if it was found that the debtor had took more than another security on his good faith. [87C] (6) The High Court erred in holding that the guarantor having lost one security, namely the pledged goods, the bail was wholly discharged.

The appellant was the son of Amritrao. The land in suit was allotted to his share by the then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for 91 714 services to be rendered by the patel and the grant was recognised as a service inam by the British Government, and (2) it was open to the revenue authorities to resume and regrant the lands in accordance with the provisions of the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900. The appellant 's case was that as a result of this partition, the " patelki inam" lands were divided and the lands allotted to the share of the appellant. The Government by its order dated August 28, 1922, excluded the "patelki Inam" lands from the resumption proceedings relating to the jagir on the footing that they were separate from and independent of the jagir. The High Court held that (1) the lands were given by way remuneration or wages for 91 purposes to be render by the Patel and (ii) the grant made was recognised by the Government, but not by the sovereign authority and neither the Inam Rules nor the provisions Of the Pates and Patharis Law. 1900 applied; and (iii) even if the said rules and provisions apply, the appellant still retained his hereditary rights in the lands. Held, that the grant of a share in the emoluments of office fell even for consideration not to speak of decision but to speak from decision. The grant was not a service grant, and no question of title by adverse possession arises against Government, even though the lands had been shown as excluded from the jagir of Nawabag in 1866. Amritrao patel vs State of Bombay, [1955] 1 S.C.R. 869, followed.

The appellant, a Hindu undivided family governed by the Mitakshara School of Hindu Law, was a member of the Hindu undivided families. He was a Cutchi Memon and belonged to the same family as the other persons who had been made insolvents. The respondents ' case that he rules of Hindu law were consistently acquiesced in and applied to their family and the other Cutchi memons settled in Madras. They filed a suit for partition of the properties on the ground that they had settled down first in Madras and then in Bangalore sometime between 1928 and 1930, and as a large part of the ,state was situate in Madras, he should prefer the Madras as against the Bombay view. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court held that the rule of Hindu laws applicable to Cutchi were not uniformly acquiesced in by the respondents ' contention that they were governed by Hindu law and stated the position of Cutchi. Held : (i) The question whether a particular statute is consistent with the Hindu Law or not, must depend on its own facts and circumstances. It is well settled that where there are two or more parties to the suit, the general trend of judicial opinion in Bombay was that both the Khoias and the Cutchi could be governed by their Mahomedan law. (ii) The rule of succession and inheritance are different from each other. In the instant case, the respondents were governed in matters of succession, succession and succession according to Hindu Law. (iii) The respondents were not governed in any matter of succession or inheritance but only in matters relating to property succession and descent as it would be consistent with Hindu law.

The appellants are manufacturers of fabrics of different types. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage. It has, however, been held that the retrospective effect given by section S I will be subject to the provisions of sections 11A and 11B of the , as amended by Act No. 1 of 1982. Under the definition "place of removal" may be a factory or any other place or premises of production or manufacture of the excisable goods etc The Explanation to rule 9 provides that excisable goods produced or manufactured in any place or undertakings at an intermediary stage shall be deemed to have been removed from such place or places and consumed or utilised for the manufacture of another commodity by deeming such production or manufacturing of the commodity at an earlier stage. In other words, if a commodity is taken outside the factory it will be removal and when the excisable product manufactured or manufactured within the factory is removed from one plant to another it will not be a case of removal. The Explanation provides that "place" may include any premises appurtenant thereto, which may be specified by the Collector in this behalf whether for consumption, export or manufacture or manufacture. It further provides that goods produced and manufactured in a continuous process shall be treated as removed from any place where they are produced, cured or manufactured or any premises attached thereto, until the excise duty leviable thereon has been paid at such place and in such manner as is prescribed in these Rules or as the Collector may require and except on presentation of an application in the proper form and on obtaining the permission of the proper officer on the form: " " The appellants are liable to pay excise duty on the yarn after it was sized for the purpose of weaving the same into fabrics. In the instant case, the appellants are not liable to payment any excise duty at the place and time of manufacture or production of the goods. They are also liable to excise duty. The High Court by the impugned judgment has rightly held that since no specification has been made by the collector of such place nor has it been shown that it is only when the goods are removed from the factory, it will become a case for removal and if the excisable commodity manufactured or cured or if such excisable goods are used in the manufacture thereof, this cannot be done without payment of excise duty, at the places and in the manner prescribed. In view of the above finding, the High Court has rightly directed that the appellants shall pay excise excise duty thereon on the cotton yarn which is obtained by them at an appropriate intermediate stage and thereafter further processed in an integrated process for weaving the said same into fabric. The question whether the commodity which is sought to be removed from a factory premises or any part thereof appurtenant thereto is liable to the payment of Excise duty arises only if the goods were removed from that factory, but not when the excise duties leviable thereon have been paid by the appellants at such intermediate stage, and thereafter, further processed into an integrated operation for weaving of the same in the fabrics. The explanation to rule 10 provides that the excisable article produced or produced in any other factory shall be liable to duty. In this case, it has been held by the High court that the commodity purchased at an end is liable for excise duty and the yarn that is produced by the appellant is also liable for payment of duty. It is the contention of the appellants that as no specification had been made in the Collector of such places or premises appurtenant to such place, the provision of deemed removal with regard to the commodity produced at intermediate stage will not apply. In our opinion, the language of rule 9(1) admits of only one interpretation and that is that the specification that has to be made by Collector is of any premises ancillary to the place of manufacture and production of excisable goods.

The petitioner filed a suit for injunction restraining the Hearing Authority appointed under section 68 of the , on the ground that the scheme published under section68 C of the Act was illegal, void and ultra vires and for an injunction restraining it from proceeding with the hearing and approving the scheme. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the suit was not maintainable for the reliefs prayed for by the petitioner since the jurisdiction of the civil courts in such matters was impliedly barred. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the suit being a suit under section 66 L of the .the Act, the Civil Judge had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit; (ii) the trial court had no power to issue an order of injunction restraining a Hearing Authority from proceeding in the hearing of the case and exercising its statutory functions. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of a civil court is exclusive in character and it is not open to a civil Court to issue any order of interim injunction restraining, the Hearing authority from proceeding under the hearing or approving the Scheme. [529G] 2.1 In the instant case, the scheme had been duly published under Section 68 C of ,the Act by an authority which had the power to publish it and that the authority which was hearing the case under section 69 D of the _Act had the jurisdiction to do so. All such objections relating to the merits of a scheme or the desirability of bringing such scheme can be raised by an aggrieved person before the Hearing Authori ty under section 67 D of , the Act and it was for the Hearing Authorities to consider such objections and representations and to pass appropriate orders thereon. [540D] 2:2 The jurisdiction conferred on the State Government (the Hearing Authority under section 71 D of .the , is exclusive, in character, and it has been not open tO a civil suit to issue a order of temporary injunction restraining any Hearing Authorityfrom proceeding with hearing of a case and exercise its statutory function. [541D] 3.1 The jurisdiction vested on the Central Government under section 70 D of ' the . is exclusive and it cannot be said that the State Legislature had the competence to make such an order. [542C] 4.2 In the present case, no question of any cause of action arises in this case. [543D] 5.3 The jurisdiction under section 65 C of . the Act is exclusive. It is not disputed that the Scheme had been published under s 68 C ,of the Act by the authority who was hearing it and had the powers to do same. All those objections relating t o the merits oi the scheme can also be raised before an aggrieved party before the hearing Authority under Section68 D of The Act and the other provisions contained in Chapter IVA of the act.

The appellant was charged with the offence of cheating punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case is that on August 29, 1963 at about 9.30 p.m. the appellant went to the house of Russel Nathaniel and his wife expressed their reluctance to bring to him the girl. On being questioned the appellant told the D.S.P. that he would pay him Rs. 5001 or in default to undergo rigorous imprisonment for a further period of six months under section 161, Indian Penal Code and ordered the substantive sentences to run concurrently. The appellant was then asked to come to the police station and thereafter the appellant interrogated the girl at the resi dence of N. Russel. The D. S.P., however, did not pay him any money to him. On August 29 1963 at 9.00 p. m. the Appellant asked Russel to bring his daughter with him to the Police Station and accordingly the appellant was interrogated by the police. After conclusion of the trial the Special Judge, Delhi accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant under section 6(2)(d) of Prevention of corruption Act and section 161 Indian Penal code. The High Court maintained the conviction of the appellant on each count. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the concealment of birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian Penal Act or any other criminal statute and if the appellant had obtained money from Russel, he could not be said that the appellant has obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to show, in the exercise of his official functions, favour or disfavour to any per son. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The order of sanction in the present case satisfies the requirements of section 6 of the Act. [639 E] 2. It was then contended that there can be no doubt that the suppression of birth by an illegitimate person was not offence under section 165 Indian Penal Ci lions Act or section 5 (1)(d). [640 B] 3. The concealment of the birth of a illegitimate child is not an act under the Criminal Law Code or any criminal statute. [613 A] 4. It is manifest that the accused was guilty of grossly abusing his position as a police officer and extorted money fromunssel Nathaiel and also a gold ring from Roshan Lal. The offence charged and that a prima facie case was made out against the appellant. [540 C] 5. In other words, the argument was that the disclosure of birth in the official capacity of a police Officer is not offence u/s 165 Indian Evidence Act or Section 5(1)(c) of Criminal Law Act. The contention was that there could be no presumption that the person who had obtained the money from a person who has been convicted for an offence and obtaining of money by the accused for refraining from any such imaginary prosecution cannot be said to be an offence u /s 165, Indian Evidence Code or section 165, Criminal Procedure Code. [625 G H] 6. The fact that the complainant was a police official was expected to maintain a high standard of integrity and to uphold the maintenance of law. Instead they proved facts disclose that there was a gross abuse of his position on the part or the appellant and in the circumstances of the case, it is manifest, that the sentence imposed is not excessive.

The appellant was prosecuted for the offence of having accepted illegal gratification as a motive or reward for doing an official act and showing in the exercise of his official functions to obtain pecuniary advantage for himself punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Special Judge acquitted him on appeal by the State Government. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the sanction accorded by the appellant was not a valid one; (ii) the prosecution had failed to prove that the appellant had accepted illegal bribe as a reward for performing an official duty and showing that in the interests of justice the appellant should be put on his trial in a court of competent jurisdiction for offences under section 161 I.P.C.; (iii) the sanctioning authority was not satisfied with the reasons given by the Special Judge; and (iv) the High Court had failed in its duty to scrutinise the evidence and come to the conclusion that the sanction was not valid one. HELD: (i)(a) The sanction accorded under section 6(c) of Prevention of corruption Act, 1950 is a valid sanction. It does not say that it is a conditional sanction. [1005 C] (b) The sanctioning authority has to consider all the relevant facts and circumstances of each case before granting sanction. If the sanctioning officer had applied his mind to the facts and the circumstances of the case he was satisfied that in view of the circumstances mentioned in the sanction, the appellant could be put under trial in an appropriate court for offences alleged against him. [1015 D] (c) The fact that the sanctioning order itself and the evidence of Mr. Bokil had failed, the appeal must be dismissed and the decision of the High court in upholding the conviction and sentence of the appellant must be upheld. [1050 E F] (d) The Special judge was of the opinion that the Sanction accorded in this case was not invalid. He applied his own mind to all the facts which concern the prosecution case alleged against the appellant with reference to his acceptance of Rs. B.okil and had accepted the sum as a bribe for performing a official act. [1105 E] (e) The order granting the certificate shows that the learned Judges who heard the application were of the view that in considering the question whether or not there was a proper sanction, it was necessary to consider whether the sanctioning Authority should have applied his minds to the fact and circumstances and the relevant circumstances of this case.

The appellant landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenants under section 14(1)(b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960. The tenant contended that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and for reconstruction. The Rent Controller held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction was not bona fide. The High Court dismissed the revision petitions filed by the tenants against the orders of eviction and set aside the orders passed by the appellate authority. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant landlord that the landlord had only a life interest in the premises and that it is inherent in such a lifeinterest that it was not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14 (1) (b) as grounds for eviction were raised in the case by proving that there was no possibility or any objection from the daughters of the settlor or from any other remainder man. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Act with which we are concerned is a self contained and complete code for regulation of rights between landlord and tenants as defined in the Act (See M/s Raval and Co. vs K. Thus a controversy that may arise between a landlord and others, who are not his tenants under the Act, is outside the ken of this Act. Such questions as are raised in this appeal by the tenant are, therefore, irrelevant in a litigation between the landlord and the tenants when a suit is instituted by the former on any of the grounds available to him under the provisions of the Act. [275 D E] 2. The question as has been sought to be established in the present case by the appellant tenant is whether there was possibility or no objection from either the daughters or from some other remainder person. On the other hand, the Act with regard to two different tenancies though in the same premises, one for residential purpose and the other for non residential purposes, is not maintainable. [276 B] 3. The expression landlord is defined under section 2(6) as follows: " 'Landlord ' includes the person who is receiving or is entitled to receive the rent of a building whether on his own ac count or on behalf or another or on his behalf and others or as an agent, trustee, executor, administrator, receiver or guardian or who would so receive the rents or be entitled to receiving the rent, if the building were let to a tenant". [276 C] 4. The words "landlord" in section 2 (6) of Act are wide enough to include the person whose property is sought to become vacant on the ground that he has been occupying the premises for a period of more than one year and has not been able to occupy the same for a further period of two years. [278 D] 5. The word "landlord ' in section 14 means a person who holds a life estate in the property and includes a person receiving or has been entitled to any rent, gift, etc. as an executor, trustee or receiver or trustee or who will so receive it. [279 C] 6. The definition of landlord is given under section 3(14) of that Act. It does not mean that the expression "landlord " in section 3 (14) includes a tenant who holds life interest for his life and who admittedly has been on his personal right under the Deed of Settlement as a trustee receiving rents of the premises from the tenants.

The appellant decree holder filed a suit for recovery of possession of the land in execution proceedings. The respondent decree holder claimed that he was entitled to the entire extent of the property and that he had no right to the whole of the said property. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the trees were not included in the 'land ' as defined under section 3(13) of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 (hereinafter referred to as the Act). The High Court dismissed the appeal. In this appeal by certificate it was contended on behalf of the appellant decree holders that the respondent decree holders had no locus standi to file a suit in execution proceeding and that the trial court had erred in holding that they were not entitled to any relief under section 18 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The definition of 'intermediary 's grove under section 2(13)(a) of U. P. Zamindari ( Abolition and Reforms Act 1950 is bhumidhari property. Rights in it are part of bhumidhari rights. Rights of it are parts of bhumiswami rights. [501B] 2.1 In view of the clear legal position, the conclusion is irresistible that even after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6(h) of The U. Pradesh Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1976, which says "intermediaries grove means grove land held or occupied by an intermediary as such". This means that "grove land" and an "intermineral 's groves are on ly collections of trees in plots of land so as to preclude cultivation in them. The uncut trees are deemed to be parts of the "land". [502C D] 2:2.1 The contention is well settled, under the general law, that trees, before they are cut, form parts of 'land" and a grove and grove land. [506B C] 2 :3.1 Under the general Law, trees, after they are cutting, form part of the 'lands '.

The appellants were charged with an offence under Section 302 IPC and sentenced to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. The trial court convicted accused 2 to 4 for an offence punishable under Section 324 read with Section 149 IPC, but the High Court acquitted them of all the charges. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the conviction of the first appellant for an offences under Section 326/149 IPC and sentence of imprisonment for two years each was not permissible. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The conviction of all accused persons for an alleged offence under section 302 read with section 149 IPC is not permissible without a specific charge having been framed against him as envisaged by law. [89B] 1.2 In the instant case, the nature of weapons with which they were armed and nature and seat of injuries inflicted by them though not on any vital part, he can certainly be attributed with the knowledge that with those injuries it was likely that death of Suku may be caused and, therefore, he could also be cloathed with the liability of causing culpable homicide not amounting to murder. None of the injuries alleged in the medical evidence were on any important part of the body though some of the injured persons had sustained injuries. The injuries attributed to accused 2 and 3 were not found to be sufficient in the ordinary course of nature to cause death. [90E F] 1:3 In the present case, none of the accused persons individually had been charged for the substantive offence of murder under Section 304 Part I against the first appellants for an act with the aid of Section 149, IPC read with Sections 149 and 149 IPC. The conviction was not sustainable. That apart, according to the medical examination, none injuries allegedly caused by them were either individually or taken collectively with the other injuries caused by blunt weapons. [91F G] 1 :4 In the trial court all the six accused were charge sheeted for an incident under Section 325 read with 149 IPC and the appellants 2 to 5 for an attempt to cause the death of the deceased. The High Court was not justified in recording a conviction against them for the offence under Sections 302/149, IPC after framing a charge against him for the offences under section 304 Part II against the appellants for other offences with the help of Section 34 IPC. [92F G; 93A B] 1:-5 In view of the sentences recorded for offence under Sec. 325 IPC against the second appellant Subran, Section 325 IPC and convicting him for an Offence under Section 307 IPC and sentencing them to suffer imprisonment for one year each, each. His conviction for an accused under Section 323 IPC was not tenable. That however, according tended to the Medical evidence, none all of the four appellants had shared the common intention of causing such bodily injury on the deceased as were likely to cause his death. The medical evidence also shows that the injuries sustained by the deceased had been caused by all the four accused and that the death had occurred due to multiple injuries which were found sufficient in ordinary course. [94B C] 1(a) In view Of the sentences awarded for offence of culpable homicide under Section 300 IPC against appellants 2 and 4, no separate sentence is recorded for the other offences except the trial Court, which tried the six appellants for the said offence, was not unjustified in recording conviction against him under Section 148 IPC without a definite charge having being framed against them as envisaged under law. The convictions of all of them for an additional offence under s.302/149 were set aside and they were acquitted of all other charges.

The assessee company was assessed to income tax for the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim of the assessee on the ground that it maintained its accounts on cash basis and since it did rot actually receive any income in all these four years, no tax is payable by it. The Appellate Tribunal held that even with respect to the accounting year relevant to the assessment year 1967 68, it had been maintaining accounts on Cash basis and as such it had committed a mistake in filing the returns for the Assessment years 196768 and 196869 69. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that since the Indian Company had credited to the assessee 's account books for the relevant years (accounting year for the Indian company is stated to be the calendar year), no tax was payable by them. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The method of accounting adopted by the assessee for the various accounting years is really irrelevant. [105D] 2.1 In the circumstances of the case, it must be held that in the circumstances, the method of accounts adopted by an assessee is absolutely irrelevant. In the instant case, the mode of accounting followed by the Income Tax officer for the accounting years 1967 69 and 1968 70 was really relevant. [106E F] 3.2 The method adopted by him for the purposes of the assessment of 196768 68 and 1969 69 to the effect that it was maintaining its accounts with respect thereto is absolutely immaterial. In this view of the matter, it cannot be said that the assessee has received the royalty amount only when it receives the same in U.K. Section 145 of the Act does not apply. [107E] 4.3 The method followed by him in the books of the Indian Companies does amount to its receipt by the assesee and is therefore taxable and that it is immaterial when did it actually receive it in UK. section 145 of Income Tax Act, nor is it necessary to express ourselves on the view expressed by the High Court that in this case, there was no conflict or inconsistency between Section 5(2) and Section 145 Of the Act nor is the assessee firm been a debtor in respect of that amount and unless the entry can be deemed to be a payment or receipt, clause (a) cannot apply. The argument that the money was not actually received, but the assessee company had not received the amount does not appear to be correct. [108F G] 4 4.4 In the present case, in the facts of the instant cases, it is difficult to accept the contention that the amount was not really received, and the assessee was a debtor or in respect thereof. The question whether there was any conflict between Section 6(2)(a) and section 145 Of Income Tax is one which must be decided on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties. [109G] 5.5 In the case of a non resident assessee like the petitioner clause (b) of sub section (2) of Section 5 has no application whatsoever and that Section 5 (2)(b) governs it irrespective of the fact whether it maintains its accounts or mercantile basis.
