The method is really relevant when did the assessee actually receive the amount in U .K. in the shape of pounds and makes an entry to that effect in its own Books at Coventry. [110G H] 6.6 In the facts and circumstances, it can be held in this view that in a nonresident assessee like a petitioner clause(a) of subsection (2), of Section5 has no applicability whatsoever and the section 5(1)(b). [109A B] 7.7 The method for accounting adopted in the instant ease is really immaterial.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction but reduced the sentence to one of imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the statement of the approver had been corroborated in material particulars and qua the appellant, (ii) the evidence of the accomplice was sufficiently corroborated for the conviction of the first accused upon which he has been charged; (iii) the conviction was unsustainable because the delay between the preparation of the knife and murder was fatal to the prosecution case. HELD : (i)(a) The statement of Santu, brother of the deceased is no corroboration of the testimony of the witness. It only means that approver made a confessional statement to his brother. That cannot be called, in the circumstances of this case, to be a corroboration of his story because the knife was got prepared by accused No. 1 and hi; motive to commit the murder because of the suspicion he had about his wife having a liaison with the deceased. [534 B] (b) The evidence of Santha, brother is no corroborated in all material particulars. It cannot be doubted that under section 133 of the Indian Penal Code an accomplice is competent to give evidence and according to the latter which is a rule of practice it is almost always unsafe to convict upon his testimony alone. [634 C D] (c) The fact that the knife had been got prepared was not sufficient to connect the appellant with the murder, under section 34 of the Penal Code. It could be said that under that section a conviction based merely on the uncorroborated evidence of an accomplice may not be illegal but the courts nevertheless cannot lose sight of the rule of prudence and practice which in the words of Lord Abinger "it deserves to have all the reverence of the law. [734 C] (d) The circumstance that the appellant might have cemented and not proceeded with the commission of the offence, is no evidence that there was corroboration of any part of the evidence against him. It is also necessary for the prosecution to establish that under the circumstances the appellant could not be convicted upon such unconfirmed evidence.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The prosecution case was that on July 8, 1961 a trap was laid and under the direction of the Deputy Superintendent of Police, P.W. Chaudhury did not challenge the findings of the High Court on questions of fact but the argument was put forward that upon the findings recorded by the High court the appellant could not be convicted of the charges because he was not a "public servant" within the meaning of section 5 of the Act. Held, that an officer in the service or pay of Government ' within the terms of section 21, Penal Code is one who is appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty. The words "public servants" include "every officer in a service or Pay of a local authority". The word "officer" in the definition of "public Servant" in section 2(12) of Indian Penal Code means an officer who is employed to some department for the performing of some official duty. A person, who was appointed to any office for performance of certain public duties, is one whose appointment is to be performed by a corporation established by or under a Central, Provincial or State Act or of a Government company as defined in section 617 of the . The word 'officer" used in section 21(9) of section 2 of the Indian Penal code is not confined to an officer appointed to such office. A public servant is one whom is appointed for performance by some public authority and is employed as a metal examiner known as Chaser in the Railway Carriage Workshops and was therefore a "Public Servant" within section 21 (9). The word `officer ' in section 20 of the Code means a person who is engaged to perform certain public duty, and includes an officer of the Government. The word is not restricted to an office which is held by a person appointed to that office but extends to an official act or duty which is performed by him personally. A "officer in the Service or pay" of a corporation is one of who is a Class Iii servant and was employed as such in the Works Manager who was an officer or servant of the State Government and the duties which he performed were immediately auxiliary to those of the Works manager who was the lead of the office. The appellant could be said to be an officer within the definition Of "public" under section 2 (12) read along with section 2, Prevention of corruption Act.

The appellant was convicted for contravening cl. 3 of the Maharashtra Declaration of Stock Order, 1964 and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. He was further convicted for contravention of cl. 2 of the Bombay Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The High Court set aside the conviction and sentence passed on the appellant in respect of contravention of cls. 3 and 4 of the said order. In appeal to this Court it was contended that r. 141 (2) of the Defence of India Rules, 1962 is not ultra vires the Defence Of India Act. HELD: Rule 141(2) is within the powers conferred by section 3 (1 ) of the . The rule is contrary to an existing act does not matter because section 43 of the defence of India Act provides that "the provisions of this Act or any rule made thereunder shall have effect notwithstanding anything inconsistent therewith contained in any enactment other than this Act". [274E] In the instant case, r.141(2), which is within its powers conferred under section 3(1) of, the Defenceof India Rules does not make any provision authorising the Court to forfeit the juar seized from the house of the appellant because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to. the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. The Rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. [274B C] In view of the provisions of r. 142(2)(a) of Defence of Indian India Rules it is not possible to say that r 141 (1) is ultra vires because section43 of the Act provides for forfeiture to the Government of packages, coverings or receptacles in which any stocks of jowar are found. The rule does not deal with the question whether a rule like r. 14(2). has been challenged, much less declared ultra vires, both in England and in India.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge, Allahabad for an offence under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to death. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the only inference which arises from the fact that violet gave the particular shout is that by so doing, she intended to facilitate the murder of Kunwar Singh, section 107 of the Penal Code which defines abetment provides to the extent material that a person abets the doing of a thing who "Intentionally aides, by any act or illegal omission, the doing Of that thing. " Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The court which acquitted Shri Ram was justifiably influenced by the consideration that though at the earliest stage he had asked that an identification parade be held, the demand was, opposed by the prosecution and the parade was there fore not held, That is not the only point in favour of Shri Ram. Soney Lal 's evidence seems to us insufficient to sustain the conviction of Shri Soneylal. [266C D] 2. The circumstance that Shri Ram had voluntarily accepted the risk of being identified, in a parade but was denied that opportunity was an important point in his favour. But the point of the matter is that the court which convicted Shri Ram and his companions could not have anticipated the presence of Kunwar singh " unless he was aware that the accused persons were lying in wait on the other side of the road and it was necessary to inform them so that they might accomplish their aim. [366C E] 3. The circumstances that Shri S Moneylal had a standing of but 2 years in the District when he is supposed to have appeared for the complainant in the particular case, are not at all to show that he was so flooded with work that he could remember no details of an important murder trial. [466C] 4. The fact that Shri R Ram had actually been identified, does not make any difference between the two. It is difficult to believe that he would have announced the arrival of KunwarSingh " unless she was aware of the nefarious design of Sia Ram and their associates. [453D E] 5. The mere fact that he had voluntarily made the risk would not make him a party to the murderous design. He might have been aware of his nef diverse design of the accused person. It may be difficult to think that he is so floodinged with works that he might remember no detail of an essential murder trial, but was denial that opportunity in the case or who used to instruct him in the matter. [454E F] 6. The question which then arises for consideration is whether the only conclusion which arises therefrom from the facts that violets gave the specific particular role, especially when Sia 's presence of the Kunwar Singh was more easily and with lesser ado. It cannot be said that he has played an important role in the murder o f Shri Ram, along with R. I. Singh. [452C D].

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34, of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court acquitted accused 2 under section 304, read with s 34, I.P.C. on the ground that it was doubtful whether 682 any one of them participated in the commission of the offence and convicted him under section 148, readwith section 149, I P.C., and sentenced him to imprisonment. In appeal by special leave to this Court, HELD : (1) The High court found that though accused 1, 3 and 4 were not identified, 3 unidentified persons must have taken part in the murder. If that be so, before a court can convict a person under section302 read with Section 34 of the I. P. C., it should come to a definite conclusion that one of the named accused is guilty of murder under section 307 read with S 34, and that along with the two or three persons convicted were others who composed the unlawful assembly but who have not been identified and so have not yet been named. [682 H] (2) The fact that the charge as well as the evidence was directed against the 4 named accused, did not mean that they did not conjointly act with accused 2 in committing the murder; nor was there any evidence in that regard. [683 C D] (3) The effect of the acquittal of some of the persons named in the charge and tried by the prosecution witnesses, and the court on the basis of the said evidence may come to the conclusion that others, named or unnamed, acted conjointly along with one of accused charged.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of iron and steel products, was granted licence for import of iron & steel products. The licensing authority issued import licence No. 2959845 for Rs.20, 12,729 in favour of M/s Industrial Cable India Ltd., Rajpura. The licence holder transferred the same in favour to M/S Metalic metal Indus tries. However, due to circumstances beyond the control of the petitioner, that it to say, by the order of the Income Tax Authorities the goods could not be released. This factor was not of the Petitioner 's making, according to the petitioner. The instant writ petition was filed under Article 32 of the Constitution on 16th April, 1988 and on 22nd April,1988 this Court passed the following order: "Pending notice, there will be limited stay to the extent that the goods name, "MSCR defective sheets/coils" which have arrived at Bombay Port per S.S.S."S. It was contended on behalf of the respondents that for the payment of duty, the liability of the peti tioner to pay the duty is the duty at the time of clearance of the goods. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The petitioner as such has no fundamental fight to clear the goods imported except in due process of law. [638G H] 2. Article 32 guarantees the right to a constitutional remedy and relates only to the enforcement of the rights conferred by Part 111 of the constitution. Unless a question of the enforcement o f a fundamental right arises, article 32 does not apply. There can be no question of enforcement of a fundamental fight if the order challenged is a valid and legal order, in spite of the allegation that it isGreater ous. I have, therefore, come to the conclusion that no question arose in this case and the writ petition is not maintainable. [625B C] 3. The Petitioner as such had no fundamental right to clear goods on payment of customs barrier and were in the process of being cleared, but could not claim any relief under Article 226 of the Consti tution. [ 625D E] 4. The petition was not maintainable because of the prohibitory orders of the Central Govern ment under section 102 of the . [639G] 5. In view of the aforesaid, it is not permissible to move this Court on the theoretical basis that there is breach of fundamental right for the enforcement Of which alone Article 32 does apply. [600E] 6. The writ petition filed by the petitioner was not under Article 31 of the ^ HELD: (1) Article 32 is not attracted. There cannot be no dispute that the enforcement or determination of a constitutional fight if an order challenged, in despite the allegation, that there was breach of law, it does automatically involve breach of Art. 32 of th e Constitution. [643E] 7. The relief under article 32 of t he Constitution is wholly inappropriate in the facts and circumstances of this case. It has further to be reiterated that for enforce ment of fundamental rights which is dependent upon adjudica tion or determination o questions of law as well as ques tion of fact without taking any resort to the provisions of the Act, it was not permissible for the petitioner to move the Court on theoretical basis because there is violation of law and determination of facts and the provision of a particular statute for which elaborate procedure is pre scribed, it cannot conceivably be contended that enforcing of those provisions of thi s would breach fundamental right. [537G H; 625A] 8. The question of infringement of fundamental fight does not arise in this petition.

The appellants were the sons of one Shri G. N. Singh who was a managing director and who had been appointed as a managing agent of the firm in respect of the bungalow. The suit was decreed by the trial Court on the ground that the sale was under section 155 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code, and therefore the sale could not be challenged as the sons were under pious obligation under Hindu law to discharge the debts of their father; that the auction sale was for a sum of Rs. 1,000 which was paid in cash by the appellants and the properties were sold in payment of a debt binding on the family and therefore they had no interest left. The High Court dismissed the suit holding that the whole estate including the share of the sons was sold in execution of the payment order and therefore qua that property the sons had no right left; and that the father 's power of disposition over the son 's share had come to an end and consequently in the auction sales the share was held to convey the entire coparcenary estate and it was remarked that it was of the utmost importance that the substance and not merely the technicality of the transaction should be regarded. Held, further, that where the pious obligation exists and partition takes place after the decree and (1) A.I.R. , referred to. The liability of a father who is a managing partner and who draws a salary or a remuneration incurred as a result of negligence in the discharge of his duties is not an avyavaharika debt as it cannot be termed as " repugnant to good morals".

The petitioners in these two cases were the guardians of law and who constitute two important segments of society on whom the stability of the country depends. The Committee recommended that the transfer of the petitioners in those cases, namely, Ms. Kiran Bedi, D.C.P. (North) and Jinder Singh be set aside and they be re examined at the end of the inquiry. In their writ petitions before the High Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the Committee should send a report recommending suspension of the D. C.P., Kiran Bedi and Jandinder Singh, section I.P.(North), and that the petitioners never intended to show any kind of discourtsey to the Committee. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the inquiry was not in accordance with section 8 B of the Act. In appeal to this Court it is contended on their behalf that (1) the Committee had no power to direct the filing of a complaint against either of the petitioner for an offence punishable under section 178 I. P.C., and (2) the petitioners were not entitled to be treated as persons governed by section 8B of the Delhi Administration Act before asking them to get into the witness box for being cross examined. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The orders of the Committee directing the filing and the criminal proceedings initiated against the petitioners before the Metropolitan Magistrate pursuant to the complaints filed on behalf o the Committee must be quashed and set aside. [501G] 2.1 In the instant case, the affidavits and other material before the Committee show that there were a large number of persons who were eye witnesses to the incidents and why could give evidence before the committee. Taking into consideration all the aspects of the case, it is obvious that the committee should not have in the circumstances of the cases directed the filing Of a complaint by either of them for an offences punishable under Section 178 I P. C., or section 178 1.P..C. [525A B] 2:2 The orders passed by the Committee are not contemplated under section 8 A of the . [502F] 3.1 The order of the committee directing the lodging of complaints and the Criminal proceedings initiated by the Metropolitan Magistrates pursuant to complaints filed by the petitioners should be quashed. [500G] 4.2 In view of the foregoing we feel that the orders of this Committee directing filing of the complaints and criminal proceedings instituted against the petitioner before the Magistrate pursuant thereto should be quash and setaside. The order passed by this Court directing the file of a criminal complaint against both the petitioners for an Offence punishable under sections 178 I, P.c., and section 1781.P .C. should be accordingly quashed and we accordingly quash the said orders of that Committee and also the criminal proceeding.

The petitioners, who are seven in number, challenged as unconstitutional and ultra vires the provisions of the Rajasthan Passengers and Goods Taxation Act, 1959, the Rajasthan Goods Taxation Rules, 1959 and a notification issued under R. 8. The first petitioner was a registered firm, petitioners Nos. 2 to 5, and petitioners Nos 6 to 9, and respondents Nos. 7 to 9. The second petitioner is a registered dealer, petitioners No. 1 to 9 were also a registered dealers, petitioners nos. 10 to 13 were also registered dealers under the Rajasthan Motor Vehicles Taxation Act. The third petitioner was also a dealer in motor vehicles, petitioners no. 2 and 3 were also dealers in motor cars, petitioners 2 to 6 were also unregistered dealers. The fourth petitioner was not a registered owner of motor vehicles but was a dealer for motor vehicles. The fifth petitioner was the registered dealer under the , Rajasthan Passengers & Goods Taxation (Amendment) Act, 1960, and the third petitioner is the registered owner under the . The fourth respondent was a Registered Firm, petitioners 1 to 5 were also carrying on business in motor cycles, rickshaw or inland waterways. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification by contending that the Act in the guise of taxing passengers and goods, taxes really the income of the petitioners, or at any rate, fares and freights, and was therefore unconstitutional. Held, that the tax is still on passengers and Goods, though what it is to be is determined by the amount of fare or freight. The tax is always on passengers but what it does is not so, is not available to the State Legislature. It is the cost of construction and maintenance which makes the difference in the tax, and no case of discrimination can be said to be made out. The last contention was that the proviso to sub section (3) of section 3 is extra territorial in nature because it makes the tax payable on fares and transports attributable to the territory of another State when the route passes through such territory even though the journey starts and ends in Rajasthan or to the officer of the Excise and Taxation Department nearest to the point of 523 entry into the State and having jurisdiction over that area. The proviso to section 3 was extra territorial, because it making the tax applicable on passengers or goods, though the measure of the tax was furnished by the amounts of fare and freight charged. It does not cease to be a tax on passengers & goods, but only lays down what the amount Of the lump sum must be, if lump sum payment is made in lieu of payment of the Tax calculated on actual fares and transportations attributable thereto. The words "in respect of all passengers carried and goods transported by motor vehicles" are wide enough to include a tax which is levied under the Entry, and thus the tax cannot be levied under section 3.

The appellant was retrenched from the service of the respondent company on 1st August, 1974. The appellant challenged the award in this Court by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The Labour Court has awarded full back wages to the workmen on its finding that the retrenchment was not bona fide and that the non availability of raw material or recurrent power shedding and lack of profitability was a mere pretence or a ruse to torment the workmen by depriving them of their livehood, the real reason being the annoyance of the appellant consequent upon the refusal of the workmen to be a party to a proposed settlement by which work load was sought to be raised(l. Pai, learned counsel for the appellant in his attempt to persuade us to give something less than full back wage, attempted to re open the controversy concluded by the order of this Court while granting limited leave that the retrenched workmen who were now reinstated shall be paid 75% of the back wages after deducting the amount paid to them as wages when recalled for work since the date of retrenchment and adjustment of the retrenchment compensation towards the amount found due and pay able. [569 D] (2) The question in controversy which fairly often is raised in this court is whether the Labour Court in the facts and circumstances of the case was justified in awarding full back Wages. Once leave against relief of reinstatement was rejected, the order passed by the Labour court holding that retrenchment was invalid and it was motivated and the relief of reinstate must follow, has become final. [570 G] (3) The only limited question is whether there should be a regular Court of appeal but it confers a discretionary power on the Supreme Court to grant special leave to appeal inter alia against the Award of any Tribunal in the territory of India. If after such a protracted time and energy consuming litigation during which period the workman just sustains himself, ultimately he is to be told that though he will be reinstated, he will not be subjected to a sort of penalty for no fault of his and it is wholly undeserved. [571 G H] (4) The Court may in the spirit of labour and management being partners in the industry direct scaling down of back wages with some sacrifice on management 's part too.

The accused was convicted by the Sessions Judge, Mahasu under section 302 Indian Penal Code for committing murder of his wife Churi. The High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the confession recorded during investigation of a case by a second class magistrate not specially empowered was admissible in evidence; (2) the statement recorded during the investigation of the case could not be put in evidence under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, as the same was not recorded in the manner prescribed by section 164. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1)(a) The statement recorded by a magistrate and signed by the accused is inadmissible in evidence. [14G] (b) The fact that the accused alone was with Churi deceased in the house when she was murdered there cannot be accepted because there is nothing to show that the police was aware of the murder of Churideceased before the visit of the accused to the house of Shri Mahajan. On the contrary, the evidence on record establishes beyond any manner of doubt that the dead body of the deceased was recovered after the accused had visited the house and with which the injuries on the body of his deceased, according to Dr. Besides that it is established by the evidence of Mangat Ram (PW 10) and Shri Mahajan (PW 15) that the relations of the complainant with the deceased, ts would be shown hereafter. were strained would, in the absence of any cogent explanation by him point to his guilt. [15A B] (2)(a). The statement was recorded by the magistrate and was signed by him. In this connection it is clear that the time mentioned by Shri Mahajan of recording of confessional statement was 11 p.m. while the intimation which was given by Mangat Ram PW 10 to the police regarding a murderer having come to the residence of Shri Hari Singh was entered in the daily diary at 10.50 p. m. while intimation was given to the Police regarding a murder having taken place during his absence cannot be said to have been taken by the police to be adding insult to the injury by an unchaste wife. [16B C] (3)(a), (b). The evidence on the record establishes that shortly before the occurrence, the accused enquired from the deceased regarding the father of the boy and the deceased thereupon abused him. The version of the prosecution that shortly after the occurrence the accused inquired from thedeceased regarding the mother of the child and the accused thereafter abused him must have been accepted because the relations between the accused with the victim, tt was strained would be, in view of the evidence, established beyond any reasonable manner of doubts that the deceased had been born to her as a result of his adulterous conduct. [17E F] (4)(a)(b) There is no evidence on which the prosecution could establish beyond any doubt that it was the accused and none else who caused injuries to Churi victim as a consequence of which she died. The fact, that the relation of the parties with the complainant, t was strained will, in this case, go to show hereafter. The accused would have had a natural affection for the child, and it is difficult to believe that he would have insisted upon Churi staying with him without the child. [18G H] (5)(a); (b): The evidence of the approver shows beyond any pale of doubt, that he was taken by P.W. 10 to Kotkhai, which had been arranged by the Publicity Department, according, to Head Constable Bhag Singh PW, lasted from 7 to 8 30 p.M. while he was intimation about a murderer being born to his wife as a matter of fact. The evidence also establishes beyond all reasonable doubt that P.Ws.

The plaintiff, who was the mortgagee of a property mortgaged to the defendant, filed a suit for redemption of the mortgage debt. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the section must apply. It confers rights on the mortgagor who redeems and directs that in the absence of a contract to the contrary, he (1) A.I.R. , and (2) C.A. No. 1052 of 1949 instituted under the Original Jurisdiction of the High court, were liable to contribute in equal shares towards payment of the mortgaged debt. Held, that the suit was not barred by section 92 of the Transfer of Property Act read with section 82 of the . The plaintiff had in substance asked for a mortgage decree up to a limit of Rs. 40,253 11 with interest against either defendant, I and II. The plaintiff did not use the word "subrogation" but merely pleaded that he had not used the word 'subrogated". The suit was therefore barred by article 105(1) of the Limitation Act. Held further, that though the claim is inartistically worded the plaintiff has in substance sought for a decree up upto a limit Of Rs. 60,25311 10 with interest from the date of payment to the date on which the mortgage amount was paid and in default of payment, limiting the liabilities of each item of property to the sum rateably due on it under section 82.

The appellant No. 1 is a Bachelor of Engineering (Civil) having secured 69.96% marks in the qualifying examination thus in all 99.46 marks out of 150.23 marks out Of 150. 23.3% of total marks. Both the appellants applied for the posts of Asstt. Engineers (Civil), and 100 Mechanical Engineer respectively, which were to be made on the basis of marks obtained in the competitive examination and marks secured in the interview, in accordance with the K.S.C.S (Direct Recruitment by Selection) Rules 1973. The selection was to be conducted on the basi sation of marks awarded in the written test and marks awarded for viva voce out of 100.23. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for vivavoce as 33.3 were excessive and in violation of the decisions of this Court. The Tribunal by its order dated 24th May, 1990 dismissed the petitions and the appellants aggrieved against the aforesaid decision have approached this Court by grant of special leave. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The selection under the impugned Rules was made according to the rules of 1973 and this practice is being consistently followed for the last 17 years and there is no allegation of any malafides in the matter of the impugned selections. However, the Rules are clearly in violation with the dictum laid down by this Court in Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., [1988] Sup. SC.R. 657 and Mohinder Sain Garg vs State Of Punjab & Ors.. , ; , referred to. 1.2 The selection were made according ly to the Rules of 1973, and this practices is being regularly followed for last 17 year and there was no allegation that any malafides were in the mater of the said impugned selections.[494D E] 2.1 In view of the fact that the result of the aforesaid impugned selections was declared in 1987 and the selected candidates have already joined the posts, it is an admitted position that if the marks for interview were kept even at 15% of the total marks, the appellants before us are bound to be selected on the footing of marks secured by them in interview calculated on the principle of conversion of the same to 15%of the total Marks. [494F G] 2:2 The selections were made as back as in 1987, and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. [594G H; 595A B] 2 :3 In view thereof it is not necessary to quash the selection on the above ground. Further the selections were also made according fo the Rules and in case the marks secured are prepared according l y then both the appellants are bound by be selected and a large number of selected candidates would have gone much lower in the merit list than the appellants. [695B C] 2(a) The State Government has already framed new rules, and as such we do not find it necessary to quashed the selections on the aforesaid ground. [965C D] 3:1 In case the appellants were found suitable in all other respects according to their Rules, they before us were found unsuitable in all others according to rules. They before us have approached the Tribu nal for relief and the case cannot be treated as they neither approached for redressal within reasonable period. [975D] 2.(b) The selection is made according per the rules. It is an undisputed position that the results of the appellants was declared by 1987 and only in the present appellant had approached this Tribunal for reliefs, the cases of other persons cannot be rejected as they ever approached for relief within reasonable ny time.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death. The High Court, on reference, held that Sadanand had continuously been detained in jail till the Collector 's murder was parked. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellants that the prosecution evidence should be rejected as when on 10th July, 1982 Sadanand was taken into custody following the raid on the Ashram and that there was a regular flow of food from outside. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The confession of a co accused is not substantive evidence against other co accused persons in the same trial. In dealing with a case involving the killing of the District Magistrate in his office better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in ac cordance with law. [446C D] 2. The prosecution has further led evidence to show that after the arrival of Sadanand at the jail, enforcement of rules became slack and there was regular flow o f food from inside. This type of evidence, even if accepted, does not establish conspiracy because Yadav, being a follower, was likely in the usual course to meet Sadanand and the fact that she were meeting at regular intervals by itself would not estab lish conspiracy. [413D E] 3. The conviction is not sustainable. [414E F] 4. In a case where the murder of the deceased person had been committed on 11th April, 1983, the prosecution has relied upon the allegation of conspiracy and confession but if the prosecution relies upon circumstantial evidence, a clear link has to be established and the chain has tobe completed, otherwise it would indeed be hazardous to accept a part of the link as a complete one and on the basis of such incomplete evidence, the allegation Of conspiracy cannot be accepted. [416E F; 414A] 5. The confessional statement of a coaccused person cannot be treated as substantive evidence and can be pressed into service only when the court is inclined to accept other evidence and feels the necessity of seeking for an assurance in support of its conclusion deducible from the said evidence, then it is permissible to turn to the confession in order to receive assurance to the conclusion of guilt which the judicial mind is about to reach on the said other evidence. [420B] 6. The question whether a particular accused person has committed the offence or not depends upon the facts and circumstances of each case. It is well settled that the confession of co accused person cannot form substantive evidence. In the instant case, Sadanand has become entitled to the benefit of our doubts and his conviction is set aside.

The appellants were employed in the same company. The company was a subsidiary of the appellant company and its employees were governed by the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The workmen were paid dearness allowance at the rate of 15 months ' basic wages and dearness allowance prevalent in comparable concerns revised them. The Tribunal fixed 20 months as the maximum instead of 15 days ' basic wage and dearness allowances. On appeal to this Court it was contended that the tribunal had not taken into account comparable concerns in the matter of competition, wages should generally be fixed on the basis of the comparable industries, namely, industry of the same kind. Held: (i) The Tribunal has not specifically considered what the wages for these categories in comparable concern are, though it appears that some exemplars were filed before it; but the way in which the Tribunal had dealt with the matter shows that it paid scant regard to the exemplars filed before them and did not care to make the comparison for factory workmen in the said way in Which it had made comparison for clerical and subordinate staff. The tribunal has relied on a number of cases in which it had dealt With the matter in which its maximum was higher than fifteen months wages. It has also taken into consideration the trend in that region, and in fixing the same scales of dearness allowance for factory employees as in the case of clerical staff. (ii) The Tribunals have not properly considered the question whether the dearness allowance fixed by the Tribunal is unreasonable or so disproportionate as compared to the total wage packet in other comparable concerns.

The appellants, who were the legal representatives of one Shiddappa and his son Mallappa, filed a suit for redemption of certain mortgaged property and possession thereof free from encumbrances. The trial Court held that the Rajinama executed by Shiddha had not extinguished the title of the mortgagors in the mortgaged property, that the plaintiffs 1 and 2 could not claim redemption of Shiddana 's share by adverse possession. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the present suit was barred by limitation as the Rajnama executed a transfer of title from the mortgagors to the mortgagees and hence the rights of the mortgagees became extinguished and that as Shiddhas alone was the registered occupant, the Raj inama could not bind Annappa. Held, that under section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code as Shudappa was the owner of the mortgaged properties and that he had acted as karta was nowhere made by the defendants appellants in their written statement and, therefore, the plaintiffs were entitled to redeem annappa 's half share in the suit land on payment of one half of the amount due under the two mortgages. The contention that the transfer of ownership from the mortgagees to the mortgagors was a relinquishment of his interest, but as regards Annaappa, it was clear that he did not purport to file, the same on behalf or for the benefit of all occupants or any particular occupant other than the 701 registered occupant and that in the matter of passing the Rajama he had been acting in that capacity and, consequently, the rights became extinguished. The conclusion of the trial Court that theRajinama was a complete relinquishment of the interest of Annappala and that inasmuch as the mortgages were subsisting, the defendants could not acquire title by adverse Possession, was erroneous and must be set aside.

The respondent, a dealer in carbon paper, was assessed to sales tax at the point and at the rate of 6 paise per rupee i.e. Rs. 2 per cent prescribed for unclassi fied goods and not at the rates specified in the Schedule to the Notification. The Sales Tax Officer, (Section IV), Kanpur did not accede to the conten tions of the respondent and holding that carbon paper was a part of the typewriter, taxed the turnover of carbon paper for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to the end of March 1967 at 6% and that of ribbon at 10%. The Sales tax Officer, however, did not agree with the contention of the appellant. In appeal by certificate, the High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the levy. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The mere fact that the word 'paper ' forms part of a typewriter is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood. [838B] (2) The word 'popular sense ' in the common parlance means paper which is used for bearing, writing or packing pur poses. It is to be construed in its popular sense, meaning, of course by the words 'pom optical sense ' that sense which people conversant with the sub ject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it. [888A B] (3) The expression 'paper other than hand made paper ' as envisaged by entry 2 of the aforesaid Notification is not determinative of the fact whether the articles are paper or otherwise.

The appellant Mills was a sugar mill at Amroha. The respondents 1 to 4 were employed by the owners of the Sugar Mills at the Sugar Mill at Amroha, and they were paid wages for the period from January 19, 1955 to February 2, 1955. On February 2 1955, the General Manager made an order dismissing the respondents 1 and 4 from service on the ground that 117 920 they had disobeyed his order of transfer and thus they were guilty of misconduct under Standing Order No. " " The appellant Mills challenged the said order before the Labour Appellate Tribunal which held that the management was within its rights and that as the respondents were not proprietors of the sugar Mills at Amroha at a time when they were not partners of the mill at Moradabad, they were properly dismissed by the management. The High Court in appeal set aside the finding of the Labour appellate Tribunal and directed reinstatement of the workers in Kundan Sugar Mills. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the right to transfer an employee by an employer from one of his concerns to another is implicit in every contract of service; (2) the employer has the inherent right to transfers his employees to another place where he chooses to start (4) a business subsequent to the date of employment. HELD: (i) The question raised was one of law, namely, whether the appellant had the right of transfer of the respondents I to 4 from one concern to another of his in the circumstances of this case. [922 B] (ii) The High Courts were not justified in holding that the appellant has the right under Standing Orders No. 926 and 927 of the Industrial Disputes (Appellate Tribunal) Act, 1950. [823 C D] (iii) The Appellate Tribunal had no jurisdiction to set aside a finding of fact arrived at by it as it did not give rise to any substantial question of law within the meaning of section 7(1) of the Act.

The appellant company was engaged in the manufacture of medical and other allied products. The Employees ' State Insurance Corporation Act, 1948 was enacted to provide for certain benefits to employees in factories or establishments situated in areas in which the provisions of Chapter IV A were in force. Section 28 lists the purposes for which the Fund may be expended and it includes among other items, (i) payment of benefits and provision of medical treatment and attendance to insured persons; (ii) payment by the principal employer of a special contribution which shall be in lieu of the employer 's contribution payable under Chapter IV in the case of factories or establishment situated in area in which they are in force; and ESTABLISHMENT to which the Act applies and the payment of contribution for that purpose. The appellant company claimed that the contribution payable by it under the or other similar payments or benefit under various other social welfare legislations must either be labelled as a tax or a fee in order to attain legitimacy or not at all. The respondents contended that the amount of special contribution directed to be made by the employer under the and other similar payment or benefit was illegal as the Act did not contemplate the rendering of any service or the conferment of any benefit to the appellant company or its employees as quid pro quo for the payment. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the contributions payable under the various social welfare legislation must eitherbe labelled as tax or fee in Order to attain legality or not and that it had been so laid down in argument by counsel for the respondent that the benefit should not be indirect and remote. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The contribution directed under section 28 of the Act constitutes only a fee and not a tax. [1088C] (2) The payment of special contributions as a fee or not is a fee. It is not disputed and indeed it is not capable of any controversy that services and benefits are indeed meant to be and are bound to be conferred on the employees and through them on the employer, in due course, when the scheme becomes fully operative in all areas. For a start the scheme is confined to a few areas and though special contribution is levied from all employers wherever they be, in the cases of employers who straightaway receive the benefits of the insurance scheme, their rate of contribution is higher while in the Case of employers, who straightaway receives the benefits under the scheme, Their rate of contributions is lower. [ 1088D E] (3) The amount of contribution directed by the respondent under section 27 of the , cannot be said to be indirect or remote. [1009G H] (4) The appellant 's argument proceeds on the fundamental misconception that the payment was of special importance from the point of view of time, but with reference to the very benefit itself and its connection with the levy. It has been so held in principle by this Court in State Insurance Board vs M/s. K.K. Modi & Ors., [1970] 1 S.C.R. 881; State of Bihar & Anr. vs Ram Kumar Modi, ; , referred to. (5) The High Courts have rightly rejected the contention of the appellant that Adhiniyam has not been enacted in the whole of India, it would not be necessary to retain this Chapter.

The petitioners are not regular employees, they do not have any specific case for absorption and regu larisation. They were being paid their daily wages in spite of their being no work for a long time. The management has throughout denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that, in fact, the petitioners have been continued on rolls on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there is no work available for them. It was stated at the hearing before this Court that there are no vacancies or work available in the establishment for absorption of the petitioners and that for quite some time they have been continuing on rolls and paid in spite thereof, there is nothing to interfere with the High Court 's decision in view of the clear findings supported by evidence that there were no vacancies nor work available. Allowing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment 'to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the regular workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same worked from him. [629B] 2. The petitioners were being regularly paid their monthly wages in view Of their being surplus to the requirement of the Project, they cannot be regularised and their retention on the rolls is purely on humanitarian ground so far. [613C D] 3. In spite of our above conclusion, keeping in view the offer made on behalf of respondent No. 2 in the counter affidavit together with Annexure R V thereto which was reiterated at the heating before us, we direct that all the 63 daily rated workmen including the 54 petitioners herein mentioned in the aforesaid Annexure R VI to the counter Affidavit be given the benefit of the Voluntary Retirement Scheme framed by respondent No 2 and they be paid the specified amounts in addition to their all other dues. Subject to this direction, the special leave petition is dismissed. No costs. P.S. Petition dismissed.

The appellants purchased the property in question from one Kazi Mohammed Ismail, the eldest son of Azam Ali. The mortgage was executed by the National Agency Co. Ltd., and it was registered as a document of title. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that when by the sale in execution of the mortgage decree obtained by the N. Baksh, they purchased the entire 16 as share from Kazi Mohammad Ismail, their eldest son, and that the co heirs were estopped from questioning the validity of the sale of the property. Held, that the proper order to pass would be to remit the matter to the trial Court for recording a finding as regards the reality of the transaction on the evidence already on the record and to pass an appropriate decree in the suit, that is, if the sale under exhibit 12(i) were held to be real, the plaintiffs would be entitled in addition to the 8 pies share decreed to them by the High Court. The proper order was to remit it for recording the finding as regard the reality or of the sales effected by him under section 41 of the Transfer of Property Act and that is if the property conveyed by exhibit 12 (i) on April 18, 1931, he figured as the first plaintiff in Suit 58 of 1931 which was filed on 28th November, 1931 without adverting to the sale being real and intended to pass title. The plaintiffs were estopped by 0. r. 13(1)(a) from questioning their validity of a mortgage decree. The High Court had rightly held that the plaintiffs were precluded by 0 r. 12(c) from challenging the validity or invalidity of the entire interest effected by them under section41 of the . It was not correct to say that the sale was made out and was real, intended to be passed title to Pir Baksh who was examined as a witness admitted this fact. The mere fact that the property was sold in execution did not make any difference between the two transactions. The sale deed exhibit 12 was executed on April 19, 1931 and it had been registered as document of transfer of interest in favour of the plaintiffs by the Registrar of Co. In view of the categorical statement in the plaint as regards indentity of the properties conveyed under exhibit 13(i), with Ashfaq 's share in the Azamabad Tea Estate, the High court was right in holding that the appellants were precluded from questioning its validity.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge for offences under sections 173(4) and 207A of the Code of Criminal Procedure. The trial court acquitted the accused on the ground that the provisions of section 173(3) had not been complied with, and that as a necessary consequence of those omissions, the entire proceedings and the trial were vitiated. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (i) the provisions Of sections 173 and 207 A(3), which are material portions of that section, have not been comply with, because, as a proper consequence of these omissions, there is no scope for the argument that the accused persons had been prejudiced in their defence; (ii) the omission was not sufficient to 37 290 vitiate the trial unless the accused succeeded in showing that they had been prejudice in their defense. HELD : (i)(a) The provisions of sections 173, 207A and other sections of the Criminal Procedure Code have not be complied with because, the omission on the part of police officers concerned or of the magistrate before whom such proceedings are brought, to 293 see that all the documents necessary to give the accused person all the information for the proper conduct of their defence, are furnished. [293 C] (b) The words "shall" occurring both in sub section (4) of section 172 and sub section(3). are not mandatory but only directory. It has not been argued that before the learned Magistrate who was holding his inquiries under section 207A(3)(4), any grievance was made that the provision of section 207 A had not be comply with. [294 D] (c) The omission on a part of the police officers to fully comply with the provisions aforesaid of the code, and the irregularity is curable by reference to section 537 of the Cr. P.C., as no case of prejudice has been made out.

The appellant was the owner of a factory and had been running a workshop for manufacturing oil. The respondent Municipality issued a notice under section 153A of the Act requiring the appellant to show cause why he should not be directed to arrange for the discharge of the effluent in the manner specified in the notice. The appellant contended that the existence of a nuisance of the kind mentioned in section 153 A(1) was a matter for the subjective satisfaction of the respondent Municipality and beyond the scope of his enquiry. Held, that the provisions of section 153B of the , are not attracted to the facts of the case. The scheme under section153A is to leave it to the subjective satisfied of the Municipality as to the existence or existence of the nuisance before a notice is issued to the party concerned. It is plain that before the appellant could be called upon to comply with the requisition of the municipality involving several lakhs of rupees as expenditure the Special Officer ought to have decide and report whether a nuisance existed or not. The question whether a particular nuisance exists or not does not arise as the person to whom the notice has been issued does not deny the existence, of the danger in question and is prepared to comply therewith without any objection. If the existence was assumed because that was a case for the decision of the Court, then it would not require a judicial officer of the rank of a District Judge to enquire and report only as to whether a reasonable nuisance existed. The order of the Special officer declining to go into the question whether the nuisance in question existed was one which ought to be set aside.

The appellant was found in possession of railway stores which by the definition of section does not include all articles which are 'the property of a railway administration but only those which were used or intended to be used for the construction, operation or maintenance of a Railway. The prosecution examined the goods said to be railway stores and kept in 11 bags and made a report to the effect that they were all railway stores being parts of a railways engine. It was the case of the appellant that he had prepared the report and signed it he made no statement to the contrary. The trial court convicted him under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955 but the High Court acquitted him on appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant: (i) that the prosecution must prove that the articles were being actually used or were intended to been used by the railway; (ii) that there was cause for reasonable suspicion of the stores being stolen or obtained unlawfully. HELD : (i)(a) The prosecution must also prove that there were no such articles which were 'the properties of a particular railway administration and that the goods were in a serviceable condition. [189 B] (b) In most cases the burden of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some, peculiarity of the goods not to be found in cases of non railway goods. Some evidence will have to be led to the conclusion that there is cause for reasonably suspicion of those articles not to he found in the case where they have become unserviceable or outmoded no person can be charged with an offence under section 4 in respect thereof. [190 C D] (c) The burden of proving in this regard may be discharge by leading testimony about the identification marks on goods or certain, peculiarities of the articles notto be found In cases of a non railway property it is only when the burden in respect of these is discharged by the prosecution that the onus shifts to the accused to account satisfactorily of his possession of the same.

The appellants were the tenants of the demised shop in Jaipur. The respondent filed a suit for ejectment against the appellants on the premise that on the death of the tenant, the appellants have no right to continue in occupation of the premises. Therein the definition of 'Tenant ' was amended by Section 3(ii) of the Amendment Act introducing to Section 3 Clause (vii), thus: "(vii) "tenant" means (a) The person by whom or on whose account or behalf rent is, or, but for a contract express or implied would be payable for any premises to his landlord including the person who is continuing in its possession after the termi nation of his tenancy otherwise than by a decree for evic tion passed under the provisions of this Act; and (b) In the event of death of such person as is referred to in sub clause (a), his surviving spouse, son, daughter and other heirs in accordance with the personal law applica ble to him who had been, in the case of premises leased out for residential purposes, ordinarily residing and in the Case of premises let out for commercial or business purposes, normally residing and In the case o f residential premises, he is entitled to remain in possession even after determination of the contractual tenancy and no order or decree for eviction will be passed against a tenant unless any ground which entitles the landlord to get an order or Decree for possession specified in the Act is established. The appellants succeeded to the heritable interest in the lease hold right in the demised premises governed by the Act subject to the rights and limitations prescribed under the Act and also subject to other provi sions of the Act. The heirs of the tenants were entitled to enjoy the protection of the Rent Acts. The tenancy rights were heritable and the heirs of such tenant became entitled to enjoyment of the tenancy right in terms of the provisions contained in Section 13(1)(a) to (k). The appellants filed a civil suit for eviction against the respondent on the ground that on death of their father, the appellant had no right or interest in his tenanted premises. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the appellants were entitled only to remain as tenants and not to be evicted as a matter of course under the ordinary law of the land and they continued to remain the tenant till date of the decree for ejectment. The High Court reversed the findings of the courts below and decreed the civil suit. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Amending Act does not apply to the facts of the case and does not have the effect of divesting their vested rights in the leased premises governed under the Rent Act. [9A] 1.2 In the instant case, the tenancy rights are heritable and they heirs of a tenant are entitled to enjoying the protection afforded to the tenant under the law. The succession having been opened to the appellants and succeeded in September 1966 to the estate of the deceased tenant without any hiatus and restriction on the heritable right held by the tenant. [10B] 1:3 In view of the termination of the lease, the rights are transferable and the heir of the landlord is entitled under the tenancy law to enjoy such protection as the tenant has thought it fit in the ease of residential premises to limit the rights of the heirs in the manner and to the extent provided in Section 2(1) (iii). The heirs and legal representatives of the appellants are entitled, by virtue of the intestate succession under , being Class I heirs, succeeded to such heritable inter est in the tenancy hold right held as statutory tenants. [11B C] 1 :4 In the present case, it was held that the tenant who continues to remain a tenant continues to have an estate or inter estin the tenanted premises and tenancy rights in respect of commercial premises are heritable.

The appellant Board was willing to extend that scheme to all the workers except the Government servants who are on deputation and those to whom the Employees Provident Fund Act applies. The workmen claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident Fund Scheme and the scheme under the Employees ' Provident Fund (Amendment) Act, 1966. The appellant Board contended that all employees of the appellant Board should had the same benefit and similar reliefs and that consequently there should not be any distinction between them. The Industrial Tribunal accepted this contention and held that all the workmen of a Board were liable to be transferred from one establishment to another both which may not he covered by the Act and such anomalies will be removed by making the benefits under both the schemes similar. In appeal, the High Court held that the State Government was the financier of the respondent Board which charges interest now at the rate of 6.25 per cent as against the previous 4 per cent per annum. The High Court also held that there should have been no distinction in respect of the employees ' Contributory Provident fund scheme and the Scheme under the Act. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the workmen that the Board had not the financial capacity to implement the Provident Fund scheme as demanded by the workmen. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The High court was right in holding that the liability to pay gratuity and provident fund can be met without undue strain on the financial position of the employer. [63E] In the absence of a detailed examination of the finances of the State it could not be said that the burden of Provident Fund and gratuity did not result in loss to the employer that burden will have to be borne by the employer like the burden Of wage structure in the interest of social justice. Even so it was noticed that the stability of the industry as well as the fact that the onus of provident fund and gratuity does not result, in loss of the employers that burden would have to been borne by an employer like any other expense including wages and if the financial situation shows that the obligation of Provident fund and Gratuity did not resulted in loss. [64F G] The Board is a statutory obligation and is a definite proportion whereas it is open to an ordinary commercial concern to credit any amount to the depreciation reserve. These and other matters cannot be properly decided in the absence absence of detailed examination or the finances, of the board. It should be directed to dispose of the matter afresh in the light of the observations made in this judgment.

The respondent wife filed a petition under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure for maintenance. The Magistrate dismissed the application on the ground that the husband having been found to be impotent, this should be a just ground for refusing to live with her husband and hence she was entitled to the grant of maintenance. In revision before the High Court it was contended by the appellant wife that the mere ground that there was a just reason for doing so was not a just cause for the refusal of the wife to live in with her wife, and that therefore she was not entitled to maintenance if she refused to live alongwith her husband merely because her husband was impotable. The High Court rejected this contention holding that the wife having been proved to be an impotant, this must be a reasonable ground for the wife 's refusal to live separately with her deceased husband and accordingly dismissed the revision application. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The decisions referred to above in the judgment taking a contrary view must be held to be no longer good law and are hereby overruled. [707E] 1.2 In the instant case, it is proved to the satisfaction of the court that a husband is impotsuable and is unable to discharge his marital obligation, this would amount to both legal and mental cruelty which would undoubtedly be a valid ground for refusal to living with her. [808B C] 1:3 The decisions in Arunachala Anandayammal vs Babu Lal Dixit, J. sounded a very pragmatic note on this aspect of the matter and in this connection pointed out that where a husband contracts a marriage with another woman or keeps a mistress this would be deemed to be a " just ground" within the meaning of the second proviso so as to make the refusal for the husband 's refusing to living separately with the husband fully justified and entitled to maintain. [908D] 1 :4 The decisions relied on by the High Courts are hereby set aside. [999B C; 999A] 1.:5 In ArunachalaAnandayammal, J sounded A very pragmatic Note on this point of the case and in that connection pointing out the scope of the Amendment of 1949 observed thus: "The Court cannot compel the wife not to stay with husband on the grounds that the she is impecotent and is able to discharge her marital obligation. This would certainly be a very just ground as contemplated by the aforesaid proviso for thewife 's failure to maintain his marital obligations, this will amount to Both legal and physical cruelty which might undoubtedly be an " just reason" within meaning of section 125(3) of the Criminal Procedure Code. [991B C]. 1:6 In the present case, the Courts cannot compel a wife to stay in with husband merely on the basis that she is forcing her in a situation where her physical and mental well being might be adversely affected, as there is no intention on the part of the husband to inflict that cruelty, she should suffer that predicament without demur and be satisfied with a grab to bite and some rags to clothe her and a roof over her head. [990C D] 1:-7 In the facts and circumstances of this case, this Court does not find any reason for the daughter 's denial to live separate with her father when it seems to us that the ground of impotence which had been held by a number of authorities under the civil law to be "a just ground", was not only for restitution of conjugal rights but also for divorce. [988D E] 1;8 In the light of our decision in Arun Venkatachala Anandayam Mal, J., it follows that the decisions referred t o above in Arun Sira Anandayam Lal, J..

The plaintiff was the owner of a portion of the suit property. The defendants were the Union of India and the State of Gujarat. The State of Saurashtra admitted the ownership of the land and structures vested in the Defence Ministry. The Government of India, by Resolution No. 77 dated 29th February, 1948, vested in it the right to give the same on rent lease and to take the income therefrom. The plaintiff filed a suit for declaration of its title and for possession of the property and rent for another portion, for the period from 1st January, 1964 till possession was delivered to the plaintiff. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the plaintiff had not shown possession of any of the structures within 12 years prior to 3rd March, 1964 when the suit was filed, the suit being barred by limitation, and that therefore it was not necessary either to deal with the argument of the defendants that the vesting that was'[ plated in the Resolution 37 dated 19th January, 1948 vested in its full amplitude, but was meant only to appoint the Municipality as agent of the State to dispose of the lands. The High Court also held that since the suit is for possession based on title to the suit land and the defendants had denied title, of the plaintiff, it was necessary for the Court to give a finding on title of the defendant even if the defendants in possession had not pleaded adverse possession. In this appeal by special leave, it is contended on behalf of the appellants that since by virtue of these orders the entire suit lands mentioned in the plaint have: "vested in and belong to the plaintiffs" which was subse quently known as the State Government, there was nothing on record to show that physical possession was with the defendant but also there could not be any legal possession with the plaintiff as the title to it is not vested in them. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The suit is within 12 year prior to the date of vesting and therefore since the plaintiff has admitted that the structures in Rasala Lines are not shown to be that of the Municipality in the Municipal records and even in the Plaint they did not claim the 232 structures as belonging to the Municipality. [225B] 2.1 In this case, the Resolution No 37 dated 29.2. 1948 by the State was only a right or an authorisa tion to sell the land as representing the Government but not a vesting of the title itself in the Municipality.[226C] 3. The resolution No. 37 dated 18th January 1948 by which the entire assets of the Bhavnagar town planning Department had been transferred to them by the orders of their Highness, Bhavnagar State in 1948 and they are collecting the Revenue from the farmers. [226D E] 4.1 The Resolution No., 37 dated 30th February 1948 was only an enabling provision for disposal of the acquired land as represented the Government. It was not intended to be vesting in its absolute amplitude but meant only for appointment the Municipality to dispose off the land. [227F G] 5.2 In this connection, it may be mentioned that the Resolution had been issued by the Government of Saurashtra to all 230 the Municipalities of Old Bhavnagar States, and the right of the Municipali ty was not vested with them on 7th July, 1952 when the suits were filed, and therefore, since the suits are for possession founded on title, the defendants have denied title of their plaintiff even if they had pleaded adverse Possession. [228F G]. 5.3 The Resolution was issued by Government of Gujarat to all 231 Municipalities of New Bhavnagar to all230 the Municipal Administration Department.

The appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Government and was performing a public duty. He was, therefore, not an "officer" within the meaning of section 21(9) Indian Penal Code. Held, that an officer is one who is appointed to some office for the performance of certain pulice duty. The true test, therefore in order to determine whether a person is an officer of the government, is: (1) whether he is entrusted with the performance or discharge of any public duty; and (2) whether it is performing duties immediately auxiliary to those of some one who was an Officer of the State within the terms of section21(9), Indian Penal code. The question for consideration before the learned Judges of the Lahore High Court was whether a Quarter Master 's clerk as such was just a Babu and no more an officer than a labourer or menial employed and paid by Government to do public work (See Queen vs Nachimuttu, ; , referred to. Held further that an "Officer" in the Service or pay or of the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer and was therefore not an 'officer ' within the definition of section 2 of the Prevention of Corruption Act II of 1947. The appellant was, however, an officer within the ambit of section 1(9). The question whether a quarter Master 'shook as such is an "person" within section 21 of the Indian Penal Act and being such public servant be fell within the expression "officer".

The Respondent along with one Gora Lal and Sat Pal, had been granted a liquor vending licence for the year 1968 69. The Excise and Taxation Department of the State of Punjab issued a notification under section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908 (hereinafter referred to as the said Act) in respect of which they had to pay a sum of Rs. 25,000/ . The Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, 1st Class, Patiala C. for recovery of revenue due to the State Government and the Collector. The suit was decreed by the trial court on the ground that the property attached and notified for sale was exempt from attachment under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of section 60. The Respondent then filed a second appeal in the High Court which allowed the said second appeal holding that the portion of the building used for residence was exemptfrom attachment and sale under clause(ccc). The Division Bench of the High court also held that "the portion of this building used by the Respondent for residence is exempt from attached and sale" under clauseccc), of the Proviso to sub s (1), of section 61. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The attachment levied on, and the auction sale notified in respect Of, the Respondent 's half share in the said property were not in execution of any decree or a decree but were in pursuance of the order made by an officer authorized to adopt proceedings under the said act for recovery. [848C D] 2. The attached portion of building used in the respondent 's quarter was liable to attachment and sales in execution thereof. The properties, if my, which are exempt from sale and in revenue recovery proceedings under section 61 would be only such properties as are so exempted by the said provisions. [820E F] 3. The property, if I have held that the Respondent had no other residential house or, therefore, his said half share was exempt therefrom from attachment and Sale under clause c(ccb) of proviso to section 60, while that portion in which the liquor shop was situated was liable for be attached and sold in execution. [821F] 4. The words "such attachment or sale" in the aforesaid proviso are "Provided that the following particulars shall not be liable to such attachment or sales, namely". (a) The expression "such attach or sale", in the proviso refers to the attachment and 'sale mentioned in sub section(1)of section 60; (b) the words "the attachment and selling" in that proviso refer to the attached property and sale mentioned in subsection (1). [821A B] 5. The provisions of section 59 of the Punjab Land Revenue Act, 1887 do not apply to an attachment and sell under any other law made expressly applicable thereto. The said attachment levied by the Excise and Taxes Department of State Government are, therefore not exempt from the attachment or Sale in revenue Recovery proceedings adopted under the aforesaid Act. [822C D].

The respondent, a tenant of the appellant, filed a suit for compensation on the ground that the lands in the original assessment had been undervalued in view of the glaring enhanced compensation awarded by the Civil Court and the High Court 's decision upholding the issuance of such notice on the wrong basis was liable to be set aside. The respondent contended that the acquired lands still formed part of the estate of the deceased which passed on his death, that the valuation for those lands adopted on the earlier occasion had not been accepted by the heirs of Rashid and as such the same had escaped assessment to duty. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the respondent had issued it on the assumption that there had been escapement of assessment to duties because the lands were undervalued in the light of the apparent enhanced compensation granted by the civil Court, and that the value of the acquired land was correctly assessed as at the date of the death but the basis on which it was issued was clearly unsustainable in law. The High Court dismissed the appeal holding that there was no mistake apparent from the record and as the respondent has merely accepted the value determined by the Special Deputy Collector in his award and the accountable person had no objection to this course, the respondent himself did not estimate the market value of those lands on the date when the death of Rashid was occurred. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High court challenging the validity of the notice issued under s.61 of the Act on two grounds: (a) it was case of change of opinion as regards the valuation of lands acquired and not a case of mistake apparent on the record; (b) it had been wrongly assumed that there has been escapment of assessment by reference to such other record was not a mistake apparent in the record of the case and as no such error apparent from record, the impugned notice was liable for be quashed. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court has attempted to distinguish the above decision by stating that in the instant case the res respondent had merely accepted his value of lands as determined by him in his Award and the responsible person had not objection to the course and valuation made by another authority namely, the City Civil Court, taken with the original compensation awarded. [330B] 1.2 The High 'Court has attempted a distinguish the decision by saying that in view Of the glaring increased compensation awarded to the respondent, the said lands had been valued in the main value of his lands as on the basis of compensation awarded and as a result thereof the enhanced compensation was sought to be included in the principal value of that estate by undertaking the rectification proceedings. [331B] 2.1 In the instant cases the wards made by the special Deputy Collector were not accepted by them and the same were pending in Civil Court at the relevant date (being the date on which the original assessments were made, and, therefore, such property had escaped Assessment to duty, and as there was escapement, assessment to Duty could not be regarded as proper evaluation of the right to receive compensation as on that date. [431C] 2:2 The respondent has only accepted the valuation made in pursuance of the impugned notices and the valuation fixed by the High ' Court as the proper valuation he must be deemed to have adopted that evaluation as his own estimated value of these lands had not adopted that valuation as on March 31, 1970.

The appellant was elected as a Director of the Bank from the Brehmapuri Agricultral Sales and Purchase Society. On 8.1.1987, the District Deputy Registrar of Cooperative Societies issued a notice to the appellant under section 78(1) of the Maharashtra State Cooperative Societies Act, 1960 to show cause within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from the Board of Directors of the bank as per the provisions of section 73FF(2) of Maharashtra State Co operative Societies Act. The appellant filed his nomination papers in July 1986 and he was elected on 18.8.1986 as one of the Directors of that Bank from Brehma Puri Agricultial Sales and purchase Society. The Deputy Registrar, Cooperative Societies, Chandrapur by his order dated 7.12.1987 removed the appellant from the Committee of Directors holding that appellant was defaulter under section 73(1)(b) of that Act on 31.3.1986 i.e. the date when he was declared elected as Director. The Assistant Registrar of the Cooperative Societies rejected the appellant 's contention that section 73F did not envisage setting aside of an election as has been done by the impugned order; that the appellant having repaid the entire loan before the impugned notice under section 80(1), on 31st March 1986, he was still defaulter under Section 73FF (2) and dismissed the appellant. The Divisional Joint Registrar of Co operative Society, Nagpur, held that appellant had already ceased to be a Director and his seat already fell vacant; and hence the appellant was not at all eligible to contest the election. The respondent 's revision petition against the order of the Assistant Registrar removing him from the committee of Directors was dismissed by the Divisional Joint Commissioner on 15.2.1988 holding, inter alia, that section 78 of the Act came into force on 12.5.1986 and the appellant could be treated as a defaulter under that section; and the mere making of payment on 21.10.86 did not mean that the disqualification on account of his being defaulter which continued from 18. 8.1986 to 21. 10.1986 was extinguished and hence, the appellant became defaulter under the provisions Of section 73BFF(1).
