The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order removing him as Director of a Cooperative Society and the High court dismissed the same holding that the appeal against that order was not maintainable. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were wrong in holding that section 75FF became applicable from 6.81986 as per Government Notification issued on 18 4.1986; that even assuming that the disqualified on account Of his being a defaulter which continues from 18 8.86 to 21 10.10, 1986 was extinguished, and hence he was not eligible to challenge the election; and that even if the disqualification continued after the election of the petitioner and section 73 BFF(I) of Act came in force, the disqualification ceased after the elections of the Board and hence section 78 envisaged such a default and the provisions thereof were not attracted. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The notice of the Deputy Registrar was in effect to say that the Assistant Registrars could not have acted under section 79(1 ) of the said Act which did not contemplate the setting aside aside of the election as had been done under the impugned orders; that section 77F did never envisage the settingaside of an Election as has already been done; and, therefore, the Special provision for setting aside an election must prevail over section 78 as there would be apparent conflict between the two and the maxim generalia specialibus non derogant general words do not derogate from special, would apply.

The respondent was in the service of the State as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. After his retirement the respondent was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. On the conclusion of the enquiry the State Government issued orders on December 4, 1982 reducing the amount of pension payable to the respondent by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. A Division Bench of that Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State 's orders dated December 4 1982 on the ground that the State had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already retired from services. The State Government preferred this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The reduction of pension by 50% was too harsh and disproportionate to the charges proved against the Respondent. [34G] 1.2 The reduction in pension by 100 per cent was too severe and disproportionate. It would seriously affect his living. [35A B] 2.3 In the instant case the purpose of the inquiry was not to inflict any punishment; instead the proceedings were initiated for determining the respondent 's pension. The proceedings were taken in accordance with Rules 188 and 189 of the Rules. [36C D] 3.1 In his report to the State government the Collector of Kolhapur held that the respondent had retired from Service on attaining his age of retirement on September 01, 1977 and charges were served on him on October 21, 1978 after about a year of his retirement. The reduction was too low and disproportionate and to the misconduct proved against him. [37E] 3:3 In his Report to the Government the Collector stated that the Respondent had retired on attaining superannuation on August 1,1977 and charges are served on the respondent on October 17, 1978. The report shows that the charge sheet was issued after about one year of retirement. This report shows the respondent having retired from the service on September January, 1977, and charges have been served on them on October 31, 1978 without any notice to him. In his letter dated December 3, 1982 the Collector had stated that he had retired in August, 1977 after about two years of his superannuation. The Government accepted the findings and passed the impugned order reducing the pension by 25 per cent. In the report to this Court the Collector observed that the charges were proved against respondent. [38D E] 4.2 It is not correct to say that the reduction of the pension was too disproportionate to misconduct and fault or financial irregularities which he may have committed during the period of his service and the Government was entitled to withhold or reduce the pension granted to a Government servant. The High Court committed serious error in holding that the Government had no power to initiate any proceedings against him as he has already retired on August, 1,77 and charges for misconduct and negligent or financial irregularity which he might have committed while in service were initiated after the respondent ceased to be in service of State 34 Government. [39E] 5.3 The State of Maharashtra has preferred this Appeal by special Leave. It is well settled that mere reduction of a pension by a Government Servant retired from his service on reaching the age Of superannuation he could not escape the liability for misconduct, and negligence or financial misapplication which he can have committed after the completion of his Service. [40E] 6.4 The State has power to reduce the amount payable to a government servant even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules.

The appellants were tenants of the premises in question. The respondent landlord filed a suit for eviction on the ground that he was not a tenant under the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the permission granted by the Commissioner under section 3(3) of the Act was invalid in law. On appeal, the High Court held that the order passed by the District Magistrate was not valid in law as it was passed without complying with the mandatory provision of the U .P. Temporary Control of rent and Eviction Rules, 1947 (U.P.) Act III of 1947). In appeal to this Court, HELD : The words of section 3 (4) read with section 16 are clear and unambiguous and they indicate that the jurisdiction of the civil courts is completely excluded in relation to the question as to whether permission has been properly or validly granted by a competent authority exercising his powers under the relevant provisions of the . [601 B] In the instant case, the question was not raised before the Civil Court. The High Court was not justified in introducing a limitation pertaining to questions of jurisdiction in determining the scope of the revisional ,visional power conferred on the Commissioner by section 3 k 3) and 16 of the ,Act. [602 C D] The amendment in question has been introduced by Act 17 of 1954. The amended provision reads thus : "The Commissioner shall hear the application made under sub section (2), as far as may be, within six weeks from the date of making it, and he may, if he is not satisfied as to the correctness, legality or propriety of the order, pass such other order as he thinks fit." There is no doubt that the object of the amendment was to confer wide jurisdiction on the commissioner. The amendment introduced by section 17 of Act 17, 1954, has been incorporated by Act 16 of 1954 and it is clear that its intention was to conferring wide jurisdiction upon the Commissioner.

The appellant was a member of the Punjab Public Service Commission. He was convicted by the trial court under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court dismissed his appeal. In this appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that before making this Reference, the President should have obtained the opinion of a fact finding body for his prima facie satisfaction that a case was made out for obtaining a report from this Court on the question of alleged misbehaviour of Shri Saini. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The power of the President to make a reference to this Court under Article 317(1) is not subject to the condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. That article provides that the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service commission can only be removed from his office on the ground of misbehaviour after the Supreme Court has on inquiry reported to the President that the member of such Public Service Commissions is guilty of misconduct and, therefore, the offence was of such a nature as to require his removal from the office of Member of the Public Service. [629G H] 2. The words "any other person" in Article 317 (1) are wide enough to include any person who has not filed an affidavit in this Court. In the instant case, it is not over by that date, the learned Judge may write to the Registrar of the Supreme court for extension of time. [613B C] 3. The recording of evidence will be over by September 30, 1983. In case it is over by the date, and the learned judge may write a to the Secretary of the Commission for extension or extension of period. The evidence will he limited to the cross examination of witnesses who have filed affidavits before this Court.[613B] 4. The record of evidence which the parties lead before them within the constraints of the following guidelines: (1)(a) The affidavits filed in this court will be treated as the examination in chief of the respective witnesses. [529G] 5. The affidavit filed in the High Court will be limited to that cross examination and not by a court of first instance. [540C] 6. In other words, no person who had not filed any affidavit in the Supreme Courts will be examined or cross examined as a witness except with the leave of this Court; and (b) Witnesses who have not filed affidavits in this case may be summoned or requested by the learned counsel for the parties to prove and rebut the facts in issue as in a regular trial. It is an idle complaint that the evidence of any particular witness is recorded by the Supreme Judge and not of a court Of first instance, except with leave of the Court. The mere fact that the affidavit of any such witness is recording by the Chief Judge will not conclude the issue as regards the admissibility or relevance of that evidence.

The appellants were the trustees of a public temple. The endowment was made for the use or benefit of the public. The respondent filed a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act No. Chatterjee, had submitted that the approach made by the High Court was wholly incorrect and it has misconstrued the evidence and documents produced in the case to show that the endowment was a private one and the deity installed in the temple was purely a family deity having nothing to do with the public, and therefore the endowment could not be said to be a public one. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the trust was of a private nature and the idol installed in it was purely an family deity. On appeal by the respondent, the High court held that the dedication was of public nature and that the temple had no connection with the religious endowment. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The question as to whether the property is dedicated for the worship of a family idol or of a community or of any community or community or a community is not relevant. [840 A] (2) Where the origin of the endowment cannot be ascertained, the question whether the user of the temple by members of the community is as of right that may be a circumstance which may in some cases conclusively establish that the property was of such a nature. [820 E] (3) The mere fact that members of a particular community are allowed to worship by itself would not make an endowment public unless it is proved that the members of that community or the brotherhood or the Government could have taken over the management.

The appellant Bank entered into certain contracts and to advance monies to Malhotra against his bills for supplies under the contracts. For the purpose of carrying out this arrangement, the appellant Bank agreed to finance the contracts and also to advance moneys to Malhotra. The appellant Bank executed an irrevocable power of attorney in favour of the appellant on July 13, 1946. On December 12, 1952 the appellant filed a suit in the court of the 1st Additional District Judge, Jabalpur against Malhotra and Takhatmal asking for a declaration that the appellant was an assignee of the biLl and that TakhatMal had no right to attach it. The trial Court held that the power of Attorney dated July 13. 1946 coupled with the endorsement on the bill dated July 19, 1948 amounted to an equitable assignment of the monies due under the bills in favour Of the appellant. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court reversed the decree and decreed the suit. In this appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the Power of attorney dated July 14, 1946, executed by Malhotra to pay the appellant bank out of the moneys receivable under the bill amounted to a equitable assignment and that the document was brought into existence in connection with a proposed transaction of financing of Malhotra 's contracts. HELD: (i) The power of the attorney coupled with its endorsement on it created an interest in a specific fund and was irrevocable. [757 E] (ii) The document was not brought into force in connection With a proposed contract of financing by Malhotra, to pay him out of his assets in their hands the moneys realised in execution of the decree amounted to equitable assignment. [777 A B] (iii) The Power of Attorney coupled with endorsement on bill dated August 19, 1947 created an equitable assignmen of the fund and amounted to An equitable assignment thereof. [779 C D] (iv) The agreement was a clear engagement by Malhotra and not an equitable Assignment of the money due under it. In Loonkaran Sethiya vs State Bank of Jaipur, , referred to. (v) The appellant bank had an interest at the rate of Rs. 100 per month in the fundS the power to attorney coupledwith the endorsement thereon created an Interest in a particular fund and could only be exercised by the appellant in his own name or in payment of such bills or other amounts and to credit to the borrower 's account the monies realised in the execution of a decree. [780 C D]. (vi) The High Court was in error in holding that there was an agreement between the lender and the borrower that the debt owing to the lender would be paid out of a specific Fund of the borrower in the hands of the Government authorities.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd., and received out of this provident fund an 439 amount of Rs. 27,948/ which represented the interest on the amount of his own contribution to the fund. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. That order was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner but on further appeal to the tribunal, the tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipt in question being profits 'in lieu of salary ', the same was exempt from payment of tax in view of section 17(3) (ii). The Tribunal held that the receipts in question were not income as defined by section 2(24). In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the assessee that the said receipt being a profit and therefore the same is "income" within the meaning of section 2 (24). HELD: The receipt of Rs 27,949/ by the assessee with which we are concerned is exempt from tax. [440 F] In interpreting the expression "Profits in lieu of pay", the legislature excluded from the scope of that expression any payments received by the assesee from a provident fund, his own contributions to the Fund or any interest on such contributions. From that it follows that the receiving of Rs, 27,946/ by M/S Gillands Arbindnot & Company Ltd., is undoubtedly an income.

The Bihar Act, 1950, was enacted to provide for the regulation of slaughter of cows and calves of buffaloes. The Act provided that no person shall slaughter any cow except a cow which is useful or suitable for the purpose of maintaining unserviceable, and unproductive cattle with a measure of assistance from the Goverment land general support from; the people. The Bihar Act was passed to provide that the slaughter of all cows would be free and compulsory and the slaughter could be carried on in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The petitioners who were butchers, tanners, gut merchants, curers and cattle dealers to carry on their respective trades, challenged the validity of the impugned Acts on the ground that they infringe fundamental rights under article 19(1)(g) of the Constitution. Held, that the ban on slaughter of buffaloes of all ages and calve of cows was not a reasonable restriction imposed on the slaughter by the State Legislature in so far as it prohibits the slaughter or slaughter of breeding bulls and working bullocks without prescribing any test or requirement as to their age or usefulness, it violated article 19 (1)(f) of Constitution. The ban on the sale of buffaloes was not valid because it was a negative and not a positive approach to the problem. The entire provision banning the slaughter and of calves and other milch and draught cattle will defeat the very object of the directive principles embodied in article 48, (ii) that a total ban onthe slaughter of she buffaloes, breeding bulls, and working cattle without prescribing no test or specification as to his age or bad usefulness was also reasonable and valid. The whole provision baning the slaughterof cows of all age and cales of buffaloes, male and female, is invalid.

The respondent was a 'workman ' within the meaning of the Central Act and an 'employee ' as defined in the local Act. The Company had its registered office at Nagpur in Madhya Pradesh, its Manager, and Assistant Manager. The respondent was employed as an employee in the appellant company at Nagpur. He was paid salary from time to time by the appellant Company. On the question whether the respondent was an 'workman within the definition of that expression in section 2(1) of the local (Act), HELD : (i) The definition of an ' workman ' is employment in the Office, Mains Department, eta., of the Company either at Nagpur or Nagpur or Wardha and that of a workman the necessary declaration by the company which would entitle him to a ticket under Standing Order No. (e) of Standing Orders. [446 B] (ii) The word "employee" is used in the definition as meaning any person employed in an office, Main or subordinate office or department of the Government either at Bombay or at Nagpur and that includes all persons employed in such offices or departments of the State Government either on contract or otherwise. [467 C D] (iii) The expression 'workman " in section 3(1)(a) of , is not defined in any Standing Order but it has been used in a wide sense as meaning an employee who is employed in a department of Government either in India or in connection with the affairs of the Union. [468 E F] (iv) The words "employed in an Office, Commercial Department, etc., are not 'workmen ' for the purpose of the Standing Orders and the inclusion of ticket numbers in the departmental musters ' in Standing Order Nos. (i), (ii), (iii), (iv), (v) and (vi) are not an essential characteristic of an employee.

The appellant, a company owned controlled and managed by a Government Company, was started in the year 1961 65. No profit was earned at least right up to the year 1966 66 when this Project went into production. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 (hereinafter referred to as "the Act") in respect of the year 1965 631 1966 on the plea that this Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment for purposes of section 16 of the Act and could not be treated as a new establishment for purpose of section16 of the . The Tribunal held that alloy steel Project could not, be treated to be an establishment separate from Hindustan Steel Ltd., or it had to be treated separately for each unit. On appeal by special leave, the appellant contended that (i) the Alloy steel project was a composite establishment in respect Of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained; (ii) the Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that merely because alloy Steel Plant was owned, controlled and conducted by Hindustan Steel Limited it had no jurisdiction to treat this company as an establishment for computation of bonus under section 16(1) of the , and (iii) the proviso to sub section (2) of section 3 will not apply in such a case. HELD: (i ) The Tribunal went wrong in finding that merely on the basis of consolidated profits of all the units belonging to Hindustan Steel, it has to be regarded as a separate unit because, under the proviso, bonus was paid in any year to the employees of all those units on the date of the commencement of the accounting year for the purpose of computation of the bonus. [655 B] (ii ) The proviso to section 3(2) only comes in the way it bonus is paid in every year to, the employees belonging to all the Units on the ground that they are treated as separate establishments and available surplus is calculated separately for the each unit, there will be no deduction @ 8.5 per cent ,of the paid up equity share capital as envisaged by section 6(d) ,and the Third Schedule of the ' Act. [613 C D] (iii ) The expression "in any year" in section 3 cannot be used to mean that all the departments or undertakings or branches of an establishment are to be considered as separate units for each Unit, and there is no provision in the Act which makes a distinction between the two categories of employees. [555 C D]. (iv) The proviso does not stand in the manner of this claim, because it bonus was payable only to, those who were treated as part of one single establishment for the purposes of computation. It does not affect the principle to be applied to the separate units of which separate accounts, separate balance sheet and profit statements are maintained. [558 D E] (v) The Tribunal proceeded on the footing that merely by reason of Alloy Steels Project being owned, managed by Hindustan steel Ltd., it has been treated as an independent establishment for all purposes of calculation of bonus. It was in the accounts of the Head Office that the entire paid up capital was credited and advances were made by the Head office to various units out of this capital or out of loans taken by the head Office to various Units out of loan taken by it, and that does not mean that the Tribunal proceeded entirely wrong.

The appellant sugar factory was manufacturing sugar from sugar cane. The cess is payable by every person carrying on any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed by such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column I of Schedule II to the Act at such rate not exceeding the rates specified in the corre sponding Entry in column II thereof as the Central Govern ment may by notification in the Official Gazette from time to time specify. " The cess was payable by all persons carrying on a specified industry. The Cess is payable on every person who carries on any industry and Every local authority, and is quantified on the principle of water consumption. " On behalf of the appellant it was contended that the sugar manufacturing industries would come within Entry 15 as "processing vegetable products industry". Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The word 'vegetable ' in Item (6) of Schedule I to the Cess Act must be construed as understood in common parlance and it must be given its popular sense meaning 'that sense which people conversant with the subject matter with which the statute is dealing would attribute to it and so construed, it denotes those classes of vegetables which are grown in a kitchen garden or in a farm and are used for the table. [529G H] 2. The expression "vegetables" in Entry 15 of Schedule 1 to the cess Act must mean as bringing into existence a new substance and does not mean 'to produce some change in a sub stance, however minor in consequence, the change may be. [630H; 528A B] 3. The words "veholdable products industry" are used in Entry 14 of Schedule III to the Central Act. The term "veignable products" is defined in the Act as meaning any industry specified in Schedule I. The definition of "processed vegetable product" in Item 15 is wide enough to include all kinds of vegetable products which are covered by other entries. [525C D] 4. The entry in Schedule 1 of the Cess Rules, 1941, does not attract the botanic meaning. The sugar manufacturing industry do not, therefore, come within the meaning of "pro cessing vegetable product industry". [530G H; 528B C] 5. The notification dated 20th December, 1977, issued by the Central Government under Section 3(1) of the Act, clearly shows that the cess is leviable on every persons carrying out any specified industries and every person engaged in any specified activity shall be liable to pay a cess which may be calculated at such rates not exceeding those rates specified therein as the State Govern ment might by notification specify. [431D] 6. The levy of cess is not a tax but a fee for rendering services rendered by a person carrying out certain specified industries. It is a fee and it is a part of the duty imposed on him by the statute. [565E F] 7. The Notification dated 20nd December,1977, issued under Section 4(1), read with Section 3 (2) of Act, does indicate that the levy of the cess was not a fee but a tax. It does not specify any particular industry which is covered by any of these entries. The power to levy cess is conferred on the State Government and it has been given to the State Legislature. [567G H]. 8. The State Legislature cannot impose a tax on the sale or purchase of goods.

The respondent landlord filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant, his tenant, from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an Advocate. The Rent Controller rejected the application holding that the practice of the profession of an Advocate was not business within the meaning of Section 10(3) (a)(iii) and, therefore, the respondent could not seek the eviction of him on the grounds of his requirement unless it was for the purpose of carrying on a business. The High Court dismissed the revision petition holding that since the respondent bona fide required the building for the purposes of carrying out his profession, as an advocate, he could not obtain the eviction. In appeal to this Court by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the use of expression 'business ' in Section 10 (3)(a)(ii) and (iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act, 1960, is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice which of an advocate or a Doctor which had nothing commercial about it was not 'profession ' within the ambit of Section 5(3)(a)(i) of that Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The expression 'profess ' occurring in Section 2(g) (iii), is used to refer to the word 'business " only and not to the expression 'Profession ' occurring therein. [14G] 2.1 In the context of the statute in which it occurs and not in the context o the statute concerned, the same meaning that the word may have when it occurs in other statutory provisions. The word must be construed in the light of the statutes in which the statute occurs and cannot be of any assistance in determining its meaning in Section 5 (3)(i). [14H; 14A] 2:2 In the instant case, the High Court was right in holding that in the matter of the Madhya Pradesh Act, the word "business" had to be given a wide meaning so as not to include any profession. [15B C] 3.1 The expression business ' occurring In Section 10 of the Act is used for a wide connotation so asto include any practice of profession like that of an Advocates or Doctor which has nothing commercial relation about it. [16C D] 2 :3 The word 'professed ' in section 10(2)(a) (ii) of Andhra Pradesh Act is not used in the sense of business within that expression in Section 4(1)(a). In Stuchbery & Ors. vs General Accident Fire and Life Assurance Corporation Ltd., ; , referred to. 3.2 The word "profession" occurring in section 2(h) (i) is used as a wide amplitude so as, to include all profession. It clearly includes the practice that the expression may have been when it occurred in other Statutory provisions. [17E F] 4.3 In Stodbery & Anr. vsGeneral Accident Fire & Life Assurance Corpn. Ltd., , referredto.

The respondent filed a suit for the recovery of Rs. 4,11,367.92 with interest and costs. The appellant contended that it was a case where money was deposited under an agreement and that it had to be paid on demand or whether it was one of the principal reasons to indicate that it would be paid at the time of the loan. Held, that there must be an unqualified demand for the whole sum before limitation can star in case of demand for return of the amount deposited. The words "deposit" occurring either in the roznamcha or in the letter dated 29 September 1942 written by Ram Ratan Gupta would not cover the advances which either party or their separate firms may have made to all or any of them or their moneys which may be in deposit with them and they shall be payable and paid in their usual course. The letter further shows that the terms were agreed to by the partners of the firm, namely, the partners who were bankers would be relieved of the situation of repaying the money immediately. The correspondence between the appellant and Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills show that there was advances which were in the nature of deposit and were not covered by the award. The letters further shows, that the term "deposit " occurring either both in the clas sions of the rozaemcha or the letter written by the appellant to the respondent recording the agreement that "a sum of Rs 4,00,000 was withdrawn on 30 September 1942 by the respondent as a banker and along with interest from time to time the amount of Rs 3,00.000 stood with the appellant in the deposit account. The payment of Rs 2,00000 would not be effective because there were common partners in the firms of the respondent and the appellant.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA. The grounds of detention were served on him only to the one point and it was clearly stated by the senior counsel, Shri Ram Jethmalani that he had a strong almost unanswerable case on merits but he was very keen to have the question of exclusion of the parole period decided since it arose squarely in this case. That having not been done, it was improper on the part of the detaining authority to pass an order of preventive detention against a person whilst he is in detention or in jail; and that having not done, the petitioner was rightly detained under section 4(1)(a) of COFEPOSA. Allowing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The fact that the detenu is al ready in detention does not take away the jurisdiction of the Detaining Authority in making an order against a man while he is already in custody does not make him liable to be quashed. [849E] 2. The facts of the present case are similar to the facts of this case and therefore, there is suffi cient material to show that the detaining author ity was aware of the fact that he was already in detention and yet he was sub jectively satisfied that his order of detention became necessary. [820G H] 3. The petitioner has not been able to make out a case for quashing the order of punitive detention. It is, therefore, not proper to hold that summons under section 108 of the Customs Act were in existence. [821B C] 4. In view of the positive case of the respondents that there was no summons and the detenu had been orally directed to attend the office by the authorities concerned, it would not be proper to conclude that summons u/s 108 of Customs Act was in existence at the time the order was served and yet the petitioner could not have been detained. [822C] 5. The Court then referred to the Constitution Bench decision in Rameshwar Shaw 's case (supra) and left it as a matter to be decided in every individual case on its own facts. The court also indicated that it was not a matter of jurisdition but had to be decide on the facts in each case. [823D] 6. In the instant case, there was suffi tient material which showed that the petitioner had confined his arguments to one point settled the writ petition as senior counsel with the allegations quoted above in paragraph 2 of the writ peti tioner had stated that he has a strong and almost un Answerable case On merits, there could be no doubt that the detention order was passed and before the actual service of the order, the peti tioners were taken into custody.

The petitioners were working as 'Daily Rated Casual Labour ' in the Posts and Telegraphs Department. The Union of India decided to absorb them regularly in its service and consequently they have been denied the benefits, such as increments, pension, leave facilities etc. which are enjoyed by those who have been recruited regularly. The petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the decision of the Union of india and the Government agencies in particular should not allow 610 workers to remain as casual labourers or temporary employees for an unreasonably long period of time, where is any justification to keep them as casual labourer for years as is being done in the Postal and Telegraph Department. Allowing the petitions, this Court, HELD: 1. The scheme of enhanced rates of daily wages will be without prejudice to absorption of casual semi skilled/skilled labour against regular vacancies as and when they occur. [607C D] 2. The benefit of increased rates of monthly wages will not be admissible to the casual semikilled/s unskilled labour in whose case the continuous spells of duty are intervened by a period of more than six months. These enhanced rates will bewithout prejudice to absorb of casual Semi skilled/Skilled labour in whom case the continuously spell of duty is intervened by an interval of time where is no justification to keeping persons as casual workers for years. [ 608E F] 3. The benefits of increased scales of daily wage will not, however, be admissible in the cases of those who had completed 720/1200 days in 3/5 years, where the continuous spell of service over a period Of six months or more with the department as on 1st April, 1986 is no reason to keep persons as Casual labourers for an unduly long period. [ 609E F; 609A] 4. The revision is done as and whenever they occur, but without any increments with effect from 5th February, 1986 on which date the first of the above two petitions, namely, Writ Petition No. It is again for this reason that managements and the State Government agencies should not allowed 610 workers who are employed as casual labour in their respective cadres but without anything more with effect From 5th of February,1986 on which dates the first petition, namely Writ Petition Nos. It will be open to the Union Of India and the other respondents to pay wages to the workmen who are working as casual employees for any unreasonably long periods of time.

The assessee was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1950 53. The Income Tax Officer issued a notice under section 22(2) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, calling upon him to furnish within such period not being less than sixty days. a return showing an income below the taxable limit. The assessee contended that he had submitted a return under section 19(3) on January 5, 1950, and with a voluntary return before the Income Tax officer there was no scope for the issuance of a notice unders. 34(1)(a). Held, that the notice under s. 22(1) was served on the assessee within the assessment years 1950 53 and therefore a return filed under section 24(2), when in fact it was filed in response to a notice issued under section 25(2). The notice could not be treated as such a return made under section 34(3). Held further, that a return which showed no assessable income could not possibly be 'treated ' as a return. A return which shows no assessable taxable income could only be filed by a person who thought that he was a taxable income and therefore the return in the case of a person whose total income during the previous year exceeded the taxable limits. The return in answer to the notice could be filed under s 24(1). Held also, further,that a return in response thereto could be made under s .24(2)(a) before assessment is made. A notice under S.22(3), if filed belatedly under section 27(2); and for this there was nothing in the Act which showed that even a return had been filed. The general notice under the section, therefore, did not apply to a return of income filed under S .24 (1)(b).

The petitioners in Transfer Case No. 219 of 1988, were appointed as Directors of the nationalised bank on different dates between 1.4.1988 and 31.3.1989. The Central Government by its notification dated 23.8.1982 issued a circular to all the banks including the petitioners therein that the panel furnished by the Union was not a matter to be encouraged in the case of other employees for selection to the Board of Directors, for the Directors must represent the interest of the bank as a whole and not of any special class of persons. The petitioners in the Transfer Case challenged the circular dated 23rd August 1982 on the ground that it violated Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution inasmuch as the said circular was issued without consultation with the Reserve Bank of India, and that the same was violative of Article 19(1)(c) of the Consti tutions Act. The Additional Solicitor General contended that the Act postulates both election and nomination of members of the Board and the choice between the two modes of appointment is left to the Central Government, and, therefore, the Act requires the Central Govern ment to make a scheme for the constitution of the board of Directors so as to include representatives of the employees and other speci fied categories. The learned Additional SolicitorGeneral contended that since the Act contemplates both election or nomination of the members of Board of Director and the option between the three modes of appoint is left only to the Reserve bank, it was incumbent upon it, until any such amend ment is made, to work the present Scheme in such a way as to give the maximum scope for the concerned employees to exer cise their choice in the selection of their representatives. Dismissing the Transfer Petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Act, by its very object, speaks of election or nominations and if read without regard to the legislative intent, as disclosed by the Act, is capable of a contrary interpretation, as is now sought to be put upon it by the Central Gover ment, and That interpretation is, in our view, wrong, and in any case out of harmony with the principle enshrined in Articles 19(i)(c), and 43(A) of th e Constitution The very object of leaving the choice to the central Government as to the mode, which is election or nominated, is to enable it to reasonably exercise its discretion in such an a way that to give best form of repre sentation to every category of persons mentioned in the Act. They are as much a part of the Bank as the management is. As soon as may be after the commencement of this Scheme, the Central government shall by notification in the official Gazette constitute the Board for a nationalised bank, consisting of (a ) one Director, from among the employees of the nationalized bank, who are workmen, to be appointed by the central Govern ment; and (b) one Director from amongst the employees, who were not workmen, To be appointed as the true representatives of employees and others, to fill up the vacancies in the Board. [857C D] 1.2 The Central Governmen t shall, by notification, constitute the board for a notified bank. The very purpose of leaving such choice to be reasonably exercised so as not to give effect to the true intent of the legislature as to its composition of the Boards of Directors. The mode of election and nominations must, therefore be such as would be ideally suitable and appropriate to the banking industry and the selectee of their respective representatives. [883E F] 1:3 It is open to the Parliament to amend the Scheme suitably for that purpose. Till any such amendment is made the Central Gov ernment shall, in consultation with Reserve Bank, make the Scheme in accordance with the provisions of the Act.] [858C D].

The assessee was imposed penalties in the sum of Rs. 1,000/ under section 220(6) of the Income tax Act, 1961 on an assessee during the pendency of an appeal before it. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the penalty and directed that the recovery proceedings be stayed till the disposal of the appeal. In appeal to the Appellate Tribunal the assessee contended that the Appellate Assistant commissioner had the power to stay the recovery of the penalties imposed. Held, that the power of stay by the Tribunal is not likely to be exercised in a routine manner or as a matter of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. The power of staying recovery during the course of an appellate proceeding has been given to the Income Tax Officer only when an appeal is pending before the Appellate authority. It could well be said that when section 254 confers appellate jurisdiction, it impliedly grants the power for doing all such acts, or employing such means as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. The Act does not empower the Appellate Authority to stay recovery of tax, though the effect of an order in favour of the assessee under section 45 of the Act is a matter for the legislature to consider. It would be that under section 225(6), the power conferred by the Act or the Incometax Appellate Tribunal Rules, 1963 powers have not been expressly conferred upon the Appellate Tribunals to stay proceedings relating to recovery of penalty or tax due from an assessee. The statute confers such a power on the Income lax Officer who can give the necessary relief to an assessee but that could hardly be put at par with a statutory power as is contained in section 220 (6) which is confined only to the stage of pendency of the appellate appeal before the Tribunal.

The respondent was charged with committing cognizable offences and was convicted under section 7 of the Police Act with a view to preventing him from acting in any manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order. The District Magistrate, Gonda, passed an order dismissing him from service. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the respondent was not holding a civil post and (2) the enquiry was vitiated by a number of serious irregularities; and (3) the specific acts with which the petitioner was charged were cognizable offences, and therefore sub paragraph (1), of para. 486 governed the situation and that as no case, as required by the said sub paragraph, was registered against the respondent in the police station, the order of dismissal was invalid. Held, that the departmental trial was only a further step in respect of the misconduct of the respondent and not a further one. The fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made enquiries do not affect the validity of the order would not affect its validity. (1)(a) In the instant case, the departmental enquiry was held subsequent to the completion of the magisterial inquiry and therefore it fell within the express terms of para 486 of the police Regulations. The respondent was a public servant and could not be dismissed from service under the provisions of para., 486 of Police Regulations. (b) The order of discharge was made under the statutory power conferred upon the Superintendent of Police by section 7 Of the Police Regulation Act, 1949, and as the Police Regulations were only directory in nature, and inasmuch as no prejudice was caused to the respondent the non compliance with the said regulations would not in any way affect the legality of the dismissal. (c) The departmental trial is held subsequent on the completionof the magal inquiry and it falls within the implied terms of paragraph 489 of the Criminal Procedure Code.

The appellant was a member of the Indian Medical Service. He was promoted to supertime grade II on February 8, 1971. The post in which he was working was converted into an unpecified post and that as it was assigned to Ophthalmology specialists ' grade posts in supertime Grade II that post could only have been filled in by promotion from amongst those holding the post in Specialists ' grades in super time grade II. The appellant contended that when a post in Ophosmology Speciality at Willingdon Hospital was created on February 1, 1971 by conversion of one post from amongst unspecified specialists' grade posts into different specialities and were filled in, it became an addition to the strength of that speciality and he should have been promoted from that date. The Central Government converted one post into a specified post in super Time Grade II and added to super time scale II that the post could be filled in only by promotion and he was not qualified for being appointed to that speciality. The respondent contended that as these 28 posts were in Specialist ' grade and the strength was reduced by 28, whenever any post out of these 28 vacancies added to the supertime scale II was required to be filled up, it can only be filled by promotion but he should be considered eligible for promotion from the date on which Dr. Sen and other qualified persons were promoted as being found qualified for the same and for the post to which each one of them was promoted. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was fully qualified for promotion to super Time grade II in February 1971, and that he should not have been considered for promotion. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that as the 28 posts which were deducted from the strength were filled up by promotion, the appellant could not be said to have been superseded by any one junior to him in his speciality, it was difficult to entertain the contention that in refusing promotion to him when some posts were converted into a specialist ' post it can merely be filled only in by direct recruitment and that the promotion of the aforementioned four respondents should be set aside. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The promotion of Dr. P. Sen was not superseded by anybody junior to the appellant in his specialties. [53A] 2.1 In passing a contention of the Appellant that in refusal to accept promotion at Simla appellant was never superseded by anyone junior to them in his specialist ' grade, it is difficult to accept the contention of Mr. Sen that in declining promotion to Dr. S. Sen he himself would not have got any advantage of being qualified for promoted to Supertime grade I in February1971 from which date he claims as being eligible for being promoted to the post of Director of Health Services, Manipur but when some one who was already in that grade is transferred to the newly created post and the post vacated by such transferred employee is offered by way of promotion which in fact was done in this case there is no violation of the rule. [54B] 2:2 The appellant was not a member in the Indian Administrative Service but was a senior to Dr.. Sen and was not unqualified for the posts of Director, Health Services Manipur, but the post was not offered to him and, therefore, he must be considered as eligible for consideration from the dates on which he claims that he had not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists " grade officers formed on September 9, 1966. [55E] 3:1 The appellant would be the Head of the Department and would continue to be in super lime grade II if he had put in 7 years of experience in the speciality.

The respondent No. 1, a small holder of land inherited by him and later transferred to his sons and wife were not hit by section 10A and section 19B of the Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 (Act X of 628 1953). The Collector ignoring the transfer of 167 bighas of land by respondent No, 2 held that the land inherited was saved from utilisation by the State. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by respondent Nos. 1 and 2 holding that the lands inherited by respondent no. 1 were not covered by section 20B of Act X of 630 1953. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant (writ petitioner) that the transfer was hit by the ceiling set and land acquired by an heir by inheritance is saved from utilization by the Government. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The gift in both the appeals fail in the face of section 19 B. [619B] 2. Section 19 B has to be enacted because the High Court took the view that area which became surplus subsequent to April 15, 1953 was not hit under the ceiling laid and land acquisition acquired by a heir by descent is saved therefrom. The scheme of the Act according to the learned Judges, was to see that no one held in excess of the permissible area and since by the gift to the son or wife the latter had only lands within permissible limits, there was no frustration of the policy of the law This reasoning is repugnant to the basic scheme because the surplus pool will be adversely affected if gifts and other transfers which would skim off surplus were to be allowed. [613C D] 3. The object of the legislation according to section 19 A is that even if the source of the excess area is inheritance, bequest of gift the capacity to own is conditioned by the permissible limit. This reasoning was repugnant to basic scheme Because the surplus Pool will be directly affected if gift and other transfer which would nab off surplus are to be permitted. [519D] 4. The Act, according to its plain language, provided that even though in the hands of the propositus, it is surplus land, if among the heirs it is not, then their transfers will not be affected by the interdict of section 10 A(a) the sins of the father shall not set the teeth of the children on edge. The drafting of the saving clause is cumbersome but the sense is and having regard to the conspectus, can only be that though in a hands of a proposituus, there is no frustration or of the Policy of the Law This reasoning has been repugnant to section 10 B(a). [520E] 5. The interpretation of the expression "any person" in section 19 is not confined to persons who are members of the family but also to persons whose lands have been acquired by inheritance. It is only a limited meaning and cannot be extended to persons belonging to the same class or classes. [540D E] 6. Section 20 B has no application to a case where the source is inherited by an individual, whether as land owner or tenant, acquires any right in excess thereof. The definition of "person" in the Act includes persons who hold lands in excess than the permissible limits. It does not include persons who have been members of a family. [542F] 7. Section 18 B has nothing to do with the vesting of any property by inheritance or gift, gift, exchange, lease, agreement or settlement any land which is comprised in surplus area at the commencement of this Act. The legislature has used the expression 'person ' in section 20 B for a limited purpose and it does not mean that persons who held lands in surplus pool are to have any right over such lands. [543G H] 8.

The plaintiffs claimed the Zamindari on the death of Amarshah in 1951 and the defendants by their written statement maintained that the genealogical table set up by the plaintiffs was incorrect, that by the order of the Governor of Madhya Pradesh dated November 9, 1951, the Zamindari was conferred upon the 1st defendant Dayaram as he was found suitable to hold the, Zamindari and the decision of the Compensation Officer regarding Malguzari lands which vested in consequence of the enactment of the Madhya Pradesh Abolition of Proprietary Rights (Estates, Mahals Alienated Lands) Act 1 of 1951 had become binding and conclusive against the plaintiffs because no suit challenging the deci sion was instituted within two months from the date thereof and the plaintiffs were on that account not entitled to claim the compensation paid or payable in respect of the Malgu zari lands; that the will dated December 8, 1950 set up in favour of the defendants represented the true relationship between the descendants of Gangashah and the ancestor Gangashashah as devisees under the will of Amirshah executed on December 3, 1950 under which his estate was devised in favour by the defendants. The plaintiffs contended that the order dated December 9, 1950, set up for Malguzar was not binding and the decree passed by the Compensation officer became final and conclusive; that after the death Of Pratapshah and Zamindari devolved upon the first plaintiff, the right to the Zamindari devolved on the 1th defendant as an impartible estate devolving by the rule of primogeniture; that in making the order the Governor had acted in exercise of the power conferred by the Chanda Patent; that he was entitled to the estate devised in his favour by Amarshih and that on the date of the notification under section 3 of the Act, the estate was impar tible and was governed by the rules of primimiture; and that the plaintiffs ' suit with regard to Malgu Zari lands was not barred by the decision in 1950. The Trial Court held that the decree dated December 3. 1950 set out by the plaintiff was not a genuine and conclusive will, and that it was not shown that in passing the order he had acted on the basis of the custom governing succession Dhanora Zamindari devolved to the defendants; that as Amarshasha had made a will dated January 27, 1951 under which their estate was administered in favour Of the defendants, the plaintiffs had become entitled to receive compensation in respect thereof and that they were under the control of the Government. The High Court held on appeal that the decision was contrary to the customs and the law governing the Zamindari; that it did not oust the jurisdiction of the Civil Court; that though the order was contrary, the will set up as a devisees and that Pratapshah had made an application for setting aside that decision, and the appellants were entitled to compensation in regard thereto. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The order of Compensation Officer under sub section (1), shall not be subject to any appeal or revision but any party may, within two month from the said date, institute a suit in the civil court to have the order set aside, and such decision shall be binding on the Compensation Officers, but subject to the result of such suit, if any, the compensation Officer shall be final and binding on all parties. [319 G H] (2) The right to property vesting in the Government by operation of section 3 is extinguished. But the right of a person who has acquired an interest in the property vests in the State. It is not necessary that he should have been a party to the proceedings before the Compensation Commissioner. He must be a party against whom the order is passed.

The appellants landlord filed a suit for recovery of possession on the ground that the standard rent was excessive and standard rent should be fixed. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that the provisions contained in sections 12 (3) (a) and (b) of the Act do not apply to the suit, but that the suit is governed by the provisions of section 12(3)(a) of that Act. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: The Bombay High Court was right in holding that the dispute in section 12 (2) (b), of the Bombay Rent Act does not apply. [766 D] In order to attract the applicability of section12(3) of Bombay Rent and Accommodation Act there must be non existence of the dispute at the date of the notice and such non existence must continue right up to the expiration of one month from the date when service of the said notice is served on the tenant. [779 G] The Bombay Rent Control Act, 1947, does not provide for any protection against eviction except in certain cases where there is a dispute as to standard rent or permitted increases recoverable under this Act. [780 A B] In the instant case, the Bombay High court was right that the question of standard rent is to be raised within one month of the service of notice under section 12 of the Gujarat Rent and Eviction Act, but in view of the provisions in sections 11 and 12 of that section the suit was governed by section 12.

The respondent company was a director of the respondent company. The shares held by it in the respondent Company were not registered in the name of the Aluminium Ltd. and, therefore, according to the principles laid down in Inland Revenue Commissioners vs B. It is not necessary that in order to have "a controlling interest" the person or persons who hold the majority of the shares must have a beneficial interest in the company when such a person acquires, by purchase or otherwise, the majority share carrying shares in that company, for the control of the company resides in the voting powers of its shareholders. The directors of the appellant company were not members of the family of the respondents and they had no controlling interest in it as contemplated by section 2 (21) of the Excess Profits Tax Act, 1940. The respondent company, therefore appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of a company at all ordinary or extraordinary general meetings of the shareholders of the Company. The appellant company was not a director controlled company and the shares held in the Respondent company were registered in its name as holders of the majority shares which, under the articles of association of the companies, carry the right to vote. The respondents filed an application before the Income tax Appellate Tribunal for the assessment years 1939 to 1943 on the ground that the directors had a controlling interest therein and that the director had no beneficial interest therein. The Tribunal answered in favour of the assessee company. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the directors were not "a governing shareholder" within the meaning of section 2(21) Of the Excess profits Tax Act; (ii) the shares were not held by them and, as such, they could not be said to have been "a control interest" in the appellant 's own name; (iii) the Directors had no control over the shares which were held by the Aluminium Company in the assessee 's name; and (iv) the director was not entitled to vote on behalf or for any other reason. HELD: (i)(a) The directors were, therefore not "the governing shareholder". [193 D] (b) In order to be entitled to have a controlling share, the person holding the majority must have an beneficial interest. It may well be regarded as having "a managing interest" within section 2 of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. [194 E F] (c) The last mentioned case was not brought to the notice of the High Court before the judgment under appeal was delivered. The facts of that case were entirely different from the facts of the case before us and that decision has no manner of application to the present case. It was, therefore unnecessary for us to discuss or express any opinion as to whether the observations to be found in the judgment in that case are or are not well founded. For reasons stated above, it is unnecessary for the Court to deal with or express an opinion as regards whether the observation to be made in the Judgment under appeal should be read in the negative. [193 G H] (d) The High Court was right in holding that the answer to the question referred by the Appellate Tribunal to the High court should be in the affirmative.

The respondent was an employee of the Karnataka Electricity Board. He opted to the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee. The amended Rules prescribed that the posts of Accounts Superintendents were to be filled by promotion of I Division Clerks on the basis of seniority cum merit on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. examination. On 30th December, 1966 some persons junior to the respondent were promoted on their passing the S A.S Examination Part I. The revised Rules prescribed the passing of the examination and Kannada language test as a consequence of the judgment of the High Court of Mysore and the Supreme Court. The respondent opted to join the Service by promotion from the cadre of Accounts Superintendent as on 30th November, 1966. On 1st October, 1957, some persons senior to him were promoted as Accounts Officers on their being passed Part II and II. On 2nd October, 1967, some person junior to him was promoted on his having passed the S B.A.,S examination Part I & Part II. The appellant 's writ petition was dismissed by a Single Judge of the Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that in view of the later Resolution of the Board dated 5th January, 1970, it was no longer open to the respon dents to rely on the resolution dated 19th May, 1969. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD : 1. The High Court was in error in construing the relevant provisions of the Regulations and the Resolutions and holding that the re spondent is exempted from passing the examination. [501F] 2.1 In any event the plea of the respondent will have to fail on the ground that the regulations framed under section 79(c) has not been relaxed by amending the Regulations. The passing of a Resolution by the Board cannot have the effect of modifying a Regulation which was passed by the Government in the exercise of the powers conferred by the statute. [511F] 3.1 The conclusion of the Single Judge that it would .mean that where the passing is insisted prior to that Resolution in the case of allotees for promotion to the cadre o f Accounts Superintendents as before be in insisted, and if passing of S. A.

The petitioner 's son Suman Behera was taken from his home in police custody. The said Suman Behra was taken to his home by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police outpost under Police Station Bisra, Distt. The prayer made in the petition is for award of compensation to the petitioner, the mother of Suman Beika Behera for contravention of fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. The State Government by its order dated 14.9.1988 directed that the amount of compensation be paid to the victims for their death. The petitioner ' s son Suman was taken into police custody in a train accident on 1.12.1987 by respondent no.6 and Sarat Kumar Barik. The claim made therein related to award of monetary compensation to Suman Behara, aged about 22 years, in police Custody. The mother of the petitioner ' son Suman Dehera was given the benefit of death of her son Suman. The father of the deceased Suman Betramhera died on 1st December, 1987 and the petitioner filed a petition under Article 32 of the constitution for determination of compensation. The Additional Solicitor General, however, did not dispute the liability of the State for payment of compensation in this proceeding for violation of fundamental rights guaranteed by the Constitution, in case it was found to be a custodial death. Allowing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The court is not helpless and the wide powers given to this Court by Article 32, which itself is a fundamental right, imposes a constitutional obligation on this Court to forge such new tools, which may be necessary for doing complete justice and enforcing the fundamental rights of the citizen. [601C] 2.2 In exercising its jurisdiction under Articles 32 and 226 of theConstitution seeking enforcement or protection of fundamental Rights, it does so under the public law by way of penalising the wrongdoer and fixing the liability for the public wrong on the State which has failed in its public duty to protect the fundamental right of the citizens. [0601D] 2:3 The court while exercising its power under Article 226 or the High Courts, being the protectors of the civil liberties of the Citizen have not only the power and jurisdiction but also an obligation to grant relief in exercise of their jurisdiction under Article 227 of the constitutional Constitution to the victim or the heir of the victim whose fundamental rights under Article 19 of the Indian Constitution are established to have been flagrantly infringed by calling upon the State to repair the damage done by its officers.to the fundamental freedoms of the people notwithstanding the right of a citizen to the remedy in public law under the Constitution by way Of penalising, the wrongdoers and fixing liability for compensation under the private law in an action based on tort, through a suit instituted in a court of competent jurisdiction or/and persecute the offender under the penal law. [ 610A] 2 :4 The court has not only power but also a duty to grant reliefs in exercise Of its jurisdiction to the aggrieved party to claim compensation under Article 31 of the India to the injured party, notwithstanding the rights available under the civil law to the affected party where the courts found that grant of such relief was warranted. [1001F] 2(a) The payment of Rs. 10,000/ as exemplary damages in proceedings under Article32 by this Court or under Article226 by the High Court, for established infringement of fundamental freedoms, is not to be understood, as it is generally understood in a civil action for damages under the Private law but in the broader sense of providing relief by an order of making 'monetary amends ' under the Public Law for the wrong done due to breach of public duty, of not protecting the fundamental Rights of the Citizens.

The petitioners were convicted for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and sentenced to death for an offences under section 307 Indian Penal code. The petitions filed by them to the President of India for commutation of their sentence to imprisonment for life, were rejected by the President recently. Before considering the merits of the application, it was necessary that such a search should be taken, a person who desires to interview a prisoner may have to subject himself or herself to the search in accordance with the rules and regulations governing the interviews. The petitioners filed petitions to the Governor for commutation and commutation of the sentence. The petition was dismissed by the High Court on the ground that the petitioners were willing to be interviewed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (1) the right claimed by the petitioner is not an absolute right, nor indeed does it confer any right on the Press to have an unrestricted access to means of information; (2) the freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution which includes the freedom to the press is not absolute right nor indeed did it confer a right on a Press to has an unrestricted right, but the right to form an opinion or opinion does not depend upon any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the Press; (3) the rights claimed by them are not the right of an interview under clause (4) of rule 549. Dismissing the petition, HELD: 1. The constitutional right to freedom of expression conferred under article 19 (1)(b) of Constitution is not a absolute right but merely a right to express any particular view or opinion but the freedom guaranteed by article 14(1) (a) is not one absolute right and it confers no right on him nor does it impose any obligation on his citizens to provide information through the medium of an Interview of the two prisoners who are sentenced to life. [1187C D] 2. The existence of a free Press does not imply or spell out any legal obligations on the citizen to supply Information to the newspapers, such for example, as there is under section 161(2) of Criminal Procedure Code. No data has been made available to us on the basis of which it would be possible for us to say that the prisoners themselves do not desire to be interview and, indeed, if it were to appear that the prisoner himself does not desire or spellout any legal duty on the Citizens to supply such information for example. [1087C E] 3. The right claimed is not the rights of other citizens but the rights guaranteed by Article 19(2)(a). But no such consideration has been pressed upon and therefore, it cannot be said that they can always and without good reasons be denied the opportunity to interview an condemned prisoner. [987D F] 4. The petitioner has been asking for permission to interview the prisoners right since the President had rejected the petitions for commutation. No such consideration have been pressed on behalf or on behalf Of the magazine India Today as also Mr. Jain who appears on behalf o the Union of India, and in our opinion should be given the same facility of interviewing the prisoners as we are disposed to give to the petitioner in the main writ petition. [999D E] 5. The representatives agree that all reasonable indulgence should be allowed to a condemned prisoner in the matter of interviews with relatives, friends, legal advisers and approved religious ministers. But no Such consideration has not been pressed before us and therefore it is not possible for this Court to decide.

The appellant was the Receiver of the estate. On January 19, 1950 the respondent mortgaged a tea garden called the "Ishanchandrapar Tea Estate" to M/s Das Bank Ltd. On February 10, 1950, the Bank applied for the appointment of a receiver. The District Judge rejected the objections and directed that the damages awarded to the respondent be recovered from the appellant. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but he also allowed the respondent 's application for damages to the extent of Rs. 22 of 1956 filed by the Receiver against that order was dismissed for default by the Judicial Commissioner, Tripura on December 18, 1959. On appeal by the respondent the High Court held that the surety bond executed by the appellant was a part of the proceedings pending before the District Judge and therefore the order for recovery of damages obtained by the Respondent against the Receiver could be executed only against the appellant to the tune of Rs 22 of1956 filed by him as directed by the court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Courts were in error in holding that the bond executed on August 26, 1950 was a complete one and therefore not enforceable at law. HELD: (i) The surety bond is a part and parcel of the proceeding pending before a District Judge. It is impossible to accept the contention that the Receiver owed no duty or obligation in respect of the tea garden. He was put in possession of the Tea garden in his capacity as a Receiver and indeed parties had made contentions from time to time as to whether the tea gardens were managed by the receiver economically and efficiently. The surety bonds would therefore cover the loss occasioned to the tea plantation due to the Receiver 's negligence in the performance of his duties. [360 E F] (ii) It is difficult to accept that the Court owed no Duty or obligation on the Receiver to enforce the bond. He is put in actual possession of a tea grove in his capacities as a receiver and indeed party had made submissions from time and time as regards whether the Tea gardens were manage by the Receivers. The sureties bond would therefore be construed strictly but it is impossible that to accept this contention that he owed no duties or obligation, in respect thereof, the appellant would not be liable for the loss caused thereto by the fire. [361 B C] (iii) It was impossible to hold that the receiver owed noduty or obligation to enforce a bond. The bail bond had, therefore, to be construed properly but it was impossible for the Receiver "s negligence" to accept it.

The appellants who are dealers in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat in compliance with the provisions of the U.P. Rice Procurement (Levy) Order, 1959, filed writ petitions before the High Court challenging the validity of the levy and contending that the transactions were not sales within the meaning of the Act. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the sales made to the appellants were sales within section 2(h) of the , and that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no "sale" within the definition of the word 'sale ' in section 2 (h). In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U .P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate of the price of wheat by the appellants, rejecting the contention raised by them that the goods supplied were not sold by them to the Controller and that no tax was exigible on such transactions. HELD : (i) The sales made by the appellant were sales in the nature of sales within Section 2(g) of U. P. Sales tax Act, 1953, and therefore, the transactions of supply did not result in sales and were on that account not exposed to sales tax. [655 B] (ii) The levy was a liability to deliver half the quantity of wheat procured or purchased by him every day beginning with the date of commencement of the Order until such time as the State Government otherwise directs. Delivery of the wheat has to be given by the dealer to the State Govt. 50% of the quantity received and thereafter fifty per cent of the stock of wheat purchased or purchased. The tax payer was under the Control Order compelled to carry out the directions of the Controller, and it had no volition in the matter. [600 C] (iii) The tax payee was under a legal obligation to deliver the specified quantities of rice on hand and he had also to supply to the Government 50% thereof every day commencing with the day of commencement. The levy did not amount to a sale within the ambit of section 2 of the .

The appellant was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was arrested on May 26, 1986 and since then he was under detention. The report of the Advisory Board was received by the Government on June 23, 1986. The detenu challenged his detention before the High Court which dismissed the petition holding that there was no valid reason for the detention of the appellant beyond the period of three months unless an Advisory Board consisting of persons who are or have been qualified to be appointed as Judges of a High Court had reported within the period prescribed by article 22(4) of the Constitution that there is in its opinion suffi cient cause for such detention. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The order of detention should have been made, knowing full well that there were no fresh facts and therefore the detention should be upheld. If a reference to an Advisory board is to be made within three weeks, it is no answer to say that the report though not obtained within three months, was obtained before the hearing of the case. If the report of such an advisory Board is to he obtained within two months, it would be no answer. [206E F] 2. The observation of the court to the extent that they go to support the contention of the learned counsel for the appel lant, but we must say that in that case, the court was not confronted with the present situation at all. This implies that the question to which the Advisory board has to apply its mind is whether on the date of its report there was sufficient cause for the detained person when the order of the detention was passed, but it does not offend the mandate of article 22 (4) Of the Constitution. [207E F; 207A] 3. The observations of the Court to the effect that if the report is obtained within one month of the date on which the second order of Detention is revoked and a subsequent order is made, it was no answer for saying that the reference though not made within two weeks, was disposed of before the hear ing of the appeal. If this is so, it will be no end to say in that event the report would be obtained after the hearing on the case, [207G H] 4. The facts that the order was passed on June 22, 1986 show that the maximum period within which the detaining authority can on its own satisfaction detain a person is three months and the detention must be upheld.[206B C] 5. If there were any fresh facts, the maximum limit for which the detention order was made, but the report could be obtained as required by the Constitution, it cannot be said that the detention became illegal notwithstanding that it was within three days from the date when the second detention order is revoked.

The respondent, a father of the respondent, was awarded a contract for carrying out certain works. The respondent had agreed to such entrustment. In the award, it was stated that the entire responsibility of solving the dispute was entrusted to him and the petitioner had agreed that both of them should abide by the award dated 20th January 1977 and that its interpretation should be left to the arbitrator himself. On the question whether there was an arbitration agreement between the parties, HELD: (1) The conduct of the parties that there was a arbitration agreement and by signing the award it could be said that the parties had agreed agreed to refer the dispute to the named arbitrator. [501C] (2) The High Court was right in dismissing the application in the manner it did. However, the way in which the proceedings under the Act are conducted and without an exception challenged in Courts, has made lawyers laugh and legal philosophers weep. With respect, we could not agree more in the facts and circumstances of this case. [540D] (3) The mere fact that the party had agreed with the acceptance of the award would not make it a proper arbitration agreement in terms of section 2(a) of the Act. But in the present context, it is clear that the conduct of parties that they had agreed on refer the disputes to the arbitration of the named Arbitrator and that he made an award. This, in our opinion, in the light of the facts & circumstances of the case can certainly be construed to be a proper Arbitration agreement in accordance with section 2 (a) and (4).

The appellants were the mortgagees of a mortgage debt. The mortgaged property was mortgaged by the mortgagee to the appellants in 1943 and the mortgage was executed on January 2, 1939. The mortgage was registered on January 1, 1939, but it was not registered as a suit for recovery of the loan advanced before or after January 1 1939. On January 30, 1939 the respondent filed a petition under article 227 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the proceedings in execution and as that was insti tuted and pending after January 31, 1939 he had no right to recover the debt from the original mortgagor.
