The trial court dismissed the petition holding that the suit was not an application at all and was not maintainable. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the petition (exhibit 2a) dated June 2, 1942, amounted to a proceeding in execution for any of the purposes mentioned in clauses (a) or (b) of section 2(22) of the Act. Held: (i) The order of January 30 1937, was made under Order XXI, rule 57, as amended by the Calcutta High Court. The words and that he had not received the notice referred to in clause (a), since section 28, sub section (1) is concerned only with assignment of debts" (pp. Stress was laid upon the expression "all the rights of the mortgagee" used by their Lordships in the passage quoted above, and it was pointed out that in the earlier decisions they held that in India a legal interest remained in the mortgagor even when the mortgage became in the form of an English mortgage, and that the interest taken by the respondent was not a absolute interest. The only question is whether the respondent as sub mortgagee is an assignee within the meaning of sub section(5) of sec tion 36.

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The appellant transferred certain properties belonging to the joint family. In 1947, after the execution of exhibit A 1 and A 2 there was a disruption of the joint Hindu Joint Family and a severance of joint status between Venkatacharyulu and his sons. In 1954, his widow and sons instituted O.S. No. 12 of 1954 against the appellant for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents dated April 15, 1946, were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes and were void. The trial court decreed the suit in favour of the appellant. On appeal by the respondents, the High Court confirmed the decree in O. S. No., 62/54 and dismissed O.A. No, 63/54. In the appeals to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the transfers were made by Venkatacharanulu in favour Of the appellant in view of past illicit cohabitation with her, such past cohabitation was the motive and not the consideration for the transfer and the two deeds though ostensibly sale deeds, were in reality gift deeds. Held: (i) The transfers under exhibit A1 and A2 were valid but in holding that the alienations were made in consideration of past cohabitations, they were invalid. The transfers were without consideration and were by way of gifts. The alienations were not hit by section 6(h). The transfers could not validate them. The alienation was without consideration. (ii)The transfer was without considering the past cohabitingation, having regard to section 2(d) of the as a subsisting consideration for his subsequent promise to transfer the properties to her. The gift was valid but under section 6 (h). (iii)The transfers were not invalid by reason of the fact that they were motivated by a desire to compensate the concubine for her past services.

The respondent, a widow of the deceased employee, filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the notice under section 226(3) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the L.I.C. had not made the payment to the respond ent. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the delay in making the requisite statement under section 227(3)(vi) of Income Tax, 1961 was due to the fact that the amount demanded by the notice issued under section226(3), was payable only to the assignee and not the defaulter. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The inordinate delay in filing the writ peti tion is the result of misconstruction of the provision and misappreciation of its liability thereunder. Performance of this statutory obligation by the L .I.c. being after inordinate delay, award of interest to the assignment of policies to whom the payment thereunder had to be made even according to the stand of the L..I. C. is, therefore, clearly justified. [114G H] 2. The delay in seeking revocation of the notices under section 225(3). was the result o ut of misconstruction on the part of the respondent and mis appreciation of its responsibility thereunder. performance of this obligation by L. I.C., in the present case being after considerable delay, Award of interest is to be considered as deemed defaulter assessee under clause (vi) thereof instead of doing so. Performance by the respondent was thus clearly justified.[114A B] 3. The unexplained delay in obtaining the requisite information under section 244(3); award of compensation to the respondent, it was incumbent on the L.,I.T.O. to make the requisite statements on oath under clause(vi) therein raising an objection on the basis of the registered assignment. It is obvious that this defence is untenable. Sub section (3) clearly shows that on a notice thereunder being issued by the I.T., in view of its consistent stand throughout that the moneys due under the policies were held by it for and on behalf o the assignee, and not as defaulter. The L.L.I., itself has taken the stand throughout, that the sum demanded by this notice was payable even according t to the stands of the assignee. This being so the making of this statement on oath by the appellant on oath of the I,.T.o. after receipt of notice under Section 226(2), the amounts of the matured policies within the time given by the l.I.'C. are, therefore clearly justified in view. performance by L . I.c., in its failure to pay to the L,I.O., without the requisite Statement on oath being made by the C.T.(as envisaged in clause (vii) of sub section (4) of Section 226 of the Act lay in its Failure to pay the L/I.I.(C.) to the Respondent. [115D F] 4. The conduct of the parties is not such as to justify the inordinate delay. It was not possible for the assignee of the policies to obtain revocation of notice by the Income tax Officer without the required statement on solemn affirmation being made, by the Appellant. It may be that the lapse in making this statement was due only to inadvertence or oversight. [116E F] 5. The mere delay in raising the requisite particulars under section 245(3 ) of the income Tax Act is the consequence of misconstruction and mispretation of its obligation thereunder.formance of this Statutory obligation by an L.l.C.(as contemplated in clause(vii) thereof, was the results of misconstruction. Performance in this statutory duty by the Respondent, therefore. clearly justified by the High court.

The appellant was the Chief Justice of the High Court. He filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of section 29(2) of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 on the ground that it was barred by limitation. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that section 29 (2)(a) applies to the case of appeals preferred under section 116 A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 and on that footing had held that the appeal presented to them by the respondent was within time if computed after making deductions permitted by section 12 of the Limitation Act. The appellant appealed to this Court. HELD: (i) The first limb of sub section (2) Of section 29 is concerned only with proceedings of a civil nature, that is, proceedings under special or local law for which a period of limitation is provided in the First Schedule. [165 D] (ii)The words "where any special or Local law prescribes for any suit, appeal or application a period different from the period prescribed therefor by the first schedule" occurring in the first limb are not expressly excluded by such special or general law. The second limb of section29 is concerned with proceedings under a particular local or special law for the which a limitation is prescribed in the Second Schedule. Therefore, what has to be seen is whether a suit, appeals or application under a certain local or other law is of a kind similar to one for which the period of Limitation is provided therefor in the second schedule. [166 E F] (iii)The first limb is concerned merely with proceedings relating to a particular type of case and that is the proceeding under special and local law. Therefore what has been seen is, whether a decree or order passed by a Tribunal sub s.(2) will apply even to a case where the First schedule to the Limitation Acts has not prescribed any period of time for an appeal in the Third Schedule. The first part of section 30 is concerned, only with proceeding under a special or special local law and that as in the 144 present case the First Schedules have not prescribed the period for an application in the Fourth Schedule. It is true that the words " where any special and Local law prescribe for any suits, appeal, or application" are used in the sense of the word "suit". But the first part will apply to an appeal under the Representation Of the People (Amendment) Act, 1950.

The appellant was a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura. He questioned the validity of the order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magistrate declaring Plot Nos. 701 and 702 in the Town Area, Baldev (Mathura) as a bus stand/halting place of Baldev, where the stage carriages were directed to stand for the purpose of allowing the passengers of Baldev to get into and to get down from the stage carriage vehicles in a writ petition, Civil Miscellaneous Writ Petition No. 501 of 1986. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that section 76 of the Act conferred wide powers on the District Magis trate to fix places for the bus stand and not in the district Magistrate. Allowing the appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Regional Transport Authority had passed the impugned order with the object of establishing a bus Stand as a Bus stand under section 76(2)(r) of the . [717G] 1.2 The District Magist trate had been authorised by the State Government under section76 of the , to pass an order fixing the Municipal Bus Stand as the bus stands. There was, therefore, no power conferred on the Regional Transport authority by section 76. [718C D] 1:3 In the instant case no order has been passed by th e Regional Transport Officer, Mathura to determine the area in question as a vehicle stand and the Dis trict Magistrate cannot be equated with the Regional Trans port Authority constituted under the Act. The District Magistrate was therefore, in error in upholding the impugned orde r dated 22.5.1986 passed by him. [758E] 1 :4. In the present case no orders have been passed on the basis of the contract entered into between the appellant and the respondent No. 2. The Regional transport Authority had not passed any order under section 78(2) (r) or under section 68(2). The High, Court was, however, in mistake in upholding t he impugned order passed by t he District Magistrate. [759D] 1.:5. In view of the fact that no order had been passed under section78(2), the Regional transport authority could not exercise the power of fixing a bus stands under section 75 of the Motor Vehicles Act. [761G] 2:6 The High court was, in our opinion, in erred in upholding th at impugned order dated 22 5.1986. [763D] 2.7 In view thereof, the order passed on 22. 5.86 by the Regional Authori ty was set aside and quashed.

The appellants were prosecuted for offences under section 7 of the and 8(1)(a) read with section 8(2) (b) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The trial court convicted all the accused persons but on appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction of Qimat Rai and of the two appellants. In revision the High Court set aside that order. HELD: (i) There was no export of paddy within the meaning of Para 2(a) of Punjab Paddy (Export Control) Order, 1959. It follows therefore that there was no exports of paddy outside the State of Punjab in this case. [635 C] (ii) The Delhi Punjab boundary was, at the relevant point of time, at about the 18th mile from Delhi. It is therefore evident that there has been no export or attempt to commit an offence. [667 E F] (iii) There had been no exports by the appellants and as a matter of law a preparation for committing an offence is different from attempt to committing it. The sufficiency of the actus reus is a question of law which had led to difficulty because of the necessity of distinguishing between acts which are merely preparatory to the commission of a crime, and those which are sufficiently proximate to it to amount to an attempt to committed it. [666 G H] (iv) There has been nothing in the Punjab Padddy ( Export Control Control) order, 1959 that there had been any export of rice outside the territory of India in this matter. It was merely a preparation on the part of the appellants to transport paddy to Delhi, 'and so there was an attempt on the parts of the appellant and as such there was a attempt to export paddy to the Delhi, [666 D E] (v) There is no export in the present case. The only question that has been raised before this Court by the respondent was whether there was any attempt on his part to commit the offence of export. It could not be said that there were any attempt to do an act which constitutes the actum reus of a criminal attempt. [665 E F G] (vi) There can be no doubt that there is no exports or attempt on behalf of the respondent and as the matter of Law a preparation, for committing offence is distinct from attempt and those Which are sufficiently remote to it amounts to an attempts to commit it.

The assessee, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1913, was carrying on business in shares and securities of the Company. The assessee was a company registered under the Companies Act. It was carrying out business in share and securities. In the assessment year 1950 56, the assessee claimed that it had earned income from the managing agency commission which had been paid by the companies to the transferees and were not liable to tax in respect of the same. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that the Sassoons had not earned any part of the Managing Agency commission which was paid by them to the transferee and were therefore not liable for tax in regard to the same, but held that the assessee was entitled to receive the managing commission as it had accrued to them during the chargeable accounting period. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner upheld the order of the Income Tax officer. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The right of the assignee to receive a entire remuneration did not depend on any specific term between the assignor and the assignee but on the fact that what was transferred was an income bearing asset which carried with it a right to the entire income that falls due after the date of assignment. [372 E] (2) The rights of the assessee to receive, the entire remuneration for the year 's remuneration did neither depend upon any specific terms between the assignee and the transferee but on a finding that what had been transferred was a income bearing assets which fell due after that date could not be said to have accrued to the Sassoonons during the accounting period.[372 F] (3) The mere clause in the Managing Agent Agreement that the employer is to be responsible only to the assignee for the payment of the entire year ''s remuneration did no depend on a specific term from the assignee and the assignment necessarily took place with the consent of the principal Mill Company.

The appellant was a resident of Pachperwa in the District of Gonda. He lost his wife years ago. His eldest son, Badri and Kirpa Shanker were living with his father. The only other inmate of the house was the appellant 's second son, Kirpa Shankar. On the morning of August 13, 1963, Sunderpatti was found with serious injuries in the room where he was sleeping and the appellant was not in the house. The appellant was also present at the time when the deceased was sleeping. The evidence showed that the appellant had illicit connections with the deceased. The High Court confirmed both the conviction and sentence. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, HELD: (1) The extra judicial confession is a statement made by an accused admitting his guilt. The Evidence Act places them in the category of relevant evidence, presumably on the ground that, as they are declarations against the interest of the person making them, they are probably true. [657 E] (2) The circumstances found by the High Court, which lead to the only conclusion that the accused must have committed the murder. [600 G] (3) The circumstance found by this Court, leading to the sole conclusion that a statement, whether communicated or not, admitting guilt is a confession of guilt. But, there is a clear distinction between the admissibility of an evidence and the weight to be attached to it. Even if so much was established, prudence and justice demand that such evidence should be made the sole ground of conviction.

The appellant was appointed as an officer of the respondent company. He was served with a notice under Rule 5 read with Rule 9 of the Orissa Insurance Co operative Society Ltd. Service Rules, 1976. The appellant challenged the said notice by filing a writ petition in the High Court which allowed the same and quashed the notice. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Board of Directors had no power to terminate the service of an employee by giving one month 's notice or pay in lieu thereof. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Board of Management did not abolish the post but put an end to the service and put an rest of the services of the officer/employee. [224E] 2.1 In the event of the Society not having any further need of the employee 's service whether permanent or temporary which shall be decided by the Board, the Principal Officer shall give 30 days ' notice in writing for termination of his service or in lieu thereto pay such employee a sum equivalent to his one month salary including allowances upto that date including allowances up to the termination of the period of notice by way of compensation provided that nothing in these rules shall affect the rights of the society to dismiss an employee under Rule 8 for misconduct etc. without any notice or salary in lieu of notice, in the manner prescribed in these Rules. [225B] 2:2 The Board 's Management may form an objective opinion on the basis of the material, that the post which the officer or the employee is occupying may continue and would be put to an end by giving One month ' notice or Pay in lieu therefor. If the provisions of law or the rule are construed in such a way as would make it consistent with the constitution and another interpretation would render the provision or the Rule unconstitutional, the court would lean in favour of the former construction. But from the facts, it is clear that the appellant was not having no further need for the continuance of the post nor put an extended end to his service. [226F G] 2 :3 The Board did not abolishing the post and put a end to its service. It merely put an effective end to service jurisprudence necessitates the respondent to recast the rules in tune with the Constitution and the law. Thereby, there would be objective consideration before taking a decision, not only regarding the need to continue the post, but also the services and of the employees. [227F G]. 2:4 The Board had no authority to terminate an employee ' service by giving him one month notice in terms of Rule 5. [228G H] 2(a) The expression "in the event" used would mean that the employee may be permanent or permanent but the absence of the need for continuance of his post would necessitate to terminate it. [229F G; 229A B] 2.(b) The word "in" employed would mean "in case of temporary or permanent, which shall not be decided in a given facts and circumstances". It is thus manifest that an employee, whether permanent, or temporary, has an option to leave or discontinue by giving 30 days notice in his writing for terminating the service. If he does so, he will ordinarily retire from the Society 's services on completion of his 55th year unless the Board reserves to continue him in office of such period as may be determined from time to time. [230C D] 2 (c) The words "in any case" occurring in Rule 5 are wide enough to include a permanent or Temporary employee, but the expression "if the provisions contained in law or rules are construed so as to make it inconsistent with the provisions and the Constitution would render such provision unconstitutional, null and void.

The appellants, who were the highest bidders on February 20, 1970 and his name was entered in the bid register and the entry was signed. The Collector issued a fresh order dated August 19, 1970 for reauctioning the shops and wrote to the Collector of Mayurbhanj to call for tenders in accordance with that order. As regards the claim for the issue of a license under section 6(a) of the Amending Ordinance, the High Court held that it was a tax which was not contemplated by section 38 of the Bihar and Orissa Excise Act, 1915, and that rule 103(1) of Board 's Excise Rules in regard to the fees for the licenses was ultra vires the Act. The State Government issued another order dated September 19, 1971 under the provisions of the amended section 29(2) of Bihar and the State Govern ment issued a new order dated April 15, 1970 under the provision of the said amended section 30(1). The Collector called upon the appellants to deposit the amount realised by auction. The appellants challenged the validity of the order on the ground that it had been passed without jurisdiction as the Collector had no authority to issue such a notice in respect of the fees payable for the licences. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that section 6 was not made retrospective and that the Board ' Excise Rules were ultra vires. In appeal by special leave, the appellants contended: (1) that the High court erred in holding that the sale notice issued by the Collector was not for the grant of an exclusive privilege to manufacture and sellliquor; (2) that section 5 of the Act did not apply to the case of the appellant because the Collector has no authority under section 22(1), as the power of the State Government in that respect had been delegated to the Board of Revenue. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: (i) The High court was right in holding against the appellants that section 4 of the amending Act of 1970 was valid and the grant was not invalid. [717C] (ii)The High Court erred in law in holding the sale notices issued by Collector were not for a grant of exclusive privilege under section 19(1)(a) but for an exclusive right to manufacture, and sell liquor. The power of ' State Government to disregard the decision in Ajodhya Prasad 's case that the amount realized by auction was illegal and that section 8 was therefore ultra vires of the powers of the Legislature. [758E] (iii)The question whether section 6 of the Amendment Act of 1971 was valid or not must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. The question whether the Collector could issue a notice under section 4(1 ) of the unamended Act is to be determined on the basis of the evidence adduced by the parties. [759D] (iv)The power of "State Government" in that regard had been entrusted to the State by virtue of section 6 and the Collector, was not concerned and did not in fact issue any public notice for purposes of sub section (1).

The appellant was convicted of an offence under section 302 read with section 34 of the Indian Penal Code and sentenced him to death. The High Court reduced the punishment of accused No. 2 to one year 's rigorous imprisonment for life. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was corroboration of the evidence of Dinkar in material particulars in regard to the connection of the accused with the crime and in regard thereto the common intention. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The discovery of articles in the godown of Takalkar was as a result of a statement by accused No, 2. The name of accused no. 3 was found in the note book of Taknkar. The relationship of father and son between accused No., 3 and accused No 2 is not to be lost sight of. (2) There was evidence to connect accused No 3 with murder. The discovery was as result of an statement by the accused No,. 2. [648 B] (3) The recovery of articles from Taknikkar was a result o statement by him at the foot of it and that was the list of the articles sold to Gadekar. There was also a piece of hand writing with the signature of accused NO. 2 at the Foot of it. [643 C D] (4) The prosecution had failed to prove the case against the appellant beyond reasonable doubt. [641 F] (5) The High court rightly came to the conclusion that there were sufficient corroboration of evidence in material facts and circumstances.

The appellant was the owner of a plot in the final scheme calculated in proportion to the increment which is estimated to accrue in respect of such plot by the Town Planning Officer. Under section 64(1) (f), the amount by which the total value of the original plots exceeds the total amount to be deducted therefrom under any of the provisions of this Act, each of such plots being estimated at its market value at the date of the declaration of intention to make a scheme with all the buildings and works thereon at that date and without references to improvements contemplated in the scheme other than improvement due to the alteration of its boundaries. The Town Planning officer made a draft scheme for the area 87 in respect thereof. The appellant 's case was that under the Act the market value of each plot included in the provisional scheme with regard to all the building and works therein at that time and without reference to improvements envisaged in the Scheme other than improvements due to alteration of their boundaries. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Town planning Officer had no power to determine the amount of compensation payable to an owner for loss of land because under section 64 (1) the market price of the land at the time of declaration of the intention to making a scheme is determined by the local authority and not by the final plot. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The Town planning officer has a duty under clause (viii) to calculate the increment to accrue from such person as the Town Development Officer may in each case determine. [723B] In determining the difference between the total of the values of the respective plots and the total number of the value of those plots included in final scheme, the Town Planner has to find out the market Value of each of the said original plots at the place on which the declaration was made. The principle for determining the compensation is the same whether an owner of land is given a reconstituted plot or not; compensation is payable on the basis of the market valuation of the plot at the relevant date. [765E F] In deciding the difference in between thetotal of the amounts included in a final scheme and the aggregate of the total values of each plots included therein, the town Planning Officer under section 32 (1)(iii) has to see out the Market value of every original plot included therein at the said date. The principles for determining compensation are the same as those applicable to all lands covered by the scheme. [764C] In fixing the amount payable as compensation on each plot used, allotted or reserved for a public purpose or purpose of the local Authority which is beneficial partly to the owners or residents within the area of the scheme and partly to general public, which shall be included in costs of the Scheme; the Town Plan Officer under Section 32 (2) has also to find that out the total sum payable as damages on each plots used allotted orreserved for a Public purpose or purposes of the Local Authority which was beneficial partly partly to them. The town Planning officer under section 33(1)(ii) has a power to fix the amount to accrue by the owner or residents in accordance with the provisions contained in section 69. Under clause (xiii), the Town plan Officer is required to estimate the compensation to be paid to the owner and partly from such persons as the town planning authority may in any case determine, and that is the guiding rule in respect Of all lands included in an final scheme. The object of the Act is to provide for the payment of compensation to the person who is entitled to obtain compensation from the local authorities or from any person benefited or partly from the public.

The appellant was the third son of Seetharama Iyer. He had no male issue but left two daughters surviving him who were minors at the time of his death. The appellant 's brother Seetharamam was married to one Krishnapuram, and he died in 1934. The first respondent filed a suit for partition of the properties on the ground that the will was void for uncertainty. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the English rule of benevolent construction that a legatee has a right to choose in such circumstances apply to India also and had further held that on the construction of the will in this case the right to select should be in the legatees and not in Seetharams or in the bequestes. Held, (per Das, C. J., dissenting) that the words "he shall deliver possession" are contrasted with the words used in the will which show that it was Seetharaba who was the guardian of the three children will be in possession so long as the three sons were minor and would deliver possession of the remaining properties to the children as and when they became major. The words " he shall deliver actual physical possession" in the Will must mean that the testator intended that each daughter should select the land devised out of the vattam is fixed. But if the intention of the testator was not to give the selection to his brother, the case would clearly be of the third kind indicated by him in the testator 's will and he would have the right of selection.

The plaintiff appellant, Mohd. Bashir and Mohd. Rashid, was the owner of a plot in dispute. The defendants were in joint possession of the plots in dispute, being co bhumidars, because after the abolition of zamindari by the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act 1950 the plaintiff appellant lost her title by operation of law. The suit was contested by the defendants mainly on the ground that the defendants were not in separate occupation of the land or plots in question and the plaintiff had absolutely no concern with them. It was further averred that though at some time before, the lands in dispute were joint but during the consolidation proceedings the plots were occupied by Adiyaz who having acquired the rights of a Sirdar under the Uttar U.P Zamindari Abolition & Land Reforms (Amendment) Act 1950, the plaintiff lost her right by operation and, therefore, she lost her Title by operation. The trial court accepted the allegations of the defendants and dismissed the suit of the plaintiff. The District Judge also found that on the admitted facts even after the creation of zamindari, the position was that in 1357 Fasli the plaintiff 's name was clearly recorded as a co sharer with the defendants. The High Court also held that the plaintiff should be deemed to be ousted from possession, was not correct. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the suit was barred by section 49 of the U. P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1953 and the judgment of the High Court cannot be allowed to stand. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The plaintiff ' s name was wrongly recorded as co sharers with the respondents and continued to be so until 1359 Fasli as would appear from exhibit 2. [867C] 2.1 In view of the clear finding of fact that a clear fraud was committed during the Consolidation operation either by the defendant or by somebody else as a result of which the rights were sought to be extinguished, the possession of defendants apart from being in the nature of constructive trustees would be in law the possession and, consequently, the conclusion that the appellant should be declared ousted from the possession was not incorrect. [888B] 2:2 The High court erred in law in holding that the present suit was not barred by Section 49 of U. Pradesh Consolidation of Holding Holdings Act 1953 or that the judgment and decree of the District Judge cannot be sustained. [879D] 3:3 In view Of the clear decision of this Court referred to above, the High court ought not have interfered with the finding of facts in second appeal. [868C] 4:4 The High 'Court erred in holding the present case as barred by limitation and the order of the trial court cannot be upheld.

The petitioner, who was a Deputy Prime Minister of India, was appointed as Deputy Prime Ministers in Haryana. He was then functioning as the Chief Minister of Haryana when the oath of office of his new assignment was administered to him by Respondent No. 1. In view of the fact that the Constitution describes him as the Prime Minister and all other ministers sign as Ministers, he described himself as Prime Minister. The affidavit of Respondent No 1 contains the sub stantial part. And according to him, as long as the substantial part is properly followed, a mere mistake or error in the descriptive part would not vitiate the oath. This Court in the reported decision said: "In view of this fact that Respondent No 2 is just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Chief Prime Minister but the description of him as Deputy Leader does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Ministers, along with his other submis sions, we think the first contention raised by the petitioner that the prescribed oath should be divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and the other which contains the Sub stanual part. The words which precede this portion are merely descriptive of the person and of his nomination as a candidate. " In view Of the clear statement made by the learned Attorney General that Respondent 1 was just a minister like other member of the council of Ministers although he has not been described in the affidavit of respondent No. 2, the petitioner himself does not press it. The petitioner himself did not press this contention. He himself does so. So far as the second contention is con cerned, the petition er himself does no press it and it is dismissed.

The appellant was a public utility industry. The workmen were employed in the factory for the purpose of carrying on their business and they were paid holidays during the period of their employment. On the night of 1st November, 1948, the management put up a notice that the stoppage of work on the 1st December amounted to an illegal strike and a break in service within the meaning of the Factories Act. The appellant contended that the termination of the services of the workmen was not justified as it was violative of article 14 of the Constitution inasmuch as they were not entitled to annual holidays with pay under section 49 B (1) of the Act. Held, that the action of the 859 workers on the night when the strike was in force was illegal and the termination was not a concerted action on the part of the workers and that the non permitted absence as a result of concerted refusal to work even for 2 to 4 hours in the course of a working day amounts to an unlawful strike. The fact that a very large number of leave applications were put in for various reasons pointed to the concerted actions and that they were acting in combination both in striking and refusing to go back to work on that night would not be treated as depriving them of the holidays under the rules and we appreciate the spirit in which this undertaking was given and hope that the workers would also take it in that spirit. The effect of the stoppage was that the workmen would also have taken it in the spirit of the rules. The stoppage of Work on 1st October, 1948 was not an concerted act on the ground that no notice had been given to the management, the Mills being a public charitable industry.

The appellant, a film producer, was convicted under section 292 I.P.C. and sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three years and to pay fine of Rs. 500/ . The High Court dismissed the petition, ignoring the contention that once a certificate sanctioning public exhibition of a film has been granted by the competent authority under the (for short, the Act), there is a justification for its display thereafter and by virtue of the antidotal provisions in section 79 I. P.C., the public exhibition, circulation or distribution or the production of the film, even if it be obscene, lascivious or tending to deprave or corrupt public morals, cannot be an offence, section 292 IPC was attracted. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1 The prosecution is unsustainable because section 79 is exculpatory when read with section 5A of the Act and section 79 of the Penal Code. [501B] 1.2 In the instant case, the prosecution is untenable because section 80 I. PP.C does not contain any provision for certification of films. It merely provides that a certificate granted under it by expert authority can be stultified by a simple prosecution of a shower of prosecutions for an offence under section 293 IPC. [504B] 2.1 Section 79 Cr. Pc. prescribes. At least as a matter of interpretation, section 79 exonerates the doer because the issuance of the certificate and its effect that the certificate holder is justified by law in committing the act, or alternatively, that he entertained a mistake of fact, namely, the issuance issuing the certificate, and its effects that the Certificate holder was justified by Law in committing it. [401C] 2:2 The Board certifies a film as suitable for public exhibition and for section 292 Cr.Pc. to punish such exhibition unless the ground covered by the two laws be different. If, as here, the Board certifies an article of food which is not obscene, it does so. Thus the trial court when it hears the case may be appropriately apprised of the Certificate under the Act, and, in the light of our observations, it fills the bill under section 79 it is right for the court to discharge the accused as the charge is groundless. [506B C] 2 :3 The prosecution was unsustainable because Section 79 is inculpatory when read alongwith section 5 A of the .P.c. prescribing. At best as a question of interpretation of section 79 Crc. PC. resolves the apparent conflict between section 292 l.P.(C.) and Part II of the , relating to certification of film. If the offence were done by one "who by reason of a mistake or fact in good faith believes himself to be justified by laws in doing it" then also, the exception operates and the bona fide belief, though mistaken, eliminates the culpability. [420D] 2(a) The prosecution has failed to prove that the performance of the act which constitutes the offence is justified under law in doing the act. [467C D] 2 (b) The Board of Censors acting within their jurisdiction and on an application made and pursued in good belief, sanctions the public exhibit, the producer and connected agencies do enter the statutory harbour and are protected because section 70 is exculpatory while read with Section 5A. [468F G] 3:1 In the present case, it is not possible to say that what was merely certified as suitable under show by a law may not go the length of holding that it is justified By some other provision, then section 79 gets attracted and the mala fide belief that the film is obscene or not, does it generate a belief induced by a mistake.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader, was appointed as an Advocate in the Patna District, including lucrative land acquisition litigation, as part of the professional 'estate ' of a Government pleader. He was permitted to represent the Government in all the civil cases. The State Government issued a notification on May 7, 1979, inviting applications from the public for appointment as Advocates and to make appointments thereto. The petitioner applied for appointment of an Advocate and was selected by the District Judge. The District Judge rejected his application. In appeal, the High Court held that the petitioner 's client 's claim as the sole representative of Government in courts is not a legal cover for seeking lucre but for vindicating the inviobility of high public office of Government Pleader by politicking men in the Secretariat or by practitioners of favouritism dressed in 'little brief authority ', a deeper issue in which the Bar has a stake and the Bench must also be concerned. The High Court further held that there should be some provision emphasising the need for positive efforts at settlement, in suits to which the Government is a party. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1.1 The petitioner ' s client ' s case is a claim of monopoly of all government cases in the Bihar courts and hundreds of cases before a plurality of tribunals, it was but right that Government did not sacrifice the speedy conduct of cases by not appointing a number of pleaders on its behalf, for the sake of the lucred practice of a single government Pleader. [763C D] 1.2 The petitioner is undoubtedly the Government Pleader and has a higher dedication to the people. [771B] 1:3 The duties of the Government Pleaders, Madras are duties of a public nature. (36) The duties and functions of the State Pleader, Madras, are duties which are of an independent and responsible character, the office must be held to be a public office within the scope of a quo warranto proceeding. [761C] 1 :4. The duties, of the Public Prosecutor, Madras and elsewhere, are of a nature. [752D] 2.1 In every suit or proceeding to which Government is an party or a public officer acting in his official capacity is a Party, it shall be the duty of the Court in the first instance, in every case where it is possible to do so consistently with the nature of the circumstances of the case, to make every endeavour to assist the parties in arriving at a settlement in respect of the subject matter of the suit. [782E] 2:3 In every suits or proceeding, to which this Government is one party or the public officer acts in his capacity as a party, it must be the obligation of the court in the second instance, to do such things consistently with its nature and duties to discharge. [791A] 2 :4 The duties are of independent and accountable character, control the price, floor to ceiling, enforce commitment to the persons who are the third world clients, and practise internal distributive justice on basic social justice so that the profession may flourish without wholly hitching the calling to the star of material amassment immunised by law from the liabilities of other occupations. [802B] 2(a) The petitioner has a number Of other duties to perform. (b) The duty of this Government Pleader is only to the Government who are his Principles and that he owes no duty to the public at all and that for that reason he would not be the holder of a Public office.

The appellants held the shares of the Bank of India in favour of the Mills. The Mills, which was a public limited company, purchased 5,000 shares of it at the rate of Rs. 100 per share and it was considered proper to invest in the said issue of the said Bank the funds of this company to the extent of 66 shares only and to distribute the right of this Company to the remaining 1,600 shares of that company in the proportion of the rights to two shares of each of the Banks per one ordinary share held by them in this company. The Income Tax Officer rejected the appellants ' contention that the distribution amounted to a distribution of "dividend" and the value of the right released in favour was indisputably the value for the purpose of section 2(6A) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. On appeal, the High Court held that the release by the Mills of the shares amounted to distribution of dividend within the meaning of section 1(6 A) of Indian Income Tax Act, and that the value Of the right to apply for and obtain two shares was indisputably dividend within that expression and was taxable as income in the hands of the appellants. The High Court also held that since the release of the share by the mills amounted to transfer of "undividend", it was still dividend within ordinary meaning of that expression, and was chargeable as income under section 12 of the Act. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The distribution of the power to apply is not a distribution or distribution of dividends but is a distribution. It does not take the form of a resolution for distribution of shares. It takes the form into account both the normal and the extended meaning of the expression. [659 B] (2) The scheme of section 34(1)(a) of Income tax, 1922, does not purport to distribute dividend within it. But by the form in which the true character of the resolution could not be altered. It did not take into account either the normal or extended meaning. [613 C D] (3) The High court was right in holding that the distributed right to the Bank was undoubtedly dividend within its ordinary meaning and was therefore taxable as Income in the eyes of law.

The appellant was elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The election petitioner challenged the election of the returned candidate on various grounds, namely (1) that he had been kept present in the Court without permission of the Court; and (2) that the High Court refused permission to examine his 54 witnesses who according to him were kept present at varied. The High Court rejected the petition holding that the appellant was entitled to be examined by a witness whose name was not mentioned in the list. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The obligation to supply the list of witnesses within the time prescribed under sub rule (1), of Rule 1 of Order XVI is in respect of witnesses to procure whose presence the assistance of the court is t necessary. If mere omission to mention the name of a witness in the lists envisaged by sub rule(1) of Rule l of order XVI would enable the Court to decline to examine such witness, it can do so under Rule 1A of Order XVII irrespective of the fact whether the name is mentioned in that list or not. Sub rule (3) of Section 87 confers a wider jurisdiction on the Court for reasons to be recorded in writing to refuse to examine any witness or witnesses if it is of the opinion that the evidence of such witness or witness is not material for the decision of the petition or that the party tendering such witness and/or witnesses is doing so on frivolous grounds or with a view to delay the proceedings. [529G H] 1.2 The obligation under sub Rule (1)(a) of Order XVIII is in relation to witnesses to procuring whose presence, the assistance by the Court is t essential. If the party wants to have the assistance, of the High court under sub clause (b) of proviso to Section Save this the Court has no jurisdiction to decline examination the witness produced by the party and kept present when the evidence is being recorded and is not closed, and the Court had no jurisdiction either to refuse or examine the witness who is present in Court on the short ground that the name was mentioned in a list envisaged by Rule 1 A. [630G H; 653A B] 1:3 The only jurisdiction the Court can decline to exercise its discretion under sub clauses (a) and (b). Sub rule(3) provides that where the party has failed to mention his name in the List, the party would be entitled to examine these witnesses and to produce documents through the witnesses who are called to produce them under Rule lA. The only Jurisdiction the Court having to decline the examination of a person whose name is not shown in the Lists envisaged by Sub rule 1A, the court may still extend its assistance for procuring the presence of such a witness by issuing a summons through the Court or otherwice which ordinarily the court would not extend for procuring his attendance. [ 653C D] 2.1 In the instant case, the High Courts have exercised their discretion in refusing to examine the witnesses produced by them and kept open the question of refusal to examine them on short ground. The order of the Election Tribunal refusing permission to examined the witness is set aside. [663D F] 2:2 The only power the Court under sub section (3), of Section 89 of the Act is in regard to witnesses who have been summoned through the court and kept pending when the case is being heard. If on the date fixed for recording the evidence, the parties are able to keep their witnesses present despite the fact that the names of the witnesses are not shown, the Court may still extended its assistance to procure the presence by issuing summons through it. [662A B; 653B] 2 :3 The power under sub cl.(a) is in addition to the power conferred on the High courts under section 89 of Civil Procedure Code.

The appellant was appointed as Principal of the College in the year 1981. The Committee of Management of the college issued an appointment order dated April 27, 1981 to the appellant informing him that the Committee of management had suspended or withdrawn its power. The Manager of the Institution issued an order dated May 1, 1981 directing the appellant to inform him that he would be a formidable rival and wanted him to be out of way. The appellant informed him that his Committee of the Management had suspended/ withdrawn its powers. The Director of Education issued an office order dated June 27,1981 to the Manager informing him about the suspension of the appellant. The High Court held that the radiogram dated April 7, 1981 contained an order of the State Government in discharge of its executive functions suspending or withdrawing power of appointment of teaching staff including Principal and therefore the Committee had no power to make any appointment and accordingly the appointment of the Appellant was not valid. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that if the appointment was otherwise invalid, though ineffective and if appellant under the orders of the High Court functioned as Principal, discharged his duties and was paid, no question of recovery of amount paid to him could arise and neither the Government nor the Committee would be entitled to recover any salary paid to the Appellant. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order contained in the radiagram was communicated to the manager of the institution. If the power to appoint was riot suspended it would not be open to the Selection Committee to make and select appellant nor the Manager on behalf o the Committee can issue appointment order. [980D] 2. The appointment was thus valid and power to do so was withdrawn or suspended. [1081B] 3. The power to grant appointment is conferred by the regulations. 16A and the Scheme of Administration envisages setting up a Committee of Board of Management and the Committee has the power, to set up a Selection Committee for selecting the candidate for appointment as Head of an Institution as provided in sec 16 F. [882C] 4. The Regulations confer power on the State government without making any reference to the Board to make an order or take such other action consistent with the provisions of the Act, the second contention of Mr. Jagannath was that the appointment had been otherwise valid though ineffective, and if the appellant under orders of High Court functionsed as principal, discharged duties and were paid,no question of Recovery of amount advanced to him would arise and no question could arise nor the Government or the Committee could be entitledto recover any amount paid by the appellant could issue appointment orders. [888D] 5. The State Government could be said to have rescinded that A regulation conferring power on appointment was not suspended but ineffective though it may not be invalid. [89F G] 6. The selection committee had no right to select the appellant nor, the Committee discharged its duties and is paid, any question of recoveries of amount made to him did arise and Neither the Government and the Director could issue the appointment order to the appellants and the appointment could be by a body not authorised to make the appointment.

The petitioners, manufacturers of tyres to whom the fabric is supplied "impregnate the fabric with rubber and weave it into a fabric in the same way as is being done by the first petitioner". The petitioners state that the manufacturers of tyre to whom fabric is sold "imPregnate" the fabric in question was exempted from Sales tax, on the "rayon cord fabric" manufactured by them. The petitioners further stated that, as some questions were put in the Rajasthan State Legislative Assembly on or about 20th April, 1971, asking for the reason why this particular type of goods of the petitioners were exempted from sales tax, the Commissioner of Commercial Tax issued a letter to the Commercial Tax Officer to levy Sales tax on the 'rayon Cord fabric" sold by the petitioners. The petitioner contended that the goods now sought to be taxed are not the "end product". In any case, its view was that, until the statutory remedies had not been exhausted, leaving some "error apparent on the face of the record", still to be rectified by the High Court, a case for interference under Article 226 of the Constitution will not arise. The respondents contended that, in the case before this Court, the "tyre cord fabric", manufactured by it is woven by its purchasers "into a fabric" in the said way as was being done on by the second petitioner. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The definition of "textile" given in the Oxford Dictionary is wide enough to include "a textile fabric". It does not mean that the product must be a fabric which is a textile? [501 D] 2.2 In the instant case, it is not so much the point of manufacture at which the Mills sell their own product which determines the nature of goods which are entitled to exemption but it is the stage reached by this product, in process of manufacture of fabrication of a "textiles", which should decide the question correctly. [502 E] 2:3 The word "t Textile" has been defined as "a woven fabric". In the Oxford dictionary, the term "tlooms" is not defined either in the Dictionary or in the English Dictionary but in the context of the definition of the term 'textile". It means a woven fabrics. [506 G] 2 :4 The word 'textiles ' has been used in the sense of "a fabric which has its own meaning and includes any kind of cloth". In other words, it does not include a fabric for the purpose of manufacturing, of the composition of the "Textile" or "any kind of fabric. [504 E] 5. The word `textiles" is used in a generic sense and it means a fabric consisting of rayon threads in the warp and cotton threads. It does no more than mean that it must be an article which has been made out of a fabric. It is, therefore, difficult to find fault with the view of the High court that on what appeared to the High 'Court to be a question Of fact, it should not decide whether the product under consideration constitutes a fabric entitled to the exemption. [403 F] 6. The case of the Delhi Cloth Mills also does not appear to be correct. It merely shows that it is meant for "tloom" fabrics and not for any kindof fabric. Therefore even if the tyre cord fabric may be the end product for the Delhi cloth Mills, the crucial question is: Does this product constitute a fabric Which is a Textile fabric which was a textile fabric and not any other kind of manufacture. [ 503 E F] 7. The High Court should have interfered as the question whether the tyre band fabric is the end products or not in the final manufacture of an other fabric was quite irrelevant.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal on contract basis in different collieries and also doing allied work. The respondent was a Senior Supervisor in the company 's establishment at Dhanbad. When the matter was thus pending consideration, the respondent seems to have written to the Government stating that it would be difficult for him to attend the Labour Court Dhanbad since he has been residing at Hajipur and it would not be convenient for him if the case is trans ferred to Labour Court Patna. The Government of Bihar transferred the case to Labour court, Patna. In exercise of powers conferred by sub section (1) of Section 33 B of the , the Governor of Bihar after careful consideration of the application of the petitioner Shri Shivajee Prasad Sinha wherein he has prayed for transfer of adjudication proceedings to Patna keeping in view the difficulties expressed by him to attending the labour court, Dhanbad regu larly due to his residence at Hajapur is pleased to withdraw the proceeding shown in Annexure 'A ' pending before Labour Court, Patna and transfer the said proceeding to the Labour court Patna for speedy disposal from the stage at which the case was transferred. The appellant company filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of transfer. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Government was misled by the representation of the workman. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the key question for consideration is whether the Government before accepting the representa tion of the appellant and transferring the case from the Labour Courts Dhanbad should have given an opportunity to the management? [529G] 1.2 The validity of reasons given by the Government in support of the order is another question to be considered. [530C] 2.1 The validity or otherwise of the reasons given in support 'of the order transferring the appel lant and transferring of the case at Labour Court Ranchi to labour court Dhanbad, regu tered under Section 5(7A) of Income Tax Act, 1922, transferred the matter from the labour Court, Dhanbad to the labour courts, Patna for expeditious disposal from that stage. [630D] 2:2 The Government was induced by the representations of the workmen. The order of transferring the cases from theLabour Court Dhanbad to Labour Courts, Patna is quashed for not communi cating reasons to the assessee. This takes us to the reasons in making the order. Reference may also be made to a letter (Annexure E) from the Assistant Electrical Engineer in proof of the electricity supplied to the quarter occupied by the workman at Dhanbad.[630B] 2 :3. The letter of the Headmaster of the School in which the children of the work man are studying is not seriously disputed. The contention that the government was misled on the representation made by the workmen is also not tenable. [613C D] 2(a) In the facts and circumstances of the instant ease, it would appear to be prudent if the principles of natural justice are followed, where circumstances permit, before any order of transferred under Section5(7 A) of the Act is made by Commissioner of Income tax or the Central Board of Revenue, as the case may be, and notice is given to the party affected and he is afforded a reasonable opportunity of representing his views on the question and the reasons of the orders are reduced however briefly to writing . [631D] 3.1 A case with a not dissimilar problem was in Pannalal Binjraj and Anr. vs Union of India, ; , referred to.

The appellant, a hotel operator, was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling cinema tickets. The hotel workers were employed by the Hotel Workers ' Union to whom notice had been given under section 12(4) of the , as amended. The dispute was referred for adjudication to the Additional Industrial Tribunal, Delhi including the terms of reference. The Additional Industrial Commissioner, Delhi, held that the dispute should be referred to a tribunal and that the reference was vague as it did not indicate how many of the 480 workers of thirty different categories working in the hotel were involved in the dispute. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The dispute which was referred to the Tribunal was not incompetent merely because it is mentioned therein that the workmen will be represented by such and such union in the disputes. It was in our opinion unnecessary for the purposes of section 10 where the dispute is of a general nature relating to the terms and conditions of employment or conditions of labour of a body of workmen, to mention the names of particular workmen who might have been responsible for the dispute, and that officer who will actually represent the workmen before the tribunal, whose number was generally large. The fact that in the order of reference the words " as represented by the hotel Workers ' union, Katra Shahanshahi, Chandni Chowk, Delhi " had been added would not make the reference incompetent merely since it is stated therein that " the Industrial Tribunal may settle the issues in the light of a preliminary enquiry which it may hold for the purpose and thereafter adjudicate on the said industrial dispute." The fact remains that the disputes which were referred for determination were between the employer, namely the management of the hotel and its employees which were mentioned as its workmen. The nature of the dispute was also specified in the terms reference. It is not necessary to mention in the award as to who were the workmen who were responsible for it. [284 D F] (ii) The question whether a particular workman is entitled to be represented through an officer of a trade union of which he is a member, does not arise merely because in the application of section 12 the words used are "as represented by" and " such union" in the context of the present case. The mere technicality of reference under the Act which does not affect the competence of the order, of reference does not make it incompetent simply because it was mentioned therein, that the workman will be representing by such, and such Union in the matter is a living person can only be served through some officer, such as its president or secretary and it is that officer whom will actually represented the workmen. [285 D F G] (iii) The fact of the existence of the union itself does not alter the position that the employer is a party to the reference. In the present cases, the dispute which had been referred for arbitration was between the management and its workmen and it went to this length that the hotel decided to dismiss a large number of workmen on October 7, 1955. The question therefore whether the reference in this form is incompetent merely on technicality, for the union not being a living man can only serve through some officers, such like as its President or secretary, and it was that officer whose number is generally large, could only be serving through some person, such that officer might represent the workman before the Tribunal, such, as itsPresident or secretary.

The appellant imported certain parts of the engine and claimed exemption from payment of Customs duty in respect of the rod bushes and camshaft bushes imported by him. The Notification grants exemption in part from payment Of the Customs duty, in respect thereof, on parts of engines mentioned in column (2) of the Table annexed to the Notification, which is relevant for our purpose not only refers to internal combustion piston engines but also to 'parts thereof '. Heading No. 84.06 refers to 'internal combustion pistson engines ' Paragraph 2 of column (3) of Table annexed thereto to the notification, which reads as follows: "Internal combustion Piston engine engines ' paragraph 2 of the table annexed to this Notification, the heading 'part ' thereof, which was relevant for the purpose not including internal combustion Piciston Engine engines, and parts thereof. Heading 84.05 refers to "parts of internal combustion engines ' Paragraphs 2 and 3 of the said Table annexed hereto are all parts of such engines". The appellant claimed exemption under Notification No. 281 Cus/76, granting part exemption from customs duty in terms of the Notification No,. 281 C.us/ 76, granting partial exemption from the payment of customs duty. The Assistant Collector rejected the claim on the ground that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the notification. On appeal by the Customs authorities, the Appellate Tribunal held that the bushes and bearings are parts of internal engines falling under Heading No 84.04 and not a few parts thereof and therefore they are distinct and separate but there is no material for holding that the trees imported by the appellant were parts of an engine or engines. The appellant 's appeal to this Court was dismissed on the question whether the appellant is entitled to exemption from duty in view of the fact that the Notification exempts also parts of machinery mentioned under Heading 8406, and not parts thereof, and that the goods are parts thereof falling under heading No. 85.06. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD: 1.1 The Notification exempts only parts of a engines mentioned under heading 84.07 but it does not refer to the parts of any of the parts mentioned in Heading No other than Heading 84,06. [227F G] 1.2 In order to avail of the benefit conferred by the Notification it has to be proved that the parts in respect Of which the exemption is claimed, are parts or any of some of them have already been included under Heading Nos. 8406 and 8406. The notification does not, however, contain or refer to any Parts of the engines mentioned therein. [228F G]. 1.3 In the instant case, there is nothing on record nor is there any finding of the Appellate Authority or Customs authorities that the plants imported by appellant are parts in parts of their engines falling within Heading No, 84.09 and not as a few part thereof. The goods are covered by Heading No 85.05. [229H; 227A] 1:4 In the absence of any clear and unambiguous provision that exemption will be granted in respect to parts of engine mentioned under headings 84.08 and 85.04, it includes the parts thereof including the parts which must be all the parts constituting the engine or engine or parts in question. [226F G; 227G] 1 :5 The Notification does not say that exemption would be granted if it is satisfied that the part of the machinery mentioned therein is parts of parts of those engines and not any few parts thereto.

The plaintiffs filed a suit for declaration that the right and management of Dargah according to Muslim Law devolved on their two sons and one daughter, namely, Sayed Gaffar Sahib, Sayed Mohideen and Fathima Bee in proportion of 2:2 respectively. The defendants claimed that they were not entitled to any right in the management or share in the offerings in the Dargah and even if they were entitled to such right they were barred by limi tation. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the plaintiffs had failed to prove ouster of Fathiman Bee from the fight or management of the Dargah. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the defendants. In the second appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High Court was right in holding that there was absolutely no evidence whatsoever to show at any point of time till her death in 1957 that Fathim Bee had no right or claim of share in her management or offerings in any Dargah and that she was expressly ousted out from the enjoyment of any share in any share of the Hundial collections as such it should be held that her rights had become barred by limitation by ouster and as such the plaintiffs who were also claiming through Fathil Bee had lost their right by ouster. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The only controversy now left to be determined is whether the High court was right In holding that a right of Fatima Bee had become extinguished by ouster or as such she was specifically denied on any particular occa sion so as to put them on notice that from that date the possession of the defendants would be adverse to the inter est or rights of the plaintiffs of F.athimira Bee. [529G H] 2. The question whether females are entitled to a share in a Dargah is not a matter which has to be decided by the High Courts. It is clear from the pleadings that relations between Fathum Bee and her brothers were cordial and assuch there was no question of any knowledge to Fathmatma Bee that she had been being ousted from her right or share. [430C] 3. The plaintiffs were carrying a mistaken impression all along that females under the Muslim Law were not dis missed from their right or interest in the Wakf. Thus it is clear that neither in the written statement nor in reply to the notice of the plain tiffs any stand was taken that the rights of Fayima Bee or plaintiffs were specifically denied and she was impliedly ousted out of the enjoyment or possession of any portion of the Wakf property. [525D] 4. The mere fact that there is no dispute now as regards the period of 27 days falling to the share of Fafmatmaha Bee, does not mean that the parties are claiming ouster on the basis of expressed denial of Fastima Bee from their rights or interest. It may be mentioned at the outset that there has been expressed denial by Fathyam Bee and his brothers were strained and as a result thereof there was an assertion in the plaint that they had asserted hostile title coupled with exclusive possession and enjoy ment to the knowledge of Fishima Bee. The said admission clearly goes to show that relations among Fathma Bee and their brothers were bitter and as Such there was nothing to show when Fathmiya Bee was a party in that suit or any such question was raised or decided that females were not entitle to any share. Thus the only controversy left to the court is whether Fathou Bee or defendants were claiming ouster of Eathima oi e from the right or title of the plaintiff of Fashmatmah Bee. This clearly goes on to show, that relations amongst Fathom Bee and the plaintiffs were cordial, as such there was not question of no knowledge to them that they was being ousted therefrom.

The appellant was employed as a railway employee in the respondent 's factory. He was allotted railway quarters of a suitable type and as he had refused to occupy those quarters he was not entitled under the rules to any house rent allowance. The Authority held that the house rent allowances claimed by the 1st respondent were "wages" within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the Act. On appeal, the Authority held in favour of the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that there had been no illegal deduction from the respondent's wages inasmuch as the respondent had been allotted railway quarter of a similar type and that even so, the appellant was not entitle under the rule to any House Rent allowance. HELD: (i) The rules which must be included in the terms of contract between the employer and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one 173 1352 of the specified places will cease to be entitled to house rent Allowance. But it has been argued on behalf Of the respondent that there is no absolute right in the employee to the house Rent allowance being admissible, namely, that the employee should be posted at some other place like Bombay, Calcutta, 1350 Madras ' etc., before the claim for house rent was arose and that there was a condition subsequent, namely that the employees posted at any one of those places will stop to be so entitled. [1353 B C] (ii) The rule quoted above is inconsistent with the provisions of sections 7 and 11 of the , and that in any event if rule 3(i) aforesaid were to be considered as a part of the terms Of the contract between employer and employee contemplate, that anemployee posted at another place will cease not to be a entitled to the House Rent Allowance. [1453 D] (iii) The Rules which must have been included in "wages", are inconsistent with sections 7, 11 and 12 of the .

The detenu, who was one Indru 's father, was arrested on February 18, 1980 by the Customs Officers. On March 25, 1980, an order of detention purported to have been made under section 3(1) of the (for short called COFEPOSA) by the State Government was served on the detenus. The detenu received a letter, dated March 14, 1980 from the State Govt., requesting him to furnish the detenus with the material relied upon by the detaining authority in the grounds of detention. On April 3, 1980 copies were supplied. On May 2, 1980 the wife of the detenu addressed a letter to the first respondent (Under Secretary to the Government of Maharashtra), requesting him not to supply the copies of statements and documents relied upon in the 'grounds ' served on them. The detaining authority, however, calledously and deliberately refused to supply them. In reply to this contention, Shri Salvi submitted that the grounds were as elaborate as possible, that the substance of the statements had been incorporated in those 'ground ' which were entirely in favour of the detenus and the full texts of which have been with held, could not, by any reckoning, expose those persons to any alarm or danger at the hands of the agents or partisans of the petitioners. The State Government refused to furnish copies and conveyed rejection of this request by a letter dated March 18,1980. On the direction of the Central Government that the State government supplied the copies, it was not necessary to furnish any copies of the statement and documents to the detenu to enable him to make an effective representation at the earliest. The detenus challenged the detention mainly on the ground that (1) the detaining authorities had failed to supply copies of certain statements to the detenus; (2) the order of the detention, purporting to have be signed by Shri Salvai, Secretary in the Home Department, to the State of Maharashtra, was void because the concerned Minister of the State had never passed any such order and under the rules of business framed by the Governor under Article 166 of the Constitution, ShriSalvi had no authority to pass the order; (3) the detenus made a written request to the detaining Authority on February 19, 1980 for supply of copies of all the documents. The first respondent challenged the validity of the order on the grounds that (i) the detention was void as the concerned minister never passed an order and (ii) the rejection was communicated to the petitioner by letter dated February 14,1980; (4) the detenu made a representation to the Central Govt., which refusal was communicated by a communication dated March 19, 1981. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the delay of more than three weeks in supplying the copies to the petitioners had vitiated the detention. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 There is no unreasonable delay of less than a month in supplying copies to detenus. [352B] 1.2 In addition to the supply of the grounds, all the basic material relied on or referred to in those "grounds" must be supplied to the detained with reasonable expedition to enable them to make a full and effective representation At the earliest, there is a reference to the earlier statements of these four persons in which they had, on the basis of some account books and documents supported the contention of the Petitioners that the latter had acquired the gems in question from those persons. [353C] 1:3 The delay of three weeks has vitiated the impugned detention. It was on this short ground, it is difficult to hold that the detaining Authorities were not justified in refusing to supply a copy and conveyed acceptance of this prayer by a letters dated March 16, 1980.

The appellant was convicted by one of the accused persons for having committed offences under section 120B read with sections 148, 149 and 307 I.P.C. The High Court acquitted him on the ground that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the Code as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 is against the maintainability of a joint appeal by the State against an order acquitting several accused persons tried jointly. The appellant contended that the Full Bench decision in Beorajan 's case was not binding on it, because the view taken by the High Court was contrary to any provision of the Act. Held, that the High court was wrong in holding the joint appeal not to be maintainable under Cr. P.C., but so holding rejected the appeal without going into the merits. The Full Bench judgment of the Gujarat High Court rightly distinguished and explained this decision. The view taken in Rabari Ghela Jadav 's Case (6) does not militate against the dismissal of a separate appeal by a State against several accused person acquitted at a joint trial. It is difficult to distinguish the previous decision of another Division Bench and holding the view that the earlier decision was wrong, instead of following the usual procedure in case of difference of opinion with an earlier decision of referring the question to a lar ger Bench. The decision does not support the maintainability or the maintainability. The appeal must be dismissed. The judgment of acquittal passed by the trial Court is set aside and the order of acquittal recorded by the appellate court is restored.

The appellant was a firm called O.RM.SP. Firm which was registered under section 26(A) of the Income tax Act, 1922 (hereinafter called the ' 1918 Act '). The assessee claimed that in the case of business carried on in foreign territory the business as such was not assessed under section 3 of the 1918 Act but only receipt of the income in British India was assessed and it cannot therefore be held that the foreign business of the appellant was charged to tax under the 1918 act. The Income Tax Officer rejected the claim holding that in view of the provisions of section 25(3) of 1922 Act, income derived from business was liable to tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that the assessee was not entitled to relief under section 25 (3) because the assessee had only taxed on remittances received from the profits of the foreign company and there was no tax on the foreign income. The High Court held that in respect of interest on securities as well, and there were no taxes on the Indian business itself under the 1922 Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant: (i) that the Indian Income tax law did not apply because the foreign trade of the assessee could be deemed to have been charged under the provisions Of the 1918 Income tax act; (ii) that in any case, the income derived by the assessee from business activities was chargeable to tax and it could not therefore be said that the Foreign business of O.M.S. Firm was liable for taxation under the 1961 Act because what was taxed was the remittances received by the appellant from the foreign firm which was discontinued in the year of account; (iii) that there was a clear distinction between the two classes of income and the income received by O.S., Firm, and the profits earned by O,S. firm, and therefore, the Indian income tax law applied to the present case; (iv) that under the Income Tax Act, the assessee is entitled to exemption under section 24(3), in respect Of interest on security as well as, there was an assessment to tax on income received from house properties owned by the foreign partner which was discontinuance in the years of account. HELD: (1) The Indian Income Tax law does not apply to a case where the assessee has no business or profession and there is no question of any tax being payable under the head "Profits and gains of business, profession or vocation".
