[912 D] (2) The exemption under s 25(4) is general. The exemption is general in nature. The income received must be held upon the facts found by the appellate Tribunal in this case that the entire income of the Indian company was remitted to the assessee and tax imposed on that income was on the basis of various heads of income derived. [913 E] (3)(a) In the context of these facts the foreign trading business of a foreign firm must be treated as being charged under section 23(1) of Income Tax, 1922. It is manifest that by section 3 Of the 1922 act the charge was made on the receipt of income in India and as the income earned by the partner was derived from the Indian trade and was in relation to the foreignbusiness it must be taken that there has been an assessment under the 1948 Act within the meaning of section 23 (1). [914 B] (b) The assessee was entitled to benefit under section 28(3)(b) in respect o interest on capital securities as per the provisions contained in section 25.

The respondent entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said Department for the construction of the Capital Project. The applicant received payment for the same in accordance with the agreed rates. At the instance of the assessee, the Tribunal referred the following question of law to the High Court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the public Works Department is a works contract." The High Court answered the question in favour of the respondent holding that the transaction was a works Contract. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The terms governing the contract to which we will presently refer are not decisive and they would be strictly in accordance With the specifications and particulars contained in the Schedule and accompaniments hereof and the contractor hereby guarantees that the said articles would continue to conform to the description and quality aforesaid for the period shown in the schedule from the data of delivery of the said items to the purchaser and that notwithstanding that fact that 163 the purchaser may have inspected and approved, the said article be discovered not to conform with the specification and the contract will be binding on the contractor. [163H; 164A B] 1.2 The contract in this case is a contract of sale and not a workscontract. The delivery of bricks after manufacture was complete until the contractor had removed all rejected materials, and shall have the approved materials, stacked or placed in such position as may be pointed out to him. [164C D] 1:3 In the instant case, the contract in question is a work contract. The property in the bricks was entirely of the appellant. The essence of the contract was, therefore, the delivery of brick after manufacture. [165E F] 1 :4 The contract was a contract for sale and cannot be termed as a works contracts. The High court was wrong in holding to the contrary. [166B C] 1.:5. In Chandra Bhan Gosain`s case (supra) dealing; with those very common features this Court observed as follows: "lt may be presumed that it was understood that in quoting his rate for the bricks, the appellant would take into account the free supply of earth for making the bricks. The materials shall remain at the contractor risk till the date of final delivery. in Chandra Bhan Bas Gosain vs Commissioner of Income tax, , referred to.

The petitioner, a member of the Legislative Assembly of Jammu and Kashmir, was elected as a Member of the Lok Sabha on 4.2.1972 by the President of India in exercise of powers conferred by sub clause (b) of clause (4) of Article 352 of the Constitution. The Proclamation of Emergency issued on 3.12.1971 by the Governor of Jammu & Kashmir was revoked by him by the Proclamation dated 27.3.1977. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said Proclamation on various grounds, namely, (1) that the duration of the House of the People could have been validly extended only when a Proclamation of emergency was in force under the proviso to clause (2) of article 83 of the constitution and since the two Proclamations of Emergency dated 3. 12. 1971 and 25th June, 1975 were either ultra vires the Constitution or had ceased to be in operation by the time the House was passed by Parliament, the House could not have effect and consequently all Acts passed by the House during the extended period including the Finance Act, 1976 (Act 30 of 1976) were ultra vires; (2)(a) that even though the said Proclams had been validly issued, the Proclamation of Proclamation of AMIE was revoked on 21st March, 1977 and the Proclamation was revoked. The Union of India contended that the two proclamments of Emergency having been duly approved by the resolutions of both Houses of Parliament approving the two resolutions of Parliament as required by clause (3) of Art 352 of Constitution as it stood during the relevant time had not been published in the official Gazette of the Government of India. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The resolution of the Rajya Sabha and Rajya Sabha approving the Proclamation were duly published in both the Houses of the Parliament. [419D] 2.1 The two Procts of Emergency were kept in force by virtue of the resolutions passed by both the House President acting as President of the India in the year 1977. Since the two sets of emergency were in operation, when the resolutions were duly adopted amounts to proof of the alleged resolutions. [519E] 2:2 The production of the two Proclamation ofAMIE and the Rajya Assembly Debates containing the proceedings of the three Houses of parliament relating to the period between the time when the resolution was passed in each of the four Proclimations of emergency had also to be published in accordance with clause (1). But the real question in this case is whether the two Practments of AMJE and Rajya Assembly approving the said resolutions have ceased to operate before the expiration of two months from the date on which each of them was issued as the resolutions. The production, of the Memos containing the proceeding of the both Houses relating to period between 1st December 1971 and 31st March 1975 respectively is kept in operation until they were duly revoked by the two Houses of Legislature. [619G H] 2 :3 The resolution passed by either the Proclomations of AML and Rajya Panchayat approving the second Resolution had also been published by the Houses. Since, the twoProclamation of Emergency had also not been notified in the Official Gazette, the proclamation of AMDE was issued. [719G] 2(a) The production and distribution of the Proctos of Emergency are kept in suspended animation until they are duly revoked. [819A B] 2.(b) The Proclamation dated 3rd December, 1971 and the resolution dated 25th July 1975 respectively were not published in any official Gazette. The period of five years (being the period for which the House may, under clause (5) of section 352 of Part II of the Jammu &K Kashmir Act, 1951, be extended for a period of one year.

The appellant was the owner of a public temple. The said property belonged to the Thoguluva Thirumalayyan, the appellant 's ancestor for a sum of Rs. 20,000/ and that it was alienable private property of the family. On the other hand, the case of the respondents in their written statement was that the property belonged not to the appellant but was an alienable property of his family. The trial court decreed the suit in favour of the appellant holding that the said premises did not constitute a temple and set aside the decision of the said authorities. In appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree of the Trial Court and held that the premises in question constituted a temple within the meaning of Madras Act 19 of 1951. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the subject matter of dispute in the suit was the private property capable of alienation as it could have in either case no market value. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The High Court was wrong in proceeding on the assumption that whether the property was a private or a public Temple, it was incapable of valuation. [157 D] (2) The appellant ' s case was that in execution of the decree in Suit No. 650 of 1882 passed against the said Kuppaiyan the property is the private properties of the members of the Thaguluva family and that the allegation of the plaintiff that it belonged to him was "false and misleading". [157 E] (3) The subject matter in dispute was the personal property of a member of the Hindu Undivided Family. It was not disputed that the appellant had purchased the property for a valuable consideration. The case of respondents in his written statement is that the suit property belonged exclusively to Thogayyava Thirumala Thirumalaiyan, and that they were in management thereof for and on behalf and behalf of their family.

The appellant was employed as a clerk in the respondent company. The respondents claimed that they should be given cash allowance in lieu of the tiffin arrangements at present made by the appellant, and they urged that the practice started by the appel lant was not obligatory on the part of the appellant to make any provision for the tafin arrangement of its employees. The Tribunal held that the appellant was under an obligation to provide some cash allowance for tiff in lieu thereof, because he argues that it is not obligatory upon the appellant either statutory or otherwise, for providing any further facility to the employees by way of giving them a cash allowance. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The Tribunal has overlooked the fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the Appellant in re employing the retired personnel and, in fact, when after the award was pronounced in the proceedings of 1956 and this question was taken up for direct negotiations between the parties, the appellant agreed to consider the claim sympathetically and make a suitable provision in that behalf. [657 B] (2) The fact that some employees have been re employed and the correspondence between the respondents on this subject shows that the respondents felt that the policy adopted by them in re employs the retired persons was not based solely on humanitarian grounds. When the respondents had raised a dispute on this point in 1960, the State Government refused to make a reference on the ground that only 4 cases of reemployment had been brought to its notice, and so, the problem did not call for any consideration at that stage. [613 C D] (3) The appellant 's grievance against the direction in the award that as. /8/ and As. /9/ per day should be paid respectively to the members of the clerical staff and the substaff on all working days, can be upheld.

The respondent, a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund, was governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules whereunder payment of provident fund credited in his account in rupees was on retirement to be made in sterling. On August 26, 1947, Browne addressed a letter to the Chief Accounts Officer communicating the sanction of the General Manager for payment of the special contribution to the provident fund to Browne in sterling in terms of r. 1413 of the Provident Funds Sterling Account Rules whereunder payments were required. The respondent was an employee of the East India Railway and was a subscriber under the State Government. On February 22, 1956, Brownee addressed a communication to the Railway Administration informing that the amount standing to his credit in the Provident fund account be remitted to the Westminster Bank, Birmingham. The Chief Accounts officer intimated the sanction for payment to Brownee on July 27, 1955, and sent them to the Reserve Bank for conversion of amounts covered by the cheques into sterling and to transmit the fund in sterling to the bankers of Browne. On March 22, 1957, Brownie addressed a notice to the respondent informing that he had been informed that the money represented provident fund money and was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was "illegal and without jurisdiction". The respondent thereupon filed an application for execution of the decree against Browne and the appellant in revision. The High Court confirmed the order passed by the executing court. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court was in error in holding that the sum represented provident funds money and were immune from attached under the Law and that attachment was not "illegality" and without Jurisdiction. HELD : (i) The High Courts were in error by holding that by sending two cheques to the Bank for convert into sterling, the debt was discharged and the money must be deemed to have been paid out to the subscriber Browne, and the amount must be treated as paid out of the subscriber credited in the provident Fund Account. [1413 F] (ii) The order of attachment of the amount into which the two cheques drawn by the Railway administration were converted on encashment was contrary to the terms of section 3 of the . The High court was in wrong in holding, that the moneys remained under the control of the Railway Administering Bank as the agent of the Railways. When the amount lying with the Reserve bank as the Agent of the railway Administration was attached the Union had clearly an interest to maintain the application for removal of attachment. [ 1413 F G] (iii) The money in the hands of the ReserveBank as the agents of the railways was attached and the Union has clearly an Interest to maintain, the application was not contrary to section 3.

The appellant was a workman in the respondent 's factory. He was dismissed from service by the management on the ground that he had been guilty of misconduct under section 2(d) read with section 3(1)(e) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947. The Labour Appellate Tribunal held that the action regarded as punitive it was bad, there having been no enquiry whatever with liberty to the employee to meet the charge. In appeal by special leave, the appellant contended: (i) that the order of termination was not a disguise or cloak for dismissing the employee and the ground given that he was a cantankerous person undesirable to be retained was good; (ii) that even in a case like the present the requirement of bona fides was essential and if the termination of service was a colourable exercise of the power vested in the management or as a result of victimisation or unfair labour practice, the industrial tribunal would have the jurisdiction to intervene and set aside such termination. HELD: (1) The Court is not entitled to interfere with a finding of fact recorded by the trial court on this point. But if such a finding is based on no evidence, or is the result of a misreading of the material evidence,or is so unreasonable or grossly unjust that no reasonable person would judicially arrive at that conclusion, it is the duty of this Court to interfere and set matters fight. [417 B] (2) The power of the Court to go behind the form of the order, look at the substance and setaside what may masquerade as termination simpliciter, if in reality it cloaked a dismissal for misconduct 'as a colourable exercising of power by the employer. If such a conclusion is based upon no evidence or isthe result of any misreading of material evidence or was the result Of a misreading or misappreciation of the materials evidence, and is so unfair or grossly unreasonable that no fair person would ever judicially arrive in that conclusion it is for this Court, to interfere, set aside the termination. [517 C D] (3) The language of the orders in such a case is not conclusive and the tribunal can go behind it to find the reasons which led to the order and then consider for itself whether the termination was a device or cloak or for dismissing an employee and, therefore completely negatives security of service which has been secured to industrial employees through industrial adjudication, came up for consideration before the Labour Appellate Tribunals in Buckingham & Carnatic Co. 2 SCR 822) wherein the view taken by the Labour appellate Tribunal was approved and it was held that even if a finding was based on some evidence or the result thereof a misreading could not interfere with such termination.[517 B C] (4) The word "dismissal" in section 2 of the Act means dismissal which is not connected with any misconduct. It does not mean dismissal which may be connected with an offence and it does not include dismissal which has already been dealt with by the enquiry officer.

The petitioners, who were the victims of a serious breach of duty in sanctioning permission for the conduct of 'eye camp ' without ensuring a strict compliance with the conditions prescribed in the guidelines prescribed by the Government in that behalf and in not effectively dis charging the duties enjoined upon them to over see the satisfactory and safe functioning of the camp. The petitioners, a practising lawyer, were charged with serious breaches of duty by the State Government and the Sub Divisional Magistrate, appropriate follow up action was contemplated by the U.P. Health Service (Amendment) Act, 1988. The Committee deliberated on the issue and its recommendations in regard to the norms for conduct and management of eye camps. It recommended that a criminal case had been regis tered against Dr. R.M. Sahay and his team and also against officers of the Government who, according to allegations, committed serious breaches in duty in sanction permission for conducting the 'eya camp ' and without ensuring strict compliance therewith. The State Government issued an order dated 9th February 1988 directing that a case be registered against Dr.. R. M. Sahay, and his report be submitted before this Court. However, the petitioners filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the said order on the ground that the State had not taken any steps to ensure compliance with conditions prescribed by it in its letter dated 9.2.1988. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Government and its authorities were acting pursuant to and under the 255 authority of Government and that on the doctrine of the State action, the activity must be reckoned as that of the state itself which must, accordingly be held vicariously liable. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the petitioners that the High Courts had failed to take into consideration the provisions of the Act and the Rules framed thereunder and that the failure of the authorities in complying with the directions given by this Court would render the proceedings as a participatory exploration for relief to the victims. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The State would approach the matter not with the spirit of a litigant in any adversy action but would look upon the proceedings and as a result thereof satisfy the conditions of those schemes. These matters would have to be gone into in the criminal and other proceedings that may be pending or in the contemplation of the Govern ment. [419G H] 1.2 The State shall take up this issue and process the claims of the victims for such other bene fits under any of the existing Government schemes providing for aid to the aged, the disabled, and the destitute, sub ject to the condi cial that the victims otherwise satisfy the condition of those Schemes. [409B C] 1:3 The State should take up the issue, not with spirit of any litigant in adversy actions but would take up such a plea as was raised before this court. These matter would have been gone into by the criminal, and other proceeding that may he pending or at the contemplation o f the Government. [420C] 1 :4. The victims should be afforded some monitary relief by the state Government. They are, otherwise, eligible for any benefit of pension under any existing schemes now in force in the State, their cases shall be considered for such benefit.

The petitioner No. 1 was the President of a Board constituted under Section 3 of the Asom Rashtrabhasha Prachar Samiti (Taking over of Management and Control) Act, 1984. The petitioner No 2 was elected as the President on 15.12.84. He challenged the validity of the said election by filing a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the learned Single Judge. In this Writ Petition it was contended that the entire area of the Samiti was taken over by nominated members and the rights of the members of the Board under Article 19 had not only been restricted but has also been taken away. It was further contended that since 1984 when the Act was passed and a notification appointing a Board was issued, the Government had no right to take any steps to restore the Society back to its elected authorities and office bearers, despite the fact that the petitioner No 1 was a member of the Committee, he could not be allowed to function. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition holding that the Act did not provide for temporary transfer of the management and control of the affairs of the Samba r Samiti from the Board appointed by the Government and all the functions, properties and affairs of th e Samiti were taken over under the Ordinance and the Act and ultimately the Act which was the subject matter of challenge in this Writ petition. Allowing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The provisions of Article 19(1)(c) of the Constitution are not intended to provide as to how when the temporary measures comes to an end the elected Byabasthapika Sabha and Karyapalika would be restored. [176G] 2.2 In the context of what was contemplated in that Act and the noti fication issued under Section 4, the Karyapalka and Bya basthap omik Sabha which were in existence in 1984 when initially the action under the emergency provi sions was taken followed by the notification under the ordinance and the statute shall be restored back and they will take over the management of the samba r. [177G] 3.1 In the instant case, the Act does not provide as how when a temporary measure comes to a end the nominated members or the Board have also the right to continue to function and office bearer, despite this fact that there was no change in the constitution of the committee. The Karyapala Jyoti and Baya bastha Prachar Parishad which were functioning in 1984 had come to an e mployment and they had sufficient time to go on and in this view of the matter the reply came to an d accepted. [178H; 177A] 3:2 In view of this, it is clear that even on the basis of the provi ded the Act, and noti ce issued under this Act taking over the administration of theSamba r, Samiti could not have been accepted to be in accordance with the Constitution to elect a Byabur tion. [179B] 3(a) The provisions contained in Article 19 (1)(b) of thi s Constitution are intended to protect the interest of the people and to ensure that the citizens are protected against exploitation by unscrupulous persons who have been illegally removed from their posts without any compensation or protection. [180C] 4.2 The Act and notifica tion issued under section 3 of The Act as ultra vires by which a Board is nominated to replace the Kary Palika and Byabaikpika Panchayat which were admittedly functioning in 1983 when initially, the action taken under the emergent provi ssions was followed by notification under Section3 of the Ordinance.

The appellants, who were the daughters of a Hindu widow, made a gift of four houses at Asansol in favour of Kamala Devi. The gift was later confirmed on the occasion of the Dwiragaman (Gowna) ceremony which took place in December, 1938 and possession of the houses was also given to her. After the marriage, however, Sumitra Devi felt ill and the deed of gift was actually executed and registered on March 10, 1940, some two years after the marriage. The appellants alleged that Sumitra Devi had made a "sankalpa" of the gift of 4 houses at Churaman in favour Of Kamala Devi and the gift was subsequently confirmed on her occasion of Dwirakaman ( Gowna). The trial court held that the gift being of a reasonable portion of the estate of Ram Kishori Lal Sao and in pursuance and fulfilment of an ante nuptial agreement made by Sumitra Devi at the time of the marriage negotiations at Deoghar, was for the spiritual 461 benefit of Ram Krishna Devi. Held, that the plaintiffs respondents were not entitled to the reliefs which they claimed. The suit was rightly dismissed. The appeal must be dismissed with costs. The question whether a gift is of such a nature as would render it void or voidable under section 14(1)(f) of the Indian Registration Act, 1908, does not depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. It is open to Sumitra Devi to fulfil that promise as a religious act which conferred spiritual benefit upon her deceased husband, irrespective of the consideration whether she made a ' sankalna " at the date of the contract or not. The gifts were made long after the marriages and the acceptance of such gift was binding on the reversioners.

The appellant, a joint candidate of the Akali Dal, was elected to the Punjab Legislative Assembly. The election petition was filed by the respondent against Tej Singh alleging that he had got circulated pamphlets and posters among the voters of the constituency wherein he had mentioned that Ruplal had withdrawn his candidature and any vote given to him (Tej Singh) would be deemed to be a vote for Ruplals. The appellant, however, denied having indulged in any corrupt practice as alleged by Avtar Singh. The High Court dismissed the election petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practices were clearly proved. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant (i) that the evidence adduced by the parties was not sufficient to prove the charge of corrupt practice; (ii) that in view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between the defeated and the returned candidates, the election would have been materially altered. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The conclusion arrived at is that Tej Singh had actually paid for the posters which were printed at his instance and Rup Lal was not collected with the printing of the posters. [446C] 2. In view of this very narrowness of votes between the contesting candidates, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of Rup Lal would have gone to Avtar Singh cannot be ruled out and that would have doubtless materially altered the result of the election. [416D E] 3. The effect of the poster was that all the voters who would have voted for Ru Plal would now cast their votes in favour Of Tej Singh. Therefore, it is clear that Ex P 1 and P 2 which contained the appeal purporting to be of Rupl Pal were in fact printed at the instance of Tej Singh and Ruplary had no connection with the same. [420F] 4. The result is that the election of the first respondent (Teja Singh) is set aside and the election is setaside.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was charged with having committed criminal contempt of court. The High Court dismissed the application for contempt filed by the appellant against Shri Bhajan Lai, who was then the Chief Minister of the State. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondent and, in our opinion rightly that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of the High Court is to punish for contempt from Article 215 of the Constitution. When no punishment is imposed by the High Courts, it is difficult to say that the High court has exercised its jurisdiction or power as conferred on it by Article 215. [893A] 2.1 In a contempt proceeding there are only two parties namely, the court and the contemnor. It may be one of the reasons which weighed with the Legislature in not conferring any right of appeal on the petitioner for contempt. But when no punishment was imposed by High Court, it was difficult to think that the said sentence should not be imposed on the alleged contemnor. [888B] 2:2 The jurisdiction conferred or power on the High courts to punish For contempt includes also the jurisdiction to dispose of the case either by punishing the contemnor or by acquitting him. [869C] 3.1 Under section 19(1) of the Act, a right of Appeal has been provided for. When the High ' Court exercises its jurisdiction and the power conferred on theHigh Court is not controlled by Article 216 of the constitution. So long as no punishment be imposed by any High Court it is impossible to say, that the Supreme Court has exercised their jurisdiction or powers as conferred upon it by article 215 of Constitution. [879D] 3:2 In a proceeding there have only two sides namely, (1) the court; and (2) the contemnor; and 4: the contemnor.[893B] 3 :3 The High Courts cannot be said to be exercising its jurisdiction nor power conferred by Article 227 of the Consti tution. [ 894D] 2(a) In a Contempt proceeding there need not be two parties, namely, one of them being the court or the contemnor and the other being the contemnor, and the petitioner in such a case can move this Court under Article 136 of the Constitu tion. The aggrieved party under section 19 (1), can only be the contemnor who has been punished for contempt of Court. [877F] 3(b) In such a situation there would be no right of appeals under section19(1). [894D E] 4.2 When the Supreme court does not impose any punishment on the purported contemnor, the High Curt cannot be held to be exercise its jurisdicic jurisdiction or jurisdiction as conferred by article 216 of th e Constitution. It does not mean that when the High Commission wrongly acquits a contemnor after hearing the parties and after considering the facts and circumstances of the ease, the Supreme Courts can be said not exercising their jurisdiction nor powers to punishfor contempt under Article 215 Of the Constitution.[894E] 5.3 In such an event there would also be no question of any right or appeal against the erroneous or perverse decision of the Supreme Curt in not exercising its jurisidicic tion to punish the contemnor for contempt, and it is for the first time that under section 20(1), a right has been conferred on him. The petitioner in this case can only move this court under Article 226 of the Con troller of Civil Procedure.

The appellant was the tenant of a building in Bombay. The rent note provided that on non payment of rent the rights of the tenant would come to an end and the lessee would be liable to pay rent at the rate of Rs. 100 per month. The appellant filed a suit for ejectment against the respondent on the ground that the respondent had failed to pay the rent due from him. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court held that the provision in the rent note that on failure of the landlord 's title to the property would come back to an effective termination and that the lease was therefore determined under section 111 (g) of the Act. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The rule laid down in sub section (g), is not based upon any principle of justice, equity or good conscience but must be held to govern even agricultural leases and where there was a forfeiture by denial of landlord ' his title would come into an end. [1028 B] (ii) In the present case the High court was fully justified in holding that the rule laiddown in sub s.(g) is not applicable in this case. The rules as to notice in writing as a preliminary to a suit were useful maxims in general and that in general they reflect the point of view from which judges would regard (1) (2) A.I.R. No rule of equity, justice or good law can be invoked in the case of a tenant of this description. [ 1028 C D] (iii) The principle of equity is applicable to leases executed prior to 1st April 1930 and to leases made prior to that date on the mandate of the legislature and that cannot be done by the filing of a suit as in English law, in all cases not governed by the . [1029 B E] (iv) In general they represent the point from which Judges would regard. (v) The rules are useful maxim in general, and that is in general it reflects the point or points of view between which judges might regard (2). A rule of justice equity and good conscience can be applied in the cases of a tenants of this kind. [1001 G H] (vi) In particular they reflect a point of fact which judges may regard (3) A rule which is merely procedural and technical, cannot be invoked if it is merely a procedural and Technical rule introduced in the section by the legislature; and that if the sun) required under the section was paid or tendered to the lessor at the hearing of the suit the court has no discretion. In this situation the High ' Court was fully right in finding that in second appeal it would not interfere with the 1028 discretion of the courts below in refusing to grant relief against forfeiture. [1002 C D]. (vii) The principles of justice and equity are not such a variable commodity, that they change and stand altered on a particular date on which judges will regard (4) A Rule of equity cannot be applied to leases effected prior to the coming into force of the , or to leases issued prior to January 1930.

The respondents were dismissed from service. The appellants challenged the order of dismissal before the High Court in a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution on the ground that the enquiry which was otherwise fair and valid was vitiated because no second opportunity was given to them of showing cause against the proposed punishment before the issuance of their dismissal order as required by the Standing Order No. Rauf (fourth charge being held not to have been proved) the punishment of dismissal in respect of Emmanual and Mohd. Ruf was erroneous while another writ petition (Misc. 17) as requiring a second opportunity being given to a delinquent at the conclusion of the enquiry into his misconduct and before inflicting upon him the punishment was imposed on Rama Shanker and Barmapradhan. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the principle of second opportunity having been given to the respondents, it should have been held that no second or second opportunity could be given to A workman at the end of the inquiry proceedings and that in the alternative the interference with the punishment inflicted upon Rama Shanker & Barma Pradhan was erroneous. In appeal by special leave, the appellants contended: (1) The concept of second chance being given only to a workman who obtained under section Counsel urged that on proper construction of the Standing order it should be held that para 3 of the S.O. says "all dismissal orders shall be passed by the Manager or Acting Manager who shall do so after giving the accused an opportunity to offer any explanation", and (2) The principle of first opportunity being available to a person to show cause against his proposed punishment of dismissing, for, it was not disputed before us that if no such second opportunity is contemplated by it then the only ground on which the inquiry has been held to be invalid by the Arbitrator and by the High court must disappear. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (i) The language used in para 3 does not warrant any such assumption and, therefore, the interpretation placed on Standing Order 17, it will be clear that the only reason on which inquiry was held to have become invalid by reason of the fact that principles of natural justice must be implied and second the infliction of graver punishment before awarding which opportunity to showcause has been provided for. [368B] (ii) The word "may" in para 2 of S.0. 17 refers only to the punishment to be imposed on a delinquent, first holding of a 371 departmental inquiry into the charges where principles of Natural justice have been implied and third the infliction or of graborder punishment before imposing which opportunity has been given for. The plain reading of the standing order read as a whole does not show that the same is to be called for prior to the recording of finding that the delinquent was guilty of misconduct. [369C D] (iii) The words "may". are used in the last part of the section which makes it clear that no order awarding that punishment will be passed unless the Manager gives an opportunity of being heard. The language employed in para. 3 does indicate that the word "shall" is intended to convey a wide meaning and cannot be construed as conferring any power on the Arbitrator to decide whether or not to decide the question of punishment. [370F G] (iv) The expression "may", in the context, means "must". It is not necessary that the words used in Para. 3 should be interpreted in their widest possible sense so as to give a wide and liberal meaning to the word 'shall '. [371C D].

The appellant was a tenant of the land in question. The respondent landlord filed an application under section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 for eviction of the appellant on the ground that he had been in occupation of the said land for not less than two years immediately preceding the commencement of the Act and that the lease deed was executed by him after his death. The Rent Controller dismissed the application holding that the tenancy was created by the landlord after his demise. The High Court held that the appellant was entitled to protection under section 6D of Kerala Land Reform Act, 1964. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the tenant had been cultivating the land for more than two decades and that he was in continuous occupation of such land for a period of not less ten years immediately prior to the commencement o f the Act. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The appellant was in possession of the lands for more or less than three years immediately before the commencement. [112A] 2.1 In view of section 6 D of the Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1969, a person shall be deemed to be in continuous possession notwithstanding any order of court for delivery of possession to another person or any court record of dispos session. The tenant holding land less in extent than the ceiling area, had executed a deed surrendering his leasehold right to the landlord but had not actually transferred possession of such lands to the owner before the date of publication of the impugned Act. [113B] 2:2 In view Of section 6 C of the aforesaid Act, a tenant holding lands less in excess than the Ceiling Area, had become a tenant notwithstanding any judgment, decree or order of Court, where, on or after the 11th day of April, 1957, a tenancy was granted by a person who had no right over the land or who was not competent to lease the land. [114C] 2 :3 In view o section 6 A of the Madras Land Reforms Amendment Act, 1968, a landlord holding land more than in extent exceeding the ceiling limit, had been given a right to continue in possession after the 12th day from the date on which he became entitled to lease that land or his authorised agent or a receiver appointed by a court describing the payment as modavaram or nashtavaram and modanashtvaram or modanastavasaram or a receipt described as M.R. receipt. The said right was not in existence at the time of the commencement, nor could it be said that he continued in possession to be deemed tenants notwithstanding any decree or orders of court. [115D] 2(a) In view thereof, the appellant had been able to establish that he is in continuous and uninterrupted occupation of land for less than ten years before the coming into force of the Amendment Act. The tenancy was not created by him within the meaning of section 7 D of Kerala Revenue Reforms (Second Amendment) Act. It was only a lease deed executed by the respondent landlord after the commencement and hence, he could not be deemed tenant. [116E] 2.(b) In the instant case, the tenancy had been created by his father after his lifetime. The lease deed in question was executed on 11th April 1957. The rent payable to the appellant for the period of 10 years immediately following the date from which the Act came into force, was Rs. 1,000/ per month. [117F] 2 (a) The respondent had not been able or willing to pay the rent for the said period. He had also not paid any amount for occupation of any land in his possession before the passing of the Amending Act. Therefore, he was deemed to have become a tenants.

The appellant was convicted under section 135(b) (ii) of the , and sentenced to six months rigorous imprisonment. The prosecution case was that the cigarette lighters and flints were imported into India without an import licence and in contravention of provisions of Government of India, Ministry of Commerce & Industry Import Control order No.17/55 dated 7 12 1955 issued under section 3(2) of Imports & Export (Control) Act 1947, which was to be deemed to be an order passed under section 11 of the Act. The goods were also confiscated. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the goods in question were actually smuggled or brought into the country without payment of customs duty at a time when payment of such duty had become obligatory; and, therefore, the prosecution could not be said to have proved that they were smuggled goods. HELD: (1) The appellant was found in possession of the offending goods on 21 4 1967 There was no evidence to show that the appellant knew that the consignment must have been smuggled or imported into the Country from another country of their assumed origin after a time while the restrictions on their import had been imposed. [529 B] (2) Section 106, read with section 114 of the Evidence Act, was sufficient to enable the prosecution to ask the Court to presume that the person who has seized the goods must have smuggled or attempted to smuggle such goods without knowing that they are illegally imported or smuggled. [542 C D] (3) The mere possession by the accused of such goods could not enable the court to come to the conclusion that the offence was not committed. [543 E] (4) Section 116 of the Indian Evidence Act is a special provision and it applies only to goods seized under the Act in the reasonable belief that they have been imported or that duty, if leviable was not P d on them. The burden of proving that the accused knew that goods must be smuggled or smuggled is on the person from whose possession the goods were seized.

The appellants, who were the President of a registered Association, filed a suit for accounts of the Cloth Association at Budhar from April 1, 1946 to June 26, 1946. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the finding of the trial court and held that the other members of the Association were not entitled to participate in the profits made on the sale of 284 bales of the Gwalior cloth and inasmuch as Nagar Mal had rendered accounts with regard to all other transactions, the suit for account must fail. The appellants appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (i) The suit before the High court was not one for accounts or of an illegal association which was in existence at the relevant period for which accounts were asked. [782 E] (ii) It is enough to point out that under the , an unregistered firm is not illegal; there is no direct compulsion that a partnership firm must be registered, though the disabilities consequent on non registration may be extremely inconvenient. [779 G H] (iii) The question whether a partnership Firm can be registered or not is a matter of fact and it cannot be decided in proceedings instituted by one member of an unlawful association against another in respect of the partnership transactions, it is competent to the defendant to resist the proceedings on the ground that illegality may be a defence. [780 G H; 782 A] (iv) The provisions of section 69(3)(a) of the Partnership Act, 1932, are not applicable to the facts of this case.

The respondents were prosecuted for offences under section 9(1) read with sec. The allegation against them was that on 8.6.1986 at 2.00 P.M., they along with two others named in the complaint, shot and killed an elephant in compartment No. 1 of compartment No,. 1 of the compartment No.. 1 of a compartment No .1 of compartment no. 1. The High Court quashed the proceedings of the Magistrate taking cognizance of the offence and ordering issue of process against the respondents. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) Section 50(1)(a) of the Criminal Procedure Code provides that when the High Court is could upon to exercise its jurisdiction to quash a proceeding at the stage of the magistrate taking cognizance, the High court is guided by the allegations, whether those allegations, set out in the charge sheet do not in law constitute or spell out any offence and that resort to criminal proceedings would, in the circumstances, amount to an abuse of process of the Court or not. [748C D] (2) The words "where such contempt is an offence punishable under the Indian Penal Code" and does not say 'there the act alleged to constitute such contempt was an offence '. [777E F] (3) Section 2(3) of Contempts of Courts Act, 1953 defines a criminal offence as meaning any act or omission which constitutes an offence under the IPC and does no mention 'There the act complained to constitute the same offence. [771A B] (4) The word "offence" in section 2(2) of Criminal Procedure is not defined in the Code but includes all acts done by a person who is alleged to have committed or is alleged, as an offence. In other words, the definition of criminal offence under section 2 (3), does not include any act done by any person with the consent of the person committing the offence. The word 'offence ' in section 3(1), therefore, includes all actions taken by a public servant in pursuance of the complaint or on his behalf in pursuance thereof. [773E F; 776A] (5) Section 20 of the Act does not refer to any act which constitutes contempt of a subordinate court. The expression "offence ' is used in section 20 of Criminal P.C. and it includes all proceedings taken by an officer in pursuance thereto. [779D E] (6) The expression 'offence" occurring in section 21 of the Code of Criminal procedure, 1973, does not mean any act committed by a party with the knowledge or consent of that person. It is only when the act constituting the offence is punishable under section 20(1). In other word, the word " Offence" has been used in the sense of the term "offence". [779A B C] (7) The definition of 'criminal offence' in section 5(2), does indicate that it includes any act by a member of an unlawful assembly or any person who was a party to the criminal conspiracy. [780D E; 778B] (8) Section 3(3)(a)(i) of Indian Penal code, 1973 defines a 'criminal act ' as meaning an act or an omission which is an act done in pursuance with the intention of causing wrongful gain and wrongful loss to the Government by any member of the unlawful assembly. [781A B; 780C] (9) The offence under sec. 9(2)(a), IPC, therefore, falls within the overlapping areas between sec 42 ', IPC on the one hand and 9(3).

The petitioner was convicted for an offence under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal, this Court, HELD: (1) A liberal policy of conditional re lease without monetary sureties or financial security and release on one 's own recognizance with punishment provided for violation will go a long way to reform the bail system and help the weaker sections of the community to get equal justice under law. [785 F] (2) The socialist republic is brought out in the Report: "The evil of the bail System is that either the poor accused has to fall back on touts and professional sureties for providing bail or suffer pre trial detention. In one case, the poor victim is fleeced of his moneys by touts, and professional surety and sometimes have even to incur debts to make payment to them for securing their release; in the other he is deprived of his liberty without trial and conviction and this leads to grave consequences, namely, (1 ) though presumed innocent he is subjected to 343 the psychological and physical deprivations of jail life; (2 ) he lost his job, if he has one, and is deprived Of an opportunity to work support himself and his family with the result that burden of his detention falls heavily on the innocent members of the family, (3) he is prevented from contribution to the preparation of his defence; and (4) the public exchequer has to bear the cost of maintaining him in the jail.

The assessee was a registered firm. The assessee claimed under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 exemption from tax in respect of 6% of its capital employed in 'Eldee ' as a newly established undertaking and sought to include in the computation of the capital so employed Rs. 3,21,460 advanced to 'Castle '. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim on the ground that in his view there were in these two undertakings the same eight partners with a share of /2/(two annas) each and that the constitution of both the undertakings being the same, 'Centle ' could not be regarded as separate entity. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected the assessee 's petition under section 66(1) of the Income tax. But the Tribunal modified the assessment and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to the assessee in the calculation of capital invested for the purpose of 429 section 15 C. The High Court, however, held that the finding of the Tribunal was one of fact as it was based on the inference arising from the non inclusion by the Income Tax Officer in the assessment in question of the income of 'Cantle ' and that "the factor taken into consideration by the Appellate Tribunal in coming to the conclusion, it did, was a relevant factor. The Commissioner appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) Under the Incometax Act it is for the Tribunal to decide all questions of fact arising out of the order of the tribunal. But where there is some evidence to support the finding on a question of law arises out of that order, it cannot be regarded either as a finding not giving rise to a question liable to be referred to the Court. [457 F] (ii) The High Courts have the power to call upon the Tribunal, to state a case and to refer it, if the Appellate tribunal has refused to state the case on the view that no question of fact arises.

The order of the High Court is set aside. The Minister, respondent No. 1, was a party to the writ petition filed by him against the Minister in charge of Irrigation Department of the Punjab Government. During the course of the heating of the writ petitions, an order was made by the High court on November 18, 1974 whereby the Minister concerned might give a personal hearing to the parties and thereafter pass the necessary order in the matter. The High Court directed that the Minister should file his affidavit. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that looking to the facts of the case if the High Courts came to the conclusion that the minister was a necessary or proper party, this Court should not interfere in the matters. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The direction for impleading the Minister as a party was given by the high court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made in the petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of the facts and circumstances of the present case, this court does not feel persuaded to interfere with the order of High Court adding the Minister. [971B] 2. The order whereby the minister concerned was directed to file his personal affidavit is setaside. The appeal shall stand disposed of accordingly. [982C D] 3. The other part of the order whereby Minister concerned was ordered to file an affidavit is restored. [993E] 4. The matter is remitted back to the High Cou rt for deciding in the light of the averments made in this petition as to whether he should or should not file an Affidavit.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. The rent was due as arrears of rent on the basis of a lease in favour of the respondent. The respondent filed an application under section 259 of the Act for realisation of a sum of Rs. 649.50 from the respondent under section 261 of the Punjab Municipal Act, 1911. The Magistrate ordered recovery of the amount. On appeal by the respondent the High Court held that arrears of land rent due under a lease cannot be recovered under section259 of the . Held, that the provisions of section 259 will apply only if such rent is recoverable by a Board or a Military Estate Officer under the Act or the rules made thereunder. The words "rent on land and buildings" which appear between the words "any tax" and "any other money" must equally be governed by the words 'claimable by a board etc." In the present case, the proceedings before the Magistrate were not one under the Code of Criminal Procedure and therefore neither could a reference be made by the Sessions Judge to the High court under section 438. The second point was that upon a correct interpretation of section259 the Magistrate had the power to recover rent due to the appellant in the manner provided for in the section. The two cases upon which reliance was placed before the High Courts arose under section 81 of the Code and therefore, neither could the reference be said to be by the High Judge to that High Court under section 439. The third point is that upon an correct interpretation Of section 259 the Magistrate has the power under section 437 to recover all arrears of rents on land or buildings only if the rent in the sections refer only to rent directly claimable under the . Act or, the Property Rules or the Land Administration Rules but under the lease in respect of rent of land or building under the management of the Board neither remedy would be available though the claim for the rent is ultimately traceable to those provisions of the , and the Rules which empower the Board to let out the land or houses upon the ground that it cannot be said that it could not be said 'to be claimable or recoverable under any express provision of the statute.

The appellant was appointed as a Section Salesman and his services were controlled by the head office through its territory office situated in Delhi. The appellant was employed for canvassing and pushing and promoting sales of the company 's product in his area. The various correspondence and other evidence produced before the Labour Court showed that the appellant was engaged for canvassing, ping and promoting the sales of company ' s product in their area. Neither the section sales . man nor the local salesmen were employed to sell the products of the Company and to collect the amount of sale. The Tribunal also found and in fact it has referred to as an admitted case of both the parties that the respondent company sells its product i.e. cigarettes manu factured by it directly through their wholesalers who in turn sell the product to various dealers appointed by the company in the area. Both the parties were employed by the appellant in order to canvass and promote the sales in this area. Even though the Tribunal noted that the appel lant was employed to do canvassing and promot ing sales for the company, it did not interfere with that finding. The Labour Court held that the termination itself was illegal. In appeal before this Court, on behalf of the appellant it was contended that the Labour Commis sioner had given findings in favour of the appeli lant on the question whether the termination alone was illegal and invalid and if not to what relief he was enti tled to. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The finding of the Tribunal for coming to the conclusion that the appellants were not a "workman" is correct. [401C] 2.1 In the instant case, the object of this enactment and the employees covered by the enactment also go to show that persons employed for sales promotion normally would not come within the definition of workmen under the Industrial Dis putes Act. The object of the enactment and th e employees covered under the enactment are also gone to show the fact that persons engaged for sales promotions normally would be not coming within the purview of the Industrial Disputes Act. [467D] 2:2 In the light of our holding that the is not applicable to him and in view of the fact tha that a long period of over 16 years had passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage. [468F] 3.1 The object and employees covered in the enactment specifically go to showing that persons appointed for sales promoted normally would come within th e definition of workman under the industrial Disputes Act as it stood in the year 1973 when the appellant 's service was terminated, in addition to whatever amount they were paying during the pendency of the appeal under orders of this Court. [469F] 2 :3 The object is also to show by ways and means to improve the sales, a study of the type or status of the public to whom the product has to reach and a studyof the market condition. The supervising work of the other local salesman was part of his work considered by the Tribunal as only incidental to his main work of canvassing and promotion in the areas of his operation. [470G] 2 4.2 In order to come within definition of 'workman under the Act, also go a to show whether persons employed For sales promotion generally would not coming under the definition o f workmen under th e Industrial Disputes act as it stands in the yeastastasthatastastabastastardastasthyastastyasthyth. The duties involve the suggesting of ways and mean to improve sales, an study of a type or Status of the Public to whom a product hasto reach and an studyofthe market condition,. The supervision work of other local Salesmen was part part of their work considered as only ancillary to his primary work of canvass and promotion.

The appellants, a private limited company, were the owners of certain lands in Madhya Bharat. The Company was granted a lease of the land on the terms and conditions stipulated therein. The respondent company had leased out the said land to the appellant company for a period of five years from 1.4.1977 to 31.3.1978. The lease was renewed by the State Government under section 181 of the M.P. Land Revenue and Tenancy Act, Samvat 2007 (Act No. 66 of 1950) on the condition that the Company shall pay the rent agreed upon between the Government and the Company subsequent to the unconditional withdrawal by the Company of its Civil Appeal No. 1 of 1961. The appellant company was granted the lease in respect of the said lands on the conditions stipulated in the lease deed. The company had also leased out certain other lands to the respondent company for the period from 1st April, 1977 to 31st March, 1978. The land was leased by the Government under Section 181 of that Act to the Company for a term of five year and the lease was extended upto 31st May, 1978 on condition that it shall pay all arrears of rent payable by the lessee in respect thereof within one month from the date of expiry of the period of lease. The appellants filed an application before the Additional Collector under section 182(2)(i) of the Act for eviction of the Company from the land in question. The Additional Collector dismissed the application holding that the land admeasuring 495.05 acres was held by the company in terms of the lease granted by the Central Government and it was not a `pakka ' tenant and did not enjoy the status of a " Gair Maurusi" tenant. Aggrieved by the order of the Additional Commissioner, the Company preferred an appeal before the Collector under Section 182(1)(i). The High Court held that the company was not entitled to be proceeded against in terms Of section 182 of the Code as it had not become a `Pakka " tenant and that it had never been an ordinary term as defined in the Madhya Bharat Act No. I have already explained above that to these lands the provisions of the Zamindari Abolition Act did not apply, since they were already held by State when that came into force. The High court also held that since the Company failed to pay the agreed rents and thus contravened the conditions of the Lease, proceedings were initiated by the 178 Additional Collector by his Order dated 1.10.1977 for eviction from the lands in question; and dismissed the appeal. Hence this appeal by the appellants. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts had found in the earlier proceeding that the Land admeasuring 495,05 acres belonged to the company under lease from the Government after it had been acquired by the government for a public purpose of the State. [180B] 2.1 In terms of sub section (2) of Section 182 that the Additional Chief Collector made his order for eviction and dismissed his appeal. The finding of the High Court to the contrary was, in our view, totally unjustified and opposed to law. [181C D] 3.2 The High 'Court had found that the State had not been holding the land under lease at any time prior to the coming into force of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue & Tenancy Act No 66 of 1951. Therefore, it was, according to the said Act, an ordinary tenant. [182D E] 4.3 In terms Of sub section 2(i) and sub section 1 (2), the Company has been holding land from the State government and it had ever been an existing lessee in relation to such land.

The Orissa Land Reforms (Amendment) Act, 1964 received the assent of the President on October 17, 1960. By section 1(3) of the principal Act it was provided that the Act shall come into force in whole or in part on such date or dates as may be appointed for different provisions of the Act. Chapter IV in the principal enactment by orissa Act 13 of 1965 empowered the State Government to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the said Act. By a notification the Government of the United State brought the Travancore Act 14 of 1124 (M.E.) into force, and referred cases of tax payers for investigation to the Commission appointed in that behalf. The Commission appointed under section 1 of the Travancore Cochin Act 14 Of 1960 was constituted on July 1, 1949. By an order dated October 17 1960 the Government issued a notification under section 3 of the Orissa Land Reform (Amendment ) Act, 1965 authorising the appointment of a Commission and referring the cases of the petitioners to the commission appointed in the said behalf. On December 2, 1963 the State of Orissa brought the Act into force by section 1 (3) on the date appointed by the State Govt. by notification. By another notification the State made the provisions of Ch. IV of the Principal Act applicable to certain lands in the personal cultivation of a person was guaranteed by the second proviso only where the land is within the ceiling limit applicable to him under any law for the time being in force or any building or structure standing thereon or appurtenant thereto, unless the law relating to the acquisition of such land, building or structures, provides for payment of compensation at a rate which ,hall not be less than the market value thereof thereof. The notification was challenged by the petitioners on the ground that it was inconsistent with or takes away orabridges any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution, and that section 47 incorporated by Act 13 Of 1965 which provided for compulsory acquisition of any land in an estate under the personal cultivating tenancy of the holder, compensation could not be more than the value of the land if such land was within the Ceiling limit applicable. The High Court held that section47 incorporated by the Act 14of 1124(M. E.) was not law in force until a notification was issued bringing into operation the provisions Of Ch.IV of the parent Act, which empowered the appointment and proceedings under the principal act. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that the Travancore Land Reforms Act 16 of 1960 was not applicable when the United States was formed, the notification bringing the Act in force was ineffective. HELD : (i) The provisions of section 1 Of the principal statute were not applicable to the landholders under any laws for the purpose of acquisition by the Government. [419 G] (ii) The Travancore Act was a law in operation, but until the power is exercised by the successor State it could not have been deemed to be law in effect and since no notification was made before Ch. V of the 1948 Act was repealed there was no ceiling limit on the landholders. [409 E F] (iii) The contention that section 1 was in operation on July 31, 1949 and the subsequent legislation sought to restrict the ceiling limits and to vest the surplus land in the Government under section 45 as amended, there was compulsory acquisition by notification, and since the subsequent Act seeks to restrict it and vest the excess land in Government under Section 45 as substituted, there is compulsory acquisition.

The widow 's estate was in the hands of a Hindu widow, and she had no interest left in her, which she could make a surrender of in favour of the reversions. The widow 'Sreeramu died on April 1, 1946 leaving behind his widow, the widow, two daughters and one daughter. After the death of her husband, the heirs of the widow were brought up by the widow for the benefit of the estate. The suit was decreed by the trial court but the High Court reversed the decree holding that the widow ' had no right to make a transfer in favour Of the reversion 's property. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that as the widow herself was in capable of disputing the title of the alienee or of the person who has acquired interest by adverse possession against her, a like disability attaches to the reversioner also who could not have obtained the properties but for the surrender made by the widows. HELD: (i) The right to challenge it is no part of the wife 's Estate at all and, therefore, could not be surrendered to the reversioners. [355 D] (ii) In case of alienation by a Hindu wife of her deceased husband 's Property without any justifying necessity or in the case of a stranger acquiring title against her the interest created is to destroy the widow's estate in the same way as if she suffered physical or civil death, there is no conceivable reason why the reversioner should not, subject to any question of fraud or collusion that might arise, be in a position to recover possession of the properties from (1) Vide Vaidyanatha vs Savithri, I.L.R. , referred to. (iii) The widow herself may be incapable of inheriting from her own grant and disputing the alienation which she has herself made; but as has been said already, surrender is not an alienation and as the reversioner does not derive his title from her, there was no principle of law under which the acts of the widows could bind him. [356 E F] (iv) The fact that a surrender is a voluntary act on the part of a widow and she is under no legal or moral obligation to surrender her estate, would not affect the right of the reversioner.

The appellants, who were the Directors of a Polytex Company, filed a suit against the respondents for a declaration that the requisitionists of the meeting dated October 1, 1985 and the Chairman of the Board of Directors of the company had ceased to have the rights of a member under section 169 of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the meeting was validly called since the Cotton Mills Company had ceased not enjoy the privileges of a shareholder by reason of the appointment of a Receiver by the Collector of Kanpur in respect of the ten lakhs shares held by the Cotton Mill Company and that the Board had no power to appoint any Receiver. The High Court dismissed the suit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the extraordinary general meeting had not been validly called as since the cotton Mills Company has ceased to enjoy the privilege of a share in the Polytex company by reason Of the appointment, of a receiver by the collector of Kanpur and that therefore the order of the Collector being an order in the nature of a charging order the Receiver had obtained an equitable right in the shares in question and there being no other legal or equitable right which would prevail over it, the Cotton mills Company had lost its right to the shares. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The order of Collector being a order in a charge order the receiver has obtained an enforceable right in his shares in respect thereof. [878G] 1.2 The attachment of the shares of the Polytechnic Company held by it had not deprived the Cotton Corporation of its right of vote at the meeting or to issue the notice under section 170 of the U. Thapar as a Director of the Company. The fact that 3,50,000 shares have been pledged in favour of the Government of Uttar Pradesh also would not make any difference Sections 172 to 178 A of the deal with the contract of pledge. [888G H] 1:3 The order passed by this Court on February 1,1985 was an order made under section 18AA (1) (a) of the Industries (Development and Regulation) Act 1951 taking over six industrial units of the Cotton Textiles Company. It is also significant that the Directors had in this case rightly treated the registered holder i.e. the Cotton Textile Company as the owner of the share in question. The costs of all the parties to the above appeal and other connected cases shall, however, be borne by the Polyineries Company. Subject to the order, the order passed in this Court shall remain in force. [898G] 2:4 In view of the foregoing the pawnee in the instant case i. e. the Government Of Uttar Pradesh could not be treated as the holder of the rights pledged in its favour. the cotton mills Company continued to be the member of the polytex Company in respect for the said shares and could exercise its rights under section 168 of the Land Revenue Act. [878G, 990A] 2.5 The Cotton Mills Co. had in fact been attached by the Collectors with the powers specified therein and that orders had been passed under section 17AA (2) read with section 190 of the Indian Industries (Regulation and Development) Act, 1951 takingover six industrial Units of the cotton Mill Company. [990B] 2 :6 The order dated February 1 1985 was an Order made under Section 18AA(1)(a) by the Board in respect to the share of the 100 shareholders out of the said 10 lakhs shares out of 10 lakhs share and also the pledge of 3, 50,000 share out of which 10 lakhs were pledged in their favour. The Cotton Mill Co. was not a holder of shares pledged in his favour.

The petitioners filed a suit in the Court of Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for a declaration that they were the owners in posses 833 sion of the suit land along with some others. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that since the question involved in the suit was merely one of title to the suit property and it was not necessary to decide whether the suit lands was shamlat deh or not, it had jurisdiction to try the suit. In appeal, the Additional Senior District Judge held that since there was no dispute between the parties, the civil court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit and dismissed the revision petition filed by the petitioners. The High Court in revision set aside the judgment of the Additional District Judge and restored the order of the trial court. Dismissing the special leave petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The plaintiffs who claimed to be the owners along with others of the land had avoided to seek a 836 declaration that the suit is not shamlat Deh vested in the Panchayat or not. They had, therefore, questioned the correctness of the entries in the revenue records which showed that the Panchayat was entitled to the land. [837G] 1.2 The plaintiffs could by drawing their plaint cleverly by not claiming a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question belonged to them or that it belonged to the Gram Panchayat. The plaintiffs cannot by drawing his plaint cle ververly, by not seeking a declaration from the plaintiffs. [889A] 1:3 In the instant case, the suit had been filed against the Panchayat and the Panchayat had expressly claimed that the land in question belongs to it as shamlat land. It will not be possible in the circumstances for the civil Court to make a declaration under favour of a plaintiffs without determining the question Whether the property belonged to a Gram Panchayat or whether it belonged exclusively to the Panchayat. [879B] 1 :4 The Gram Panchayat had not been impleaded as a defendant. The plaintiff in that case had not claimed that he was the owner along with any others of his suit land. The defendants could by no stretch of imagination be said to have either acquired title or interest in it. [869D] 2.1 In the present case, there is no dispute about the fact that the plaintiffs were claiming to be owners along With some others of their suit land had failed to seek any declaration from them. The Gram panchayat had expressly asserted that the property was shamil deh and it had been vested in it by virtue of section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the Act. [859E] 2:2 In the absence of a clear finding by the trial Court, the plaintiffs could not by drawing the plaint clevingly by claiming a relief that the plaintiff had no right or title in it, without deciding whether the land belonged to him or that he belonged to it. The civil court has rightly held that the jurisdiction of the civil courts had not be taken away by virtue Of section 13 of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961. [899G] 2 :3 In view of the above decision, the question is whether the civil Courts have jurisdiction to decide such suits in a suit filed against a Panchayat and not by the Civil Court.

The appellant Board had been conferred statutory power under Section 49(1) of the . The Board was empowered to determine the conditions on the basis of which supply is to be made. " In exercise of this power, the Board issued a notice dated 28th April, 1989 calling upon the consumer to deposit the amount in dispute within 15 days from the date of receipt of the notice. The consumer deposited the amount with the Board and filed an application before the Board for permission to deposit it on the ground that the Board was keeping the security deposit and deprived the consumer of the use of the money which is alleged to be earning interest with the respondent Board. The Board rejected the application on the grounds, inter alia, (1) that there was no legal obligation to pay interest on a deposit made by the consumer with the Electricity Board in terms of Clause 20(a) & (c) of General Conditions of Supply; and (2) that the supply of electricity and the conditions of supply were statutory. The High Court dismissed the application holding that the consumer had not been given an opportunity to file objections against the proposed levy. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant Board that there is no legal duty to pay the interest on deposit made with the Commission in terms Of Clause 20 (a) and (c). Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The condition of supply requiring a consumption security deposit has a direct bearing on the operations of the Board which are to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus. [278 F] 2. The conditions of Supply requiring a production security deposit have a direct nexus with the position that without a law in that form and with that amplitude smuggling might not be possible of being effectively checked, the question arises whether the law could be held to be violative of the freedom guaranteed by Article 19(1)(f) &(g). [278 D] 3. The nature of consumption security deposits is such that it represents the moneys of the board. The purpose of deposit is to secure the payment of consumption charges. G., Ramaswami, learned counsel, appearing for the appellant, has a right to receive the amount deposited by the consumers with the licensee in terms o Section 49 (1). [279 C] 4. The obligation to Pay interest to the consumer proceed on the assumption that the Electricity Act is not violative of any fundamental rights guaranteed under Article 19 (1)(g) & and (g) as imposing an unreasonable restraint. It stands to reason that if there is a revision in the rate of tariff there must be an upward revision in consumption security deposited since it has direct bearing to the level of supply in consumption of electricity. The liability to pay Interest to the consumers proceed on account of default in payment of interest would be admissible. [279 D] 5. The terms of supply providing for non payment of electricity are not so unconscionable as to shock the conscience of the Court. The essential conditions of the supply requiring an consumption security amount has a definite bearing on its operations and cannot be struck down as arbitrary on the sole ground that it is liable to be appropriated for the satisfaction of any amount liable to pay by the Consumer to the Board. [280 F] 6. The term "in addition" in Section 49 of the Act means "any sum payable to the Government by a consumer under an agreement or contract from the time of deposit". It does not mean that the payment is made for a price paid or promised to be paid by the purchaser. The words "in lieu of any sum payable" are used in the context of wide scale theft of energy, tempering with meters and such other methods adopted by the Consumers. [281 C] 7.

The petitioners were working as officers in the Telecommunication Research Centre of the Posts and Telegraph Department which is directly under the control of the P&T Board of the Ministry of Communications, Government of India. The direct recruits to which category the petitioners belong are not given any Special Pay in these grades and they are given only the pay at the pay scales prescribed for them. In the counter affidavit filed by the Union Public Service Commission it was stated that all relevant things such as qualifi cations, functions, duties and responsibilities are the same as between direct recruits and the transferred officials and that the transferred official had to be paid extra amount by way of Special Pay at the same rates at which it is paid to the transferred officers working in that centre with effect from the date on which the transferred officer commenced to draw the Special Pay upto date and to continue to pay it in future also as long as the transferred employees continue to get it. The petitioners have raised two grounds, namely, (1) the denial of promotion to them on account of irregular implementation of the rules of promotion contained in the Recruitment Rules and the second relating to violation of Article 14 and Article 16 of the Constitution by not grant ing them the same special pay which is granted to the trans ferred officers who are working in the telecommuni cation Research Centre; (2) the discrimination between the direct recruits & the transferred Officers regarding the payment of Special pay was attempted to be justified by the Government in the Counter affidavit filed on behalf of the Union of India and that it was not the case of the Government that the petitioners were not competent and are not able to discharge their duties.
