Allowing the petitions, ^ HELD: 1. The petition ers (direct recruits) who are specifically recruited to the Telecommuni tation Research Center are entitled to the Special pay at that rates at Which it is payable to the transfer officers working In that centrewith effect from 1st January 1973. [275E] 2. There is no justification to deny the Special pays at the higher rates to the direct recruit working in a department with effectfrom the date of which the transfer officer commenced or to continue in pay it. All the direct ent recruits are graduate engineers and have been working throughout in the Telephonecommunication Research Center. It is paid for the special pay upto date payable to them. [276F] 3. The arrears of Special pays upto date due to the promotee officers shall be paid within four months from today. [278G] 4. There was no justification for denying the Special Compa ny at the said rates to direct recruits working in their organisation with effect fro the date from which the transfers officers have been drawing the SpecialPay upto date. The arrear of Special Pension upto date pay payable to direct recruit shall be payable within four weeks from today.[278F] 5. There are no justification why the petitioners should not be denied the Special Leave Petition.

The appellant was employed mainly in a managerial administrative capacity drawing basic pay (excluding allowances) exceeding five hundred and fifty rupees per month. The respondent, who was an employee of the appellant, had not complied with the provisions of law in that he did not make an application under section 42(4) of the Act which was a condition precedent to approaching the Labour Court and prayed for setting aside the order of the Labour court. The High Court held that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42 (4) including the proviso before he could apply to the Labour Courts for relief under section 7 8(1) D. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme of section 78 (1) seems to be that disputes should be settled as far as possible and primarily through conciliation and agreement it does not stand to reason that an employee should be able to side step all this by a direct reference to the labour court. [782 E] 2. The Scheme of section 8(2) seems very clear that disputes falling under clause (a) of paragraph A of sub section (1), must be settled in respect of matters covered by section 42 and under sub section(2), every application under sub s.(1) has to be made in the prescribed form to the representative of the employees. The object is that disputes must be decided as far possible and ultimately through conciliation, and agreement, it does appear that an employer should first make an order of dismissal, discharge, retrenchment or termination of service or suspension as the case may be, and ending on the date on which the Labour ' Court orders such payment, such sum not exceeding four thousand rupees by way of compensation, regard being had to loss of employment and possibility of getting suitable employment thereafter. [788 F H] 3. The provisions of section 78(1), therefore, do not stand in reason that a Labour Court is to have power to decide all the disputes covered by paragraph A. As the scheme of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act is that dispute should be settle as far and primarily by conciliation and agreed agreement it did not stand on reason that no agreement was arrived at. [789 F] 4. The purpose of section 79(1)(a) seems clear to be to provide for a speedy remedy to an employee who has been dismissed, discharged or retrenched from employment on account of any dispute relating to change in respect or alteration in respect thereof. [882 G H] 5. In the instant case, the scheme is that claims should be decided by conciliation, conciliation and settlement. It does not stands to reason because an employee can be able only to step all these by a direction to see whether it was possible to come to any agreement and an application to the workmen court could only be resorted to after efforts had been made to settle the dispute and no agreement had been arrived at.[882 H] 6. The Act is a welfare legislation which provides for better protection of the interests of employees in industrial establishments. It is not intended that a workman should be given full opportunity to approach an employer or a Labour court for relief. [825 E F] 7. In view of the solemn assurance given by the appellant to this Court, it did appear that the scheme was that disputes could be settled only as far according possible and basically through conciliation; and agreement. It did not mean that an application should be made by the employer intending to effect any change in regard to matters covered under section 43(1).

The appellants filed a suit for eviction of the respondents on the ground that they were tenants from month to month. The respondents served a notice on them claiming the right to contin ue in possession after 31.7.1971 as tenants from year to month and further held that the appellants would have to make another application under section 12(3) of the Act for evicting the respondents if they did not vacate within the time allowed by court. The appellants then moved the Patna High Court in its revisional jurisdiction, inter alia, contending that the respondents ' application was not maintainable before the Munsif and the entire proceeding was mis conceived. The learned Judge who heard the case held that in absence of a month 's notice under section12(1) from the tenant, the application of the appellants was not entertainable by the Munsif. The High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the respondents. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether a landlord after the expiry of the period of a fixed term lease is entitled to move the court by an application under Section 12 of the . because even on assuming the argument of the respondent to be correct the appellants should succeed. [934D] 2.1 In the present case, it is the Civil Court, Ranchi which is the appropriate court either for filing a suit or making an application Under section 12. The jurisdiction of the civil court is not confined merely to the amounts of court fees payable by the parties in the first court and by the defendants before the Judicial Commissioner and the High Court, but that should not come in the way in construing the correct nature of the proceeding. [1034E F] 2:2 In the instant case, the question does not affect the substantive right of the parties as the controversy was concluded by the first appellate court in favour of the appellant. The occasion for filing an applica tion under section 11 and as we have made an assumption in favour o f the respondents that section 12 has no application to the present cour t. [109B] 2(i) In the facts and circumstances of the case, in our opinion, the proceeding has to be treated as a suit and the judgment of the learned Munsif as a decree therein. The order passed by the court would have the effect of a final order under section 47 which would be appealable as a result of which no revision would lie. [110C D] 2.(ii) In view of the fact that the matter is covered by section 12, and as there was an error in asking the appellants to file such an applicat tion, it was held that section12 has no applica table to the respondents to file the application. [1134F G] 3:3 The question does neither affect the rights of the res pondents as the dispute is concluded by a first appellate Court in favour to the appellants. The suit filed by them as an application for eviction under section 13 and an application u/s 12 are to be filed. In the circumstances, the proceedings have to be regarded as a plaint and the impugned proceeding as the one in a suit followed by an appeal and a second appeal. [111G H] 4:4 The question is whether the petition which was filed by appellants as an applicati tion under Section12 of the , before the Civil court was maintainable, should be treated to be a plaint or the impugned proceedings as the two remedies are open to a landlord thereafter. [114A B] 5:5 In the case of a suit under section11 and an appli cation under section 14 are to he filed. The only difference is that if the matter in question is covered under section 10, and the order passed thereunder would have ted effect of an final order u/ss 47 which will be appealable.

The appellant Society filed a suit against the respondent for an immovable property through its Secretary, which was numbered as Suit No. 11 of 1973. The trial court after holding that the appellant 's application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure was not maintainable, proceeded further to consider the question as to who was the duly elected Secretary of the Society and entitled to prosecute or withdraw the suit. The High Court agreed with the trial court that the application under Section 15 1 was not entertainable, proceeded to consider whether the trial Court had committed any error in deciding the question of granting permission to the withdrawal of the suit under its inherent power. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In order to decide whether a party makes an application before the court for setting aside the decree on the ground that he did not give his consent, the court has the power and duty to investigate the matter and to set aside the order if it is satisfied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree. [237E] 1.2 In the instant case, the trial judge was clearly wrong in dismissing the appellant's application as not maintainable. The Trial Court was thus clearly wrong by dismissing the appellants ' application as being not maintainable and the High Court should have inter vened in its revisional power on the assumption that it had no jurisdiction to do so. [238G] 1:3 In the view of the High Courts that is the position, but it declind to exercise its revisional powers on the basis that it has no jurisdiction, the prayer for withdrawal of a suit was not made on behalf of the appellant at all and the impugned order was passed as a result of the court being misled. [239D] 1 :4 The High Courts were, therefore, not right in holding that it did not exercise a jurisdiction vested in it by law. [240E] 2.1 The trial Court was, therefore clearly wrong In dismissing the application as non maintainable and directing the trial Judge to decide the matter on merits. [241B] 2:2 It is well settled that the High court while confirming the order, said that in the exercise of inherent power under Section15 1 of CPC a court can vacate an order obtained by fraud on it. The courts below were, however, not entitled to hold that the only remedy of the petitioner was to file a fresh suit. [243C] 2 :3 In view of this position, the High ' Court should not have interled with the arguments of the learned counsel as the disputed question has to go back for reconsideration. The main question which requires consideration is whether the High Curt had committed grave error in dismissing his application as a non maintainable one. [244D] 2(a) In the light of the decision of this Court in C.W.P. Beyond pointing out that even according to the impugned judgment of the trial courts, the errors in the judgment of trial court are serious, we do not consider it appropriate to deal with the argument of the counsel as it had failed to exercise a power vested in him by law [243H] 2.(b) The High C Court was clearly right in dismissing this appellant ' s application as neither maintainable nor the trial cour ts jurisdiction vested therein by law, and the only relief which could be obtained by the party is to institute a suit. If the case of the party challenging the decree is that he was in fact a party to the compromise petition filed in the case but his consent has been procured by fraud, the Court cannot investigate the same in exercise of its inherent powers, and, the only right to the party being to institute the suit is to file an application.

The appellant was a citizen of India and was declared to have ended on April 1, 1946. The Ordinance was promulgated in exercise of the emergency powers vested in the Governor General under section 72 of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, by which one must look to its terms as they originally stood to justify the continuance of the ordinance in question after April 1. 1946 whensoever it may have been promulgated. The appellant was convicted and sentenced for an offence under section 161 I.P.C. and was sentenced to imprisonment for life. He appealed to the High Court which held that the Ordinance had not lapsed on April 11, 1946, because the Ordinance did not cease to be in operation after the expiry of six months from its promulgation. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Held: (i) The Ordinance having continued in operation even after the declaration of the Emergency having come to an end was made on April 10, 1953, the Ordinance ceased to be operative until it was repealed. (ii)The Ordinance had continued in force even after that date and the Ordinance having been promulgated between June 27, 1940 and April 1 1946, the said notes continued to be effective as legal tender in India though the position in Jammu and Kashmir in regard to the same could not be affected by reason of the , not having been made applicable to the State of Jammu and K. (iii)The words " for the space of not more than six months" occurring in section 72 during the period specified in section 3 of the Indian and Burma (Emergency Provisions) Act, 1940, were omitted from section 72 by section 1(3) of the India and Burma and (Eemergency provisions) Act. The words "for the space for not morethan six months " occurring in the said section were omitted with the words " after April 11. 1946, while determining the duration of the Ordinance which had been promulgated on April 12, 1946 and April 2, 1946 respectively.

The appellants were convicted for murder under section 302 I.P.C., and sentenced to death by the trial court. The High Court confirmed their conviction but reduced the sentence of death to a term of imprisonment for life. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the High Court was in error in confirming the death sentences passed under section 368(a) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973; (2) the sentence imposed by the Trial court was not proper or uncalled for; and (3) the view taken by the High court was erroneous. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were justified in confirming their death sentences. [1076G] 1.2 In Rajendra Prasad 's case (supra), the Court held that it did not lay down any legal principle applicable to any legal problem disclosed by the facts and circumstances obtaining in such cases. But in the great enthusiasm for doing so, the pendulum has swung to 1076 the other extreme and the guideline given is that the 'special reasons ' must relate "not to the crime as such but to the criminal" for which there is no warrant in section 354(3) of Cr.P., 1973. [1007G H] 1:3 The High court, therefore, was justified in upholding the death sentence passed under Section 368(b) of Criminal procedure, 1973. But the question whether the death penalty should be awarded or not must, in my view, be left to the discretion of the Judge trying the accused and the question of sentence must depend upon the facts of each case. [1017A B] 1 :4 The High 'Court was justified by confirming the conviction of the two appellants under section 364 I. P.C. on the ground that there were "special reasons" within the meaning of section 354, sub section (3), of the code of Criminal Procedures 1973. If the general observations on sentencing jurisprudence made in Rajendra Prasad "s case, there are no rationes decidendi, much less any ratio decidendi. This may be a 'progressive ' stance, which is out of place in a judicial pronouncement, which ought to be based on the facts & circumstance of the case and the law applicable. But when a sentence of imprisonment is passed it is subject to confirmation by the Court under section 366(1) of Code and the accused also has right of appeal to the High Courts under 5.5. It would therefore be manifest that it is neither feasible nor legally permissible for this Court while hearing such an appeal to lay down that on grounds of compassion and humanism the sentence awarded must relate not to the Crime as such, but to criminal" occurring in the majority judgment, it must be pointed out, if I may say so with respect, would be unwarranted and contrary to section 302 of the Indian Penal Code read with section 354 (3). [1018C D] 1.:5. The Court has to choose between a sentence awarded for life and a sentence imposed on an accused are constitutionally valid. But this does not laydown many legal principles applicable to all Courts in the country. If, the general observation on sentencing law made inRajendra Prasad ' s case (Supra) is to be regarded as "law declared By this Court ' within the ambit of article 141 so as to bind all Courts In the great enlightened circumstances for imposing death penalty must relate, not to crime as a rule of universal application, but also to the Criminal" for whose there is none warrant in Section 354(1). [1008G H; 1019A B C] 1 2.6 The High "special reason" must relate 'not to 'the crime as defined by article 141 of the Constitution so as not to affect the criminal '

The appellant was charged with having committed a criminal offence under section 409 of the Indian Penal Code. The Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., Lucknow, on an enquiry held by him, found that the appellant had entered into partnership with others under the name of Gautam Cycle Mart, Meerut, in contravention of the Government Servants ' Conduct Rules. He also found that there had been an enquiry in 1949 by Shri A. Inspecting Commissioner and about others in 1952 by Shri R. N. Srivastava, another Inspecting Commissioner, and that the charges were actually framed and fully enquired into by Officers whose integrity and sense of justice was not challenged. The appellant filed a suit for declaration that the order passed by the Commissioner of Incometax, U., Lucknow on 2nd April, 1956, reducing the appellant in rank from the post of an Income tax Officer to that of an income tax Inspector was void and inoperative. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that the inquiry had been conducted in 1952 and not in 1939, and the appellant could not be given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the High Court did not deal with a number of submissions made because they had, apparently, been forgotten. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The question whether an order refusing grant of certificate of fitness of the case for appeal to this Court could vitiate the whole departmental trial is one which should be, initially raised in the departmental proceedings. Unless such a point could be raised, there could be no declaration that it would vitiate the entire departmental trial. [658C] (2) The order refusing to grant certificate of special leave to appeal by this Court on the ground that some material facts were suppressed or misrepresented for the purpose of obtaining special leave. [613B C] (3) It is only when an opportunity denied is of such a nature that the denial contravenes a mandatory provision of law or a rule of natural justice that it could vitiate it. In the case before us, it has not even been shown how the witnesses whose production was said to have been disallowed could help the appellant 's case on specific charges. All these are questions of fact which should he, initially, raised in this Court. [558C D] (4) The High Court refused the certificate ofitness of the appeal for appeal under section 66(1)(a) of the Act. It was not hearing an appeal against the findings of the departmental authorities.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The contracts between the appellants and the M.M.T.C. were inter se inter se in the course of export. The appellants entered into direct contract with their foreign buyers. The M.T.,C. entered into a direct contract for sale of the goods to their foreign buyer. The agreement was executed by the appellants with the M/s. F.O.B. and the appellants were also required to bring the goods on board the ship. The agreements between the parties indicated that the appellants ' contract of sale occasioned the export and that the contract of the appel lants with the foreign buyer was integrally connected with the contract entered into by the M..M. T.C., with their Foreign buyer. In the special leave petition, the appellants challenged the assumption made by the High Court to the effect that all contracts between them were similar. The principal question in these appeals is whether the appellants are the last purchaser of goods within the meaning of section 2(1)(a) of the Andhra Pradesh General Sales Tax Act, 1957 (Act No. XIV of 1957). Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The contract of sales between the M and the foreign buyers was in the nature of a contract between the Corporation and their foreign sellers on F.o.B., basis. Under the contracts between M and its foreign buyer, the seller 's duty is to place the goods "free on board" a ship to be named by the buyer. This Court in Serajuddin 's case (supra) laid down that the normal presump tion attaching to F. O.B, contracts is that property in the goods passes only when they are put on board a ship. [444C D] 2. The terms of the contracts were not in the way of the contract between M & the foreign sellers. Under these contracts between S.T..C. and their Foreign buyers, the duty is payable to place them on board. A perusal of the agreements shows that the contracts entered into between the two parties were inter inter se. The relevant clauses of the agreement are: "the Purchaser"s contract with the Corporation; "the purchaser" 's goods " free on board", and "the seller"s duty was to place goods on Board a ship, to be mentioned by the buyers. This means that the sellers ' duty is not to place or to place any goods onboard a ship at all. The contention of the appellants that they were integrated F.Os.B and F.F.O.,B. contracts with their Indian buyer was negatived by this Court in B.C.'s case. [445E] 3. The High Court was right in holding that the agreements between M/S. F & F.L.C.; and the S. T..C., were integrated contracts in the sense of export, because the export sale is an independent one between the corporation and their Indian buyers. [441F G] 4. The question whether the contracts are integrated or not depends upon the nature and character of the transaction. If they are different contracts, as they are in the present case, the last buyer within the state is the M M. T.,C., and the purchaser within the latter is the manufacturer of goods. [442F G; 442A] 5. The distinction between a contract of transfer of property in goods passed by a merchant and a contract for export is that the transaction must be one which is entered into with the buyer, and the contract must be executed on board, a ship would be regarded as an independent contract between both the parties.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi 521 Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. He was terminated by letter dated 12th October 1974 with effect from 19th October, 1974 with retrospective effect from 1st November, 1974. The appellant challenged his termination before the Labour Court which held that he had rendered service for 240 days in a period of 12 calendar months preceding the date with reference to which calculation was to be made, and that since he had not rendered uninterrupted service for a period less than 240 days, he could termination of his service. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the termination was invalid. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the respondent had worked for 240 months in a continuous period of twelve calendar months commencing and counting backwards from the relevant date being the date of retrenchment, and therefore, his case fell within section 25B(2) (a) and he should be deemed to be in continuous service under an employer (a). Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The termination of service of the respondent was ab initio void and inoperative. [535C] In the instant case, the termination of the service of appellant was ab legally void and ineffective and a declaration was made that he continues to be In continuous service for one year. If he had, he would be deemed not to be on continuous service within the meaning of sub section (1) and his case need not be covered by sub section(2). [536D] The termination was illegal and inoperative and a further declaration is made that the workman concerned continues to remain in service with all consequential benefits.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953. The appointment was terminable with one month 's notice and on February 5, 1955 the appellant was served with a "charge sheet" by the Settlement Officer, Bhatinda that he had received Rs. 150/ as illegal gratification from one Darbara Singh and bad demanded Rs. 30/ as unlawful gratification from two Ude Singh. The appellant submitted his explanation to the charge sheet. The Enquiry Officer found that the charges were proved and the appellant 's services were terminated in exercise of authority reserved under the terms of employment, and no penalty was imposed upon the appellant. The Deputy Commissioner, however, did not act in exercise Of this authority :the appellant was dismissed or removed from service but his employment was terminated by notice of one mouth " without assigning any reason" without assigning reasons. The order of termination was confirmed by the Deputy Commissioner on March 30, 1955. The appeal filed by the appellant to the High Court was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the order dated March 17, 1955, was not the order pursuant to which employment was terminate ; and that the provisions of article 311(2) had not been complied with by the Enquiry Officer, the. High Court held that the appellant had no right to hold the post he was occupying and by the impugned order the appellant could not be dismissed or discharged from service. HELD : (i) The order dated April 17,1955, was made with the object of ascertaining whether disciplinary action should be taken against the appellant for his alleged misdemeanour. It was clearly an enquiry for the purpose of taking (1) (1958) S.C.R.828. such an enquiry and order consequent upon the report made in the enquiry will not fall within the principle of Ram Narayan Das 's case. [723 E] (ii) The third proposition in the latter (Gopi Kishore Prasad 's) case refers to an enquiry into allegations of misconduct or inefficiency with a view, if they were found established, to impose punishment and not to an Enquiry whether a probationer should be confirmed. But an order discharging a probationer following upon an enquiry to ascertain whether he should be confirm is not of that nature x x x] The third principle in the former (Gomi Kishore PRASAD 's), case refers only to an inquiry into allegations against misconduct or irregularity with a decision, if it were found proved, to imposing punishment and cannot be regarded as one by way of punishment.

The appellant State Government was promoted to the post of Professor in the colleges. The appellant State filed a writ petition challenging the promotions of respondents Nos. 1 and 2 on the ground that it had not been consulted in accordance with its requirement, and that the Public Service Commission for the State of Jammu and Kashmir, hereinafter referred to as the Commission, has been consulted by the Commission in accordance With its requirement. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Commission was not consulted in regard to the principles to be followed in making the promotions in question or on the suitability of candidates for such appointments, promotions or transfers; (ii) on the principles laid down in section 133(2)(b), it will be enough to consider whether that section has been correctly interpreted and whether the Public Services Commission for Jammu and Srinagar Kashmir,hereinafter referred to the Commission had been consulted. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, ^ HELD: The State Government at first framed rules on November 15, 1968, for selections to be made to posts of Professors in the Colleges. " It is not provided by section 133 that all the members of the Commission should have interviewed all or any of the candidates, or that it was not permissible for the Commission to entrust the selection to a committee consisting of only one of its members, so long as the commission reserved to itself the right to approve or disapprove the committee 's report and actually discharged that constitutional responsibility. It would thus appear that the State Government referred the selections to the Public Selection Committee which was "formed" by the commission under section 133 of the Constitution and as the writ petitioners have not ventured to take a plea to the contrary, it is not permissible to refer to any averment in the writ Petition that the selection made by it was invalid for that reason. [875 D E] (iii) The State has stated in its reply to the writ petitions that for every post of Professors, names of four Lecturers strictly in order of seniority, were sent to the commission "at its direction" and they were interviewed and examined by the Selection Committee, which was constituted under the Chairman 's note dated June 2, 1969. [88 E F] (iv) The Commission was therefore consulted on the eligibility of the candidate for promotion as Professors. [87 D] (v) The High court erred in holding that section 133 does not arise in this case because it is a matter relating to the interpretation of clause (b) of sub section (2) of section 133, and its true and correct interpretation would be that "it is applicable only to 'making promotions and transfers from one service to another".

The petitioner was the Chief Minister of Bihar. He made a speech in the Bihar Legislative Assembly when M. P. N. Singh, one of the oldest members of the Assembly made a speeches in the House of Commons and made a statement that he had no privilege to speak and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of the House or any committee thereof. The petitioner alleged that the speech was not published in the Gazette as required by article 194(3) of the Constitution. The Committee of Privileges of the Bihar Assembly held that the petitioner 's fundamental right under article 19(1)(a) was preserved despite the provisions of article 194 (3). The petitioner challenged the validity of the Act on the ground that it violated articles 14 and 19 of the constitution. Held, that the powers, privileges and immunities of a House of Parliament and of members and committees of a house of such Legislature are conferred by the latter part of article 105(3), on each House of the Legislature and the members and Committees thereof and by the former part of Article 194(2) on a House or a Committee thereof and the Members and committees thereof and, by the later part of clause (3) on the House. The privilege conferred on the Legislature of a State is subject to the freedom conferred on a citizen under article19(1) of that Constitution and, therefore, if the House has the power or privilege to prevent the publication of its proceedings, or at any rate of the expunged portions of it, the Legislature has also a similar privilege or power and it can exercise it notwithstanding the fact that it infringes the fundamental right of a citizen.

The appellants were working as Readers in different faculties in the said College on the date of transfer in the scale of pay Rs.510 860/ and Rs.600/ respectively as on the dates of take over, namely, March 9, 1971, and April 9, 1970 respectively. The Government of Orissa took over the management of the college on and from March 9. 1971 and a formal agreement was executed between the managing committee of the College and the Governor of the State. The College after taking over was administered as a Government College. The Director of Public Instructions (Higher Education) Orissa, issued a letter to the Director of public Instructions (Secondary Education) for consideration of their suitability for appointment as Readers. The appellants filed writ petitions in the High Court challenging the validity of the said circular and also the validity o f the said order. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the Government had no power to issue the said Circular, and that the High court erred in directing the Gov ernment to take into account, as experience, the service of the Respondents while they were in the private college since, according to him, the necessary qualification was eight years experience in Class II, Orissa Education Serv ice (O.E.S.). The appellants preferred appeals before this Court by special leave. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The condition of draw ing of Rs.100/ or more on the basis of salary aspect under the said circulars had to stand the test of Article 16 in the case of two (1) ; (2) The teaching experience of the Readers in the Private College is completely effaced to the extent that they will not be even eligible, on the plea of absence of teaching experience in Government service, for consideration for appointment. [775G H] 1.2 In the instant case, the High Courts have rightly held that all the Respond ents are eligible to be referred to the Public Service Commission for the post of Reader. Whether they will be suitable for appointment Readers will be a matter entirely for due and proper consideration of the Public Services Commission whose recommendations will be considered by the Government in the matter of final absorption. [771A B] 1:3 The condition regarding draw of Rs,600/ or less on the dale of taking over, which has been laid down in the aforesaid circular as a particular qualification for eligibility for appointment to the post is arbitrary and discriminatory. [762C D] 2.1 In the case, there was no material before the High courts to show that they were not relied upon by the State in connection with the appointment of the respondents as Readers after the College had been taken over by the Govern ment on March 9; 1971. The said circular took recognition of the service in the Government service and was drawing Rs. 600/ , the minimum according to the aforesaid Government circular, on that date, was eight year experience in class II, and the minimum equivalent according to that Government circular was only a confirmed Lecturer whereas, as already shown, five of the Respondent were confirmed Readers though drawing salary less than Rs.200/ on the said date. [752E F] 2:3 In the present case, it is not clear from the record that the Respondents were appointed as Readers on 4 9 1969 and were drawing a salary of less than what was laid down by the Director Public Instructions for appointment in Government College, first time presented before the take over. That action based on the salary aspect had to. stand the tests of Article 14 in the instant cases.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1) of the U.P. State Road Transport Corporation Act, 1948. The scheme was published in respect of the route a scheme had been prepared and published under section68C of Chapter IV A of . The Corporation applied for grant of temporary permits to ply the passengers on Khurja Pahasu Chhatari Dabai Rajghat Sabha route (route for short) which applications came to be rejected by the State Transport Authority and their appeal to the State Appellate Tribunal was dismissed. In the appeal to this Court it was contended that in respect Of the route no scheme had ever been published and therefore an application for temporary permit for the period intervening between the date of publication of the approved or modified scheme has to be made to the state Transport Authority under section 69 F(I A) of Chapter III A of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: The State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court fell into error by interpreting section 68F(1 A) only to mean that even though there are 7 vacancies and the Corporation applied only for 3 temporary permits, once the Corporation made an application under section 66 F(2), the State transport Authority cannot grant permit to any one else. [985 H] The State Road Authority or the Regional Transport Authority as the case may be will have to examine the application for permanent permits made by persons other than the Corporation and if they are found to be competent, eligible and qualified they may have to be granted permits for the benefit of the large travelling public. In that event the State Government will have no power left in 985 the State Road authority to grant temporary permits till the approved scheme is published. But if the Corporation applies for all the permits but only for some, the inevitable conclusion is that for the remaining strength the Corporation has made no application for the temporary permits and section 68 E(1 C) would be squarely attracted. [864 D] The High Court was right in interpreting section68 F(i A) merely to mean "that even though it there are 8 vacancies and, therefore, the Corporation should grant temporary permit to all persons other then the Corporation will have only to grant permits to persons other similarly situated." [987 H; 988 B C] The Corporation has power under sub section (1 C ) to grant permanent permits to any person in respect o the area or the route or part thereof specified in the scheme. If the Corporation is willing to operate vehicles to the maximum strength undoubtedly the State 's remaining permits will have, to grant permit, to the Corporation under section 67 F(l A) to the exclusion of others. But section 68 C(1A) clearly envisaged a situation where application for a temporary permit is not made under section 71F(IA), by the Corporation. If that is so, the State Corporation will be entitled to all the temporary permit till the approval scheme is notified.

The appellant, a son of Sarup, filed a suit for partition of his property in the hands of his maternal grandfather 's father. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal preferred by the appellant. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the property inherited by respondent 10 was not ancestral property qua the appellant and so it allowed the appeal. HELD: (i) The decision of the first Full Bench in Narotam Chand 's case (1), should be treated as good law. [1006 D] (ii) The principle of stare decisis is applicable to a decision on the point of the relevant custom. It is not necessary that the question as to whether property inherited from a maternal grandfather is ancestral property or not must depend upon the facts and circumstances of each case. [1018 E F] (iii) The doctrine of stare judicata is in applicable and should present no obstacle in holding that the earlier cases of the Full Bench were not correctly decided. [109 G H] (iv) The question as regards whether property from maternal grand father is ancestral or not cannot be determined on a consideration of the evidence adduced by the parties. [1108 F] In dealing with the point as to what the daughter 's son inherits from his maternal grandmother is ancestral, it must be confined to the property descending to the father from his male ancestor in the male line. The question whether property was ancestral property is not ancestral but a decision based on what the majority of the judges considered to be the general principles of the customary law and upon the argument abinconvenienti. [1110 G] (v) The decisions of the High Courts are wholly unsustainable as a decision of a Division Bench of the Punjab High Court was wholly untenable.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum on charges under section 449 and section 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of 14th November 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, these appellants came there and while one of them Abdul Odud pressed his knees and Ekram and Habibullah pressed his chest and hands with Matiullah inflicted an injury on his neck with a dagger. The trial court convicted the appellants under section 302 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for two years under section 307 read with s.34 of Indian Penal code. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) A charge under section 324 read with S.34 is not sustainable in law unless murder has actually been committed. [981 D] (2) The words "in order to" have been used by the legislature not only in section 449 but also in two succeeding sections 450, 451 and again in section 454 of the Code. Therefore, when it is found that the four appellants attacked Haji Ebarar Ali in furtherance of the common intention of all of them to kill him and some of them held him down while one used the dagger on him each of the four was in law considered to have done this act of using the dagger. [980 G H] (3) The word "in" is not defined in the Code but it means a person who has a particular intention or knowledge which is likely to be committed by him when that individual has a specific intention or know which is intended to be used by him in order to attract the provisions of section 34. [970 E] (4) The object of the house trespass is to commit theft if it is done "in pursuance of" to" the committing of any offence punishable with imprisonment. Section 451 makes punishable the commission of an offence punishable under section 450 of the I.P.C. if it was committed "in Order to" a person when that person has a certain intention or information which is capable of being used by a number of persons, jointly it can have no application. But, once it is decided that the act is so done by a series of persons in furtherance thereof the legal position that results is that each person shall be held to have committed the entire criminal act. [969 G H; 981 A] (5) The intention of the legislature was not to use the dagger must in law be considered to be having done this Act of using it as if the act had been done by himself alone.

The appellant, a Sarswat Brahmin, was the son of one of the sons of the respondent. The respondent contested the suit mainly on the grounds (i) that the properties in suit were not ancestral and (ii)that the appellant was not a collateral of Gurdial at all. Held, that the appellant 's right to succeed to her father 's ancestral propertie 'section is not a mere declaration of the custom but a sound piece of evidence in proof of the special custom set up by the parties. The general custom of the Punjab being that a daughter excludes the collaterals from succession to the selfacquired property of her father, the initial onus, there fore must be on the party who is the res pondent and has, therefore, failed to discharge the onus that was thrown on her as a result of the production by the appellant of the Riwaj i am of 1913 and, consequently, the appellant must succeed. The appellant ' s right to succeeds to her son 's selfacquired propertiority is not merely a declaration of custom but also a sound document in proof thereof. The presumption as to the correctness of the entries in the Romaj i nal book so as to shift the onus to the daughter who is a party to the proceedings, must be based on the evidence adduced by the party and it cannot be said that the burden was thrown upon her as an independent or reliable document. The onus of proving the custom is not on the person who asserts the custom. The burden of proof is always on the parties concerned and the onus shifts to the party concerned. In the present case, the respondent did not lead any evidence in support of the plea that the collateral was not self acquired property of his father but was merely a statement of fact which was believed by the Settlement Officer as well as the High Court. The statements in a Riwraj i ams of 1913 were beyond the fourth degree and it was enough for the Court to say that irrespective of whether the properties were ancestral or selfacquired the collateral ones in that case could not succeed to the collateral.

The respondent was the Managing Director of Messrs Bird and Co. Ltd., and of Messrs F. W. Heilgers and Co., Ltd., which were acting as Managing Agents of several Companies registered under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The appellant 's case was that the instrument in question did not comprise distinct matters for the purposes of section 5, and that the instruments were chargeable with the aggregate amount of duty payable if separate instruments were executed in respect of each of those capacities. Held, that the document in question does not comprise different matters and therefore the instrument cannot be split up into separate instruments each comprising or relating to a distinct matter in so far as the different capacities of the donor are concerned. The fact that the donor of the power of attorney executes it in different capacities is not sufficient in my opinion to constitute the instrument one comprising distinct matters and thus requiring to be 855 stamped with the total amount of the duties with which separate instruments Each comprising or pertaining to one of such matters would be chargeable under the Act within the meaning of section 4. The words "distinct matter" in section 5 are not intended to refer to a single power of Attorney but to a series of acts which can be done by the donor himself, whatever be the capacity or capacities which he enjoys and cannot be divided up into individual acts which the donor is capable of performing whether in his individual capacity or in his representative capacity as trustee or as executor or administrator are also comprised within the instrument and are not distinct matters to be dealt with as such so as to attract the operation of section 6. The word "distferent matter" means all acts which may be done either by the donee himself, what is contemplated by section 5 or by the authority conferred thereby. The expression "distinction" in the context of a particular provision must mean that all the distinct acts which are capable of being performed whether in their individual capacity and in his own name as trustee, executor or administrators are also included within the same instrument which is executed by him, and if that is the position, it is but logical that whatever acts the donor was capable of discharging whether in the individual capacity he is capable for per forming and which he appoints his attorney to do for him and in respect Of every transaction entered into by him in his personal capacity. The mere fact that a person executes a power of power of an attorney in respect o all the matters in which he could act, it does not mean that he, as trustee is capable Of performing whether under his individual capacities or in their representative capacity, as executor and administrator are included within that instrument.

The assessee was a Mahalaxmi Mills Ltd., in the other two appeals. The assessee claimed that no deduction should have been made on the strength of the words which would have been allowed to him if the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was in force in the past as in fact no claim had been made or could be made for such allowance, was rejected by the Income tax Officer. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that this expression "or which would not have been granted to him" did not permit the Income Tax Officer to make any deduction under section 66(1) of the Indian Incometax Act, and disallowed the claim on the ground that no claim was made or was could be raised for such allowances, but allowed a certificate that it was a fit case for appeal to the Supreme Court. The High Court held that the expression "any law relating to tax on profits of business" in section 13(5)(b) of Indian Income Tax Act, 1961, which was not in force at the relevant time did not authorise the Incometax Officer to deduct any depreciation under this bead. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the assessee that no deductions should have be made on account of the word "or" which would had been allowed if proper claim had not been made and substantiated, assuming the Indian income tax Act 1922, as in law no claim could be advanced for such deduction, was rightly rejected by this Court. HELD: (1) The words "any laws relating to income tax and super tax or any law relating thereto" in paragraph 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order, 1949, which were not in existence at the time when the Ordinance had been promulgated, did not require that the Income should be deducted in ascertaining the written down value. [230 E] (2) The word "any other law relating" in para 2 of section 13 of the Ordinance was not intended to include the depreciation allowed under a law which had been law of a Part B State before it became included in the Part B States, and so, depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a part B State would come within the first portion of the clause. [231 E F] (3) The expression "all depreciation actually granted under any law or rule relating to Income tax and Super Tax or any Law relating to taxation on profits" in cl. 2 of article 19 of the Constitution, must be construed as including all depreciation actually paid under any such laws or rule of a particular Part B state relating to the income tax, super tax, or any other law which was law of part B States before it become included in Part B A State. [232 D] (4) The High Courts have rightly decided that the depreciation availed of by the assessee under the Bhavnagar War Profits Act was a deductible amount in computing the written off down value of the assets. [233 E F].

The petitioner, a contractor of the Mysore Construction Co. (M.C.) was awarded contract for construction of a building in the Mysore State. The work was to be completed within three months from the date of completion of the work. The petitioner submitted his tender on the basis of the prequalifying requirements as laid down in para I of the N.I.T. and also the other documents called for vide para 5(c) of the Notification Inviting Tenders (N.I.) and also a copy of the Tender Notice issued by the Karnataka Power Corporation Ltd. The respondent No. 1, who was the lowest tenderer, had submitted his bid on the same date. The tender was accepted by the respondent No 1 and the petitioner was declared successful in the said work. Thereafter, the petitioner filed an application before the Karnataka State Electricity Board for supply of the contract documents. The respondents refused to supply the documents as demanded by the petitioner. The petition er challenged the award on the ground that there is no difference between the requirements in paras I and V and the pre conditions of eligibility to submit a tender form were only the three conditions set out in para V of the notification Inviting Tender (NI. T.) and that the details called for in para VI could be supplied at any time. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that it is only para I that stipulates the pre condition and that all the documents referred to in the other paras can be supplied within a period of three months. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the High Court had erred in not considering the question as to whether there is any difference between requirements in para 1 and para V and that only para 1 & 2 could be said to have satisfied the pre eligibility requirement of para I and that even para I set out the general procedure which the K.P.C. was following in regard to N.1.T., and that, therefore, the preconditions for supply were only three conditions laid down therein and that there was no difference in the requirements of paras I & V and, therefore the pre em entation of the tender documents could not be said that there has been any difference in respect of the requirement of paras III, V or VI. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Courts have rightly held that it was only para l that stipulates all the pre pre conditions and that every document referred to therein can be supply at any stage before the final award of the contracts. [237B] 2.2 In the instant case, the lacuna in furnish ing the information has been set right subsequently by the tenderer before opening of the price documents, the Chief Engineer had 240 come to the conclusion that the firm had fulfilled all prequalivi ses and as such the tender of M/s M.C.,C. had been found to be in order. [238D E] 3.1 In the present case, there are some other requirements in the N I.T.. which have to be complied with before the applicant can be eligible for supply. It is clear that at least some, if not all, of the documents mentioned in para l, are intended to verify the fulfilment of the three prequalified conditions of para 1. The more harmonious and practical way of construing the NI.t. is by saying that, before the tender books can be supplies, an intending ten der should satisfy the KP. C. by supplying such of the document called for by in para 5 as are material in assessing the fulfilment o f the condition in para II, that he fulfills the three requirements set out therein and, as such, the tender Of M/S M.

The appellant was a displaced person. He had been in possession of certain properties and the Custodian General issued notices to him under section 38(1) of the East Punjab Act XIV of 1947, asking him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from service. The appellant filed an application for confirmation pending on the date when the Central Act XXXI of 1947 came into force. The Custodian General rejected the application and confirmed the order of confirmation against which no appeal was filed by any one. The Additional Custodian General in revision, set aside the order and directed that the appellant be reinstated in service with effect from the date of his reinstatement. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the application for confirming the order passed by the Custodian in 1952 and which remained pending until Act XXXI Of 1950 came into operation had to be disposed of in accordance with sections 5 A and 5 B of the Ordinance; (ii) the order under appeal was one passed by virtue of the wide powers of revision vested in the CustodianGeneral under section 27 of the Central Ordinance XIV of 1949, as amended in 1948; and (iii) the revisional power vested in him under s.27 of the Act could not be exercised in a judicial manner unless such policies or directives were embodied in rules made by the Central Government under section 56(2)(q) and that no such rules were prescribed by the relevant dates and that even the Custodian GENERAL himself in his order under revision discounted the usefulness of any reference to notifications and directives for the purposes of this case. Held, that the application of the respondent for confirmation was one made long prior to the time when the office of the Custodian was set up and he was clothed with powers of Revision. The order under challenge was one in which no revision was filed against the order confirming the original order of dismissal passed by him on an application made long after the date on which the Central ordinance XXXI of 1949 came into existence.

The appellant company was a registered Company under the Indian Companies Act, 1913. The respondent company claimed bonus for the relevant four years on the ground that it had no right to claim bonus under the Bonus Act. The Industrial Tribunal rejected the claim holding that the demand pertaining to the practice or custom prevailing in the establishments before 1965 was not such a matter as has to be adjudicated and it also did not fall under the provisions of Bonus Act, but held that the claim for bonus could be based either as a matter of pleading implied agreement between the employers and employees creating a term of employment for payment of Puja bonus. The appellant company preferred an appeal before the Industrial Tribunal which dismissed the appeal holding that there was no material to show that the dispute was not one relating to customary bonus or those based on conditions of service. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the question whether customary bonus could have been claimed as a customary bonus did not arise at all and such customary and traditional bonus would depend on the content and terms of that custom or the tradition on which the claim is made. HELD: (1) The subject matter of dispute, as referred by the Government, deals with bonus based on custom or condition of service and in that light, the question of payment of bonus based upon profit to employees employed in establishments '. [657 F] (2) The object and reasons of the Bonus Scheme indicate that the subject matter is 'the question of Payment of Bonus based on profit to workmen employed in factories '. The object of the Act and its scheme, it is not possible to accept the construction suggested on behalf by the respondents that before the Arbitration Board no case of customary or traditional bonus was urged for the year 1965 and so, this Court took the view that so long as award stood, the same claim under a different guise (the Shops Act) could be subversive of the rule of res judicata. [613 A B] (3) The question about policy of the Parliament that was agitated in that case turned on the availability of the as an independent method of claiming profit bonus de hors the Bonus Acts and the Court took this view that it would be subversive Of the scheme to allow an invasion from the flank in that manner. If, therefore, Parliament wanted to retain the right to claims bonus by way of industrial adjudication for those who are either excluded or exempted from the Act, it would have made an express 612 saving provision to that effect as it has done for employees in Coal Mines. Shri Pai 's argument is that before this Court, no case was urged on behalf the respondents and so long that award stood,. the same claimant under a separate guise (The Shops Act), could be violative of the general principles of resjudicata.

The petitioners in the Writ Petitions were direct recruits appointed to the Superior Judicial Service of Punjab and Haryana and second, between December 31, 1976 and March 31, 1975. The High Court by its order dated February 12, 1978 amended rule 12 by providing that the seniority of the members of the service, whether direct recruits or promoted officers, shall be determined by the length of continuous service (in a post in the service irrespective of the date of confirmation) and until that is done, promotees cannot be confirmed even if vacancies are available within their quota in which they can be confirmed. The petitioners in W.P. 266/79 challenged the validity of rule 12 on the ground that it was not open to the High Court to give an arbitrary date of confirmity to the promotees. The writ petitions were dismissed by a Single Judge of the High court holding that the rules governing seniority between direct recruits and promotees appointed to Superior Judicial Services of Punjab, before December 31. 1976 would be governed by a rule of rotation only and not by the rule of reservation. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the retrospective effect was given to the rules from April 9, 1976 for the mere reason that on August 25, 1976 the High 'Court had issued a notification fixing seniority of promotees and direct recruits who appointed to a post on or after December 31., 1976 in accordance with the amended rule. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The retrospective effect is given to rules from May 9,1976 for the simple reason that after every two promotees are confirmed one direct recruit has to be confirmed and until this is done they cannot be confirmation even if vacancy is available within the quota in Which they can he confirmed. [1038E] 1.2 In the instant case, the retrospective operation was given only to the Rules from April 8, 1976. The seniority list will be drawn by the High Courts on the basis of the dates of confirmation allotted to them in compliance with the aforesaid direction (a). and (b) of such of the petitioner, respondents and others who were appointed to that service by promotion and by direct recruitment. [ 1039F] 1:3 In the present case, it appears to us that the prospective effect was not given to rule 8 from April 1, 1970 for the merely reason that some amendments were going to be made hereafter to the Rule of rotation. The retrospective operation is given only in respect of the rules which are already in force on, or after May 9. 1976. [939F G] 2.1 In the absence of any direct decision on the question whether the Governor has the power to frame rules regulating the seniority between promotees and promotees, the High, Court was not justified in applying the rule by fixing seniority at the time of confirmation so as to enable the High to give a arbitrary date for confirmation to the petitioners. [936F] 2:2 The retrospective amendment is given effect to from April 10, 1976, for the obvious reason that whatever amendments are going to been made hereafter by the Governor of Haryana, the quota rule prescribed by rule 8 justifies without more, its extension at the stage of confirmation. It may be recalled that in Punjab continuous officiation on a post In the Service is the criterion of seniority. And though that is not the requirement of the proviso to Article 309 of the Constitution, we hope that whatever amendment are goingto be made now to theRules will be made in consultation with the High Curt. [995G H] 2 :3 The High Courts will re draw the inter se seniority (i) of the said petitioners and respondents as were promoted or appointed to posts in the Service on or before December 30, 1976 in compliance With the amended rules 12.

The respondents Nos. 4 & 5, B. Kumara Swamy and G. Amarender, in this appeal filed a special provision in respect of the State of Andhra Pradesh empowering ing the President to organise class or classes of posts in a civil service of, or any class or class of civil posts under, the State Government for equitable opportunities and facilities for the people belonging to different parts of the state to make an order in that regard requiring the State Govern ment to so organise class and classes of civil post under, and class or Classes of civil Posts under, a State Government. The respondents Nos 4 &5, B Kumara Rao and G Amarender filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the said provision. The Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the provisions of paragraph 3(1) of the Order were ultra vires the powers conferred on the President by sub s.(7) of paragraph 5 of the Andhra Pradesh (Scheduled Castes, Scheduled Tribes and Backward Classes) Order, 1987. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that: (i) The power under proviso to paragraph 3 of the order referred to hereinbefore, is only to organise a separate cadre in respect o any category of posts or class or categories of civil services; and (ii) the State Govt. has no power to organise any class, classes or classes or civil posts in the State into different local cadres for different parts Of the State to make a order in particular (a) requiring the state Government to so organize it. No. Dr. No, Dr.No. Dr, No. Smt. K.S.N. Rao and others vs The State of A.P., ; , referred to. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The power to initiate class or category of civil service is only in respect to a class or group of posts under the State. [501G] 1.2 In exercise of the power under paragraph 3 (1) the President may require the State government to organise one cadre when more than one cadre in relation to such category exists in each department; so that State Government may organise one Cadre when morethan one cadre is in respect for different categories of posts exist in a zone under para 3(2) of Order. [525A] 1:3 The power given to the State Gover nment in subparagraph (7) is only for organising a separate class or Class or classes o f civil posts, under the state into different Local cadres. Similarly, the power given by an order to require the state government to so organizing it. In exercise Of the power conferred under proviso by an Order to require State Government to organise the local cadres in relation t o any class and class of posts, and Class or Classes or classes thereof, the President has been given power under Proviso by an ardment to require that the StateGovernment shall have to place necessary material before the President; the President shall consider that it is expedient to organise such class or groups of posts as may be specified by the State Gov ernment in accordance with para 3 (2) before the expiry of the twelve months from October 20, 1975. No.(5) The State Government shall have power under sub s(7) before expiry of twelve months period prescribed in sub paragraph (1). [525B C] 1 :4 In exercise o r.

The appellant was the auction purchaser in execution of a mortgage decree. The mortgaged property was sold by the mortgagor to one M, who had been the auction purchasers. The mortgage was executed on November 23, 1941 and the sale deed was executed in favour of M. On December 11, 1942, M filed a suit for possession of the mortgaged property. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal by special leave it was contended that the decree which had been passed in the mortgage suit was binding on the mortgagor and that the Patta being subsequent to the plaintiff 's mortgage thus came to an end and he was entitled to recover khas possession from the defendants. HELD : (i) The question whether the mortgagor in possession has power to lease the mortgaged land has got to be determined with reference to the authority of the mortgagor as the bailiff or agent for the mortgagee to deal with the property in the usual course of management, would be operative against the mortgagee. [110E F] (ii)The true position has been stated by this Court in Madan Mohan Singh vs Baj Kishore Kumar, ; , that a mortgagor is not restricted in the management of the property by making a mortgage and that so long as nothing takes place to impair the value or impede the operation of the mortgage the mortgagor would be well within his powers in making a lease for a term. Mukherjee J. had occasion to consider this very case in Madanmohan Singh vs Raj Kishore Kumar (I.L.R. , referred to. (iii)The question whether a mortgagor was not restricted by the provisions of section 66 of the Transfer of Property Act and that too long as anything takes place,to impair the property or impede its operation, the mortgagor does not exceed his powers. [1112 G] (iv)The case of Banee Pershxd vs Beet Bhunjan Singh, A.I.R., Cal. 92, referred to (v) The true position had been stated in the following terms by this court in MadanMohan Singh vs Jal Kishore Kumar and others, ; and it was held that the mortgagor dealt with the mortgaged properties in the ordinary course of his management could be rightly deemed operative against him. [111 G H] (vi)The fact that M filed the suit for recovery of possession of four villages of which the defendants were in wrongful possession did not affect the rights of the mortgagee, and that M had ample opportunity to redeem the mortgage if they so desired but did not choose to exercise their right of redemption, that the execution sale of Gadi Sirampur including the four villages in question was binding upon the mortgagor. [114 A B] (vii)The suit for specific performance was decreed by the trial court and the decree passed by the High court dismissing the plaintiff appeal was set aside.

The petitioner, a contractor, was appointed as an arbitrator. The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of the contract and for damages. The petitioner contended that Clause 68 of the Contract provides for appointment of an arbitrator and when the petitioner had legally invoked clause 68 and issued notice to the respondent for reference to arbitration. The trial court dismissed the suit holding that Clause 67 of the Agreement provided for appointment by consent of the parties and not by consent, and that the arbitration agreement was void as it did not comply with the provisions of section 14(2) (b). The High Court in appeal held that the period of limitation for commencing an arbitration runs from the date on which the cause of action accrued, that is to say, from the day when the claimant first acquired either a right of action or a right to require that an arbitration takes place upon the dispute concerned. In this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that Clause 69 of the agreement provides for the appointment of arbitrator and since the respondent had legally exercised his discretionary power under section 8 of the Act, he was bound to appoint an arbitrator; and that in any event, by a conjoint reading of sections 5 and 12 (2) it is clear that the court has been given power in given circumstances to grant leave to a contracting party to have the arbitrator or umpire removed and the arbitration Agreement entered into with other contracting part revoked. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of the Limitation Act would apply to arbitrations as it applies to actions in the High Court and the making, after a claim has become statute barred, of a submission of it to arbitration, does not prevent the statute of limitation being pleaded. [363D] 2.1 In the instant case, the proceedings before the arbitration are like civil proceedings before court within the meaning of section14 of the . The proceedings before arbitration are both like civil suits before the court within whose jurisdiction the claim is not to be brought after the expiration of a specified number of years from the dates on which it should have accrued but for that term in the agreement. [364E] 2:2 In the case of arbitrations, the claim was not to have been brought after expiration of the specified number or years from date when the claim accrues. The period of Limitation for commencing arbitration runs between the date of the cause and the date when it should has accrued but only for that period in the contract. [365G] 2 :3 In the present case, by consent the parties have substituted the arbitrator for a court of law to arbiter their disputes or differences. It is, therefore, open to the parties to plead in the proceedings that they have substituted their arbitrator for an arbitration. [366H; 367A] 3:4 The provisions contained in section 14 of the , Limitation Act will apply to arbitration as it applied to actions under the High Courts and the make, after the expiry of a certain number of year from the commencement of the period when the cause or action accrued. [367B] 4.1 Section 14 of Limitation Act applies to arbitrations and notwithstanding any term in an arbitration agreement to the contrary, cause of arbitration for the purpose of limitation shall be deemed to have accrued to the party in respect of any such matter at the time when it would have accrued But for that clause in the Contract is not applicable, of arbitrations. [368C] 4:2 The provisions relating to arbitration proceedings are like Civil Procedure Code, by analogy to arbitration proceeding, and like interpretation was given to section 14 (1) (a) to Section 14(3) (c).

The appellants, who were the mortgagees of certain lands in Bihar, applied for a decree against the Estate. The trial court held that the objection was barred by the principles of res judicata and further on July 23, 1960 for default of the judgment debtors. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the trial court and restored the decree to its original number. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the execution was barred under section 4(d) of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950 (to be hereinafter referred to as the Act). HELD : The provisions contained in section 16 in regard to the scaling down of debts due by the proprietors and tenure holders clearly indicate that another object which the Act wanted to achieve was to give some redress to the debtors whose estates have been taken away from them by the notifications issued under section 3. Therefore, in construing section 4 (d) it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions of the Act do not fall within the protection of the said Act and again at page 578 "Having regard to this scheme, it is difficult to confine the application of section 4 only to execution proceedings in which the decree holder seeks to proceed against the estate of the debtor. [69 H] The words of section 6 are wide enough to include claims made against the estates which have vested in the State and no others. [70 E F] In construing section 3(d), it would be necessary to bear in mind the object of the statute which was merely to provide for the transference to the State of the interests, of the proprietors, tenure holders and so, it would also be reasonable to confine that application only to the claims made by the estates who have vested under the State.

The appellants who were allocated to the I.P.S. or Central Services Group 'A ' and who have appeared in Civil Services Main Examination of a subsequent year under the interim orders of the Tribunal, were allotted to the Indian Administrative Service Group 'B ' and they had succeeded in Civil Service Main Examination subject to the provisions of Rule 17 of the C.S.,E.P., Rules, 1954. The respondents who had been allocated to I.A.S or Central Service Group "A ' or I.I.P.'S. and who had appeared in civil Services Main examination of a later year under interim orders passed by the Tribunal and were within the permissible age limit and have succeeded are to be given benefit of their success subject to t he provisions of Rules 17, 18 and 19 of the Central Civil Service (Prelimi nary) Examination Rules, 1955. The appellants who had not been allocated in any of the State Services, Group ' A ' or II, could not have been given benefit o their success in the main examination since the Tribunal has upheld the validity of the second proviso to Rule 4 of the Rules. In the writ petitions filed by them before this Court, it was contended that (1) the High Court had erred in holding that the respondents were entitled to be extended the benefit of the reservation under Article 16(4)(a) of the Constitution; and (2) the respondents had failed to establish that they were not within the prescribed age limit. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The Tribunal has allowed the candidates who have been allocated from the IPS or Central services Group 'C ' to sit at the next Civil Service Examination subject t o the condition that they must be within the per missible age limit without having to resign from the service to which they have been allotted, nor would they lose their original seniority in the service. [58D] 2. The High Court has rightly held that the Tribunal had erred by holding that those candidates were not eligible to sit for the main Examination since the tribunal has upheld t he validity of second proviso. [59E] 3. The direction should be issued to the respondents to permit the applicants to appear in the preliminary C.A., if they are unable to take training with their own Batch. Those applicants who have already been allocated, and who joined Group ' 'A service subsequently on allocation either on the basis of the previous examination or the subsequent examina tion or the consequent examinations as the case may be, will become eligible to appear again in the next CSE (Main) Examination subject only to the provision of Rule 4. [60E] 4. The proviso appended to the said rule, a candidate who has been allocated by the Central ServicesGroup 'A to a service Group ' on the results of an earlier examination will be eligible to compete for IAS, IFS, IPS and Central Services, and considered only for those appointments. A candidate who is appointed to a Central Service group 'B' on the result of an initial examination will not be eligible for appearing again in that Service or the service in which he has been allotted. [61F G] 5. The word "may be allowed to sit in the first Civil Service examination subject to th e provisions of rule 17 of C.C.S.(E.A.) Rules, and that the said candidate when allocated to a Service on the ground of his earlier examination would become eligible for consideration to appear at the subsequent Civil Services Examination subject lo the provisions o r Rule 17. [62G H] 6. The words "may not be allowed" in the second subse quent proviso are wide enough to include candidates who had already been allotted to a State Service Group or Central service Group. [63E] 7.

The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short) by an order dated 25.11.1986, passed by the Advisory Board. The grounds of detention were served on him on 26.11 1986 and he was informed that his request for assistance of a friend at the hearing had been turned down. On 27.11., 1986, the appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of detention. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the detaining authority was not in a position to reject the request of the detenu and that the application had been rejected. In this appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the refusal by the Board to permit the appellant to be represented by a lawyer was bad and continued detention of the Appellant became vitiated. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of the High court is set aside. [792B] 2.1 In the instant case, on 25th November 1986 while the detaining Authority was assisted by a Deputy Collector and a Superintendent of Central Excise, was the request for the assistance of the friend in order to ensure due observance of the policy of law that a detenu is not entitled to representation through a lawyer. The Advisory Board has, of course, to be careful in permitting assistance of an advocate. Regard must be had to the substance and not to the form since, especially in matters like the proceedings of Advisory Boards, whosoever assist or advises on facts of law must be deemed to be in the position of a legal adviser. [788E F] 2:2. The refusal by a detaining authority or the Government to permit such assistance to detenu was not justified. It did not preclude the Board from allowing such assistance. Regard should be had, to the context and not the form as since, particularly in matters involving the proceedings relating Advisory Boards etc., whosoever assists or advates on facts in law must also be deemed so to be In the position, particularly, in matters of like the proceeding of Advisory Board, whatever may be the substance. [789B] 3:3.
