The failure by the detaining authorities or the government to appear before the Advisory board with the aid of a Legal Practitioner or a legal practitioner would be in breach of Article 14 if a similar facility is denied to the detenu. Regard has been to the fact that it was for the Advisory Boards and not for the Government or the State to afford legal assistance to the prisoner. Regard ought to be had not to, the substance or not to The form since the detaining Board had, ofcourse, to consider the request made by a legal Practitioner or an legal advisers before the Board through a legal expert it could have, if he was so minded, made a request to the AdvisoryBoard for permission to be heard by a Legal practitioner. [781C D] 4:4. The detaining authority and the Government should have the facility of appearing before the advisory board with aid of an legal practitioner or a lawyer or a Legal adviser would be In breach of article 14 if the detaining officer or the Board takes the aid, of a statutory adviser before the Committee with the help of a lawyer, but that the said facility should be denied to detenu. [784E F; 778A] 5:5. The obligation cast on the detaining body and the government is not absolute and unconditional. It is not for this Court to examine and assess what prejudice has been caused to the appellant on account of such denial.

The appellants were the owners of certain mills in Calcutta. The mills were requisitioned and acquired by the Government under r. 75 A (2) of the Rules framed under the Act. The appellants claimed ownership through the mills on September 30, 1946, as provided by r. 76 A(2) Of the Rules. The Government issued notices to the owners and the mills for the acquisition of the property in the goods. The owners filed objections before the Land Acquisition Officer claiming ownership through them. The Land Acquisition officer held that as the goods requisitioned and were subject to pucca delivery orders, they did not pass on September 29, 1946. The Collector dismissed the objections holding that the requisitioning orders were only issued against payment, and that the property was not acquired under r 75 A(1) of Rules framed thereunder. The appeals filed by the owners were allowed by the Land acquisition Officer. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Government of India had no power to acquire the property as required by r 75A (2), and that in view of the usage that pucca delivery Orders were only passed against payment and were sold and dealt with in the market as absolutely representing the goods to which they relate, and as the mills were estopped from challenging that the properties in the articles had passed (see Anglo India Jute Mills Co. vs Omademall (I) , the Government which was entitled to acquire them under r . 75 A of the rules framed under it did not apply its mind to the question whether the Government would be precluded from acquiring the property on September, 30,1946, as required in r. 74A(2). Held: (i) The order of requisition passed by the Collector was valid service on the mills as owners for the purpose of r. 25 A (3), and therefore there was no acquisition following on the service of the notices in this case. The notice of acquisition in this respect was effective service on them as owners, for the purposes of r .75 A (4) would apply and the property passed to the Government on September 15, 1946; (ii) The Government had no authority to acquire any property under r.. 75A(1), and it could not be said that the order of requisitioning was invalid.

The assessee was a Private Limited Company. The assessment year concerned is 1963 64. During the assessment years 1964 65, a notice was issued to the assessee under Section 23A of the Income Tax Act, 1922. The assessee contended that it may become liable to pay additional tax under the said provision, and that the said sum of Rs. 4,50,000 continued to remain and was shown as a provision set apart to meet the taxation liability which the assessee called a contingent liability. The Income Tax Officer did not agree with the contention of the assessee and held that no action can be taken against the assessee in respect of the subsequent assessment year (1964 65) and disallowed the claim for additional tax. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, dismissed the appeal holding that no order levying additional tax was made on or before the date relevant to the assessment year 1963 64, and therefore, the said amount being a provision made towards a liability which had attached on account of the issuance of a notice under Section23A was indeed a provision and not a reserve. The Tribunal held that the sum of money being a reserve and should be included in its capital for the purposes of the Act. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that inasmuch as no order imposing additional tax had been passed on or after the date of the said judgment, the assessee could not be treated as a "reserve" within the meaning of Section 23(A) and not an "reserving". Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in holding it to be a provision. [113E] 2.2 In the circumstances of the case, we must hold that the High Court rightly held it to have been a provision, but not a "Reserve" nor was it set apart or appropriated as a reserve; and that it did not call it a reserve nor was there any appropriation as a reserved. [114F] 2:3 The assessee itself called it a provision which provided for a liability against the profits to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P & L. accounts and the balance sheet. On the other hand, reserves are appropriations of profits, the assets by which they are rep resented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business. [115F] 4.1 In the instant case, the High court was right. [116G] 2(a) The assessee himself called it "reservation" and did not ask it a "reserved". It did not require it a reserved or appropriation. [117A B] (b) The expression "resisting" is used in the context of business. In other words, the broad distinction between the two is that whereas a provision is a charge against the profit to be take into account towards gross receipts, in theP & L account, a reserve is in appropriation of profits and the asset or assets bywhich it is represented being retained, to form parts of the Capital employed in that business. The provisions are usually shown in the balance sheets by way of deductions from the assets in respect thereof. [118C D] (c) The broad distinction must be that whereas an provision is charge against profits tobe taken into consideration against gross receipt in the A & L Account, a reserved is in appropriated of profits the assetor asset or asset by which it is representing being retained To form part Of the capital invested in the Business. [119D] 2.(a) In other word, the general distinction between provision and reserve is stated in the following words: "The distinction between a provision (and a reserve) is stated In the balance Sheet by way Of deductions from assets in the Income Account, the asset/or assets by whom it is represent being retained.

The petitioners in these writ petitions were appointed to temporary posts on the basis of competitive examinations and those that were recruited by selection, but both by Union Public Service Commission. The Railway Board had taken a decision to the effect that the Officers so absorbed into the Indian Railway Service of Engineers would be given weightage in seniority "on the basis Of half the total years of continuous service in working posts in Railways prior to their permanent absorption into Class. The petitioners in the writ petitions claimed that officers were appointed on temporary posts and that their seniority had to be reckoned on the principle of 'equal pay for equal work". The Union Public Services Commission, however, rejected the claim of the petitioners on the ground that the officers so absorbed were placed above those appointed on the same basis as temporary Assistant Engineers. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the classification of temporary Assistant Officers separately from the Indian Railways Service of Engineer Class I was neither discriminatory nor violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution, for the reason that it had nexus to the object sought to be achieved, which mainly was efficiency of service, and that both the services had started separately and never became one. Allowing the appeals by special leave, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The classification of Temporary Assistant Officers is not discriminatory nor violation of Articles 16 and 16. [1022C] 1.2 The seniority of the absorb temporary Assistant officers would ordinarily reckon from the date of their absorption as stipulated in their appointment matters and as held by this Court with weightage of half the length of service subject to a maximum of five years, it would otherwise be imprudent now, at this point of time to dig up old issues. [1122D] 1:3 The seniority has to be counted from the dates of absorption as provided in their appointments matters and the seniority of those absorbers is to be computed from their date of absorption into the service matters and on that basis it would be impriudent now at this stage of time, at present, at point of point of first time to draw up old issue. [1222D E] 1 :4 The seniority in the Indian railways Service of Engineering was to be determined from the year of their appointment as temporary Assistants subject to maximum of 5 years. This Court has also held that the seniority had been reckoned on that principle. [1323F] 1.:5 In Katyani Dayal 's case, this court took into account the long wait involved in the process but all the same approved of measures of the Railway Board in lessening the Iona wait by giving them weightage of one half of the length as temporaryAssistant Officers subject to the maximum of three years. [1423F G] 1:-6 The seniority had not been reckoned at this time to look for a substitution at our end, as that would unsettle a settled position, established more than a decade ago. It needs mentioning that the appeals being decided instantly are against the judgments and orders of the High Court rejecting writ petitions of the appellants 1027 before it on the aforesaid basis. [924F] 2:7 The seniority is to he reckoned from thedate of absorption of temporary Assistants. subject to an maximum of ten years, because of its being questioned elsewhere. [969G H] 1):8 In Katkyani Dayal vs Union of India and Ors., ; , followed.

The appellant was charged with offences under section 9 and 11 of the Saurashtra Ordinance, 1947. The Special Court held that the offence was one under section 5(1) of the Act and that it was not competent to try the case. On appeal by special leave, HELD : (i) The notification issued by the State Government under section 4(1)(a) of that Ordinance was, therefore, different from the notification issued under section 6(1). [457 F] (ii) The words "offences" in section 11 of that Act are wide enough to include all offences which are punishable with imprisonment. It is obvious that this part of section 11 does not offend against the equal protection clause of our Constitu tion and the notification which has been issued under that part of the section cannot be held to be invalid or ultra vires. [456 F] The words 'offences ' in section 5 (1) are wide and comprehensive enough to cover all offences punishable with death, imprisonment for life or imprisonment for a term exceeding seven years. It does not mean that the legislature has left it to the State Govt. to classify offences or classes of cases for the purpose of the Ordinance, for the State is in a better position to judge the needs and exigencies of the State and the Court will not lightly interfere with the decision of the Government. [441 G H] (iii) The word 'offence ' in article 14 means "to try" and it includes all offences committed by an accused person or persons who are charged with the offence. It cannot be said that the Legislature has left the State to classify offence or classes o f cases for t he purpose of t he Ordinance, because, as the legislature had left it, to the Government to classify them or classes thereof, makes it the duty of the state government to classify offenders or classes or classes Of offences or class of cases.

The appellants were convicted under section 396 I.P.C. and sentenced to death for the offence of murder, and the High Court confirmed their conviction and sentence. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (i) the evidence of P.W. 2 who undoubtedly came near the scene of occurrence is not reliable; (ii) the prosecution has proved the case against the appellants satisfactorily and beyond all reasonable doubt, and (iii) the High court had erred in rejecting the evidence as it was corroborated by the evidence on record. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The evidence of the eye witnesses lend assurance to the evidence that they were seen by P.Ws. 1, 7 and 8 immediately after the occurrence which had gone on for about 15 minutes. [935C] 2.1 In the instant case, the prosecution had proved the presence of the accused appellants in the house at the time of the occurrence. The testimony of P W. 2 is corroborated by evidence of PW. 1 who undoubtedly was present in the eastern kotha where the main part of the incident has taken place and must have had sufficient opportunity to indentify, with the help of the lantern which was burning, the appellants who were previously known to her and not strangers and she had received as many as 19 injuries during the course of the commission of the offence could have seen any of the culprits and could not identify them. [ 935D] 2:2 The evidence on the record is consistent with the evidence adduced by the prosecution. The High Court has rightly rejected the evidence tendered by the eye witness PW 1 who actually saw the occurrence and had not mentioned the name of any of those accused to other villagers who entered the house of the deceased soon after the culprits left the place. [961D] 3:3 In the present case, it is quite possible that all the 9 appellants were in the western kothas of the house in the tin shed at the relevant time and it was not improbable that these appellants were seen near the site of occurrence. Therefore, it could not be said that they had been seen by any of them during the occurrence or had not stated the name or names of any accused to whom they entered the room of the victim soon after their assailants left the scene. [964E] 4:4 The evidence adduced on behalf the appellants lends assurance to their evidence lends assurance, to the testimony of PW 1 lend assurance that the witnesses were seen at the scene immediately after occurrence and it is not improbable whether these appellants could have been in a position to identify them or not strangers. [963G H] 5:5 In the absence of any cogent reason for rejecting the prosecution evidence, the High 'Court has rightly held that no reliance could be placed on the evidence. The reasons given by the learned Judges of the High Courts for rejecting their evidence are not convincing. [996D E] 6:6 It is well settled that in an appeal against acquittal, it should be slow to interfere with the findings of fact arrived at by the trial court unless there are compelling and substantial reasons for doing so. In the case of acquittal, the appellate court has full power to reverse or affirm the finding of acquittal recorded by the lower courts. [995E] 7:6 The High 's approach in dealing with an appeal filed against acquittal is not proper. It should have been a judicious approach and should be avoided while dealing with appeals against acquittal.

The appellant Corporation was engaged in the business of manufacturing and selling cement. The workmen were appointed as Assistant Engineers on probation for a period of two years. On the expiry of the period of probation, they were confirmed by an order dated October 30, 1982. In the meanwhile, the State Road Transport Corporation created under the State Act entitled the Transport Corporation to the Transport Undertaking Act, 1950 ( 'Corporation Act ' for short) is in appeal by special leave and the common decision of a Division Bench of the High Court was upheld by this Court. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The expression 'retrenchment ' must include every termination of the service of a workman by an act of the employer even if such termination involved was a consequence of transfer or closure of the undertaking was to be treated as 'ret retrenchment ' for the purposes of notice, compensation etc. [793A] 2.1 In Hindustan Steel Ltd. vs Shambhu Nath Mukherjee, ; , followed. 1.2 The expression "termination of service for any reason whatsoever" in section 2(oo) of the covers every case of termination of service except those not expressly included in section 25F or not expressly provided for by other provisions of the Act such as sections 25FF and 25FFF. [788B] 2:2 In Hindustan Steels Ltd. 's case, this Court held that retrenchment as defined in section 3(oo), includes every termination by the employer of the services of a probationer by an action of the employee on reaching the age of superannuation if the contract of employment between the employer and the workman concerned contains a stipulation in that behalf; or (c) voluntary retirement of the workman on reaching his age of retirement, if the Contract of employmentbetween the employer & the workman involved contain a stipulation In that behalf, termination of services except those which have been embodied in the definition, discharge from employment or termination of such service of probationer would also amount to retrenchment. [789E] 2 :3 The excepted or excluded cases are where termination is by way of punishment inflicted by way Of disciplinary action, voluntary retirement, of the workmen, retirement of a worker on reaching that age of superannuaries if the employer had not terminated the services by act of employer even though such termination involve a stigma. [893F] 2(a) The excepted and excluded cases were where termination was by way o punishment inflicted on the workman, voluntary resignation of the worker on attaining the age Of superannuation or termination thereof is to be regarded as ' retrenchment '. The excepted categories are those which had been embodied into the definition in section2(oo). [894C] 2.(b) The excluded or excluded classes of cases are Where termination is for a reason whatsoever, otherwise than as a punishment inflicted inflicted by an employer, voluntary, retirement or termination or of service of probation or where such termination involves a stipulation of dismissal or removal from service. The excluded category of cases is where termination involves the termination of employment of a person on the transfer or termination by way either disciplinary action or voluntary retirement. [820E] 3:1 In the instant case, the services have been terminated on the ground of unsuitability and it was not a case of disbanding surplus labour force and, therefore, did 788 not amount to termination. The exclusion or excluded categories are where the termination involved is a consequence by way or disciplinary action voluntary retirement or resignation of service or termination. [821F] 3.2 In the present cases, the order of retrenchment was treated by Parliament as 'deemed retrenchment ' and it upheld the Award of the Labour Court which set aside those orders and gave appropriate relief to the appellant Corporation. [822G H] 4:3 The decision in Sundara Money 's Case was approved in the aforementioned three cases.

The question referred at the instance of the assessee to the High Court relates to the assessment years 1953 55 and 1960 56. In the assessment proceedings for the four quarters ending March, 1959 the assessee applied to the Commercial Tax Officer for cancellation of the registration of the appellant as a "dealer" under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act in respect of unconnected or unclaimed goods, and was accordingly registered. The Commercial Tax officer rejected the application on the ground that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the assesse s 's activities, and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. On appeal by the assessee the Additional Commissioner of Commercial Taxes held that the transaction did not indicate that the Railway concerned was carrying on business as a dealer liable to assessment under the Act, and accordingly ordered cancellation of registration of appellant as an "dealer". The High Court dismissed the revision application holding that the sale effected by the appellant were sales under the provisions of Section 56 of the Bengal Excise Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the assessee that the expression "dealer ' in section 2(c) of the Bihar Finance ( Sales Tax) act, 1941 is not defined in the Act and therefore a sale of goods takes place. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether the assessee Railway in each case is a " dealer" for the purpose of as sessment under the Indian Railways Act, 1941. [780C] 2.1 In the instant case the assessee Eastern Railway disposed of scrap and unserviceable material lying with it. The case is covered directly by the decision of this Court in the District Controller of Stores, Northern Railway Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxes Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423. In view of the decision in the State of Punjab vs C.A. No. 1069 of 1975 arising from the decision it is not necessary to refer to the facts in the present case. [788F G] 2:2 The question as to whether the appellant Railway in any case is an " dealer", for the purposes of as Section 56(c)(g) read with C1. (g) of section 2 of the Indian Railway Act, 1939. [789B] 3.3 In the case of the assesses South Eastern Railway, what were sold were unclaimed goods. The Railway was a carrier of the goods and if at the stage of delivery goods remained un claimed for a period the Railway was entitled to dispose them of. There can be no doubt that the activity of so disposing of the property was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It seems to South Eastern railway was a "business" for purposes of theBengal Finance ( sales Tax) and 1941. In this case, what was sold were unserviceable goods. [822C] 4.4 The case falls directly within the ambit of the definition of "dealer " under the Bihar Sales Tax Act, 1940. [823B] 5.5 The question is whether the activity carried on by the respondent Railway in respect Of unconnected or unpaid goods under the provision of Section56 of the Railways Act is a dealer" within the meaning of section 3(c).

The appellant, a Director of the Indian Bank, was authorised to purchase securities on behalf of the Insurance Company. The appellant was authorised by the Chairman to sell securities on his behalf and to issue instructions regarding the purchase or sale of securities. He had been instructed in September 1954 that the shares would be purchased at Bombay and that after Dalmia 's approval the vouchers about the purchase of those securities should be prepared. The Bank of India, however, did not pay any amount to the appellant as required by section 409(1) of the . The appellant filed a complaint against the respondent for the offence under sections 409 and 420 I.P.C. on the ground that he had been authorised by Dalmia to purchase or sell securities in contravention of the manner in which he was to deal with that money. The trial court acquitted the respondent but convicted him under section 409 I. P.C., and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for one year and a fine of Rs. 500/ . In appeal, the High Court held that the appellant had been authorized by Dalmia and added that the investment of funds would be in the discretion of Agents and the Insurance company was not authorised to sell or sell any securities on their behalf unless he was authorised under the Chairman 's instructions regarding purchase or sales of securities and that the funds of the insurance Company were invested in securities. Held, that the High Courts had rightly held that it was not possible to believe that the securities had either been sold or pledged and that therefore Chokhani did not include those securities in this letter. The circumstances showed that they mentioned Bhagwati Trading Company as that represented the true state of affairs andigence had to inform the Delhi Office of the Bharat Union Agencies about the source of the money he was receiving for the Union Agencies to meet its losses.

The appellants were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the erstwhile State of Saurashtra and Kutch. By sub section (1) of section 115 it was provided that conditions of service applicable immediately before the appointed day to the case of any person allotted to another State shall not be varied to his disadvantage except with the previous approval of the Central Government. Under the , the appellants were allocated to serve under the orders of the State Government and continued to render service in the Districts will not, in our judgment, affect the right of the personnel to be absorbed in equivalent posts in the Secretariat and on terms not== coercing them to perform service in connection therewith. The appellants were appointed as ministerial staff in the ministerial service of the Part B State of Gujarat under section 81 of the Bombay Reorganisation Act. By virtue of sub section(7) it was made clear that conditions Of service applicable before the date of the appointed date to the cases of any persons allotted to other States shall not, except with prior approval of Government, be varied or modified to his detriment except with previous approval in writing of the Government. The State Government by its order dated August 19, 1966 directed that the appellants should be treated as permanent employees and their pay and seniority in the subordinate offices of the Secretariat of the Gujarat State Secretariat shall be fixed at Rs. 1,000 per month. The respondents challenged the validity of the order on the ground that the transfer of the former Saurashtra and Saurashtra States Secretariats to the Gujarat Secretariat per se was not open to objection. Held, that the High Court was right in holding that when the ministerial services were allotted and assigned duties in various districts it will not be open to the officers of the subordinate office to challenge the authority of the government either to transfer officers from the Districts or to post and assign them duties in the offices of subordinate offices. The Government of Gujarat had no power under article 309 of the Constitution to adopt any other method of recruitment of the members of the ministerial staff.

The petitioners, who were dealers in cotton and sell them at the rate of Rs. 250 per metric tonne, purchased cotton and sold them at a higher rate than the State Government. The petitioners contended that the tax was levied on the basis of the turnover of the petitioners during the period from April 1, 1967 to March 31, 1968, and that the sales were made in the course of inter state trade or commerce, and therefore, they were not liable to pay sales tax under section 5(2)(a) (vi). The State Government rejected the contention. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the Act itself did not indicate the stage at which the tax could be levied and because under section 15(1) of the Central Act there could be no liability for payment of tax unless this stage was so stated in the Act or the rules thereunder, and as such the tax cannot be said to be higher in the case of imported goods. HELD: (i) The normal rule under the Act is to levy the tax on the first purchaser. If a person has purchased cotton or sells it after the period provided for in section 5 (2)(b), that party is liable to make payment of the tax and in the first instance, and then claim refund, at a later stage. [553 C D] (ii) The discrimination is also between the first purchase in the cases of imported cotton and last sale in the Case of local goods. If the Central Government makes it mandatory that the Tax can be collected only at one stage, in our opinion, it is not enough for the State to say that a person, who is not liable under section 4(2) (a)(vi), must nevertheless pay it in the second instance and then claiming refund, At a later point. [552 E] (iii) The tax cannot therefore be said either to be lower in the category of goods or sales tax. [554 C D]. (iv) The distinction between the two classes of cases is that if a person purchases cotton and sells it at the first sale, the stage of purchase is purchased by the last dealer liable to tax and the stage is purchase by the next dealer liable for paying the tax. It is said that the discrimination is only between the second purchase in one case and the last sale of such goods by the third dealer liable. [558 G H] (v) The discriminatory treatment is also on account of the fact that the taxing authority has not prescribed a time limit for making the assessment.

The respondent mortgaged the property in dispute to the appellant who was defendant No. 1,08,098. The mortgage debt was one and indivisible and even though different amounts were mentioned as payable by two groups of defendants in the decree, the decree holders were bound under the terms of the decree to release the entire mortgaged property even on payment of certain specified amounts by 'them proceeds clearly on the assumption that the mortgage debt and the security had been split up. The respondent filed a suit for recovery of the amount due under the decree as scaled down in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the decision of the District Judge, but held that defendants 2 to 7 were entitled to have the debts scaled off and set aside the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the mortgage decree was scaled up by the High court in favour of defendants 2 and 3 only and the amended decree directs that the said defendants do pay into court the sum of Rs. 1.05,000 and odd and it is on payment Of the amount directed to be paid by defendants 2, to 7. (2) the amendment made by the Code of Civil Procedure was not applicable because the mortgage was schedaled down under the provisions o the Agriculturists ' Relief Act, but only in case where the decree holder had failed to pay the amount within a period of one month from the date of the judgment and the suit was dismissed against him. HELD: (1)(a) The High Court was right in holding that by virtue of the amendment the mortgage could not be scaled out under the Agriculturists' Relief Act but only with respect to cases where the debt has been scaled over, and in case they did not pay this amount, the whole of the mortgaged property including their interest would be sold for the entirety of the mortgage debts for which defendant No, 2 was not an agriculturist himself. [299 D] (b) The decree contains no such clear directions but reading the decree together as a whole and having regard to the actual decision in the case, this must be taken to be its plain implica tions. The subsequent agreement between the parties arrived at in course of the execution proceedings by which the decreeholders agreed to release interest of defendant No 2 and that of defendants 3 to 7 separately on payment thereof by 'him proceeds clearly On the assumption, therefore, it is not possible for the respondent No. 2 to have paid this amount. [297 E F] (c) The subsequent agreements arrived at during course of execution proceedings between which the mortgage creditor agreed to released the interest of the respondent no. 2 and also that of defendant Nos 3 to 5 separately on payments of certain stipulated amounts by way of security by 'their proceeds clearly indicate that the decree contains nothing more than a clear direction but reading it as a part and having respect to the real decision in this case, the finding of the High Courts is right and should not have been disturbed. [298 G] (d) The amendment made in section 47 of the Code was not retrospective because the amendment was made retrospectively with effect from April 1, 1938. It was only prospective in operation.

The appellants, who were the respondents in the suit before the City Civil Court, were tenants of the premises in question under the first respondent. The first respondent filed a suit for eviction of the appellants on the ground that the first appellant was a tenant within the meaning of the Act and that the second and third plaintiffs were lawful subtenants of the first plaintiff and were entitled to possession, use and occupation of the said premises as sub tenants thereof. The City Civil Judge held that it had jurisdiction to entertain the suit but dismissed the suit on the view that there bad been no lawful subletting by the first appellants of the building to the second, and that there had been a lawful subletting, by the second appellant of the property in question to the third plaintiffs as the provisions of section 10 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel Rates and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947 (Bombay Act No. " The City civil Court held that the suit was not one between a landlord and a tenant because the defendants of this suit did not admit that the appellants were the tenants of premises within the ambit of the provisions Of the Act. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the City civil court had jurisdiction under section 28 of the City of Bombay Rents Hotel, Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control (Control) Act, 1948, because there bad already been a lawfully sublet by the appellants to the first and third defendants as the provision of section 28 did not apply to them. Held:(i) The City of Nagpur vs R. M. D. Chamarbaugwala, ; , followed. (ii)The suit related to possession of premises to which the provisions o. 28 were applicable and in that suit claims and questions arising out of the act or any of its provisions had to be dealt with. It was not necessary for the City Court to decide whether the plaintiffs were the tenant of the buildings in question. The provisions of the section on the other hand clearly indicate that all claims or questions arising from the Act or any o.l its provisions, even though they may be in the nature of a title to the premises, were to be determined by the courts specified in section 28 and no other. (iii)The City Civil court could not decree the suit of the plaintiffs unless their claim to remain in possession was established under the Act, or any other. The High Court correctly decided that the suits filed by the plaintiffs could not be determined on the basis of the evidence adduced before it.

The appellant was a managing director of the Company. On July 7, 1955, Dadoba transferred his business to the Company and he further contended that the appointment of the appellant Govind as the managing director by the will of Dadoba was void. The appellant contended that an appointment by a director of another in his place by act inter vivous be an assignment of the office of a director within section 312, and had only contended that such an appointment would not be an assign and would not therefore be rendered void by the section. Held, that the proviso to section 86B does not assist the argument that in section 312 of the new Act the word "assignment" in the main part of section 86 B of the old Act meant a "transfer of his office". The rule of construction on which the High Court relied was that when one finds a proviso to a section, the presumption is that but for the proviso the enacting part would include the subject matter of the proviso. In other words, it seems to be the policy of the Act that to a certain extent the appointments of directors have to be made by the shareholders. The rule does not permit an appointment of an alternate director by a person who has been appointed otherwise than by the company in a general meeting. Where however a director has been so appointed otherwise then, the shareholders cannot claim to have a say in the appointment by him. In the present case Dadoba had power under the articles to appoint a person to be his managing director and in exercise of that power he bad appointed the appellant as the Managing Director to hold the office after his death.

The appellants are the tenants of the premises situated at No. 6 Kasi Chetty Street, G.T. Madras. They carry on business there. The respondent landlord filed an eviction petition against the appellant and one other partnership firm carrying on business in the name and style of M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart on the ground that they had unlawfully sublet the said shop to M/S. Adivas Glass Mart and were liable to be evicted for HAMEEDULLAH ful subletting under the provision of Section 10(2)(ii)(a) of the Tamil Nadu Buildings (Lease and 419 Rent Control) Act, 1960. The Trial Court held that the appellants had unlawfully and without the consent of the respondent sublet the shop let out to M./s Adivas glass Mart and they were liable for be evicted under section 10(1)(ii) (i)(a). The Appellate Authority dismissed the said appeal upholding the finding of unlawful subletting by the appel lants. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the application against the partnership firm was not maintainable without joining its partners as re spondents. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of order 30 of the Code of Civil Procedure are not applicable to the proceedings under the Rent Act either and hence, the ratio laid down in the aforesaid decision is directly applicable to taine proceedings under Rent Act, either and thus delay matters for a number of years. [420B] 2.1 In the instant case, no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it is indeed not open to the appellants to raise such an objection at a very late stage and thereby delay matters For a number Of years. It was only by virtue of the provisions of Order 30 of Code of C.P.C., that a firm can sue and be sued in its own name without the partners being impleaded. In these circumstances, this contention of Mr. Nayar must fail. [ 420B] 3.2 The appellants are not entitled to raise this plea at this stage at all. It is indeed open to Mr. Sethi to raise the said objection at any stage of the proceedings. [421C D] 4.3 In the case before us, no objection has also been raised in the Trial Court or even in the first Appel late Court, nor in the second appel late court, it would have been open to them to raise it at a later stage and thus delays matters for another number of year. It would be only just and proper if the appellants are permitted to amend the eviction petition and join the partners as fresh partners. [467D] 4:4 In the present case, there is no evidence in the case to come to the conclusion that had the account books and ledgers been produced, they would have shown that rent was received by the appellants from M/ s. Adars Glass Mart which would justify the finding that had he the account book and led Officers were not produced. They would have showed that rent is received by them from M.S.Adeshwar Glass Shop which would substantiate the finding. [468G H] 5.5 In the aforesaid circumstances, there was no substance in this contention. There is also evidence to show that M/ S Adivas Engineering Mart was carrying on trade at the said premises and that firm was carried on business at the aforesaid premises even for some time during which the appellants firm had ceased to carry on the business there and that firms were carried on by the respondent herein even for certain time during that period. [469G H; 469A] 6. In view of this, it is not open for Mr. imagination to raise any such objection at this belated stage and consequently delay matters.

The Andhra Pradesh Land Reforms Act, 1960 was enacted to provide for the imposition of ceiling on land situate within the urban agglomerations. Section 2(n) (A)(ii) defines a family unit in the State of Andhra Pradesh including land situate in urban agglomeration and includes land situate therein. Section 3(f) defines "family unit" as meaning any land held by a person in excess of the ceiling area. Section 4(1) provides that where a family is not a member of a family, the whole of the Andhra Pradesh Act would apply to land situate outside the urban area and the Andhra State Act would continue to be applicable to determine the ceiling on holding of land. The Andhra Pradesh Ceiling on Land Holdings Act, 1961 was enacted with reference to the provisions of the Central Act. Section 5(1)(a) defines family unit as meaning a family consisting of a father and mother and includes a son born out of the wedlock. Section 7 provides that every individual who is not member of any family unit shall be an extent of land equal to one standard holding. The ceiling area in the case of every individual, who is a member or a family after the commencement of the Act was required to be determined and if there was any surplus it was to be surrendered to the State Government. Section 8 provides that the ceiling shall be payable on all lands held by him as a family Unit. Section 9 provides for the determination of the total area of land in excess whereof the ceiling limit is fixed. Section 10 provides for payment of compensation to every individual. Section 11 provides for an appeal against the order of the Collector, and section 12 provides for appeals against orders of the appellate authority. Section 13 provides that no person shall be entitled to any compensation or other sum payable under the Act in respect of any land which is not included in the family unit. Section 14 provides for a revision of the order passed by the Collector. Section 15 provides for appeal to the High Court from an order of a subordinate officer. Section 16 provides for revision of orders of appellate authority and section 17 provides for review of orders passed by such authorities. Section 18 provides for power of revision. Section 19 provides for making of rules. Section 20 provides for matters relating to the determination, payment of land revenue etc. The Rules provide for appeals to the Appellate Tribunal against orders passed under the provisions contained in the Act. Rule 22 provides for procedure for appeal and revision. Rule 23 provides for filing of appeals by the State. Rule 24 provides for disposal of appeals. Rule 25 provides for preparation of draft rules. Rule 26 provides for publication of draft Rules. Rule 27 provides for issue of notice to the persons interested in the land. Rule 28 provides for appointment of a person as an appellate authority, and Rule 29 provides for determination of appeals and revision by the Appellate Authority. Rule 30 provides for hearing of appeals on merits. Rule 31 provides for stay of proceedings before the Appellate Board. Rule 32 provides for deposit of amount deposited with the Collector and Rule 33 provides for grant of stay of execution of orders. Rule 33 deals with appeal to High Court against orders under the Andhra Land Reforms Rules, 1960. Rule 34 provides for suspension of execution pending disposal of an appeal by the appellate Board. The appeals are filed in this Court challenging the validity of the proceedings taken by the Revenue authorities. The questions that arise for consideration were: (1) whether the Andhra Act sought to impose ceiling on lands situate within these urban agglomities; and (2) whether it was ultra vires and void as being outside the legislative competence of the State Legislature? HELD: 1.1 The Andhra Act is an expensive concept and any area with an existing or future population of more than one lakh could be notified to be an urban agglisable Area under section 2(j). [1157C] 1.

The respondents were workmen of the appellant company. The dispute was referred to the Industrial Tribunal for adjudication and it was held that all the workmen who turned up on or before October 2, 1953, must be taken back in employment without condition and of the two men who came later, some claimed to come back to their services as of right without any explanations and none of the workmen had done any actual work for the period. The Tribunal however found that the workmen themselves tried to coerce the Company by 'slow down ' tactics etc., for the periods between October 2 and November 2, 1952, and that they reported for duty on October 1, 1953 but failed to produce evidence satisfactory to the Company of their absence as required by the notice dated September 17, 1953. The Industrial Tribunal held that the termination was justified. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Industrial Tribunals had in each case considered the justification for absence without leave and in view of the circumstance that the men were in custody, the Company was not justified in refusing leave. Held: (i) The Industrial Tribunals have taken a decision to terminate their services of Chattoraj on the ground of his prejudicial and subversive activities, as in this case, the work of the company will be paralysed if the Company is forced to give leave to all of them for a "more or less indefinite period. If, on the contrary, the Tribunal proceeded on the footing that the company had decided to terminate the services of the Chattorraj on the grounds of his adverse and subversive activity then on being satisfied that Chattorj was guilty of such activities the proper order would have been to give the Company permission to dismiss Chattorapaj. The decision of the Industrial tribunal to terminate his services was justified, because it found that Chattaj indulged in activities prejudicial to the company and it is now recognised that deliberate 's slow down ' methods and an incitement to other workmen to adopt such tactics both amounts to misconduct. If a large number of workmen are arrested by the authorities in charge of law and order by reason of their questionable activities in connection with a labour dispute, as In this case the work was not paralyzed if the company is forced by giving leave to All of them For a " more or less mere indefinite period". If the Tribunal proceed on the basis that the Company had decided not to terminate Chattorgarh on the plea of his reversion, it was for the Company to decide whether the charges had been proved and the Industrial Court should not have interfered with the decision of that company unless it found otherwise. The question whether the workmen were entitled to be taken into employment without any condition is a matter which must be decided by the Tribunal in each individual case. In the absence of exceptional or special circumstances or of grave injustice, the proper orders would have to give effect to the finding of fact. [696 B C] (ii) The Tribunal having found that there was a suspension order against Chattraj indulged in activity prejudicial to other workman to adopt those tactics both amount to misconduct and not merely because Chattapaj indulged into activities prejudicial or subversive to others to adopt them such tactics either amounts to victimisation. If on the facts, the Industrial Disputes Tribunal proceeded to terminate services of Chhattaj on being satisfies that Chattaraj was guilty Of such activities then on be satisfied that the decision was mala fide or amounted to victimisation, it would have resulted in a finding of guilt. [596 C D] (iii) The contention that the Tribunal had in every case considered whether the charge had been established and the industrial Tribunal should not interfere with the order of termination is justified.

The appellant University of Rajaswas invited applications for the post of Professor in the department of Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under Section 5 of the Urea Kant was mentioned in the reserve list by the Selection Committee. Dr. Urea Kumar who was already selected and kept in the reserved list was appointed as Professor in a department of the University. He was appointed on the ground that the Selection Commis sion had not been constituted in accordance with law and objection was also raised that once a selected person joins the post, the reserve lists exhausted itself. Dr Urea Chand who was earlier selected and placed in the select list was appoint ed as Professor. The appellant University filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the validity of the Selection Board 's order dated 10th July, 1978. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that once an selected person join the post then selection made by the Committee is exhausted and the reserve s list is of no avail and becomes extinct. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant University that once the selected person joined the post earlier selection made in the last decade from the reserve pool, the reservation list exhausted itself and the subse quently the Syndicate by its resolution dated 10 th July,1978 decided that the reserve List recommended by the selection Committee shall be valid upto six months instead of six months in a resolution passed on 3.12.1983. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The very purpose of preparing a reserve list would be defeated if the view taken by the High court is accepted that once selected person joining the post again selection made under the last year from the reserved pool is exhausted, and the reserved List is of nothing avail and become extinct, there was no meaning or purpose of keeping the reserve for a long period of one year. [421D] 1.2 The very object of preparing the reservelist would be frustrated if the views expressed by the University are accepted that when a person selected by the interview committee has joined that post then selections made by him are exhausted and in accord ance with the provisions of Section Uma Kant is found suitable for the posts concerned and shall be entitled for appointment if any 424 vacancy is caused during the validity period of the reserve. [409D] 2.1 In case of every selection of a teacher or of an officer in university, a Committee would be constituted of the persons mentioned in sub clause (i) to (v) of Section 6. The Syndicate in its Resolution dated 10.7.1978 had resolved that the reserved lists recommended by Dr. Section 6 shall be effective upto six month from the date of approval of the Syndicate which was subsequently extend ed to one year instead of four months in the resolution passed by the Syndicate on 3rd December, 1983. [411E F] 2:2 The purpose of preparation a reserve List would be served if the opinion expressed by Dr U.rea Kumar is accepted. In case there is no doubt that according to the university such a procedure is in vogue in all the universities of Rajasthan that a reserve lists is used for the appointment on a vacant post caused during t he validity period, and numerous appointments have been made in last decade, from the reservation lists. [413E F; 413A] 2(a) The very objective of preparing an reserve list will be defeated when the view expressed by this Court is accepted to that once another person selected for the vacancy can at all be expected not to join for such a long time of one month.

The petitioners, who were owners of certain lands in the development plan originally published on January 9, 1964 by green colour without assigning any purpose and the reservation and re designation of these lands for recreation centre and green belt by the first, second and third respondents in the Development Plan finally adopted was in contravention of section 9 of the Act. The petitioners challenged the validity of the combined operation of sections 4 and 11(3) of the . Held, that the local authority could not protract the acquisition of any land designated for a public purpose under section 7 of the , for 14 years and if resort was had to power,% under section 17 of revising the development plans at the end of this period of 14 years. The preparation of the tentative plan or the final development plan was not something which was left to the pleasure or discretion of the local authorities. If the provisions of the statute were borne in mind and the rules framed thereunder complied with, as appears to have been done in these cases there was little or no scope for the local authori ty acting arbitrarily under section 13 of the act. The preparing of the final plan or a final development scheme was not nothing which was at all left to his pleasure or discretionary discretion of local authority. If there was some doubt about the correctness of the draft, it is difficult to envisage what other authority could be entrusted with the work of appeal or revision. The prepare ment of the provisional development plan or final development plans was not a matter which was within the domain of the State Government under section 12 of the ; Held, further, that by the combined effect of sections 3 and 11 (3) the local Authority could protract its acquisition of land designated as for public purposes under section7 of the West Bengal Town Planning Act at least for 14 year and thereafter indefinitely indefinitely. The submission that by section 13 the local body could protracting the acquisition was not one which was entirely misconceived.

The territory of the State of Kutch merged with the Dominion of India. The Indian territory was a part of India and had always been so from the establishment of the two dominions, that India has exercised effective administrative control over it and that therefore giving up a claim to it involves a cession of Indian territory which can only be effected by a constitutional amendment. The dispute between the parties was whether the Great Rann of Kutch was part of the territory of India or not. The Tribunal held that the Great Corn is part of Pakistan, and that the area was in different state at different seasons in the year 1948, for part of it was water and for the remaining part it was land. In appeal to this Court on behalf of the appellants it was contended that by the alignment of the boundary under the award, territory which is Indian is now declared foreign territory, and apart from the survey maps there is no evidence that it is part or whole of the Great Map of Kutch. Held, that the territory in this sector is contiguous to and in fact is an extension of the mainland of Sind, and therefore, the rule earlier laid down by this Court applies. The claim made by the claimants that in imple menting the award of the International Tribunal an attempt was made to cede any part of that territory before 1948 or was in de facto occupation and in respect of which sovereign authority was exercised by the Maharao of Kutch, is within the competence of the Executive wing of Government and no constitutional amendment is necessary. The question whether there will be a cession or not depends upon the nature of the terrain, the location of the border of what was called Rann, the highly discrepant and conflicting claims made from time to time by the British authorities as well as the Kutch State authorities before the State merged with Dominion of Indian India in 1948. The fact that it was territory over which the Maha Rao of Kutch exercised sovereign rights and which by merger of the territories became Indian territory, is not evidence of the fact that the inlets were territory over where the Maha nate of Kutch had sovereign rights, acceptance of the award is not required to be implemented by a Constitutional amendment.

The mortgagor had leased 200 bighas of coal bearing land out of his holding in Mauza Bahaldih to certain lessees for an annual royalty of Rs. 2,000 payable in two equal instalments, the first in the month of Aswin of Vikram year and the second in the year Chaitra. The mortgagee did not pay the principal or interest to extend the period of limitation for the suit. On April 7, 1937, the mortgagor filed a suit on July 12, 1946, in the Court of Subordinate Judge at Dhanbad for a decree for enforcement of the two mortgages by sale of the mortgaged properties. The trial court rejected the defence raised by the contesting defendants and held that the suit was within limitation both on account of part payment of principal and interest and upon the cause of action furnished by the dispossession of the mortgagee in respect of the Bahaldh property. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant (i) that the mortgage "was partly simple and partly usufructuary" and even though the plaintiff could not rely upon part payment, she could still maintain the suit relying on the dispossession, of the mortgagees from Mauza Bahahdih or part payments of principal or Interest after the mortgagor had parted with his interest in the mortgaged property Mauzas Bansjora and Simitanr; (ii) that by the covenants in the mortgage deed dated June 14, 1922, a usufructuary mortgage was created on the mortgagor 's interest in Mauza48, and by the attornment made pursuant to paragraph 7 of the mortgage, the mortgagee had parted away his interest with his right in the property Mauzaas BansJora and (iii) that in any event even if Mauza Baharaldih was 639 one of the mortgages mentioned in the plaint, the plaintiff having lost her interest in Mauzhatras Bansjor prior to the payment of Rs 600 by the mortgagor on April 7 1937, as evidenced by the endorsement on the first mortgage deed, the appellant 's suit to enforce the mortgage dated August 27, 1922 was barred by limitation. HELD : (i)(a) The right to sue where the mortgagee is deprived of the property security or where he is not secured in his possession of the mortgagor property or where possession is not delivered to him as agreed, the claim maintainable by the mortgagee was one for compensation and the period limitation for a suit to recover the mortgage money is governed by article 120 of the Limitation Act from the date of destruction or deprivation of the security or disturbance of their possession by the creditors of the borrower, dispossession having taken place in 1937 the suit filed on July 11, 1946. [696 B] (b) The decree passed by the High Court will be set aside and there will be a decree in favour of the plaintiff only in respect for the mortgage of dated August 28, 1922.

The appellants were employees of the respondent company. They were charged at the rate of Rs. 2 per month for the transport of employees from Chinchvad Village to TELCO factory at Pimpri and back. The appellants contended that these amounts were realised by the appellants only from a particular category of employees and no charges were levied in respect of those employees who were in supervisory grades. The Commissioner dismissed the appeals holding that the challenge to the tax sought to be realised by them was not tenable and the appellants were liable to pay the tax as also the penalty. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the transport provided to the employees from Pimpri Railway Crossing and onwards to TTCO factory, they were charged only at the rates of Rs A charge of Rs 2 per day was levied for the Transport of employees; (2) the tax could be levied only if the passengers are carried on a public service vehicle. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The transport service in the present case which was registered as private service vehicle falls squarely within the ambit of the aforesaid definition. [362E] 2.1 In the instant case, it is not disputed that the transport service provided to T employees by the appellant was reserved for them only and no other member of the public even if he wanted to pay full charges could be carried on the said vehicle. The transport services in the instant cases which were registered as Private Service Vehicle falls squarely under the ambit Of the aforesaid definitions. [363E] 3.1 Section 2(7) of the Act defines 'public service vehicle ' thus: "stage carriage ' means a motor vehicle carrying or adapted to carry more than six persons excluding the driver, which carries passengers for hire or reward at separate fares paid by or for individual passengers, either for the whole journey or for stages of the journey. and includes such a carriage or other omnibus when used as a contract carriage within the meaning of the ". [362G H] 3:2 The term 'public services vehicle ' has not been defined either by the Act or by the Rules but that too does not create any difficulty, because having regard to the Preamble of the enactment we are of the opinion that the tax can be levied on only passengers who were carried on by a stage carriage which is of the nature of a public utility vehicle. It cannot by any process of reasoning or stretch of imagination be deemed to include employees of a private company who are given facilities not as members of the Public but as holding a special status, namely, the employees of that company. The Transport service in this case was registered in the name of the company and it is therefore not disputed whether the transport vehicle provided to them by the employees could be a public services vehicle carrying passenger. [361G H; 362A] 3 :3.1 It cannot be said that the Transport Service provided to employees by TTM was reserved exclusively for them and no others member of public even though he wanted for paying full charges would be carried in the said vehicles. The road service in TTTCO was not a public transport vehicle within the definition of the expression 'public ' vehicle '. [360H; 362B] 3(a) The transport Service in the case of supervisory staff falls squarely covered by the ambit o the aforesaid provision. [364C D] 3 (b) The word 'public motor vehicle ' is not defined either in the Act nor by the rules, but that however does not creating any difficulty because having regards to the preamble of the statute we are inclined to think that the Tax can be levy only on passengers who are carried by a Stage carriage which was of the type of a Public Service Vehicle.

The appellants, who had objected to the grant of a no objection certificate for the site on which the cinema house was to be constructed, applied under section 5(3) of the Madhya Pradesh Cinemas (Regulation) Rules, 1972 for a licence for a quasi permanent cinema to respondent No. 3 Prem Narayan son of Ganpatlal Chouksey, proprietor Chitra Talkies, Lalbagh, Burhanpur (M.P.) against which a petition under 795 Article 226 of the Constitution by the appellants was dismissed in limine by a speaking order by the High Court of Madhya Pradesh at Jabalpur on 6th March 1978. The State Government did not give any opportunity to the successful objectors and decided the appeal at their back and thus the decision was rendered in violation of the principles of natural justice and the order granting licence for quasi permanent Cinema by the State Government is invalid. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellants not being entitled to challenge the grant or refusal of a cinema licence to the third respondent, yet in the appeal preferred by the 797 third respondent under sub section (3) Of section 5 the State government did not giving any opportunity of hearing to the objectors and decide the appeal on their merits. [895B] 1.2 The appellants were not entitled to raise the plea that the grant was in respect of a permanent cinema or a touring cinema. They could not now be permitted to plead a right to oppose the grant. [820C D] 2.1 Rule 6 declares that the "no objection" certificate is without prejudice to the right of the licensing authority to refuse a cinema license under rule 102. I leave the question open whether a person who has objected to a location of the cinema at the site notified by the applicant. Since those grounds were available to them during the proceedings for considering the grant, they cannot now be allowed to plead any right to resist the grant granted of a "noobjection certificate" certificate. [821F] 2:2 The order granting the no objection Certificate is without jurisdiction and it is not a fit case for the interference of the High court. [822C D]. 3.1 In an appeal filed by an applicant, who has been refused a cinema Licence, the local residents, who have objected to grant of "no Objection" certificate and had been over ruled, can contest the claim of the applicant to a cinema lease. The appellants cannot now now be granted a noobjection certificate on the same grounds which they took against the " no objection" Certificate and have been over held. [823D] 3:2 Rule 6 prohibits the grant by a licensing authority only at the instance of a person aggrieved by the decision of the Licensing Authority refusing to grant a cinema or an touring Cinema licence, as the case may be. The Act does not confer any right of appeal on a person whose might have raised objections before the licensing authorities against the grant granting of a 'no objection certificate or a licence,as the case might be. [829F] 3.2 Rule 7 declares that "the grant of no objection' certificate is subject to the provisions of section 5 and shall not affect any right which may accrue to the licensee in respect thereof." The appellants could not therefore challenge the validity of that grant on the ground that there was a mosque, and a temple in the vicinity of the place where the proposed cinema house is to be built. [828G] 3 :3 In an application under section 6(3), the State Govt did not make any objection for the location of a building at the proposed site notified under rule 3. The order refusing the grant does not give rise to any right in favour of the applicants.

The plaintiffs instituted a suit (O.S. No. 46 of 1957) against the defendant alleging that by a contract dated August 3, 1957 the defendant had agreed to assign to the plaintiffs his leasehold interest under a mining lease in respect of 184 acres of land in Kudrekanave Kaval, Hosadurga Taluk and for claiming specific performance of the contract. The Trial Court decreed the suit. In appeal, the High Court held that there was no concluded contract between the parties. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants that there had been a contract as alleged in the plaint. HELD: (i) A plaint in a suit for specific performance should allege a concluded contract, see the Code of Civil Procedure 1st Schedule Appendix A, Form No. 47 of 1957 was not a suit to enforce specific performance. [757 B] (ii) The Plaint in a Suit for specific relief should allege an acceptance by serving a copy of the plaint through the medium of the Court. [758 C D] (iii) In the peculiar facts of Bloxam 's case a contract to take shares was concluded by an oral application for shares followed by allotment though no notice of allotment was given to the applicant. There was no completed contract between parties.

The appellants were the owners of sugarcane purchased by them from the respondent. The price of sugarcane was fixed at Rs. 1,000 per quintal. The appellants paid the price to the sellers. The sellers did not pay the price of the sugarcane purchased within the time prescribed. No. 11 of 1966. Iyengar filed a complaint against the appellants under section 3(2)(b) of the Act on the ground that they had failed to pay to the seller the price for the sugarcane sold by them, within the period prescribed. The Magistrate convicted the appellants and sentenced them to imprisonment for three years. On appeal the High Court held that the investigation was not in accordance with law. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the complaint made before the police did not disclose a cognizable offence and as such the police could not have taken up the investigation of that complaint. HELD: (i) The question whether the cultivation and sale of sugarcane can be regulated under section 2(2) (b) is in accordance With law. [767 B] (ii) The regulation of the price at which sugarcane may be bought or sold, and in addition to the Sugar Control Order 1955 which was issued by the Central Government on 27th August, 1955, it also issued the Sugarcane Control Order, 1955. It also issued a Sugarcane Control order 1955 on the same date investing it with the power to fix the price thereof as also the power of regulate the movement of sugarcane. [676 G H] (iii) The Parliament intended to bring under control the cultivation of sugarcane as also to the sugar Control Order 1954 which was passed by the State Government on 28th August 1955 invested it with that power to regulate the sale, supply and distribution of foodstuffs. That being so it was well within the competence of Parliament to enact the Act and hence the power conferred on the Government ,under section 3 of the Bihar Act cannot be challenged as invalid. [677 E F] (iv) The contention that in view of section 11 of the , no cognizance could have been taken of the offence alleged is premature. There was no substance in the contention that the complainant made before him did not mention a Cognizable offence and that as such he could not take up the proceedings of the complaint. [667 B C] (v) The provisions of section 3 Of the Act were clearly inconsistent with the provisions of the Order and the Act. [674 D E] (vi) The power conferred by section 11 on the State Govt., under section 6 of the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 cannot be questioned as invalid because it was not within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of Parliament. [679 B C].

The appellants, a State Government Undertaking, filed writ petitions before the High Court claiming that the industrial undertakings started between 30th June, 1969 when the order dated 12th January, 1977 was issued could not be deprived of the concessions given to them by the former order as the said grant of concessions constituted a promissory estoppel against the Government on the basis of which they had acted by starting new industries requiring investment of considerable funds and the Government was not entitled to go back or that promise as it had sought to do by the order. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions holding that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Government of Karnataka that the concessions granted under the said order dated 30th May, 1969 were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Doctrine of Prom promissory Estoppel is not applicable to the present cases because it is found by a Government of Mysore that the concession granted under that order had been misused and unfair advantage was taken of that concessions by way of refunds, though in a more limited manner and that is not even the case of the appellant. Dismissing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1. The doctrine ofpromissory Estoppels is not available to the appellants because it has been found by Government of India that the said concession was being misused or undue advantage taken of by the newly established industries. [948C] 2.1 In order to test the validity of the order of 30th September, 1969, one has to see the substance of the concession given under the order and not merely certain words used out of context. Although the benefit regarding sales tax granted to the new industries is by way Of refunds of sales tax paid to the extent provided in the Order, it is clear that in effect, the benefit granted is in the nature of an exemption from the payment of the sales tax or reduction in the sales Tax liability to the amount stated in the order but can be found on the examination of the relevant Act, the exercise of the power must be attributed to that source. [940D E] 2:2 The doctrine must be regarded as good law in view of the recent decision of this Court in State of Bihar and Anr. vs Usha Martin Industries Ltd., [1987] 65 STC, 430 where a Division Bench comprising three learned Judges of this court upheld and applied that doctrine also grants concessions byway of refunds. It is clear from Section 8A that in order to examine the validity or otherwise of the said orders, it has to be attributed, to that sources. The exercise of power must, therefore, be attributed not only to that Source but also certain words incorporated out of the context. [990G H] 2 :3. In view of this, there is no substance whatever in the contention that the State Government had no authority to provide for the grant of refunds and that promise was clearly there in Section 8 A. [999C D] 2(a) The doctrine cannot be regarded good law now, he conceded that doctrine must also be regarded a good law as good Law in view Of the recent decisions of this High Court in Union of India vs Usha martin Industries Limited, [1987], 65 STC 430 where the source of power under which it is issued is not stated in an order but could be found On the examination, the relevant provisions, in this connection, are Section 8B of the Act and that empowers the State government to notify exemp 951 tions and reductions in the levy of tax on sale or purchase of goods that are made exigible under the provisions contained in Chapter 3 of the aforesaid Act.

The appellants were tried for the offences under Sections 147, 148 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. on the allegations that they caused the death of Madda Laksha mandas of village Ramaraogudem on November 1, 1980 near the Tobacco garden of A 1. The Trial Court acquitted A 7 of all the charges. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 4 to A 6. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) Section 141 I. P.C., does not bar a conviction under 7 Section 302 readwith section 34 I. PP.C if the evidence discloses commission of an offence in furtherance of the common intention of the persons all. [896F] (2) The non applicability of Section i49 I.A. is no bar in convicting the appellants under 7 section 302 read alongwith Section 34 I P. C. if the eviden tions disclose commission of a crime in furtherance o f the common object of the unlawful assembly was concerned. [889G H] (3) The High Court clearly fell into error in confirming the conviction of A 3 to A6 under Sections 148 and on applying 149 I,P.c. [871A B] (4) Section 149 does not exclude a conviction for an offence under 7(a). If the evidence disclosed commission of any offence in pursuance of the said common intention, all. are liable to be punished as sharers in the commission of offences.

The assessee, a company incorporated under the Indian Companies Act, 1956, was carrying on business in the manufacture of sugar and molasses. The assessee claimed that it had purchased the sugar from its own funds and that it was not liable to tax under the Gift Tax Act, 1958. The Income tax Officer assessed the sum of Rs. 48,500 to tax relying on section 52 sub section (2) of the Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer but reduced the amount of Rs 48,000 from Rs.48,500 and directed that the assessee should pay a sum of money equivalent to the value of the capital asset as on the date of transfer. In appeal by the Revenue, the Tribunal held that the income tax officer assessed the sums of Rs, 48, 500 to tax based on section 53 sub section(2) and taking the view that this sub section did not require as a condition precedent that there should be under statement of consideration in respect of the transfer and it was enough to attract the applicability of the sub section if the fair market value of such property as on date of the sale exceeded the full value of consideration declared by the assessee. The Revenue appealed to this Court. HELD: (1) The language of sub section 2(2)(a) is plain and unambiguous. It does not require that the full amount of consideration received by the appellant should be included in the total consideration for the transfer which has accrued to or is received by him and it must be confined to cases where the actual consideration received for the transferred is under stated or in other words, the consideration actually received by that assessee is more than what is declared or disclosed by him. [655 C] (2)(b) The expression "consideration" used in sub section 1(1) of section 52 does not mean that the entire amount must be included for the purpose of determining the value under the gift tax Act. It only means that the consideration received should be taken to be the full price of the consideration so received and it is not enough to invoke the applicability Of sub section [656 D] (3) The words "consideration for the sale" in section 52(2), are wide enough to include all transactions which have been entered into by a person with the object of avoidance or reduction of liability of the assessee to tax. [600 E F] (4) The word "consideration ' is used in the context of the definition of consideration and not in the sense of any other term. It is not necessary that the whole amount must necessarily be included as part of the value so received by a party with whom the transaction has been entered, but it is only necessary that such part should be added to the total value so ascertained.

The appellant was charged in the Court of Presidency Magistrate as follows: "That you on 3 12 1968 at 8 a.m. at Bandra in contravention of provisions of section 2(1)(f) and 7(i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, sold 450 grams of Til seeds to the Food Inspector and that the Til seeds were unfit for human consumption, and thereby committed an offence under sec. 3(2) read with section 7(1) (a) of Prevention of food Adulteration Act." The Magistrate convicted him on two grounds: (i) that there was a tall; about the actual purpose for which the Til plants were kept in the accused 's shop, and (ii) that the Food inspector had not stated that he had only black Tils used for Pooja. The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there is such vagueness and apparent contradiction in pictures conveyed by Tambe and the Food Inspectors that Tambe 's testimony tends to demolish more than to corroborate the version of the Food Analyst on points of fact in issue. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) The evidence of the prosecution witnesses was not sufficient to prove that the article which is the subject matter of an offence is ordinarily used for human use as food whenever reasonable doubts arise this question. [319D] (2) It is a matter of common knowledge that black Til seeds are not used as food. It is also true that when the case of the accused supported by his cash memo, is that the particular black Tles were sold only for pooja for being burnt like incense or thrown into fire in the course of pooja. it cannot be said that this case had been repelled by the mere statement of the food Inspector that they can be used as a food also. [519D E] (3) The fact that the signatures of Tambe are absent on all those documents on which they would have been present if section 10(7) of Act had been strictly complied with.

The appellant was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th January, 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31st August, 1966, on the ground of limitation.
