The order of dismissal was communicated to him on 19th September, 1960. The plaintiff 's suit was one to obtain a declaration that the order of dismiss ment was bad and he continued to be in service. The trial court decreed the suit on the plea of limita tion. The High Court dismissed the appeal on the view that it had no jurisdiction. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant that the principle of merger applicable to decrees of courts would not apply to orders of departmental tribunals and, secondly, that the original order merged in the order passed in appeal therefrom and in the final order of revision was negatived by this Court on two grounds; (i) that the doctrine of merger applies only when the appeal or representation provided by law is disposed of, cause of action shall first accrue and where such order is not made, on expiry of six months from the date when the Appeal was filed or representation was made, the right to sue shall first accrues. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The question for consideration is whether the impugned order in the proceedings under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court was an order prior to the Constitution and, therefore, the High court could not exercise its jurisdiction or was it one pending at the commencement of theConstitution and the revisional order being after the Constitution came into force, the writ petition would be maintainable. [54G H] 2. The cause of actions shall be taken to arise not from the dates of the original adverse order but on the date where the appeal is filed or represent ed. If such order was made it will first accrue. [55A B] 3. In every such case only when a statutory remedy is provided by statute, cause o action shall second accrue and Where such order Is not made the right of sue shall then first accrue; where such an order is made,on the expiry of 6 months from date when cause of Action shall be computed to have first arisen. [56B] 4. The Civil Court 's jurisdiction has been taken away by the Act and, hence as far as Government serv ants are concerned, Article 58 may not be invocable in view of the special limitation. [57C D] 5. In the instant case, the claim had been dismissed on the basis of limitation and our conclusion is that the suit was within time, the decree passed by the State Government had merged into the order dated 13th of January 1966. The suit was filed within time. The appeal was therefore within time and the High Courts were set aside and the matter is remitted to the trial Court for disposal in accordance with law.

The respondent filed a suit for specific performance of an agreement to sell. The appellant contended that the decree was not a decree of affirmance but variation in the decision of the trial court which confirmed the decision was a minor variation and since the variation in question was to a very small extent and may be of very minor significance, it was not affected even if the variation was made in favour of the intending appellant and whether the variation had been obtained by parties by consent or a part of the subject matter covered by the decree. Held, that the word "decision" does not mean the whole of the decision but the decision on that part of it must be taken to have been arrived at by reference to the whole; and if there is a variation in regard to it is an integral part of that decision or the decree, the appellate court is not a Court of appeal. The word "judgment" does mean the entire of the judgment and the subject matters which are actually proposed to be brought to this Court in appeal. It may also be necessary to make it clear that if an appellate decree confirms the decision Of the trial Court but merely makes a variation, in regard thereto, the court is entitled to consider only that part which is proposed to come to this court in appeal and not by reference or to the entire subject matter of the appellate decree. The position with regard to interest, however, is different; for instance, in respect of a claim for interest before the date of the decree which is a part and in that sense if an Appellate decree confirms it, such variation cannot affect the character of the appeal which would in law amount to a decree or of affirmation.

The five revision petitions filed by the appellants were dismissed by the High Court. The High Court held that the revisional jurisdiction under section 115, Code of Civil Procedure in respect of an order of the District Court under section 25, Provincial Small Cause Courts Act was not maintainable. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that the High court had exclusive jurisdiction under Section 115, C.P.C., in a revision petition filed by them against the revisional orders of the two courts below; and that the District Judge had no jurisdiction under s 25, Presidency Small Cause Court Act, 1947, to entertain a revision application against an order passed by the District Magistrate under section 26, Provincial, Small Cause courts Act, and that as such the High Courts had exclusive Jurisdiction under section 114 read with section 115 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The revisional power conferred on the High courts from time to time is exercised by the Supreme Court from time To time. In respect of cases decided before 20th September, 1972 and also all cases arising out of original suits or other proceedings of any valuation decided by the two Courts below, the case would be amenable to the revisional power of the High 'Court under section115, Code, of Civil procedure. [36G H] 1.2 The High court has exclusive jurisdiction over a revisional order made by the subordinate Court under that section. It is a point for consideration that had section 25 in its application to the State of Uttar Pradesh continued in its original form the High would have exercised the revisional powers under section25, and no question could have arisen of invoking the revisional authority under section 5 of the Provincial Small Causes Courts Act. [37A] 1:3 The High ' Court is not vested with revisional jurisdiction u/s 115, Civil Procedure Code over a revision order made under that Section. [38B C] 1 :4. In the instant case, the High "Court" has exercised the appellate power under section 35 and no questions could have arose of invoking revisional power under s 115 of Code. [39D E] 2.1 In the present case, an order was passed under section 24, Provincial of Small Cause Jurisdiction Act by a District Court exercising the jurisdiction of a Judge of Small Causes. The revision petition under section 116 is not maintainable against a revisional application under section 30, the appeal and the associated special leave petitions must be dismissed. No question could arise of invoking of the revisional provision of the said section. [40E] 2:2 In case this Court is of the opinion that a revision Petition under section 117 is not tenable against a Revisional order under section 50, the revision petition and the connected special leave Petitions must be rejected. No. 2844 of 1979 that in case this court is of opinion that an order made thereunder by a subordinate Court or Additional District Judge exercising the powers of revision under section 125, Code is amenable to revisional jurisdiction of the high Court under Section115 of the Civil Procedure. No such question could not have arisen in view of the fact that section 25 has been amended and the result was that : (i) The High " Court" had exclusive power under Section 25, and (ii) The District Judge would have exercise the revisional Jurisdiction under Section 35, and any question could be arose of invoke the revisional Power of the State. [41F G] 2 :3 In the context of their individual facts, it is desirable to appreciate the relevant jurisdictional features of the Revisional power enjoyed by the high court from time TO time. The Code of civil Procedure (Amendment) Act, 1973, however superseded the scheme of bifurcation of revisional jurisdiction with effect from 1st February, 1977 and, with certain modification the position reverted to what it was under the original section 115.

The respondents, who were the owners of certain lands in Jaipur, filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the notification issued by the State Government of Rajasthan under section 52 (1) of the Act for the acquisi tion of certain land belonging to them required by the Urban Improvement Trust , Jaipur for a public purpose. The Special Officer held that the proposed acquisition was not bona fide and their real object was just to get the land released from acquisition on one ground or the other. He rejected the prayer of the respondents for release of the land and recommended that the entire land be acquired by the Government under section 53 (1). The appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the legality of the notice issued by them under section 51 (2) of Act for acquisition of their lands at Jaipur and sought to challenge the validity. The Single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the alleged need of the respondent was just a pretence and he was satisfied on the material on record that the land was really not needed by them bona fide, and their true object was merely to get it released from the acquisition on some ground or other. The State Government preferred an appeal before the Division Bench which dismissed the appeal holding that there was total lack of inherent jurisdiction on the part of the (1 ) ; , 602 the Calcutta High Court to entertain such petition . Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The impugned orders passed by the learned Single Judge of the Calcutta high Court are set aside and the proceedings before the Calcutta Bench are quashed. [605B] 2. The entire cause of action culminating in the acquisition of the lands under section52(1)of the Act arose within the State of Rajasthan i.e. within the territorial jurisdiction of the Rajasthan High Court at Jaipur Bench. It was not necessary for the respondents to plead the service of notice on them by the Special Officer , Town Planning Department , Jaipur under section 54 (1), for the grant of an appropriate writ, direction or order under article 227 of the constitution for quashing the notification dated February 8, 1984 issued by State Government under Section 52(1). If the respondents felt aggrieved by the acquisition proceedings of their land situate at Jaipur, and wanted to challenge their validity of notification issued in pursuance thereof, the remedy of the appellants of the grant was to file such a petition before the RajasthanHigh Court , Jaipur Bench, where the cause of actions wholly or in part arose. [ 602C D] 3. The respondents did not raise any objection as to the power and authority of the State Govt. to acquire the notified land under section 49 (1)(a) of The Act or the legality and propriety of the notices issued by it under section 55(2). They did not file any reply to the writ application before the High court. [ 603D] 4. The whole cause of the action culminating into the acquisition was resulting in the acquiring of the said land under Section 53 (2).

The appellant landlord purchased the building in 1968 and that it was covered by the new Rent Act. The first ground was based upon sub s.(2) of section 2 which provides that nothing in this Act shall apply to a building during the period of ten years from the date on which its construction is completed. The second ground was founded upon sub section (2) which provides for that nothing contained in this section shall apply, to a suit for eviction of a tenant except on the specified grounds as provided in the section. The appellant landlord contended that the building had been constructed by a co operative society and the landlord had purchased it from the society and, therefore, the new rent Act had no application to the building. The Additional District Judge accepted the contention of the appellant landlord and held that the buildings were not ten years old on the date of the suit and was exempted from the operation of the new Act. On appeal by special leave, this Court, HELD: (1) The building in question was subject to assessment therefore it will be deemed to have been completed on the day on which the first assessment thereof comes into effect and where the said dates are different, the earliest of the said date, and in the absence of any such report, record or assessment, the date, on which it is actually occupied (not including occupation merely for the purposes of supervising the construction or guarding, the building under construction) for the first time. [343 D E] (2)(a) The new Rent Acts will not apply to buildings during a period of 10 years from 1st October, 1971. [344 G H] (b) The construction of a building shall be deemed not to have become ten years ' old on 1st April, 1972. The question in the present case is whether by seeking the benefit of section 39 of the Act there was a change in the cause of action. [345 D E]. (3)(a). Sub section (1), viz., the arrears of rent, if at the first hearing of the case the tenant in default pays all arrears of Rent to the landlord or deposit in court the entire amount of rent and damages for use and occupation of the building due from him, such damages for using and occupation being calculated at the same rate as rent together with interest thereon at the rate of nine per cent per annum and the tenant 's cost of the litigation after deducting therefrom there from any amount already deposited by the tenant under sub section(1) of s.30, the court may pass an order relieving the tenant against his liability for eviction on that ground. [346 D E F] (4)(a), The new Act will not be applicable to a case where the building has not become ten year old on 31st March, 1972 and is exempted from operation of section 40 of the . [345 G] (5)The new Rent Control Acts will apply to the buildings during the 10 years.

The appellant entered into three contracts for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings stores and other works at Ranchi. The first contract was with the respondent company for the execution of certain works at Jamshedpur. The second contract was executed by the appellant in respect of the work done by it. The third contract was also executed by one of its officers. The appellant contended that he as not, and relies in support of his contention on a notification dated April 1, 1937 issued by the Government of Bihar, had been specifically authorised to execute the agreement. Held, that the document actually before the court, is, what it purports to be, "a certified copy", and that under section 35 of the Stamp Act there can be validation only of the original, when it was unstamped or insufficiently stamped, that a document in court which is a copy cannot be validated and "acted upon" and that the law does not provide for the levy of any penalty on lost documents. The law is no doubt well settled that the copy of an instrument cannot be validation: That was held in The Rajah of Bobbili vs Inuganti China Sitaramasani Garu (I.L.R. , followed. The Court has to consider whether the document which was sent by the arbitrator to the court is the original instrument or a copy thereof. It is not necessary that the original document must be produced and, if it does not fall within that item, it must fall within entry 12 of the Indian Stamp Act.

The respondent was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works Department in the State of Punjab in the year 1979. He retired from service on 31st March, 1983. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of his retirement and also the order dated 3rd April, 1985. The High Court quashed the proceedings against him. In appeal to this Court it was contended that keeping in view the scope of Article 309 as also the purpose of Rule 2.2, the said rule cannot be interpreted to be a rule placing an embargo on prosecution of a government servant if the conditions stated therein are satisfied. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The third proviso to clause (b) of Rule 3.2 is in the nature of a beneficent legislation and in case of doubt has to be interpreted in favour of the person for whose benefit the rule has been framed. This purpose can be achieved if the said proviso by adopting the rule of reading down is interpreted to mean that even if a government employee is prosecuted and punished in judicial proceedings instituted in respect of cause of action which arose or an event which took place more than four years before such institution, as has been held by the High court can be treated to be an rule regulating the condition of service of such a person. [920G H] 1.2 The third Proviso to clause(b) is in nature of an beneficent Legislation and in cases where doubt has been raised by the petitioner for quashing of the prosecution, it would not be entitled to exercise the right conferred on it by the substantive provision contained in clause (a) with regard to pension of such government servant. [1020G] 1:3 The third provisos to clause 2.1 are in the type of a welfare legislation and are intended to provide an exception to the power of the government in the matter of withholding or withdrawing etc. of pension of a retired government servant contained in clauses (b), (c) and (d). [1021G H; 1022A] 1 :4. The third exception to clause 'b ' is in respect to the benefit of a Government servant contained In clause (c). The said proviso cannot be construed as laying down an absolute or general embargo on prosecutions instituted in connection with cause of actions which arose, or an incident which tookplace more than 4 years before the institution of the departmental proceedings. [ 1022B] 1.:5. The fourth proviso to Clause (b)(ii) is not in the form of a proviso to Rule 2(2). In view of what has been said above and keeping in mind the scope and object of Rule making power under Article 309, the third proviso cannot also be interpreted as laying an absolute and general embargo upon prosecution. [1122C] 1;6. The filing of challan, however, was delayed on account of the steps taken by the respondent for getting the First Information Report quashed. Since the High Courts quashed the prosecution of Mangal Singh Minhas on one ground alone based on its earlier decision in Des Raj singhal and did not consider other grounds, if any, that may have been raised, by him for quashing the prosecution on grounds, it is not to place an embargo upon prosecutions. [1222D] 1:-7. The order of the High Judge quashing the First information Report as against Kailash Nath, respondent in criminal appeal No. 422/88, and did Not consider other ground, if some, that might have been raising by him in respect thereof for quashing quashed of the proceedings, would not cover events of grave misconduct or negligence committed by the government servant more than three years prior to the institution. [1322D E] 1 8.

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act 1913, to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 3,000 preference shares of Rs. The preference shareholders were under the Articles of Association entitled to a fixed dividend of 71 per cent on the face value of the shares, with no right in the balance of the profits. The respondent company filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution challenging the validity of the order passed by the Income tax Officer and the High Court held that the respondent was one in which the public were substantially interested, and there fore the income tax Officer had no jurisdiction to pass the order under section 23 A of the Act for any of the three years. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the Explanation to sub section (1) of section 23A was in reality a clause which defines what a company, in which, the public are substantially interested. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The definition of "public" in section 2(15) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922 before it was amended by the Finance Act, 1955, stood as follows: "Public limited company shall be deemed to be a company in which not less than twenty five per cent of the assessable income of that previous year, as reduced by the amount of income tax and super tax payable by the company in respect thereof he shall make with the previous approval of the Inspecting Assistant Commissioner an order in writing that the undistributed portion of the chargeable income of the Company of that earlier year as computed for income tax purposes and reduced by such amount of Income Tax and super Tax payable by it in respect thereto he shall, make with effect from the date of the general meeting aforesaid." The definition is wide enough to include a company which has not less then twenty five percent of its voting power. [723 B] 2.1 In considering whether shares carrying not lessthan twenty fiveper cent of voting power are held by persons other than the controlling group, the shares yielding a fixed rate of dividend have to be excluded. But shareholders who are entitled to an fixed rate are not directly interested in such accumulation: it matters little to them whether the dividend is immediately distributed to the ordi nary shareholders or is accumulated, and therefore in assessing whether the twenty five percentage of the voting power is vested in persons other then the controlling Group, the share yielding a specified rate of dividends have to he excluded. [750 D F] 2:2 The definition in section 23(A) of 1922 Act is in reality an clause which defined what a Company, in whose case the public is substantially interested is. (2) Where not less exceed twenty five% of the share capital of such subsidiary company is held by a single individual or group of individuals acting in concert, the company would be regarded as one in whom the public have not substantially interested and to a subsidiary company of such a company if the whole of theshare capital of that subsidiary company was held by the shareholders. But shareholder who are not entitled to any fixed rate is not directly affected in such accumulations: it matter little to him whether the dividends is immediately distributable to or acquired unconditionally by or beneficially held by them. [751 G H] 2 :3 The total voting power was 5,500 one vote, for each share, ordinary and preference alike and twenty five cent of that voting power has been held by single individual and a group of shareholders acting in jointly concert, is not a question which therefore cannot be decided by this Court.

The appellant was a del credere agent of the first respondent. He had been authorised to take delivery of the goods on behalf of another quota holder Beharilal Bajirathi. The first respondent, who was the managing agent of Dwarkadas Khetan & Company, sent a letter to the first appellant informing him that he had received payment in advance from Shree Kishan & Company and that the 13 bales should be sent to "our godown ", Whether the " our " refers to Dwarkadash Khetan & Co. and that he has been authorised by the quota holder to take possession of these 13 bales. The goods were delivered on 28th February, 1947, and so the first respondents were not the agents of the quota holders. The appellant was convicted under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He appealed to the High Court which dismissed his appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the sale agent bad informed the first appellants that he would have been authorised, (2) as the form required information regarding physical delivery to the quotaholder or his agent and as Dwarkadis Khetan was not the agent of a quota holder, the statement was inaccurate and misleading. HELD: (i) The entry in column 3 is not intended to be confined to quota holders or their agents but means what it says, namely the person to whom physical delivery of goods has been made whoever he may be. [833 C] (ii) The entries in column 4 are not intended for being confined to a quota holders and they means what they say, namely, the person who to whom actual delivery of that goods has actually been made Whoever he may not be. It is clear from the entry in Column 3 that the entry is not meant to be restricted to quotaholders or their agent but means whatever it means, it is clear that the entries in columns 3 and 4 are intended to include only goods allotted to quota holder or their Agents but means nothing more than what they mean, namely. the person, to whom delivery of possession has been given, who may be present at the time when the name of the person is delivered. [820 E F] (iii) The statement in column 2 headed Full name and address of person to whose delivered the name was made Whoever must be entered in column 5 and that this godown belonged to Dwarkeshwar Khetan &Company.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 5(1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. He was prosecuted under section 161 I.P.C. for having committed offences punishable under sections 161 and 165 I. P.C., read with section 5 (2) (a) of that Act. The trial court acquitted him on the ground that he had been guilty of corrupt practice as defined in section 5 of the Act, and that he was not a public servants within the definition of "public servant" within sub clause (d). The High Court dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the ninth clause of section 21 of the Indian Penal Code had no application because the word "obtains" on which much stress was laid did not exclude the idea of acceptance of what is given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element of effort on the part of the receivers one may accept money, that if offered, or solicit payment of a bribe, or extort the bribe by threat or coercion; in each case lie obtains a pecuniary advantage by abusing his position as public servant; and that even if Dwivedi was not punishable under section 5, read with s.5(1)(d) as he did not abuse his position, he would nevertheless be liable under section5 (1) of Act because the liability of a public Servant has been made absolute and it is wholly immaterial in what capacity he has committed the offence under sub clause(d). Dismissing the appeals, HELD : 1. The word " Obtains" does not eliminate the idea that acceptance of whatever is given, although it connotes an element or effort on his part. [775 D] 2. It would, therefore, be reasonable to put on clause (c) a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section. The abuse being either by corrupt or illegal means or by other means of the nature mentioned in Narayanan Nambiar 's(1), case. lie obtains pecuniary advantage from abusing his office as a public officer. [779 E] 3. The use of the word 'obtains ' on which considerable stress was placed does not exclude that idea of accepting what is stated or offered, though the means employed are corrupt and illegal. [780 G H] 4. Section 5 (1)(c) of section 405 of the I. A. Act has to be looked at. It is true that in clauses (a), (b) and (c), the abuse of position as a Public servant is clearly implied. It will, therefore be reasonable if it is so, the abuse being by corrupt means or illegal device or by any other means. [781 F] 5. The words "obtaining" on clause(c) are wide enough to cover all cases where the abuse is either by pecuniary or illegal methods or by others abusing his official position as such. [783 E] 6. In clauses (b), (d), (e) and(f) the use of these words show that the clause was wider when it came to the case of an officer who was remunerated by fee or commission for the performance of any public duty and it was not necessary that the remuneration by any of fees or commission should be paid by the Government as is now necessary under subclause (a). The abuse of the position would be the necessary ingredient of the offence; the abuse having been either by corruption or illegal use, the misuse being either either by misrepresenting himself in the discharge of his own duty he has not committed an offence under section 4(1 ) (d)(i) of Prevention of criminal misconduct.

The petitioners in each of these applications were engaged on terms of casual labour for periods varying between 10 140 and 16 years in the Construction Department of the Signal Unit in Northern Railway. All the writ petitions having disposed of by a common judgment as questions of law and fact involved therein are similar. The petitioners alleged that despite the fact that each of them has put in continuous service for quite a long period, the Railway Administration, respondent herein, had not treated them as temporary servants and had applied discriminatory rates of wages. They have asked for a direction to treat the petitioners at par with maintenance workers and to declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked them for their absorption in regular cadre in the permanent category as per the circulars issued by the respondents. The Union of India, Ministry of Railways, has filed these applications under Article 32 of the Constitution praying for a writ of mandamus directing the Railway administration to treat them at par and have prayed for their regularisation in the regular cadre. The main contention raised on behalf of the Administration is that the petitioners are project employees and do not belong to the open line acquired temporary status. They had asked for permanent absorption against permanent vacancies which mostly occur in open line acquire temporary status, but there was no break in such continuity the previous service is also taken into account. Allowing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The Railway Administration should take prompt steps to screen such of the petitioners who have not yet been tested for the purpose of regularising their service. [144G H] 2. The scheme for absorption in Yadav 's case which has been framed and is operative. Casual labour seems to be the requirement of the Railway Administrations and cannot be avoided. Several instructions issued by Railway Board and the Northern Railway Headquarters were placed before us to show that the Administration was anxious to take appropriate steps to remove such difficulties faced by the casual labour but there is perhaps slackness in enforcing them. [145A B] 3. The Railways should take expeditious steps to scre such of those petitioners who had not yet completed their service, and if necessary they may be accommodated against permanent posts which mostly occurs in open lines as well as willing project casual labourers on completion of 180 days of continuous employment previously. [146B C] 4. The benefits of Discipline and Appeal Rules are also applicable to casual labour with temporary status.[145C] 5. The benefit of Discipline & Appeal Rules is also not available to casual labourers acquiring temporary status for the conferment of attendant benefits like regular scales of pay, increments etc. [147F] 6. The retiral benefit of pension is not admissible to either category of employees.

The Forward Markets Commission, constituted under the , framed bye laws of the Association for the purpose of carrying on business in certain commodities. The Forward Markets Act, 1951, was amended by the Bombay Agricultural Produce Marketing (Regulation) Act, 1953, which came into force on January 21, 1956. By section 12(1), the Central Government made a bye law relating to the framing of bye laws and it provided that the rules made under the Act shall be subject to the condition of previous publication. The appellants who were members of the Forward Markets Committee, challenged the validity of the said bye law on the ground that they were not in either case Subordinate legislation under section 11 or 12 as the case may be, of the Act and they could not have been conferred the power which it purported to do under the amended bye law 52AA. Held, that the Government had no power under section 12 of the , to make a byelaw with retrospective effect and, therefore, the new bye law made on January 1, 1956, in so far as it purports to operate retrospectively is invalid. The provisions of section 12 are not ultra vires the powers conferred by section 12. The power of the Central government to make bye laws under section 4(f) is undoubtedly co extensive with the power of a Association to frame bye law framed by the Government under section 3 of the Bombay Agriculture Produce Marketing Act, 1948 and it cannot be said that unless retrospective operation was given to the provisions of sections 12 and 13, the objects of the legislation would be defeated or the purposes for which the power was conferred could not be fulfilled.

The assessee, a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd., was a shareholder. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declared as dividend for each of the three years in question and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the entire sum for each year was income in the hands of the assessee, but only a part of it being dividend, within the meaning of section 2(6A) of Indian Income tax ACt, 1922 was liable to be grosed up. The High Court also held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by the company for grant of long term leases after the 31st March, 1948, was not taxable as dividend but as income of the assesee from other sources. In second appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the distribution to the assessee of the amounts attributable to land acquisition compensation received by it as consideration for grant or renewal of lease after the31st March 1948, being in the nature of capital gains of the Company which comprised salami or premia received by them as consideration, for grant and renewal of longterm leases after 31st march, 1948 was not in the hand of the company receipt of dividend within the ambit of section 12 of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1961. HELD : (1) The High court had to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of salami was capital gain or whether any part of compensation received for compulsory acquisition of land was capital gains. [775 D] (2) The question of law raised was whether distribution of dividend out of capital assets was taxable as dividends, and if dividend be distributed to the shareholders of the companies out of those capital gains, to 'the extent of the distribution out of the capital gains the dividend must be deemed exempt from liability to tax under section 12 as dividend income liable to tax.

The Karnataka Forest Act, 1963 incorporated in its definition of forest produce Sandalwood oil and agar wood. The expression "forest produce" is defined to include "Sandal wood" and "sandal wood". The term "forest produces" has been defined as meaning "a forest produce which includes, that is to say, the 'enumerated items in Clauses 1 and 11 "wood oil" being a forest produce. Section 2(k) defines "forest" to include any land or building or part of a building or structure or part thereof, whether used for the purpose of agriculture or horticulture or animal husbandry or dairying or poultry farming or dairy farming or poultry farm or poultry breeding or poultry feed or poultry poultry farming and includes also any other forest produce including a forestry. Section 3(1) defines 'forest" as meaning any land, building or structures, trees, shrubs, grass, grass or garden, land, sea, pond, well, tank, pond or well, whether in the course of trade, manufacture or processing, and includes any other produce which is used for agricultural purposes. Section 4(1)(a) defines a forest as meaning a forest land, land or any building or land, including a hut, shed, structure or any part thereof. "The expression 'forest produce ' has been used in the Act to include wood oil. The wood oil is a natural produce of the forest directly derived as an exudation from living trees in the forest belonging to the family of the Dipterocarpucoae trees while sandal wood oil was a bye product from sandalwood (Santalum Album) by industrial process. It is further contended that the word 'timber ' defined in section 2(f)(i) of the Act means "a Forest produce" which includes wood oil, deodar oil and pine oil, apart from oleo resin and wood oil derived from exudations from living tree in the forests belonging to family of Dipteregarpuccoae Forests while sandalwood oil is also a bye products from sandalwood. It must be noted in this context that there are several types of essential oils in India, the important being Sandal Wood Oil, agar Wood oil and deodarि oil apart from 0leo tree and wood Oil derived fromexudationfrom living trees In the forest area. An interpretation clause of the inclusive definition is not meant to prevent the word receiving its ordinary popular, popular and natural sense whenever that word would be properly applicable, but to enable the word as used in section 3(i) (1) (a) (i) to (i). The restricted meaning canvassed by the counsel would defeat the purpose and the literal interpretation giving narrow meaning to the word wood oil ' should be excluded. In Fatesang Gimba Vasava and Ors. vs State of Gujarat and ors. , the division bench construed whether bamboo would include in its ambit cut pieces in the context and the purpose the Act sought to serve and the family to which sandal wool oil belongs being an essential oil would include wood Oil. The Court, therefore, held that WITHIN wood oil being the bye product derived commercially manufacturing process is not wood oil as defined under section 2 (f) (ii) of The Act.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 and sentenced to transportation for life. The Sessions Judge acquitted the accused but on appeal to the High Court, the order of acquittal was reversed and they were convicted under s.302 read with s 34 and awarded a sentence of imprisonment for life and a fine of Rs. 500/ . In appeal to this Court it was contended that there was no evidence against the appellants sufficient to warrant a conviction and (2) that there were no compelling reasons justifying reversal of the judgment of acquittal. HELD : The High Court should not set aside an acquittal unless there are " substantial and compelling " reasons for doing so. [858 D] In the present case, the evidence in the present cases was of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt could properly be drawn. [ 859 E F] The second point on which the judgment is challenged is the lack of compelling reasons for setting aside the acquittal. This court will not interfere with the findings of the High Courts because its conclusions on the evidence as to the guilt or innocence of the accused differ from that of the trial Court. But where the evidence is such that no Tribunal could legitimately infer from it that the accused is guilty this court would set aside the conviction. [820 E F; 859 A B] The third point on Which the judgment was based was the lack in compelling reasons. This Court will not re examine an acquittal if there are ' substantial and exceptional grounds for doing it. But the High court should not interfere, unless there were " substantial or compelling " reason for doing that so. If this Court would have set aside a conviction, it would do so materially from his reliability that it would be dangerous to accept his testimony as being of any great value which is still more diminished by the finding as to guilt or guilt of the Accused.

The appellant company was an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act. The factory at Jamshedpur was an industry under the Indian Factories Act, 1948. In Bihar alone, it had two factories one at Jamshedpur and the other at Ranchi and had depots at Patna and other towns. The company at Jamshedpur is an establishment within the meaning of section 2(k) of the Industrial Disputes Act. Certain disputes having arisen between the management and the workmen employed in that factory and represented by their union the Indoxco Labour Union, Jamshedpur made a joint application dated September 7, 1963 to the Government of Bihar for a reference under section 10(2) of . The notification thus makes it clear that the disputes referred to the Tribunal were disputes set out in the said agreement and state 554 ment and were between the company 's factory at Ranchi. The dispute raised by the union was whether the workmen of the factory at Sarai, Jamshedpur were entitled to special leave under section 9(2)(a) of , but the Tribunal refused to grant special leave to attend the meetings of the executive committee of the union. On appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the dispute raised in the present case was in respect of the employees of the company wherever they may be stationed; and that as the said reference was made in October 1963 i.e., after the said purported amendment, "the mention in it of the dispute as a dispute between the Company and Indox co Labour Union does not materially affect the position that the disputed dispute raised was in relation to the employees employed in the factory wherever they might be stationed. HELD: (1) The Tribunal 's conclusion, therefore, that the union 's constitution was duly amended on either January 6 or 21, 1963 or that, therefore the/ndian Oxygen Workers Union represented the workmen concerned was mentioned in the agreement and the said statement and not that of the Indian Oxygen Workers ' Union is erroneous and cannot be sustained. [501 D] (2) The dispute referred to it was only those set outin the said Agreement and the statement and no award made by the Tribunal in respect thereof could operate only in respect Of the workmen who had agreed to refer those disputes for adjudication. [558 E F] (3) The reference extended to them also and the Tribunal ' s order would cover them also.

The assessee was carrying on business in timber at Abdullapur. The firm of Lala Hakam Mal Tani Mal was dissolved and on that account the assessee was entitled to relief under section 25(4) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922. In 1943 there was a partition of the Hindu undivided family and five members of that family entered into an agreement of partnership to carry on the business in the name of R. In 1948 there was another partition of that firm and five shares were allotted to each of them. The assessee was assessed to income tax under the Indian Incometax Act, 1918, in respect of the income from business inter alia in timber. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm Messrs Hakammal TaniMal was dissolved on March 31, 1939 before the Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 came into force and on April 1, 1939, after Act 7 Of 1939 was brought into force relief under s 25(3), or in the alternative under section25(4). Held, that the assessee had commenced doing business immediately after the dissolution of the firm from April 1. 1939, and immediately thereafter the business of the assessee started. The partnership therefore came into being at the material time when the Indian income tax ( Amendment) Act 6 Of 1939 came in force and it could not be said that the business was carried on by the assessee at the commencement of the Income Tax (Amendment). Act 7of 1939, as amended by Act 7 o 1939. The partners were not independent entities but were independent persons. The agreement of dissolution was not a separate partnership of the partners. The partner was constituted to carry out the business immediately before the dissolution from April I, 1939. No date of the oral agreement constituting a separate firm of the partner is set out in the instrument. The deed did not contain any indication that the partnership was dissolved or was dissolved.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the Mysore Motor Vehicles Rules, 1945 for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by Regional Transport Authority, Shimandhar, by its order dated May 3/4, 1963. Some of the respondents preferred appeals against the said order to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and obtained stay of the order of the State transport Appellate Tribunal. The appeals were dismissed on February 27, 1967. Thereafter some of the Respondents preferred further appeals to the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal against the order granting the permit. The State Transport appellate Tribunal held that there was no period of limitation under rule 119 of the Karnataka Motor Vehicles rules, 1945 (old Rules) after a lapse of such a long time from the date of grant of the permit and that the issue of the permits was made beyond the prescribed period of Limitation under rule 120 of the Act. The High Court dismissed the appeal on February 28, 1967 holding that there had been no period for limitation under Rule 119 of Mysore Motor Vehicle Rules, 1944 after a period of such long time. Allowing the appeal by special leave, HELD : (1) The appeal before the State Government against the grant of permit to the appellant stood restored. [64D] (2) The order granting permit to him stands restored. There is no dispute that section 64 of the , is the only section creating rights of appeal against the Grant of a permit and other matters with which we are not concerned here. There was, therefore, a clear error of jurisdiction on the part of both the Tribunals in interfering with the grant granting of the permission to the Appellant. [65E] (3) The High court was right in dismissing the writ application of the appellant which ought to have been allowed. Although arguments were addressed by counsel with regard to old rule 151 and rule 119, it did not feel called upon to pronounce upon the legal effect of these rules in this appeal.

The appellant contested the election on the ticket of the Republican Party. He was then a sitting member of Parliament. The appellant alleged that at the Hapur meeting respondent Prakash Vir Shastri and his supporters delivered inflammatory speeches against the appellant and thereafter the said respondent Shastri 's supporters entered the office of the Sta tector, to which the appellant belonged, assaulted the workers of the appellant. The witnesses on behalf of the appel lant contended that there was no discussion of the oral evidence of P.W. 18 in the Vir Arjun of 8 February 1967 and thereby the appellant was denied the opportunity of meeting that case. The High Court accepted the contention and dismissed the election petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf Of the appeli lant that (1) there was a discussion of oral evidence on behalf o the respondent, (2) there is no evidence that the assault was by the workers or supporters of respondent Prakashvir Shastri; (3) there were no complaints by the appellant to the Election Commissioner, secondly, there was an allegation by the appe lant to the election Commission, thirdly, there is nothing in the Indian Evidence Act which would indicate that the oral testimony of P W. 18 was not admissible in evidence and (4) there could be no question of any kind of corrupt practice. HELD: (1)(a) The allegations are that on 2 February 1967 an election meeting was organised in support of the candidature of the candidate of respondent 's party. The alleged incident at Chhajjupur is unacceptable because, first there was not a complaint by the Appellant to the Commission, secondly there was nothing in Indian Evidence which would show that the appellant had committed any corrupt practice in relation to the personal character and conduct of the respondent. [895 A B] (b) The allegation are that at 2 February, 1967 an Election meeting was organized in support othe rations at Hapur. The evidence on record shows that the supporters of Prakash Vir watch created disturbance with the result that the meeting could not be continued and the supporters were alleged to have chased the appellant 's workers. [889 F] (c) The alleged incidents are that there were an assault on Shamshad Elahi, a worker of the Appellant. The allegations relate to the Nagola incident. The allegation is that on 18 February 1967, an election meetings was organised at Hapur and no election meeting held in support thereof could be continued. [879 G H] (d) The appellant failed to prove that respondent Prakash Chand Shastri committed any illegal practice in connection with personal character or conduct of respondent. He failed to establish that respondent No. 1 had committed corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(3)(a). The alleged assault on xxxxx Elahi the appellant is unacceptable. [869 G] (e) The news item in the newspaper ' Exhibit 22 was an appeal on behalfof respondent Prakash Singh. The appeal must be dismissed.

The appellant, who was the auction purchaser for delivery of possession of the property auctioned purchased by him, filed an application under Order XXI Rule 95 of the Code of Civil Procedure for delivery and delivery of the same to him. The said application was rejected by the District Judge on December 12, 1980 holding that in view of Article 136 of the Limitation Act, 1963, Article 136 prescribing a period of limitation of 12 years for the execution of the decree and not Article 134 of the would apply. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the application for delivery filed by the auction purchasers was barred by limitation as prescribed by Article 134(a) of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The application for setting aside sale on the ground of fraud was made after the sale was confirmed and the decree holder respondent having filed the application under order XXI Rule 94 of the C.P.C., it should be held that the applica tion was quite within the period of Limitation as prescribed in Article 136. [712G] 2. The Full Bench took the view that after the insertion of Explanation II to Section 47 of the Civil Procedure Code, an application for set aside sale can also be made within a period o f 12 years from the date of decree irrespective of the date when sale is confirmed and all questions relating to the delivery of posses sion of the immovable property to such purchaser of immovable property would be questions relating t he execution of a decree. [761G H] 3. The High Court was in error in holding that after a sale becomes absolute on the dis missal of the application of the judgment debtor 's claim for settingaside the sale, another application for striking aside the sale by the judgment creditor is not maintainable and the period o limitation as provided under Article 136 will apply. [762B] 4. The view expressed by the Full Bench was strongly relied upon by the learned Counsel for the respondent de cree holder and it is submitted that even though the appli cation for setting up aside sale was made within one year of the dismissal of the second application for taking a plea of fraud, the Full bench took the same view that the period under Article 180 of the old Limitation Act should be computed from the dates of the order disallowing the application to set aside the auction sale on merits. [763C] 5. The judgment of the High Court is set aside and the judgment of thi s Court is restored.

The appellant was the election agent of a constituency in Kerala. He filed an election petition challenging the election of the appellant to the Kerala Legislative Assembly from Mattancherry Constituency No. P 14 and P 15, alleging that he had committed corrupt practice within the meaning of section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951 (hereinafter referred to as the 'Act '). The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the evidence adduced by the election petitioner was not sufficient to prove the corrupt practice. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that the publication was intended to create an impression and did create an believe impression that the incident had taken place a day prior to the election, and that it did so. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The contents of this wall poster directly named the first respondent as the murderer of the four victims, and if it is proved that the said poster was affixed prior to or the election by the workers of the appellants with their knowledge and consent as alleged in the petition, nothing more has to be established to hold the appellant guilty of the corrupt practices within the ambit of section123(4). [775C] 2. The publication was meant to create a impression and does creating an impression that it is then true of the plaintiff 's election. It is not necessary to prove that those with special knowledge of the extrinsic facts were likely to interpret or understand the words complained of were reasonably calculated to prejudice the prospectus of the defamed candidate 's Election. [776F] 3. The appellant 's cross examination of this witness was directed to prove his case that he has not taken the photographs even on 25th and 26th March, 1987 but at a much later date and just prior to filing of the present election petition. It was also his case in the Court that exhibit P 1 was printed and pub lished only a day before the election and what is further, he had gone to the extent of saying that it was the appellant himself who along with his election agent and other workers had gone there to their residence to deliver the said copy. The High court has recorded a finding that the contents of exhibit P1 were true. [774A B] 4. In a libel action it may further be necessary to establish that those With special knowledge, the extrinic facts are likely to construe or understand that the words alleged were reasonably intended to prejudice a candidate ''s election. There is no doubt that the copy of exhibit PW 1 being pasted near the wall poster along with exhibit P I being pasted one week prior to election and nothing more had to be proved to hold that thosewith special knowledge about the extraterinsic materials were likely or understood to cause any candidate, or in relation to the candidature, or with drawal, of any candidate. [764C D] 5. The words complained ' were reasonably explained by this Court in paragraph 84, and it is not possible to understand as to how this witness could have seen the wall posters together with exhibit PW1 being pasted One week prior thereto and just before the filing of this election petition, no more. [753E F] 6. In the instant case, the contents were not printed and P 1 had stated that he was going to examine witnesses only in connection with the pasting of the poster on the said one wall and no more; nor even any other witness has stated that they had seen the actual pasting. It may further also be necessary for prove that the word complained of was reasonably calculated, to prejudice or understand to the words spoken of were likely 'to interpret or understood in a defama tory sense in an election action, it may not be necessary that to do so and all that is necessary is to prove such facts.

The respondent No. 5 submitted a plan to the Municipal Corporation of Greater Bombay for the construction of a five star hotel. The Commissioner rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said land under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing. Being aggrieved by the rejection of the plan, the respondent No 2 set aside the order of the Commissioner rejecting the plan submitted by the respondent no. 5 for the purpose of construction of an five star Hotel. The Municipal Corporation accepted the appellate order and did not challenge the order granting sanction of the Plan submitted by respondent No 5 for construction of the hotel on the said plot. Being dissatisfied with the rejection, the appellants filed a writ petition in the High Court which was dismissed by the Division Bench of the High court. In this appeal by special leave it is contended that even though the proposed revision could be taken into account as one of the relevant factors, the same could be considered as one for the relevant factor and not the relevant material. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question whether or not sufficient quantity of land has been kept reserved for park and recreation ground has been adequately considered and taken into consideration by the High Courts. [922D] 2.1 In granting sanction to the plan out of 44,820.49 sq. yds. belonging to the respondent NO. 5 and conditioned by the Respondent No. 1, it will be improper to reject the plan for want of a draft revised development plan. The respondent No, 2 directed sanction of a revised development Plan out of 43,820 sq. yards belonging to respondent No., 1. It is, therefore, apparent that in granting sanction, the Municipal Commissioner would be entitled to rely upon the same in rejecting the Plan. [822E F] 2:2 In granting permission to the building plan, it is not necessary for the Municipal corporation to rely on the same. The High Court has rightly rejected the application for approval of the plans submitted by Respondent No 5. [820B C] 3.1 The respondent no., 2 directed sanctioning the development Plan of the respondent Rs. 1 lakh in respect of the land granted in favour of respondent No.. 5. It was, therefore apparent that even in granting the exemption to the Respondent, the Corporation had prepared and published on April 30, 1984 a draft modified development plan, which has since been published and the plan made available by the Municipal Council. The plan, as sanctioned by the Corporation, had since been printed and the plans made available for inspection by the appellant No. 2. [821B C; 822A] 3:3 In granting the sanction to respondent Rs 1 lakh, the Respondent no. 2 directed the sanction of revised development plans out of 45,820 square yards in respect thereof in accordance with the direction of the Municipal council. The Plan was prepared and the draft revised Development plan had since be published and it was the plan which has been duly approved by the municipal council.

The appellant union was a registered trade union. The workmen were re employed in the respondent 's factory on April 8, 1980 when they were closed down. The appellant union filed two complaints against the employers alleging that the employer had committed an unfair labour practice by imposing and continuing a lock out as provided in Item 6 of Schedule II of the Act. The Industrial Court framed an issue whether the employers had committed any unfair labour practices by imposing or continuing a strike as provided under Item 6, Schedule II read with Items l(a), l(b) and 2 of Schedule I of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971 ( 'Act ' for short). The appellant contended that the industrial undertakings had never been closed or at any rate have resumed working in full and that the old workmen were not being re employed. The respondent raised an objection that the employers were willing to take back all the old employees and in order to satisfy the court about the bonafides of the employer he pointed out that nearly 16 old workmen, who responded to the advertisement in a local newspaper had already been re employed and that almost 16 old workers, who replied to the advertisements in a Local newspaper have already been de employed. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The true test is that when it is claimed that the employee has resorted to closure bonafide wants to re open, revive and re start the industrial activity he can not do so on the pain that the closure would be adjudged a device or pretence to determine whether the employer is guilty of unfair labour Practice. [69D] 1.2 The duration of the closure may be a significant fact to determine the intention and bonafides. To accept the view taken by the Industrial Court would lead to a startling result in that an employer who has resorted, bonafide wantsto re open revive and resod the industrial activities he can neither do so nor on the Pain that the closing down of the industrial business was a consequence of imposing lock out or the owner employer had decided to close down the industrial establishment. [70E] 1:3 The duration is not decisive of the matter. To accepting the view of the Industrial court would lead a startleling result, in that a employer who had resorted to closed closure bonafide needs to re opened, revive, and re started the industrial operation he can no do so. [71F G] 2.4 In lockout the employer refuses to continue. to employ the workmen employed by him even though the business activity was not closed down, and continues to employ him even if the business activities were not closed. The essence of lock out is the refusal of the employee to continue to employ workman. Imposing and continuing the lock out are necessarily temporary or for a period. [72G H] 2:5 In lockouts there is only closure of the place where as in case of a closure there is a closure of business itself permanent and irrevocable. The duration, of the closing may be an important fact to determining the intention of the employers at the time of closure but is not determinative of the matters. To acceptance the view that the termination has to be irrevocable, final and permanent and that lockout is necessarily temporary and for a periods. [73G H; 74A] 2 :6 The true tests are that when there is an employer resorted to closing down the business, the industrial court in orderto determine whether it is guilty om a device, or pretenceto determine determine whether such closure was a device and a pretence to decide determine whether a closure was for a device.

The assessee company was incorporated on July 29, 1924 as an investment company. The objects of which are set out in el. III of the memorandum of association and more particularly in sub cl. 1, 2, 15 and 16 of that clause. 2,000 were the objects of a company incorporated on June 29, 1928 as an Investment Company, the objects set out therein in el.(III) of the Memorandum of Association and more especially in sub cls. 1 to 2,15 and 16. The assessee company applied to the Appellate Tribunal under section 66(1) of Income Tax Act, 1922, for a reference of the following questions of law for the opinion of the High Court: "(i ) Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the assessee company can be treated as an investor; (ii) Whether the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, securities and immovable properties of the assessee Company can be taxed as business profits. " The Appellate Tribunal held that in the case of the appellant company not only the Memorandum Of Association gave the power to the company to deal in investments but the case was that it was a dealer in investments and properties and not merely an investor. It also held that the assessee 's case was one which fell within the ambit of section 66 (1) because the objects contained in the memorandum were not the properties of E.D. It further held that there was material on the record to support the finding of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner that the appellant had incurred losses or made profits and that therefore because of the objects incorporated in the Memorandum, the assessee could not be treated to be an investor." The High Court also held against the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that (1 ) the question as to what were the characteristics of the business of dealing in shares or investments and whether as a result thereof the assessee had to be treated only as a dealer; and (2) the profits, and losses arose from the sales of shares and securities and properties of A.D., and therefore, the profits arising from sale of these shares could not he taxed as income. HELD: (1)(a) The question as regards what were its characteristics was a mixed question of fact and law and that this Court allowed the appeal on the last occasion and set aside the judgment of the Bombay High Court dated June 15, 1952 and directed the Appellate tribunal to state a case on the following points of law. [675 D] (b) The final conclusion of the Tribunal can, therefore, be challenged on the ground that the relevant legal principles have been mis applied by the Tribunal in reaching its decision on the point; and such a challenge is open under section 67(1). [676 E F] (c) The High Courts were not competent on the questions as framed at present. It was because the question involved in this case was not a question of pure fact but was a matter mixed question between fact and laws that this court allowed the appeals on the first occasion and setting aside the order of the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal dated June 18, 1952. [76 H] (d) The contention that the question whether the profits or losses arising out from the selling of shares were business profits cannot be sustained. It is because the questions involved in the present case was a pure question of law and this Court allowing the appeal, on the second occasion set aside that judgment and directed that the AppellateTribunal should be asked to make a fresh statement of the cases on the aforesaid questions of fact. [77 E F; G] (e) The nature of the question is not a mixed issue but a mixed one of fact or law and it is a mixed matter of fact, and law that this is a question which has been decided by this Court in the earlier case.

The appellant was appointed to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. In 1949 he was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge, and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District. On April 28, 1954, the appellant filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution for a writ quashing the order of suspension dated January 28,1954, on the grounds, firstly that under the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953, which came into force from October 1, 1953 the enquiry against the appellant was without jurisdiction and secondly that the order in question was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the constitution. Held, that the High Court could not hold a preliminary enquiry into the conduct of a judicial officer, but under Rule 13 of the Madras Civil Services Rules it is the High court of Judicature at Madras that is constituted as the authority which may impose suspension pending enquiry into grave charges under rule 17(e) against the Members of the State Judicial Service. The order passed by the High Courts on January 28 1954, was merely one of suspension pending final orders by the Government and such an order is neither one of dismissal nor removal from service within article 311 Of the Constitution. But under Rule 4 (1)(a) of the Andhra Pradesh Civil Services(Disciplinary proceedings Tribunal) rules, 1953 it is not the High ' Court of Judicature to decide the matter finally, that is, constituted as a authority which might impose suspension Pending enquiry into serious charges under Rule 17(d). The order made by the State Government on January 27, 1954 was merely an one of removal pending enquiry against a member of the Judicial Service and such such an action is neither either dismissal nor removed from service.

The appellant, a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Company, died on May 13, 1945. The Income tax Officer issued notices to the legal representatives of the deceased and the general provision in section 24B provided that where a person dies, his executor, administrator or other legal representative shall be liable to pay out of the estate of the said deceased person to the extent to which the estate is capable of meeting the charge the tax assessed as payable by such person. The appellant contended that the income received by him before his death and received by his heirs and legal representatives after their death in that previous year became assessable to income tax in the relevant assessment years, but not receipts by the legal representative after the expiry of the account year in which he died. Held, that section 24 B did not authorise the levy of tax on receipts by a legal representative of a deceased person in the years of assessment succeeding the year of account in which such notional income must be deemed to have been received by the dead person and therefore they were not liable to be taxed as income of the assessee. The expression "assessee" in section 2(2) as substituted by the Indian Income tax (Amendment) Act 25 of 1953 with effect from April 1, 1952, means a person by whom income tax or any other similar 601 every person in respect of whom any proceeding and this Act has been taken for the assessment of his income or of the loss sustained by him or of any loss sustained to him. The charge to income Tax has therefore to be in accordance with and subject to the provisions of the Act, and the Legislature has not provided that the Income tax officer must have provided that he should have provided for the levy and collection of tax from the estate after the expiration of the year in question in which the notional income should be deemed as having been received. The words "assessee ' in section 25B were used to refer only to a person who died before the expiry or the date on which the order of the Income Tax Officer pursuant to which income was to be deemed distributed becomes effective and not to a legal heir.

The appellant was a Ruler of the State of Baster. He was a maufidar and was also a mahaufadar. The State Government issued an order under article 132(1) of the Constitution declaring that the village in question had never been assessed to land revenue but no evidence had been led to this effect. The appellant challenged the validity of the order on the ground that he was still a Ruler and absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of his petition under articles 226 and 227 of the constitution. The High Court held that if the appellant was an ex Ruler, there was nothing to show that with reference to any village held by him it was entered in the wajib ul arz with respect to any of his maufi villages that he had a right to recover rent or revenue from persons holding land in such village. The question whether the villages mentioned in Schedules B and B were assessed to lands revenue, which was denied on behalf of the appellant, was also considered by the High Court. Held, that the High court rightly held that the petition was not maintainable as these villages had not yet been recognised by the Government of India as the private property of the petitioner. The contention that even if he was regarded as a mahafidar it was not entered in his wajab ul ar z with respect t to any other village held on behalf or for purposes other than the Constitution, could not be accepted. The definition of 'proprietor ' in the Act does not include a grant from a State or a Ruler to a person holding land as defined in article 366(22) of that Constitution. The word 'maufidar ' is necessarily confined to a grantee from the State or Ruler of a State. It includes any person who for the time being is recognised by such President as the successor of such Ruler, and includes any other person who, for the purpose of the privy purse guaranteed he is a Ruler as defined under article 366 (22)of the Constitution.

The respondent was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director, Botanical Survey of India, Eastern Circle, Shillong. By order dated January 29, 1991 he was transferred to Phri (Uttar Prades). The respondent submitted that the guidelines contained in Government of India O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer. tie complained that some other officials who had been serving at Shillong for a longer period, have been allowed to continue at Shillong. He submitted that he was liable to transfer anywhere in India is not in dispute. It is not the case of the respondent that order of his transfer is vitiated by mala fides on the part of the authority making the order, though the Tribunal does say so merely because some guidelines issued by the Central Government are not followed, with which finding we shall deal later. The Administrative Tribunal quashed the order of transfer on the following reasoning: (i) The decision of this Court in Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta [1992] 1 S.C.C., 306 rendered by a Bench of which one of us (J.S. On a perusal of the judgment, we do not think it supports the respondent 's contentions instead of supporting them. (ii) The Administrative Tribunals are not an Appellate Authority sitting in judgment over the orders of transfer. In this case the Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the orderof transfer. The order of the Tribunal reads as if it were sitting in appeal over the order dated April 3, 1986. The respondent is liable to be transferred anywhere in Indian service and avoid transfer to a different place on the ground that the spouses thereby would be posted at different places. (iii) The administrative Tribunal is not an appellate Authority sitting over the decisions of the Courts established by law. In the case where a person makes any representation with respect to his transfer, the appropriate authority must consider the same having regard to the exigencies of administration and enable the two spouses to live together at one station if it is possible without any detriment to the administrative needs and the claim of other employees. (iv) The Tribunal has also exceeded its power in interfering in the order passed by transfer. (v) The guidelines say that as far as practicable, husband and wife must be posted in one pi" as faras practicable, but that does not enable any spouse to claim such a posting as of right if the departmental authorities do not consider it feasible. The only thing required is that the departmental authority should consider this aspect along with the exigencies and enable them to live separately at one place without sacrifice of the requirements of the administration and needs of other employee. After giving preference to the career prospects by accepting such a promotion or any appointment in an all India service, subordinating the need of the couple living together at two station, 'they cannot as of rights claim to be relieved of the ordinary incidents of all India Service and avoid transfers to a separate place on that ground. (vi) The said observations in fact tend to negative the respondent's contentions instead o supporting them; (vii) The judgment also does not support the Respondent 's contention that if such an order is questioned in a Court or Tribunal, the authority is obliged to justify the transfer by adducing the reasons therefor. It does not also say that the Court or the Tribunal can quash the order if any of the administrative instructions/guidelines are not follow, much less can it be charactrised as malafide for that reason. To reiterate, the order also doesnot support the Respondents ' contention that the Administrative Tribunals were not anAppellate Authority sitting at judgment over their orders of transfers.

The appellants were convicted under Section 302 read with Section 34, IP.C. and sentenced to undergo imprisonment for five years. They were convicted by the Trial Court. On appeal, the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1to A3. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The participation of the appellants in the occurrence which resulted in the death of Jawahar has been proved beyond doubt. [319D] 2.1 In view of the nature of injuries on the person of the deceased and the facts and circumstances of this case, the 3 offence committed by them came within the mischief of Section 325 read with 34, IPC. Thirteen external in juries were found on the dead body of Jawahar. Out of those 11 were on lower legs and arms. The High Court while consid ering the nature o f offence observed as under: "These accused and their associates who be set themselves on Jawahar could never have intended to cause such injuries as would be sufficient, in the ordinary course of nature to cause death, if such was their intention, they could have certainly killed him especially after carrying him into the cholam field and left him dead there instead of merely causing grievous and grievous injuries to him. Even according to Jawahar 's statement (Exhibit P 6) all that first accused had remarked was that the attack on him was in retaliation for the injuries Jawahar had caused on the first accused a few weeks earlier. " Agreeing with the above observations of the High court, this is set aside. The conviction and sentence of the appel lants under Section 304 Part I read with section 34, Cr. P.C., read with Sec tion 34, is setaside. The appellants shall deposit Rs. 7,000 each before the Trial Commis sion within four months from today. In the event of non payment of fine the appellants shall undergo rigorous imprisonment for 5 years.

The appellant Bank was constituted under the Banking Companies Act, 1949. The Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Ordinance, 1969 was promulgated by the Governor on December 1, 1969. Section 3(27)(a) of the Ordinance provided that the provisions of the Act shall apply to a corporation which is an autonomous body. Section 4(e) of Ordinance VIII of 1969 provided for the constitution of a Board of Directors and sub section (1) thereof provided that in respect of any banking company, the Central Government may by notification in the Official Gazette appoint a person to be its Chairman and Vice Chairman of such Board. The appellant Bank filed a suit against the respondent Bank for recovery of the amount due from it under the Ordinance VIII. The suit was decreed by the trial court. In appeal, the High Court held that the words `special Indian law ' in section 4(a) were placed after the words "an Act of Parliament of the United Kingdom and before the words 'Royal Charter or Letters Patent ', they must be held in view of the setting that the expression `formed in pursuance of ' in Section 4 (e) was meant to refer or relate to a special law enacted by an Act of British Parliament for India. In this appeal by Special Leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant Bank that as the words were `formed before the word `an Act ', the provision of section 4 (a) would not apply inasmuch as the appellant bank was formed by or under and not in pursuance to the Banking companies Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The provisions of Ordinance X of 1969 are not applicable to a banking company which is the creature of a special Indian law, whether it is created in pursuance Of or by or Under the special Indian Law. [969G] 1.2 The words `any special Indian laws ' refer and relates to a law made by the British Parliament. It will be highly unreasonable and illogical to think that as a corporation has been formed by and under a specialIndian law, it will not come within the purview of section4(e).
