[968G] 2.1 In the face of the provision contained in section 3( 27)(a), as it stood on the day the Act was passed, it must be presumed that the legislature intended to protect the British economic interests and although such a law could permissibly be enacted under the Constitutional Scheme of the 1953 Government of India Act, that law after the inauguration of our Sovereign Democratic Republic cannot but be held to have become void as making invidious discrimination in favour of the British Corporation offending against the equality clause under Article 14 of the Constitution. [969A] 2:2 The provisions contained in Ordinance VIII are not inapplicable to corporations formed or created by any special Indian statute which, in the instant case, is the Banking Company Act. No other point has been urged by either party in this appeal. In view of this discussion made above, it may be stated that the observations made by this Court in Krishna Murthy 's case for holding the latter part of section 3 (27)(b) to be void as having become void under making a discrimination in respect thereof offending against equality clause Under Article 14 Of the Constitution and, accordingly, void. [970G H] 2 :3 The words "any special law" refer and relate to an Act made by Parliament or Legislature of India or Legislature. Therefore, the provisions contained therein are not relevant to the appellant ' Bank and, therefore, there is no question of scaling down the debt due to the Bank by the respondents. [971G] 4:4 The words 'any special foreign law ' refer or relates to any law made in pursuance thereof or by a special person under the law and not by the law itself.

The petitioners, who were manufacturers of sugar in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar, raised the following points in support of their contention that the impugned notification is illegal and invalid (1) The impugned notification was beyond the ambit of authority conferred on the Central Government under section 3 of the Act; (2) the impugned Notification was not within the ambit Of authority conferred by section 3. HELD : (i) The object of the impugned Act is to provide for control of production, supply and distribution of trade and commerce in essential commodities in the interests of general public so that the price at which the factories were compelled to sell their products may be maintained or increased, their equitable distribution secured and they may be available to the general public at fair prices. [134 E] (ii) The main object of section 3 is to secure fair prices for the consumer, i.e., the general Public at fair price; but if fair prices are fixed in this area, price all over India is practicalLy fixed, and it is not necessary to fix prices separately so far as factories in other States which are said to be mainly deficit, are concerned. [135 G] (iii) The contention that there is discrimination is purely theoretical, in view of the economic factors which control the price of sugar In this country, the price control is imposed on factories in Punjab and Uttar Pradesh. [136 C D] (iv) The press note issued by the Government on July 30, 1958 shows that the Government was of the view that prices should be pegged at the level at which they were in the week preceding June 27, 1958, and inasmuch as they fixed prices below that level or even below the level of which they had been at the end of May, 1958. The contention of the Government is that as soon as the price is controlled in Punjab the price for the whole of India is fixed, for other States are deficit and import sugar from these States, particularly Uttar Pradesh, and North West Bihar. [137 G H] (v) The argument that there was discrimination is merely theoretical, because it compels factories to sell sugar at a loss, (vi) it fixes the price arbitrarily, and (vii) there is no reason why the Government should go on also to fix wholesale or retail price.

The workmen of the appellant company, were employed in the manufacture and sale of sugar. The workmen represented by Bengal Chemical & Pharmaceutical Works Limited, Calcutta, were employees of the respondent company. The dispute was referred to the Industrial Tribunal under section 10(1) (d) of the Industrial Disputes Act, 1947, for adjudication. The Tribunal held that the working class cost of living index in the year 1951 was taken as the basis and that the date of agreement was the crucial one for ascertaining whether there was substantial change in the working classes cost of labour index in 1957. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the award dated June 21, 1951, was not terminated under section 19(6) of Act and therefore the reference was bad in law; (2) the Tribunal wrongly relied upon Exhibit 3, corrected on the basis of the information given by the State Statistical Bureau, West Bengal for ascertaining the working division cost of working class costs of living Index since August 1954 up to March 1957. HELD: (i) The Tribunal wrongly relying upon Exhibit 2, corrected in the Monthly Statistical Digest, West West Bengal, for ascertaining that there was a substantial change of the workingclass cost of live index in that year and complained that similar entries for all the relevant years had not been produced; and (3) the date on which the agreement replaced the earlier award and therefore, the date from which it was so transferred must be the crucial part for ascertaining Whether there was any substantial change. [148 B C] (ii) The expression "any dispute" in section 33B of the Act is wide enough to include a reference to an industrial dispute. It does not mean that a dispute should be referred to a Tribunal constituted under the Act and that it must be deemed to have been referred to it by the appropriate Government. [149 C D] (iii) The word "Tribunal" in Section 33B, inserted in the Act by the Amending Act, was prospective in operation i.e., it would apply only to proceedings initiated in the tribunal constituted under section 7A of the , and that proceedings pending before the tribunals constituted under that Act before the commencement of the Amending act would be disposed of as if the Amending Acts had not not been passed. [150 C D].

The appellant, a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of the tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism. The said management continued as before and the fact that an Executive Officer had been appointed under the scheme made no difference to the actual administration of the Mutt. It was no doubt urged before the learned Judge that the appellant 's writ petition should not be entertained because he had a definite adequate alternative remedy under the latter Act, but this plea was rejected by the learned judge with the observation that where the fundamental right is clearly infringed, it is the duty of the Court to interfere in favour of the citizen unless there are reasons of policy which make it inexpedient to do so. The appellant contended that the scheme having been framed as early as 1939 under the relevant provisions of the earlier Act which was valid when it was enacted, could not be challenged on the ground that some of its provisions contravened the fundamental rights guaranteed to the citizens of this country under article 19(1)(f). Held, that the schemes to which section 103(d) applies have to be deemed to be settled or modified under the provisions of section 103 (d) and that is why section 103 was not actually enforced before the 26th January 1950. The scheme was framed and the Executive Officer was appointed as early in 1939. If the Executive officer could not take over the actual management of the Math and its properties, it was partly because the appellant had continuously challenged the implementation of the scheme by legal proceedings and partly because he has otherwise obstructed the said implementation. But it is clear that when the scheme was made and a challenge made by the appellant to its validity failed in courts of law, his property rights had been taken away. The deprivation of the petitioner 's property rights was brought about by invalid orders and it was in respect of such invalid orders that the Court held that the petitioner was entitled to seek the protection of article 19 and invoke the jurisdic tion of this Court under article 32.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha, M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells, till May 25, 1986. The appellant continued to work as Hindi teacher in the school on July 12, 1982. The managing committee even passed a resolution on July 6,1987 requesting the educational authorities of the State of Orissa to approve the continuous appointment of the appellant as Hindi Teachers with effect from July 12.1982. The management of the school approved the continuous appointments of the appellants as Hindi teachers but no action was taken by the said authorities. The respondent filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi Lecturer with effectfrom July 12 1982. A Single Judge of the High court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant was not entitled to be regularised in terms of the provisions of Section 3 of the Orissa Aided Educational Institutions (Appointment of Teachers Validation) Act, 1989 (hereinafter called 'the Validation Act '). The Division Bench held that the appointment by the managing committee on ad hoc basis must be on or after the 1st December, 1976 but not later than 31st December 1984. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court erred in denying the benefit of the Validation Act to the appellant on the ground that his initial appointment for 89 days was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the select list. [934G] 1.2 The State of Haryana will do well to consider the cases of all those who have completed one year or more as ad hoc teachers after December, 31, 1984 and come out with a scheme or any other appropriate measure to regularise their services. [1035C D] 1:3 The High court erred in denied the benefit to the appellants on the grounds that his original appointment for 91 days was accompanied by a resolution dated July 6 1987 requesting the Educational authorities of State ofOrissa to approve continuous appointment as Hindi lecturer but no approval was taken from the educational authority for the period subsequent to 1986. [734D] 1 :4. The High ' Court erred while denying the benefits of the validation Act to those members of teaching community who are being exploited for years together by keeping 999 them in short spell appointments like 89 day posts as here with one day breaks and in the process denying them their rightful dues and other service benefits. [834F] 1.:5. The State will do justice to the students studying in the schools under the control of the managing committees. [936G] 2:6. The school is still utilising his services though there is no approval by the educational Authorities for the periods subsequent to1986. The case of the respondent is, thus fully covered by Section 3(1) of the validating Act. [948C D; 935A] 1:-7. The validity of the Validating Act to validate the appointment of teachers in a substantive vacancy because of the invalid Act does not arise. [949E F] 2.8. The Validation Act has been enacted by the Orissa legislature with the obvious object of granting relief to those persons who have already completed one years or more ad hoc teacher after December 31,1984 and come into force with a Scheme or any appropriate measure for regularise their service. An appointment on 89 day basis with one month break which deprives a teacher of his salary for the Period of summer vacation and other Service benefits is wholly arbitrary and suffers from the vice of discrimination.

The appellant was defeated by respondent No. 1, who was defeated on the ground that he was disqualified from being a candidate for being a member of a Panchayat Samiti and was based on Rules 3 to 7 of the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads, Non official Members (Payment of Allowances) Rules, 1965 which were as follows : "3. The Chairman and Member shall be paid mileage allowance in respect of a journey performed within the district, including attending of meeting, supervision of plans, projects, schemes and other works and also for 'the discharge of all lawful obligations and implementation of Government directives : Provided that the Vice Chairman and Members shall not be entitled to any mileage allowances. " The appellant challenged the validity of r. 3 on the grounds (1) that he had failed to establish that the allowances paid under rules 3 to 6 made the office of Chairman of a panchayat Samiti an office of profit, and (2) that the payment of mileage Allowance was in excess of the amount of expenditure which he would have incurred for 'he purpose of performing the journeys in order to discharge his official duties. The High Court held that the allowance paid under r. 2 to 7 made the Office of Chairman was in addition to the payment for the journey performed by him and that consequently, there was no question of any disqualification arising out of the office which he could have incurred in connection with the discharge of his official duty. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1 ) the allowances payable under rules 2 to 6 were not in addition or in addition; (2 ) that the Chairman must be making gain out of payment to him of daily allowance, daily allowance or any other allowances to which he might have been entitled in orderto compensate him for expenses incurred in relation to the discharge and performance of his duties. HELD : (1)(a) The appellant has failed to prove that the amount received as daily allowance was in fact excess of what was actually required by r. 7(2); (b) the Chairman should be making profit out of such payment to the Chairman of the Panchayat Samiti; and (c) the payment must be made at a higher rate to the members of the staff of the panchayat Samiti. [655 B] (1). The appellant had failed in establishing that the amounts received as travelling allowance or daily allowance were in excess Of the amount which he incurred for the purpose of performance of the journeys. He has failed in proving that out of his payment as daily allowances the Chairman will in fact invariably make a saying, it cannot be held that this payment would result in gain so as to make the office an office profit. [613 C D] (2)(a). The High court was perfectly correct in arriving at the conclusion that this allowance of Rs. There is also no evidence from which an inference may be drawn that out Of the amounts paid as daily Allowance the Chairman would in fact make a say, it can not be held to have been made gain out by so as To make the Office an office or profit. In the course of his submissions, learned counsel tried to urge that the payments of travelling allowance and daily allowance under r 3 to7 were in addition and to the payments for the purposes and journeys mentioned in rule 5 was in connection only with additional expenditure and out of pocket expenses of the Chairman and, while no evidence has been advanced to show that out o the amount receipts as daily wages were in fact made by a Chairman for travelling allowance, the Chairman could not make a sense of profit. The appellant failed to produce any evidence from where an inference might be drawn whether out of expenditure or daily allowances is in excess or not.

The appellant was tenant of a residential building. The tenanted premises was let out to the appellant for running a Dal and Oil Mill. The trial Court held that the partition wall in the hall did not constitute material alteration, it further held that tin shed marked by letters ABHG had been constructed by the appellant with the consent of the erstwhile landlords predecessor in interest of the respondents but the tin shed marking with letters CDGH had been built by the appel lant subse quently without respondents ' consent which materially altered the accommodation and on that findings the trial court decreed the suit. The High Court also held that since two sides of the tin sheds were resting on the pucca wall it constituted a material alteration in the accommodation, and on this finding the first appellate court decreed it. In appeal to this Court by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the construction made by a tenant in the shape of kitchen and bathroom did not form part of the building, and that the tin roof marked with letters ABGH had not been constructed without respondents consent which substantially altered the structure and on the findings the first Appellate Court decreed the appeal. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The basic sine qua non for eviction is that the tenant has without the permission of the District Magistrate but if the tenant, without the landlords permission made or permitted to make construction which in the opinion of the court has materially altered, the landlord is free to file suit for tenant 's eviction without obtaining permission of a District Magistrate. [975D] 2. The essential element which needs consideration is as to whether the constructions are sub stantial in nature and they alter, the form, front and structure of the accommodation. The crucial element which requires consideration is: whether the construction is sub statial in character or not. If so, whether those constructions are of such a substantial nature which make material alterations in the building. [1075E] 3. The question would depend on the facts and circumstances of each case, the alterations in this case must mean material alteration. [1002B] 4. The Court must address itself to the nature, character of the construction carried out by the tenant. The Legislature intended that only those constructions which bring about substantial change in the front and structures of the premises should provide a ground for eviction. The object is to ensure that the building is not used as a place of residence but it has been constructed on the open land adjacent to the accommodation so that it may be used as an office of profit. [1012C] 5. In determining the question whether the structures materially alter the structure or not, the Court must examine itself to consider whether theconstruction materially altera tions as the construction carry out by such a tenant without causing any damage to the premises. The nature of constructions, whether they are permanent or temporary, is a relevant consideration in determining the questions of 'material alteration '. [1022D] 6. In deciding this question the Court has to consider itself to whether those structures which bring into substantial change either in the form or structure of building should provide an ground for tenant "s eviction, but every construction or alteration made by any tenant in a building does not provide a grounds for eviction; instead the constructions complained of, must be of such nature and character as to materially alter, and the extent to which they make changes in the structure.

The appellant company filed a suit against the respondent firm for setting aside an ex parte decree on 22 4 1975 against the appellant. The Trial Court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975. The High Court allowed the revision set aside the judgment of the Trial Court and upheld the passing of the ex parte order. In this appeal by special leave, the appellant company contended: (1) that the summons in question was not properly served on it; (2) that since Navlakha was an employee of the company sitting in its registered office in Calcutta the summons will be deemed to have been duly served; and (3) that there was no agent empowered to accept service of summons on his behalf. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The word "Principal Officer" in clause (b) has got to be understood in the background of the provisions of the Code in Order 5 which is meant for issue and service of summon on natural persons. [1032C D] 2. Rule 17 of Order 5 does not an exhaustive provision providing for all modes of service on the defendant in the sense as to what is meant by service of Summons on the Secretary, Director or Principal Officer in Jute and Gunny Brokers Ltd. and another vs The Union of India and others it was held that the words "Principal officer" in cl.(b) of Rule 2 would include managing agents and it can, under this rule, be on a juristic person. [ 1032C] 3. Rule 2 is not an inclusive provision providing that all modes Of service on a defendant by post to the registered office of the Company unless the contrary is shown, will be presumed to be service on that company itself. In Rule 17, it has been provided: "Where the defendant or his agent or such other person as aforesaid refuses to sign the acknowledgement, or where the serving officer, after using all due and reasonable diligence, cannot find the defendant, and there is no agent empower to accept Service of the summons on behalf of the defendant nor any other person on whom service can be made, the serving Officer shall affix a copy of the notice on the outer door or some other conspicuous part of the house in which the defendant ordinarily resides or carries on business or personally works for gain, 1032 and shall then return the original to the Court from which it was issued, with a report endorsed thereon or annexed thereto stating that he has so affixed the copy, the circumstances under which he did so, and the name and address of the person (if any) by whom the house was identified and in whose presence the copy was affixed. " [1033D] 4. Rule 18 is an exhaustive one providing for service of notice on natural person. The meaning of clause (a) has been got to have be understood as in the context of the provision in Order 6 which is intended for issue or service of notices on natural people. Sending a summons by post will be assumed to be Service on the Company itself. [934E F] 5. Rule 20 provides that "Where, the defendant and his agent/or such other persons as aforesaid refuse to sign any acknowledgement, the served officer shall affix an copy of such notice on a outer door and some other prominent part of it, and then return to the court from which the Court was issued with a copy endorsed thereon.

The appellant was the owner of a land in dispute. The respondents filed a suit for declaration that they were in possession of the land in question and that they had no right to possess the same. The trial court decreed the suit holding that there was an apprehension of breach of peace existed at the time the order was passed. The High Court allowed the petition and remitted the case to the Magistrate. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that as there was no clear finding by the Magistrate in the final order that there had been an apprehension or breach of the peace existed, the Magistrate called upon the parties to file their written statements and then after a full enquiry as provided by section 145(5) Cr. It was further contended that the Magistrate had not given any finding on this aspect of the matter and therefore the final decision was bad and the High Court rightly allowed the appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court in revision cannot go into the sufficiency or otherwise of the materials on the basis of which the satisfaction of the Magistrate is based. [952B] 1.2 In Hari Ram & Ors. vs Banwari Lal & Ors., ; , relied upon. Hari Ram and Ors. V Banwari Lal, ; , followed. Hariram & Ors.'s case was decided by a Division Bench of the High court on the same facts. The decision in Hari Ram 's case did not lay down any proposition that once a Magistrate finds that there is a breach of law it is not necessary that the dispute should continue at every stage of the proceedings unless there is clear evidence to show that the disputed land has ceased to exist so as to bring the case within the ambit of sub section (5) of section 145 of the Code of Criminal Procedure. [962D E] Hari Ram vs Banwari lal & Ors, ; ; , referred to.

The appellant was a resident of the State of Madras. The income tax authorities assessed him to income tax for the years 1941 42, 1942 43 and 1943 44. He claimed that he had sold his goods in British India in British Indian and that the profits could be taxed only if they were remitted to British India. The Income tax Officer rejected this claim on the ground that the transactions between the appellant and its nonresidents were benami transactions and not sales of the assessee. The Appellate Tribunal held that the transaction was benami transactions, but the High Court in appeal held that section 14(2) (c) applied only to non residents and that it was only section 14 (2) that would apply to residents and applied to have that question referred to the court under section 66(1). In reference the High court held that sections 42(1) and 42(3) applied both to nonresident persons, and that therefore a finding of fact on a question of law could be challenged in a reference under section 67(1), and that there was no question which could be referred to it. The appellant appealed to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) The finding of the Commissioner was correct. It was not open to the Tribunal to review its own judgment on the facts found, on the application of the proper principles of law, and it was not a pure question of fact or mixed question of Law. The decision in Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co., (1) was not even so much as referred to in the (1). It was only this question that was pressed on the strength of the decision in Commissioners of Income Tax, Bombay City vs Ahmedabhai Umarbhai & Co., , and it could not be said that sections 41(1)(c) and 43(3), ap plied only to Nonresidents and the decision of the High Courts was not therefore open to reference under Section 66( 1). (ii) The question whether section 42(I) and section 42 (3) were applicable to non residents, and the decisions in St. Applying this decision it was open to review by the court only on the grounds that it is not supported by any evidence or perverse but also on the basis of the finding that it has not been treated as profits by the assessee and the authorities in St., applied section 66 (1), which applied both for non resident persons and nonresident.

The assessee was appointed as a General Manager of the respondent company. The remuneration of the General Manager carried the responsibility equal to that of the Director who was given the charge of the conduct of business after the death of Shri Vaish, the General manager. The Income Tax Officer determined the sum of Rs. 70,465 paid as commission to the General Managers and the assessee preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who by his order dated October 31, 1949 found that Rs. 37,733 paid to the general Manager was an amount laid out or expended wholly or exclusively for the purpose of the business of the assessee and was wrongly disallowed by the Income Tax Appellate Tribunal. The Appellate Assistant commissioner held that the post of General Manager carrying the responsibility of the management after the deceased had been old and dilapidated and in the first 14 months the mill made no profit and Shri Vaish was paid nothing beyond the salary and car allowance. The High Court answered the question against the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the amount of Rs, 37,0733 paid by the GeneralManager was an income laid out wholly and exclusively for purposes of the trade of the company and was rightly disallowed by Income Tax Tribunal; (2) the salary paid to Shri Vaish in excess of tiffs amount Was not really paid wholly for the purposes of carrying on business. HELD : (i) The principle of this decision applies to the present case and it must accordingly be held that in the circumstances established by the assessee the entire amount of commission was laid out exclusively and exclusively towards the purpose for which the business was carried on, and the special aptitude of the employee, future prospects of extension by the business and a host of other related circumstances. [521 B] (ii) The case of the Revenue, however, is that a higher rate of commission of 25% was fixed for Shri J.P. Vaish because the mill was old and old andwas dilapidated and it never made profit of even a lakh of rupees in the past and that the rate of 25%, was fixed in order to create special interest of the general manager for accomplishment of the task entrusted to him. Private Ltd., (2), in applying the test of commercial expediency for determining whether an expenditure was wholly or partly laid out for the purpoSe of business, profession or vocation as required under section 10(2)(Xv) of the Income tax Act has to be adjudged from the point of view of the businessman and not (1).

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. He was actually represented in the proceedings before the Tribunal by an officer of that Union, its Secretary, who was incharge of the conduct of the proceedings on behalf of the company. The appellant filed his application to the Patna High Court on March 13, 1957 praying for a direction to the Tribunal not to record the compromise in so far as it related to the appellant 's case and to give its award without reference to the settlement and on proper adjudication of the matter. The Tribunal rejected the prayer for representation by a person of his own choice instead of Fateh Singh, the Secretary of the Union and thereafter in making an award on the basis of the reference. The High Court dismissed summarily the application holding that the Tribunal committed a serious error in rejecting his application for separate representation. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (i) the Tribunal erred in rejecting the appellant "s prayer for relief on the ground that he had not authorised Fateh Singh to enter into any agreement in his case and praying that the agreement filed in respect of his case should not be accepted; (ii) the tribunal erred in refusing the appellant to make a statement on behalf, of the Company that in addition to the sum of Rs. 1,000 which the company had agreed to pay to the respondent as a term of settlement the company will pay a further sum of money to him as a condition precedent for making an application under section 36 of the Industrial Disputes Act; (iii) the award was not made by the Union or a number of workmen and that the appellant did not want his case to be represented by Fateh Singh. Held, that the High Court erred in holding that it had committed any error in refusing to entertain the appellant's prayer for a writ. Chakravarty, J., dissenting), that section 36 Of the Industrial Dispute Act recognises this position, by providing that the workman who is a party to a dispute shall be entitled to be represent by an Officer of a registered trade union of which he is a member. It has been suggested that the Union 's Secretary Fateh Singh himself had made the complaint against the appellant which resulted in the order of dismissal.

The appellants were the tenants of a joint Hindu family. The suit was decreed against both the defendants and for arrears of rent against defendant No. 1. On appeal by defendant No, 553 At the hearing of the appeal of the surviving appellants, the only point which was urged for consideration was whether the surviving appellant could have instituted the appeal against the entire decree in view of O. 4 of the Code. Held, that the High Court could not have heard the appeal on the ground common to all of them and could have reversed or varied the whole decree in favour of all the original plaintiffs and could only have granted relief with respect to the rights and interests of Kedar Nath as well. The provisions of O., XLI, r. 4 when an appeal is filed by all the plaintiffs or defendants, if all the appellants or the defendants dies and the appeal abates so far as he is concerned under O.XXII, r, 33 is of no greater help to the contention of the appellants that their appeal could continue even though the appeal by Kedar Nath had abated, as the Court could have passed a decree in respect of the rights & interests of the deceased appellant and could not had passed a final decree in his favour. The appeal by the surviving plaintiffs was not competent in the circumstances of the case and, therefore, the provisions of 0. XLI, R. 4 were not intended to apply to an appeal which was not a competent appeal against a party under the Code or under the Letters Patent of the High court.

The landlord filed a suit for eviction of the tenant on the ground that the lease had expired by efflux of time limited thereby under section 111(g) and no notice terminating the tenancy under section 106 was needed. The trial court decreed the suit holding that the tenancy stood determined by forfeiture, not in terms of section 111 (g) because the TP Act did not apply to the present lease and the principles of justice, equity and good conscience were not desiderate the technical requirement of a notice in writing of an intention to determine the lease. The High Court held that the provisions of sections 106 and 111 of the TP act would regulate the matter as could be held to be consistent with the rules of equity, justice and good law. In appeal by certificate under article 133 of the Constitution, it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that the suit was barred by limitation because the lease having expired by lapse of time, the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting in terms thereof could not be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a written notice as contemplated by section 111. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The question whether the provisions introduced in sub section (g), of section111(g), are but a statutory recognition of a principle of justice equity and fair conscience is the alter ego of section 112(g). [920C] 2.1 In the instant case, no notice whatsoever was sent to the tenant of the application for eviction when the notice was sought to be justified on the grounds that no such notice was necessary because the tenancy stands determined either by efflux or by forfeiture following the breach by the tenant. The statutory law as it now stands, however, is that the happening of any of the events specified in section 111 does not, ipso facto extinguish the lease but only exposes the lessee to the risk of forfeiture and clothes the lessor with the right, if he so chooses, to determine his lease by giving notice in that behalf. The essential principles, not the technical rules, of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882 or the rules made thereunder form part of justice. [921D] 2:2 In regard to notice to quit and notice of forfeiture, the appellant accepted the application, not of the Rent Control Law but of the rules and regulations of justice and fair play. The conclusion emerges that the landlord 's termination of the lease in this case is good even without a written intimation. [ 922D] 3:3 In the present case, the tenant has to stand or fall by his submission that justice, Equity and good mind is the alteration ego and not merely because it is merely procedural and technical rule introduced in the section by the legislature and is not based on any well established principles of equity. The basic principle, not technical rules or technical rules of the landlord form part thereof, form part and parcel of justice; equity and justice are the altere ego. [961E F] 4:4 In regard, notice to demand for possession of the premises in question was a statutory notice. The tenant has also to stand and fall by him his submission, not on the technical grounds, but on the application of the principles embodied in section 112 (g). The basic rule is that a written or oral notice is no part of equity; justice, justice, equitable and good sense. The principle of law, equity, good conscience and good justice are both integral and essential features of the transaction.

The respondent was dismissed from service on the ground of conduct which led to his conviction on a criminal charge. The High Court held that the Governor had no power under article 311(2) to give him an opportunity of showing cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the Governor has no power to give the said Shri P. K. K., K.K. K, K. M. K.. K. Hore and B. K K. D. K.' K. J. The respondent contended that (i) the High Court had erred in holding that the order of dismissal was illegal as it did not comply with the requirements of article 311 of the Constitution; (ii) the order passed by the Governor under sub clause (c) of the proviso to clause (2) of Article 311 of Constitution was without jurisdiction and, therefore, the order was liable to be quashed. HELD : (i). The satisfaction under the unamended provision, therefore that the respondent had to arrive at was that it was not expedient to hold such inquiry; or (iii) the satisfaction required was that in the interest of the security of the State it was expedient to give an opportunity to show cause against his action proposed. [489 G] (ii). The Governor has to arrive on the material before him and he is satisfied that in view of the nature of the charges, it was necessary to hold the inquiry under the principal clause. He is also satisfied that there was no justification for holding such an inquiry. [490 E F] (iii)(a) The satisfaction contemplated by the amended article 311 is not a condition precedent to the exercise of his power under sub cl.(2). The order passed under the amended provision, however, does not show that it has been made in accordance with the provisions of article311(2). [489 C D] (b) The Governor had to come to the conclusion that there were no sufficient grounds for holding the inquiry. He was also satisfied by the evidence adduced during such inquiry that the charges against him were proved. [487 E F; 488 A B] (c ) The satisfaction of the Governor in the present case, therefore. that the satisfaction under sub clauses (2), (3) and (4) of article 310 of the constitution was not necessary to give that person an opportunity. [488 C D].

The petitioners, who were the Shia Wakfs of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi, filed a suit for declaration that they had been in possession and enjoyment of the land in dispute as Shia Waqfs for purposes of performing their religious ceremonies and functions over the plots and structures thereon under the decree of competent Civil Court for the enforcement of which the instant Writ Petition has been filed. The petitioners contended that the Shias ' community of MohallaDoshipuri, Varanasi was a wakf property and that the mosque on Plot No. 8 was not a Shia Wakf property within the meaning of section 2(1)(d) of the U.P. (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972. The respondents contended that they were entitled to customary rights in respect of the lands in dispute under the provisions of the Act and that they could not be deprived twice over with the same kind of litigation and in any event, they had no right to claim any customary rights. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the petitioners had failed to prove their existing customary rights to perform their religious rites and functions on the other plots and structure thereon. In appeal, the High Court held that the respondents were entitled for customary rights under section 144 of the Code of Civil Procedure and that in view of the fact that they did not raise disputed questions of title and the Allahabad High Court had decided them for the first time in the writ petition, irrespective of whether the assumption made by this Court was right or wrong, the fact remains that there was no adjudication or decision on merits as a result of the final order passed by this court in the appeal, which was confirmed in the Review Petition. Allowing the Appeal, HELD: 1.1 The Notification dated 26th February, 1944 issued under section 5(1) of U. P. ( Regulation of Letting Rent and eviction) Act by the Sunni Board is of no avail to the Sunnis for the purpose of defeating the customary rights of Shias to perform religious ceremonies on the plots or structures thereon. [735G] 1.2 The Notification issued under Section 5(I) of Act by Sunni Board of Waqf is of a no avail, to the petitioners and through them the Shib Wakfs of Varanasi is directed, if action under section 145 Cr. Pc. is taken against the two Boards (Shia Central Wakf Board and Sunni Central Wakf board) notices were issued to them and they were also heard through respective counsel. Thirdly, the earlier decision of this Court in Civil Appeal No.941 of 1976 did not record any decision on the rights of the parties on merits but the Court took the view that the parties should be relegated to a civil suit on the assumption that the appellants before the AllahabadHigh Court (in W.P.(No.2397) had raised disputed questions about title and they had misled the Court into believing that the Notification issued by the Shian Board on 1st December, 1956 under Rule 5411(vii) was the Notification under section5(1). [736H; 737A] 1:3 The petitioners and respondents 5 and 6 have been heard through their respective counsel and they are also im 1135 pleaded as parties to the petition who have filed their affidavits in the matter and have been hearing through various counsel. They have been represented through their counsel. Therefore, the present petition by res judicata or principle analogous to res judicata cannot be regarded as between the same parties who are before us; further, where it was felt by this High Court that proper adjudication would not be possible without impleading the two Board (Shia Waqf Board) notices are issued to the parties and they have been hear through their counsels.

The assessee, a company registered under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was assessed to income tax for the assessment year 1957 58. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim of set off on the footing that when in the assessment years 1957 58 the loss was claimed it was excluded in the computa tion of income as capital loss and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner while disposing of the assessee 's appeal had stated that it was a notional capital loss. The Appellate Assistant Commis sioner dismissed the appeal by holding that there was no genuine loss; it was essentially notional in nature and that the claim for set off to be admissible had to be notified by the Income tax Officer under Section 24(3) of the 1922 Act to the assessee by an order in writing. In the appeal before the Appellate Tribunal, the Revenue contended that the assessee had filed its return showing the loss and that it had filed a return showing loss and, therefore, the claim was not admissible. The High Court dismissed the reference holding that the benefit conferred under Section24(3)(a) of 1922 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 Act and notwithstanding the wordings of section 80 of the latter Act, the High Court was Fight in holding that it did not amount to an adverse order, the Income Tax officer was not entitled to take advantage of his own failure and reject the assessee "s claim of carry forward and set off of loss on the ground that loss had not been determined as required under Section 25(3). The Revenue appealed to this Court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 In order to be eligible for setoff against capital gains, it is necessary to ascertain whether there has been a genuine loss or not. [1166C] 1.2 The assessee had produced its return show ing the loss as computed by him for the purposes of this section. It was not disputed that the amount claimed was a sum which was not deductible under Section 23(3), but it was only a notional income. [1067D] 1:3 In order that the Tribunal should have determined the loss, the assessee must produce evidence to show that there has not been any genuine loss. [ 1068C] 2.1 The word "capital gains" in sub section (2A) of Section 24 of 1922 is a phrase used in the sense in which it occurs and includes all profits and gains arising out of or relating to the business of the company. It means any loss, injury or damage arising out from or relating thereto. [1001D] 2:1 The words "in respect of any assessment year" occurring in sub clause (a) are not defined in the Act but are used in a wide sense and include all profits which arise out of the business carried on by the company or its directors or other persons. [1006E] 2 :2 In order, therefore to be entitled to set off against capital gain, it must be shown that there is a genuine difference between the loss sustained and the loss suffered. The word 'capital gains ' in sub Section (2) of section 24 of the Act has been used in wide terms and includes any profits and losses arising out or relating lo the business. [1016E F] 2(a) In order for set t off under sub section(1), there must be a genuine distinction between the actual loss sustained by the assessee and the actual amount thereof. The expression "capital gain" in clause (b) of sub section 1 means any sum which is not deductible from the profits and gain arising out Of or relating with the business, profession or vocation carried on under the head "capital asset". [1017E F]. 2(b) In the instant case, there was a genuine dispute between the assessee company and its directors.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air) (DTD & P). The Defence Science Services had three units under it, namely, 1) Defence Research and Development Organisation (DRDO), 2) Director ate General of Inspection (DGI) and 3) Directorate of Tech nical Development and production (Air), (D.S.) and 3), Directorate of Scientific Development andproduction (Air). The recruitment was made always to the Defence Production Service, and after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of the service, in any of the said three units. All, the service conditions of the persons working in the three units including scales of pay, superannuation age etc. were the same and were regulated by the same set of Rules, viz. Defence Science (DRDS) and DQAS, and Rule 13 in DRDS which reads as follows: "Other conditions of service: (1) The conditions of Service of members of the Service in respect of matters not expressly provided for in these rules shall mutatis mutandis and subject to any special orders issued by the Government in respect o f the service. (2) The Conditions of service of the members of service in respect t he matters not specifically provided for therein, shall mutatis down and subject also to any general orders issued from the Government In respect of the services not expressly provide for in the Rules, shall abide by such special orders as may be issued by Government in regard to the service." The respondent was appointed as a Junior Scientific Officer in the Department of Defence Science and Production on October 13, 1966. He retired from service on attaining the age of 60 years. On January 10, 1986 he filed an application before the Central Administrative Tribunal for quashing the order dated January 10 , 1986. The Tribunal held that the re spondent was not liable to be retired at the age o f 58 years his superannuation age being deemed to have been increased to 60 years in view of OM dated 24.12.85 read with OM dated 10.2.86 referred to above. On appeal by Union of India, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The denial of the benefit of enhanced superannuation age to the members o f one 24 unit while the same is granted to the member of another unit amounts to discrimination violative of Article 16 of the Constitution. [785C] 2.1 In spite of the decision of the Tribunal and even pending this appeal when no stay was granted, the Appellant Union of ly retired the respondent at the time of attaining the superannuation age of 58 years. The denial by the Union of india retirement to the employees working in different units amounts to discriminatory violative of Articles 14 and 16 of th e Constitution. The decision of Tribunal is both proper and valid and there is no substance in the present appeal. [758E F] 2:2 In spite Of the decision o the Tribunal, and even Pending this appeal, when no interim stay was sought, the appellant Union of Ii ty had retired the Respondent at the said age of 57 years. [759D E] 3.1 There is no dispute that the Government has power to vary the service condition of the employees from time to time. The question involved in the instant case is, however, not whether the Government had such power. The fact that the respondent was a Senior Technical Officer does not mean that he was also entitled to the said benefit. [761F] 3:2 The denial to the benefit given by enhanced superannuation ages to the Members of one 24 units while the latter is granted only to the persons belonging to the different units, viz., DAQAS and D.S.

The appellant was elected to the Sangli City Municipality. The election of councillors to the Municipality was held under the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965 (hereinafter referred to as the Act). On that date the court adjourned the hearing of the case for 969 recording the evidence of these two witnesses in respect of whom an application had been made by the election petitioner on the previous day. The appellant presented an application to the High Court under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution praying for quashing the order of the Judge; but the High court dismissed the writ petition in limine on October 4, 1968. In appeal to this Court it was contended that having rejected the application of the election applicant on the 21st August for issue of summons to these two persons, the trial judge had in the exercise of jurisdiction vested in him refused to issue summonses to them when he was asked to do so on August 21, 1968; and that the first publication having taken place on the 8th June the time limit of ten days fixed under section 21 sub section (1) of the Act began to run from that date and the petition which was filed on the 24th June was beyond time. HELD: The High Court was right in refusing to quash the order. [975 D] In the present case, there is no merit in this point raised by the learned counsel. It is for the appellant to have come to his own conclusion as to the period of disqualification prescribed by section 21 (1). [976 E F] The first publication had taken place at 8th May, 1967 and the second publication having been taken place in that day and the Petition which was presented on the 25th June, 1968 was beyond limitation. If the distribution of the pamphlet be accepted, there can be no doubt that the appellant was guilty of trying to arouse religious sentiments of the voters of the particular ward a majority of whom were Muslims. There is much force in this contention. [963 E F G] In view of the fact that the evidence about the distribution had been meagre and not beyond reproach it was not for the High Courts to take the view that the order ought to be quashed on the ground that there was no evidence.

The petitioner company was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. By a notification dated March 31, 1956, the State of Uttar Pradesh imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said notification by way of a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that there was no power in the State to issue the impugned notification under section 3 A on March 31. 1956, as that section was itself to come into force only on April 1, 1956 and that in consequence the impugned Notification was not saved by the new Act. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the petitioner that (i) the Validation Act was ultra vires because it was passed beyond the saving of the Validation Acts; (ii) the validation Act was not ultra vires the powers of the legislature under entry 54, and as there was a difference between the existence of a power and its actual exercise, that while by reason of Act XXIV of 1957, a power had been conferred on Government to issue a notification on March 1,1956, the notification actually issued on that date could not be referred to that power; (iii) the impugned notifications were ultra vires as they were beyond the scope of entry 54 and as such void. HELD: (i)(a) The Validation Act is intra vires and the validity thereof must be judged on the construction of Entry 54 in List II or List III of the Seventh Schedule, and any other provisions of the constitution bearing on the question. [934 C] (b) The validation Act is not ultra within entry 54 of List II for the reason that it operates retrospectively. It operates retrospectively and the Validation Ordinance is therefore not a law in respect of tax on the supply of materials in a contract for the construction or sale of works simpliciter, on the footing of a sale was held to be outside the saving Of the Validation act. [1034 D] (c) The impugned notification dated April 31, 1957, was intra vires as it was not issued beyond the period prescribed by section 3A of the Act. [963 E F] (d) The validity of a Validation Act in respect o tax on supply of goods, which the Act assigns exclusively to the Provincial Legislatures, is plenary and unrestricted subject only to any limitation which the Constitution might impose, and in the exercise of that power it will be competent to the legislature to impose a tax (1) ; , , , ; , (2) a tax on sale of goods as known to law, on that occasion of sale, and that therefore it could not have been imposed with retrospective operation. [964 E F; 935 A] (e) The State Legislature was competent to enact the Validation legislation in respect Of sales tax, and the validation Ordinance is also not ultra.

The appellant was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 I.P.C. and sentenced to imprisonment for life. He preferred an appeal against the conviction but the High Court affirmed it in appeal. In this appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the sentence imposed by the Sessions Court was not excessive. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The crime is a serious one and the punishment must be deterrent. It may be marginally extenuatory to mention that modern Indian conditions are drifting into societal permissiveness on the carnal front promoting proneness to pornos in life, what wit libidinous 'brahmacharis ', womanising public men, lascivious dating and mating by unwed students, sex explosion in celluloid and book stalls and corrupt morals reaching a new 'high ' in high places. The current efforts of Governments, Central and State, to reform jail regimen, we hope, will give a better deal to the caged community. For these reasons, in this case, the incriminating company of lifers and others for long may be counter productive, and in this perspective, we blend deterrence with correction and reduce the sentence to rigorous imprisonment for two years. [691G H] 2. The appellant is not a 'habitual ' and has no vicious antecedents except this fugitive,INSTy molestation which is bad enough in a society where women are often socially weak and sexually victimised. It is difficult to appreciate how the crime can be said to have been committed by a negative reduction in the prison term. What is more important is a set of positive prescriptions which will ensure his turning a new leaf. One major method in securing this goal is to keep alive the family tie of the person in prison so that he may not deteriorate into a non person. Within limits of the Prison Act and Rules thereunder, the State Government or the Inspector General of Prisons will ensure that on parole, furlough or orders, the young appellant turns a new born leaf of normal life. [600C D] 3. The task is not done by a positive reduction in prison term, but what is more vital is a sets of positive prescription which will secure his turning an oldishing child, given propitious social environs, curative and congenial work and techniques of internal stress release or of reformatory self expression. One minor method in obtaining this goal was to keep good alive the families tie of person in jail so that they may not stagnate into any non person.[600D E] 4. The present efforts of Government, Central, State and State have, as yet, no convincing national policy on female flesh and sex sanity. This reflection apart, we must, as part of the sentencing package, design a curative course for this prisoner to rid him of his aphrodisiac overflow and restore him into safe custody. The factual background of the case does not warrant any interference in this appeal. [599E F] 5. The offence is one of rape with violence, of the private person of a woman an outrage by all canons. In prison treatment must, therefore, be geared to psychic healing, release of stresses, restoration of self respect and cultural normalisation, apart from being deterrent. The human element in this regard is not excessive but it is marginally disproportionate. [ 600D] 6. The victim and her parents have forgiven the criminal. They have forgited the molester who is a first cousin, says counsel. An affidavit from the father in law of the woman has been filed and, if needed, counsel is ready to produce the victim 's statement that she has forgiven him into the safe citizenship. The Court must restore the man.

The assessee was a limited company dealing in land. It maintains its accounts on the mercantile system. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.24,97,249 as compensation payable to the assessee. The assessee preferred an appeal before the Arbitrator, 24 Parganas, Calcutta. This represented the difference between the sum of Rupees 7,37,190 payable to it in terms of the award dated July 29, 1956 of the Arbitrator and a sum Rs.12,276 out of that amount which had already been assessed to tax. The Income tax Officer treated the sum as liable to income tax during that year on the basis that the income accrued to the assesseee on the date of the Award. The Appellate Tribunal rejected the first contention and held that the compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee, and was, therefore, a trading receipt of the business carried on by the assesee. The High Court dismissed the appeal. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The legal position was explained in further detail by the Gujarat High Court in Topandas Kundanmal vs Commissioner of Income tax, Gujarat, [1962] 1 SCR 676 that the award made by the Collector was merely an offer or tender of the compensation determined by the Civil Judge though an appeal was pending against that award. [396B C] (2) The right to receive payment is in dispute and it is not a question of mere quantifying the amount to be received, and cases where the right to receiving payment is admitted and the quantification only of the amount payable is left to be determined in accordance with settled or accepted principles. [397C D] (3) The claim by the claimant, after taking possession, at a particular rate or for a certain sum is not compensation. It must not be forgotten that, even if a court was awarded enhanced compensation, there is a right of appeal by the Government to the High Court and the High Courts may either disallow that claim or reduce the compensation. [398D] (4) The mere claim by an assessee after taking of possession at a certain rate or FOR a certain amount is not Compensation. It cannot be forgotten, even though a court is awarded enhanced award, there are a right to appeal by it to the Supreme Court and, the High courts may either dismiss that claim, or reduce it. [399F] (5) The question whether income could be said to have accrued to an assessee on the day when possession of the land was taken by the government for the purpose of assessment to tax in the year of assessment is not an issue of mere identifi cation. It is sufficient to point out that there is no liability in praesenti to pay an enhanced compensation till it is judicially determined by a final court since the entire question, namely, whether the offer made by Land Acquisition officer was inadequate and the claimant is entitled to an additional amount of compensation. The legal fiction is explained in detail by this Court in Harish Chandra Raj Singh vs The Deputy Land Acquisition Officers & Anr., [1962) 1 SCR 677; referred to. (6) The High Courts are right in the view taken by it and, therefore this appeal must be dismissed.

The appellants landlord filed a suit against the respondents for eviction of the respondent tenant on the ground that he was entitled to possession on one or other of the statutory grounds mentioned in the Act. The trial court decreed the suit and the High Court confirmed the decree. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that under the terms of the compromise under consideration in that case the respondent had withdrawn all his defence to the application filed by the landlord and submitted to a decree for eviction unconditionally. But if the tenant in fact admits that the landlord is entitled to have such a decree under the law, it is open to the Court to act on that admission and make an order for possession in favour of the landlord without further enquiry. HELD: (1) The provisions of Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure are not intended to be used as a shield against any person who has been evicted by the tenant. [881 E] (2) The object of the Act is to protect a tenant against eviction and that protection of the tenant is inherent in the language of Order 21, Rule 2 when it says "Where it is proved to the satisfaction of the Court that a suit has been adjusted by any lawful agreement or compromise". the Court can pass a decree on the basis of the settlement. The protection of a tenant is implicit in the words of Order 22, Rule 1 when it states "where it is established to the satisfied of the court that a ground for eviction has been established". [820 E F] (3) The expression "any other law or contract" used in Order 23 Rule 3 means any law or agreement which prevents the tenant from vacating the accommodation in spite of the fact that none of the grounds mentioned therein exist. In order to get a decree or order for eviction against a tenant whose tenancy is governed by any Rent Restriction or Eviction Control Act, the Court must indicate either on its face or in the background of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly is agreeing to suffer a decree of eviction because the landlord, in the circumstances is entitled under law. [821 E F; 882 A B] (4) The words "any law or order" used by Order 23 rule 3 are wide enough to include within its ambit any law which prevents a tenant in vacating the premises in spite Of the fact of that none has been mentioned therein. If on the other hand, the court is satisfied on consideration of the terms and conditions of the agreement and if necessary by considering them in the context of the pleadings and other materials, that the agreement is lawful, as in any other suit so in an eviction suit the Court is bound to record the compromise and pass a Decree in accordance therewith.

The assessee company was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of tea. The assessee company had purchased shares for the purpose of managing agency of the company. The company did not declare any dividend for the year in question. In so doing be ignored, the loss in the value of the shares held by the company in Elphinstone Mills Ltd. was due to the loss of Rs. 12,00,000/ on account of depreciation in the valuation of the share of the assessee. The Income tax Officer, however, again invoked the provisions of section 23A (1) and levied additional super tax @ /4/ per rupee on the surplus of Rs, Commissioner took the view that the loss incurred by the assessee was a capital loss. But all the same as there was no commercial profits in the relevant accounting years it was not reasonable to expect the assessee company to declare any dividends in respect of those years in view of the capital loss incurred and he,. therefore cancelled the orders of the Income tax officer under section 23 A (1). The High Court held that in view Of the capital losses of Rs 12,000 and Rs. 13,63,874/ were not allowable as a deduction under section 10(2) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the expression "losses and smallness of profit" in section 23 (1), must be construed in its ordinary sense and not in its popular sense. Dismissing the appeals, HELD : The word " loss" is used in a wide sense and includes all matters relating to the business of the Company. [864 D] In the present case, the assessee had suffered a capital gain of Rs 13,00 lacs on account Of depreciation in its value of shares held in Elpinstone Mill Ltd. of Bombay. The loss was due only to the losses incurred by it and to the smallness and of the profits made. [874 E] In view of section 22A (2) the assessee suffered a loss of about Rs. 10 lacs on the ground that it relates to the price paid for the shares purchased for the sake of acquiring the managing agency. The question is not whether the value Of the shares may not go up in future but whether the Directors were justified in not declaring dividends in view o the capital gains incurred and they, therefore, cancelled the order of the Incometax Officer under section23A (I).

The appellants filed a suit for declaration that the land in dispute was not his personal property and that he had no right to file an appeal under section 39 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954. The Civil Judge held that the Civil Judge was not justified under section 15 of the , in modifying the award merely because he disagreed with the finding. He also held that section 37 of the Act applied to arbitrations referred to in section 12(4) of the . The District Judge allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Civil judge modifying the decree, and the award announced by Shri Vikram Singh was accepted. In a revision filed before the High Court under article 227 of the Constitution, it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) section 37 applies only to arbitrations under the Consolidation of Holding Act, 1953, and (2) section 39 applies to arbitrations which are not governed by consolidation, and that the provisions of sections 15 and 39 of U. P. Consolidation Of Holdings Act apply to arbitrations made under the Act. Held:(i) The effect of section 37 is inter alia to apply sections 15, 16 and 39, of the to the proceedings under the . In the present case, section 12 (6) must be read with section 37, of U..P. consolidation of Holdings (U.P.) Act, 1952, and if it is so read it is quite clear that what is made final is the decision of the arbitrator as it emerges after appropriate proceedings, if any, have been taken under the provisions Of the .

The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. Till 1974, the promotion post of superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. This was so according to the practice followed by the Corporation without making any rules or regulation in that behalf. The petitioner challenged this resolution by a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that no classification could be made among the Executive Engineers on the basis of their educational qualification for the purpose of promotion to the post. In appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The rule providing that graduates shall be eligible for such promotion to that exclusion of diploma holders does not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution. [775G] 1.2 The contention that in the absence of rule or regulation the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. The principle that in a case where no separate quota for promotion to a post is kept for degree holder Junior Engineers and diploma holder Junior Engineer, it could be prescribed on the ground of educations does not offend Articles 14 or 16 of Constitution. It is well settled that for the purposes of promotion, a valid classification can be made amongst the members holding the same post on the principle of educaations. [758G H] 1:3 The rule provides that graduates should be eligible to such promotion as they are Degree holders or Diploma holders. Hence, the observation are per incuriam as regards the next contention, admittedly neither the practice adopted till 1988 nor the resolution passed in accordance with section 64 of the Act. It was a case of the direct recruits and promotees integrated into one cadre. Hence the observation is per incuriam. [759A] 1 :4 The principle of seniority in service jurisprudence has been clearly laid down by this Court in H.C. It may be observed that in State of Mysore & Anr. vs P. The. The Court then referred to Roshan Lal Tandon, ; and distinguished it on the facts by pointing out that it was a Case of direct recruitsand promotees integrated together into one class. [761B] 1.:5. In state of Mysore and Anr. , this Court had clearly held that such a classification is permissible and does not infringe Articles 14 & 16 of The Constitution. The proposition that in view of the above, the petitioner Graduate Engineers as a separate category amongst Junior Engineers cannot be classified for purposed of promotion on a basis other than that in case before the them the classified for purpose of Promotion on a base other than the basis merely of their qualification which is not permissible in law though the creation of selection grade in the same category on the foundation of merit and on seniority is well known and permissible. [762D E] 1):6. The rule prescribing service conditions does not contravene Articles 14, 16 and 16. [763F G] 1:-7. The contention of the petitioner that he was diploma holders Junior Engineers as per merit cum Seniority cannot be accepted because he had got the said resolution and was promoted to the said post on that date. It would be a case if direct recruits & promotees are integrated into a common class of Assistant Engineers, they can be classified on the footing of educational qualification. [765F] 1 8.1 In view of this, the observations made in H C.C., it is well established that for promotion, the valid classification could not be made between the Executive Engineer on the one hand and the Junior Engineers on that basis.

The petitioners who were working as Judges of the Supreme Court and were appointed as Judges in the High Courts, filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that it was the constitutional obligation of the Union of India to provide the sanctioned Judge strength in the superior courts and the default, if any, was a matter of public interest and the writ petitions requiring a direction to the Union o f India to fill up the vacancies were maintainable. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioners that the constitutional duty of the State to provide for the sanctioned judge strength in superior courts, and the failure, if anything, was not a matter which could be considered by a larger bench; that the decision of this Court in S.P. Gupta 's case relating to the status and importance of con sultation, the primacy of the position of the Chief Justice of India and the view that the fixation of Judge strength is not justiciable should be re considered by the larger bench. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The Constitution has been enacted for the purpose of providing the sanctioned Judges strength in inferior courts and to make such appointments without any delay. [460E] 2.2 In order to achieve this object, it is necessary that the role of the institution of the chief Justice of the High court and the Chief Minister of the States be recognised as of crucial importance in the matter of appointments to the Supreme Courts and the High courts of the states. If the recommendation is to emanate di rectly from a source other than that of theChief Justice of a High Court or the Chief Ministers justifying the same should not be reopened and if in a given case the Union Government is of the view t hat the matter requires to be looked into again a reference should be made to the Chief Judge of the concerned High Court. [461F G] 2:3 The Constitution provides that "there shall be a Supreme Court consisting of a Chief Justice and, until Parliament by law pre scribes a larger number, of not more than seven other Judges." From time to time the Chief Justices of the high courts and of the Judges of this High Courts as the Central Government may deem it neces sary to consult, are merely constitutional functionaries having a consultative role and the power of appointment resides solely and exclusively in the Central Govern ment. The matter is not, therefore, to be considered that the final say is the exclusive prorogative of the executive Government. [462G H] 2(a) The Constitution does not provide for any kind of consultation or consultation with the Chief Judges of a high court or the High Judges of such high courts as the Supreme Public Service Commission may deem fit. It is clear on a plain reading of these two Articles that the Chief Law Minister of India, the Chief Secretary of the Central Public Service Commis sioner and such other Judges of high courts are merely Constitutional functionaries having an consultative function and the powers of appointment reside solely and solely in the State Government. The role of a institution of Chief Justice may not be necessary to be examined in the view of the fact that by the Amendment the ChiefJustice of India would become the Chairman of the Commission. [463G H; 464A] 2 (b) The constitutional purpose and process it becomes imperative that the roles of the institutions of the Government of India be recognised, as of vital importance in matters of appointments appointments to Supreme Court, and, there can be a fresh look at the matter only if the Chief Chief Justice Of the High ourt permits such a review of the case.

The respondent was appointed as an Enquiry Officer under the Chief Executive Officer 's Order dated January 9, 1979. The enquiry officer held that such an enquiry is incompetent and without jurisdiction and, therefore null and void. The respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the order of discharge on the ground that the original order was without jurisdiction or competence and, as such, null and invalid. The Single Judge allowed the writ petition holding that the enquiry was incompetent and not without jurisdiction. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that since the respondent had retired from service in 1986 and if the order imposing punishment is quashed he would ordinarily have to be paid his wages etc., upto the date of his retirement. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in quashing the impugned order of punishment but it should not have ordered payment of 'all consequential benefits flowing from the declaration that the impugned orders were bad in law. [635B] 2.1 In the circumstances, the course suggested by Shri Shetye can be usefully adopted. [613C D] 2:2 The respondent had admittedly retired from services in 1986, and if he was so entitled he would normally have to pay his wages and also upto thedate of retirement. [535D] 3.1 It is for this reason that the High Courts were right in directing payment of all consequential benefits. [540C D]. 2:3 The respondent succeeded in getting the order quashed on a mere technicality and that too on the conten tion belatedly raised before the High court for the first time and, thus, the High Curt was in error in direct ing payment of the consequential benefits to which the respondent would be entitled on superannuation. [542C D; 542A] 2 :4 The respondent failed to raise any objection against the continuance of the enquiry by the said Enquiry Officer and therefore the High ' Court ought to have remitted the matter to the competent Disciplinary Authority to take a fresh decision based on the report of the Enquiry Officer. No useful purpose, therefore, can be served by adopting the procedure suggested by Mr Shetyee as the respondent has admittedly retired since 1986 and, if the orders imposing punishment are quashed he will ordinarily have been paid his salary etc., up the date when his retirement was. [543C D E] 2.:5 The High Courts should not allow the respondent to question the competence or jurisdiction of the competent authority of Shri U.B. Menon as the res pondent had admittedly superannuated from service.

The appellant, a Municipal Corporation of Delhi, was granted permission to carry on the construction of a building or the use of the site for the building. The plans submitted by them did not contravene any of the provisions of sub section (2) of section 336 or section 340 of the Corporation Act. They stated that according to the Master Plan prepared under the Delhi Development Act 1957 certain areas including Chawri Bazar would be the Central Business District of Delhi and that the proposed user, mentioned by them in the plan sent for sanction was not in contravention of the Master plan. The Commissioner refused sanction on the ground that the Master plans were prepared under section 7 of the Delhi Municipal Corporation Act, 1957 (Act LXVI of 1957) (hereinafter referred to as the Development Act). The appellant filed a writ petition before the High Court challenging the order of the Commissioner refusing sanction. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the order was legal and justified by the provisions, of cl. The appellant contended that the Commissioner had no power under section 336 of the Municipal Corporation Delhi Act to sanction the plans submitted for the construction or execution of a work unless such a building is in conformity with the Master Plans. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The Commissioner has to give sanction for the erection of a buildings or the execution of the work unless it contains a proposal regarding the width that a road should have, all use of land adjoining that road is prohibited for an indefinite period. If neither of the plans provide for the particular use of any land or building in the area or Zone, section 14 will quite naturally stand attracted, because any user of land is indicated in a Master Plan, a different use of that land cannot be permitted.
